en: Prosperity!
Salutations to the venerable Rāmānuja.
The *Śrutapradīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrībhāṣya* composed by the venerable Sudarśana Bhaṭṭāraka.
First Chapter, First Section.

May my intellect take the form of devotion toward the Supreme Brahman, Śrīnivāsa—who performs the divine play of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of all worlds; who is solely consecrated to the protection of the multitude of various beings who bow before him; and who is brilliantly illuminated in the crest of the Vedas.
I bow to the bestower of boons, whose crest is the mountain-like elephant, the beloved of Kamalā, the ocean of compassion,
who grants the desires sought by all supplicants, and who removes the suffering of those who prostrate before him.
Having studied the meaning of the Commentary on the Vedānta Sūtras under my teacher for a hundred years,
I shall now, as if by his word acting as a lamp, reveal it according to my own understanding.

Desiring to perform an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) characterized by the worship of his chosen deity for the sake of completing the work he intends to begin without obstacle and for its widespread propagation, and wishing to briefly indicate the subject matter to be treated so as to focus the minds of the listeners, he says "akhila... and so forth. With the first quarter-verse, there is a summary of the meaning of the first two chapters; with the second, that of the latter. That which "becomes" (*bhavati*) is the "world" (*bhuvana*), the entire aggregate of effects. The word "akhila" (entire) is used to exclude only a few causes, such as the four-faced Brahmā and others.

The term "sakala" (all) is used to exclude the sense of being merely common or frequent. The term "akhila" (entire) is an expression of negation (*vyatireka*), as in the phrase "there is nothing unknown. The term "nikhila" (complete) is not used so that the word may begin with the letter *a*. Even when its capacity to denote the Blessed Lord is not intended, the letter *a* possesses an auspicious character (*māṅgalikatva*). The negative particle (*nañ*) denotes something other than auspiciousness depending on the specific object of negation, but not inherently. However, in this context, because it negates deficiency and thus refers to completeness, it is indeed auspicious. Birth is threefold.

*Sthemā* (maintenance) consists of the various forms of preservation carried out through the agency of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), Viṣṇu’s incarnations (*avatāra*), and so forth. *Bhaṅga* (dissolution) takes the form of the periodic (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and primordial (*prākṛta*) types. Although liberation (*mokṣa*) is included within dissolution, it must be stated separately—just like the subject matter (*viṣaya*)—because it is the primary purpose of the scripture; therefore, it is improper to include it by means of a term that applies to multiple objects.

For this reason, the ancient teachers (Pūrvācāryas) spoke separately [of these qualities]: "To the sole cause of the world's birth, maintenance, and destruction; [to Him who performs] the world's arising, maintenance, dissolution, liberation from saṃsāra, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), entry, control, sustenance, and the like are included; for it is more appropriate to accept the very meaning already stated by [the author] himself in his own voice elsewhere, where he says: "[The Lord's] play consists of the creation, maintenance, withdrawal, entry, and control of the world."

The word *līlā* (sport) is used to exclude [the notion of] dependence and other such qualities, according to the manner stated as "immeasurable" (*aprameya*) and "not subject to injunction" (*aniyojya*). The mention of "birth and so forth" (*janmādi*), rather than stating "being the progenitor" (*janayitṛtva*) and the like, is intended to signify the material cause (*upādāna*); for the Śruti says, "May I be many, may I procreate. By the word *līlā*, the status of being the efficient cause (*nimittatva*) is illuminated. Furthermore, by this word *līlā*, which removes the objection that activity is impossible for one who has attained all desires, the meaning of the second definition is also indicated. Now, he summarizes the meaning of the second pair [of definitions] with the word "vinata" (humble).

By the two words *vinata-rakṣāpa*, the meanings of the third and fourth characteristics are indicated. "Vinatāḥ" means those who have bowed down or become humble, namely the lay-devotees (*upāsakas*); their twofold nature is as will be explained later by Bādarāyaṇa in such passages as "because of the possibility even beyond that. "Bhūtāḥ" means those whose existence has been attained through the knowledge of the Lord; this is the sense, according to the Śruti: "If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existent. A "vrāta" is a multitude belonging to those who are humble and have become [enlightened] (*vinata-bhūta*). Thus, the compound is *vinatabhūtavrāta*.

By the word *vrāta*, the intended meaning is "the ancestors clap their hands [in joy], thinking: 'He is a beast, a human, a bird,' and so forth. *Rakṣā* (protection) is characterized by the attainment of what is desired and the warding off of what is undesired. The word *eka* refers to preeminence; for it has been said: "Even if I were to give up my life, or should I choose to restrain myself, my wife, or my son, I would never [restrain] a servant or a laborer"—thus, that initiation (*dīkṣā*) of which this is the primary rule is described as such. By the word *dīkṣā*, the sense of being indispensable is implied; for its declaration is: "This vow is mine."

Now, he states the meaning of the four aphorisms that serve as the introduction to the treatise—beginning with the word *śruti*. For the purpose of those [aphorisms] is indeed to establish that the treatise ought to be commenced, by way of refuting both the absence of any means of knowledge regarding Brahman and its being known through other means of knowledge. The word *śruti* indicates its distinction from other means of knowledge; for it is called *śruti* because it is eternally heard (*śrūyate*). By the word *śiras*, there is the mention of a portion that has no other purpose. *Vidīptiḥ* means a special kind of illumination (*viśeṣeṇa dīptiḥ*).

With the intention that even the worshipability [of the Lord] through forms such as Agni is understood from the Vedānta, and with the intention that Brahman is by its very nature the infinite human goal, its "special radiance" (viśeṣeṇa dīptatvam) is stated. The word *brahmaṇi* is a general term; the word *śrīnivāsa* is a specific term. Here, the principle of *chāgo vā mantravarṇāt* is intended. By the word *śrīnivāsa*, both etymologically and conventionally, there results the exclusion of the identity of the three deities (*trimūrti*), the state of being surpassed by others, and so forth, as well as the connection with the eternal manifestation (*nityavibhūti*).

The term "in the other" (*parasmin*) refers to the state of being the goal (*prāpyatva*), as established in the section concerning the bridge and measurement (*setūnmāna*). Now, regarding the subject to be expounded—which consists of both the means (*upāya*) and the end (*upeya*)—he specifies the aspect of the means indicated by the word *vinata*: "the intellect in the form of devotion. Here too, the maxim of the goat and the animal (*chāgapaśunyāya*) is intended. By these two words, there is an exclusion of the notion that mere knowledge of the meaning of the sentence constitutes the means, [which would imply] a conjunction of wisdom and ritual action (*dhī-karma-samuccaya*). He says "mine" (*mama*) with the intention of acknowledging his own inferiority. The sense is: let it be so; this means directed toward this object is sweeter than any other result.

Thus, the ultimate subject matter has been shown, and the purpose here has been stated very briefly. Now, stating the intermediate subject matter of his own work and its distinction from other works to be explained, clarifying the concise purpose of the treatise, and demonstrating the uniqueness of his own composition compared to other commentaries, he implicitly performs an auspicious invocation in the form of service to the Guru, beginning with the words "Pārāśarya":

"The nectar of the words of Pārāśarya, extracted from the midst of the milky ocean of the Upaniṣads, which restores life to the self whose vital breath has departed due to the kindling of the fire of saṃsāra..."
May the wise ones of the earth daily drink this [work], which was well-guarded by former teachers, situated far from the contradictions of many opinions, and brought forth in its own words.

Vyāsa’s identity as Bādarāyaṇa is established by the Śruti. Furthermore, the word *pārāśarya* indicates his preeminence from birth. The word *vacaḥ* (speech) extends to its meaning, just as the word *veda* does in the compound *vedavit*. If one were to justify [the term] as "the nectar of speech" (*vacasaḥ sudhām*), there would be an impropriety regarding the context of the metaphor and the non-primary sense of the word *sudhā*. It is a metaphorical representation of nectar because it is the cause of immortality. The word *upaniṣad* is intended to signify that this [work] presents Brahman immediately, even before the earlier portion [of the Veda].

The word "milked" (*dugdha*) intends that the Upaniṣads constitute the essence of the Vedas, as in the expressions "from the Vedas, like [milk] from the *āraṇaka* grass" and "like nectar from herbs. The word "ocean" (*abdhi*) refers to their infinity. By the word "middle" (*madhya*), the preeminence among all the Śrutis is intended, because that which is in the middle is compatible with all locations. By this, both the fact that his own subject matter is rooted in authoritative scripture and its specific scope have been demonstrated.

By the word *uddhṛta* ("extracted"), which denotes the lifting up of what is submerged in an extremely deep place, the grasping of the meaning in its entirety is indicated. He states the ultimate purpose with the words "saṃsāra... (the ocean of worldly existence). The fire-nature of *saṃsāra* consists in its being composed of the threefold suffering (*tāpa*). Furthermore, the word *vidīpana* ("blazing") illuminates the internal subdivisions therein, its state of never having been extinguished at any time prior to the attainment of knowledge, its manifold nature, and its uninterrupted continuity.

Those who, since beginningless time, have not attained the Supreme Self through any one of the various modes such as hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, have their vital breaths departed. This is because of the Vedic usage: "The vital breaths are the Supreme Self; they enter into the vital breath itself. By the term *saṃjīvinī* ("life-restoring"), it is intended to express that this work is the cause of supreme liberation. He states that his own composition is rooted in the authentic tradition (*satsaṃpradāya*) with the word "previous" (*pūrva*). Here, the service to the Guru is performed by way of praising him. The word "previous" is used to exclude [other teachers] such as Śaṅkara.

The sense is that it is not only protected by instruction, but also by the composition of this treatise. To the question, "If so, why has it not become widely known? he replies: "Because of the many opinions" (*bahumati*). The "conflict" (*vyāghāta*) of the opinions of many people refers to their mutual contradictions; because of these, [the truth] remains at a distance. The sense is that it is not merely a failure to understand correctly, but rather that there has been a misunderstanding. The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to highlight the difference from his own previous works. He does not say "by my words" (*mamākṣaraiḥ*) in order to maintain consistency with the title *Sudhā* (Nectar).

The meaning is: "by means of the immortal syllables that are the limbs of the Gāyatrī. "Sumanasaḥ" (well-minded ones) refers to those who are discerning in distinguishing between the essential and the non-essential. "Bhaumāḥ" (earth-dwellers) refers to those residing on the earth who have studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (Aṅgas) and the Śiras, and who have heard the Mīmāṃsā of ritual action (Karma-mīmāṃsā); the sense is that there is efficacy for [this work] even in other places and times through its recitation and so forth. "Pibantu" (let them drink): the meaning is that even the hearing of this is of the nature of bliss, like drinking nectar (sudhā). "Anvaham" (daily): because of its excellence as an object of enjoyment and because of its profundity.

The former teachers have condensed the extensive commentary on the Brahmasūtras composed by the venerable Bodhāyana; following their interpretation, the words of the Sūtras will now be explained. ||1||

To the objection that "let the works of the ancient teachers (pūrvācāryas) be set in motion; what is the point of the labor and pride involved in composing another work?", he replies with the words "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavat*). Here, the term "ancient teacher" is explained. The word "Blessed One" (*bhagavat*) signifies one who possesses superior knowledge even compared to Śaṅkara and others. The works of the Teacher Dramiḍa and others are extremely concise. [The present work follows] according to their view, and not through his own imagination. The meaning is that the syllables of the Sūtras must be construed in accordance with the roots and suffixes, and not joined together in an arbitrary manner.
By means of the two prefixes *vi-* and *āṅ*, expansion and contraction are intended according to what is required. He takes up the word to be explained:
"Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (1.1.1).

In this context, the word *atha* (then) signifies immediate succession; the word *ataḥ* (therefore) indicates the causal status of what has preceded. For one who has studied the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs and its esoteric portions (*śiras*), the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) necessarily follows immediately thereafter. ||1||

Since the excellence of renown is rendered ineffective by the denial that there was no prior understanding of what preceded, doubt and error persist; therefore, he explains the word *atha* in order to eliminate those two, saying: "In this context" (*atrety*). The proposition is that the word *atha* signifies "immediacy" (*ānantarya*). By the word "it occurs" (*bhavati*), its natural sense is indicated. "In this context" (*atra*) refers to the commencement of the inquiry into the meaning of the latter part of the Veda, which serves as a rebuttal to that denial. By this, it is implied that the inquiry into the meaning of the former part of the Veda has already taken place.

Thus, by indicating the exclusion of this [present] *atha* from such [ordinary] uses as "Now, the instruction of words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*) through the force of the term *brahmajijñāsā*, the word *atha* is shown to be preceded by the word *ataḥ*. By this, it is made known that the general preceding context (*vṛttasāmānya*) is denoted by the word *ataḥ*, because of the natural tendency of the word *etad* (and its derivative *ataḥ*) to refer to what has been previously mentioned.

Thus, it is stated by implication that the word *atha* has the sense of "immediacy" (*ānantarya*), as obtained through the juxtaposition of two words that denote a general category while implying a specific mode of conduct. Therefore, because the roots and suffixes in expressions such as *atha maunam* are seen to have multiple possible meanings, he explains the word *ataḥ* with the word "from this" (*ata iti*). Here, the phrase "this occurs" (*ayaṃ bhavati*) is to be supplied. In this context, the words *atra* and *bhavati* function as before. "This" (*ayam*) refers to that which is preceded by the word *atha*.

The meaning is that this follows from the natural force of the root and suffix, the natural force of the word *atha*, and the inherent power of the compound term *brahmajijñāsā*. Nor should one suspect a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*) on the grounds that the determination of the meanings of the words *atha* and *ataḥ* are mutually dependent; for the natural force of these two words in expressing "immediacy" and "the state of having been accomplished" is understood through linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), and thus they are not mutually dependent.

Explaining the narrative indicated by the words "herein" (*atretyādi*)—both that which has already occurred and that which is yet to occur—as well as the relationship of cause and effect between the two, [the author] establishes the immediate succession of what is to follow with the verse beginning "Having studied" (*adhīta*). By the word *sāṅga* ("with its ancillaries"), it is signified that the study is the cause for the initial, superficial comprehension (*āpātapratīti*); by the word *saśiraska* ("with its head," i.e., the Upaniṣads), it is shown that the sequence of the two parts of the text follows the sequence of the commentary, that they constitute a single unified work, and that the study must be complete. By the two terms "investigation of ritual action" (*karmajijñāsā*) and "investigation of Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*), the past and the future portions of the work are respectively indicated.

By the word *kevala* (mere), there is the absence of knowledge of Brahman; by the two words *alpa* (small) and *asthira* (unstable) in contrast to *ananta* (infinite) and *sthira* (stable), there is the relationship of cause and effect; and by the phrase *anantarabhāvinī* (occurring immediately thereafter), there is the fullness of the cause resulting from the two words *atha* and *ataḥ*. For when that [cause] exists, there is the immediate succession of the fruit. The term *anantasthiraphala* (infinite and stable fruit) is an adjective qualifying Brahman, or else it qualifies the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*); its being such is mediated through that [Brahman]. "The desire to know Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*): here, the genitive case in *brahmaṇaḥ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). ...
Because there exists a counter-exception stating that "the sixth case ending in construction with a *kṛt* suffix is compounded. ||1||

Now, while determining the meaning of the compound which serves as the reason for its being a single word (*ekapadya*), he analyzes and points it out in order to exclude other case-endings, saying: "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*). And removing the suspicion that it might have another meaning, he says: "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*); for regarding the question "from what?", he says: "by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*" (Pāṇini 2.3.65). The sense is that when [Brahman] is the object (*karman*), its status as the object of cognition (*viṣayatva*) and its status as the purpose (*prayojanatva*) are established.

Although a specific injunction (*pratipadavidhi*) is stronger than a general injunction (*sāmānyavidhi*), because compounds are prohibited in such specific instances, the means (*upāya*) and other factors connected with Brahman are nonetheless established as objects of inquiry (*jijñāsya*). This is because even a mediated relationship (*paraṃparā-sambandha*) is included within the category of "relationship in general," and by implication, the status of Brahman as the object (*karman*) is also entailed. Anticipating this objection regarding its general sense, he says, "Even though... (*yadyapi*). In the phrase "even in the inclusion" (*parigrahe 'pi*), the word *pari* indicates the establishment of the status of the related factors as objects of inquiry, while the establishment of [Brahman] as the object is indicated by the root *gṛh*.

The word "of the sixth [case]" (*ṣaṣṭhyāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The intention of the author of the *Bhāṣya* is that because only that which is denotative (*ābhidhānika*) is to be accepted, the case-ending of the subordinate term (*upapada-vibhakti*) is meaningful, just like the case-endings of the factors of action (*kāraka-vibhakti*), such as the second case for the object (*karmani dvitīyā*) or the sixth case for the agent and the object when a *kṛt*-suffix follows (*kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti*). By the use of the particle *eva*, it is intended that that which is the cause of immediate cognition is stronger than that which is the cause of delayed cognition.

The meaning is that since the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is implied for both the primary and the non-primary [factors], it is logical that the primary factor is denotative while the others are merely implied. Anticipating the objection regarding the prohibition of compounding (*samāsa*), he refutes it with "na ca" (and not). A "reinstatement" (*pratiprasava*) is an exception to an exception. Even though a case-ending (*vibhakti*) that is not actually employed lacks denotative power, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is explained here in order to determine the specific intended meaning based on grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*).

However, when the meaning of a case-ending is indicated by a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), not only factors such as semantic fitness (*yogyatā*) are required, but grammatical authority (*anuśāsana*) is also necessary; therefore, it has been explained in accordance with that.

By the word "Brahman," the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*)—who, by His very nature, is free from all defects and possesses an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities—is denoted. ... ... ... ... He alone is the object of inquiry for those afflicted by the three types of suffering, because He is the means to attain immortality. Therefore, the Lord of All alone is the Brahman that constitutes the object of the desire to know. (2)

Now, since both words taken together are subject to doubt and misconception—due to the first word being well-known as having multiple common meanings and because others have explained it otherwise—he explains it [with the word] "Brahman. In accordance with the Śruti, "having encompassed the worlds," the term "Puruṣottama" (Supreme Person) is used. The meaning of that word is His distinctness from all other conscious and unconscious entities.

Since even grass and other such things possess "otherness" (anyatva) relative to what is different from themselves, he states their distinction by means of possessing both sets of characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatva*) in order to exclude them, beginning with the words "by nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*). The term "entire" (*nikhila*) excludes those who are bound (*baddha*) and so forth. The phrase "by nature" excludes the liberated (*mukta*). The term "limitless excellence" (*anavadhikātiśaya*) is used to exclude that which is eternal but possesses a limited excellence. Such qualities are innumerable for each [deity]. The word "multitude" (*gaṇa*) intends a collection of qualities consisting of various modes and distinctions within a single quality.

For qualities such as *vaśitva* (mastery) are indeed included within *satyasaṃkalpatva* (the power of true resolve); thus it is stated that [the Lord] is understood through the primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*). Desiring first to establish the capacity of the word [to denote the Blessed One] based on the capacity of the word itself and the capacity of the meaning, and keeping in mind that [the term] is used figuratively elsewhere, he states that the word "Brahman" is applied by connection with [certain] qualities, beginning with the words "In all cases... (*sarvatra*).

"In all applications" means in all objects [of usage]. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And [the word] 'bṛhat'. To the question "Why should this not apply to others as well?", he says: "And that (sa). The particle *ca* serves to dispel doubt. How is the restrictive particle (*evakāra*) used here? For it is employed elsewhere as well; to this he replies: "Therefore (tasmāt). Why should all [words] not have primary denotation? To this he replies: "Because of multiplicity. For it is an application that cannot be established otherwise (*ananyathāsiddha*) that leads to the postulation of a [specific] power (*śakti*). The point here is that in this case, however, it can be established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*).

There is no consequence here of postulating multiple powers, nor is there any lack of primacy elsewhere, because there is primacy everywhere through the very same power residing in the parts; to this, he says: "By the Blessed One... [etc.].

The meaning is as follows: just as the word *paṅkaja* possesses the universal *padmatva* (lotus-ness), which excludes blue lotuses (*utpala*) and the like while including the red lotus (*tāmarasa*), so too, since it would be necessary to postulate multiple powers for a word if there were no basis for its application that both conforms to its objects of usage and excludes non-objects, and since such usage can be accounted for otherwise, the word is primary (*mukhya*) when applied to an object possessing a full set of grounds for application and secondary (*amukhya*) elsewhere; this is just as the word *Bhagavat* has been determined to be. Now, he establishes the capacity of the meaning itself with the words "by heat" (*tāpa*).

Indeed, one imprisoned in a jail should not petition for the release of his shackles; rather, it is he himself who, upon the cessation of those very shackles by whose command they were imposed, is the one to act. Intending this, the scripture beginning with "him thus" (*tam evam*) is cited here. It concludes with "therefore" (*ataḥ*); the meaning is: on account of both the force of the word *ataḥ* and the force of the sense. The desire to know is *jijñāsā*. Since desire has as its primary object that which is desired... [the] Mīmāṃsā-śāstra begins with "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) and ends with "No return, on the authority of the scripture; no return, on the authority of the scripture" (*anāvṛttiḥ śabdād anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*), following a specific sequence determined by particular logical connections.

He explains the second word by dividing it into its root and suffix: "jñātum" (to know). Although the fact that desire is an effect [of knowledge] is already understood, the meaning is that this is an injunction regarding a part that was not previously established, similar to the expression "having bathed, one should eat. The mention of the desiderative suffix (*san*) is intended to indicate that inquiry is prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*). Thus, even in the phrase "the desire to know dharma" (*dharmajijñāsā*), the knowledge consisting of inquiry is what is enjoined; for it is stated elsewhere that "inquiry must be performed. However, valid cognition (*pramiti*) is established as a matter of course as the fruit [of the inquiry]. For this is indeed *mīmāṃsā*.

"Here"—that is, in the introductory aphorism (*upakrama-sūtra*). By this, the claim that this aphorism is concerned with a specific object of inquiry (*jijñāsya-viśeṣa*) is set aside; for once its necessity as an undertaking is established, the determination of the specific object of inquiry follows. That determination is carried out later, beginning with the aphorism "Because of seeing [Brahman], not that which is non-scriptural" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*). Alternatively, he connects the meaning of the sentence: "Mīmāṃsā" and so forth constitute the proposition (*pratijñā*), while the rest serves as the supporting argument (*upapādaka*).

By the two terms "prior portion" (*pūrvabhāga*) and "subsequent portion" (*uparitanabhāga*), it is shown that the nature of the commentary consists of a sequential arrangement and the study of interconnected sections. The fact that the subject to be explained (*vyākhyeya*) possesses such a character—which serves as the cause for this—was stated previously during the word-by-word analysis (*padayojanā*). Both [the commentary and the subject] must be understood in both ways (sequential and interconnected). This formulation is made for the sake of brevity in the text. He confirms the promise "in accordance with that view" by means of the commentary text itself: "He says that... (*tad āha*).

He shows in the commentary that [this work] consists of the investigation of karma, the immediate succession [of births], the projecting karma, and the single treatise [on dharma]: "And he will say," etc. *Lakṣaṇa* refers to the chapter (*adhyāya*). "Connected" (*saṃhitam*) means bound together in the form of a commentary on a single subject to be explained—this is the sense. *Śārīraka* is the *Brahmamīmāṃsā*; it is so called because its subject matter is Brahman, whose body is the world. "By the sixteen-lakṣaṇa" means by the sixteen chapters.

Anticipating objections regarding the contradiction of meaning, the difference in subject matter, the difference in purpose, and the difference in authorship that would oppose the unity of the treatise, he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). "Therefore" means: because the unity of the work is established by its nature as a single commentary upon a single object of exposition. "Intended to be explained" (*pratipipādayiṣita*) means: desired to be explained, i.e., the intended scope of the purport (*tātparya*). [The objection is: "The refutation of the deity and so forth is intended for other purposes, such as praising ritual action (*karman*) which yields results independent of knowledge of the deity."

However, there is no intention [of the sūtra] to exclude the deities and so forth; rather, the point is that Jaimini accepts Brahman, as seen in passages such as "But Jaimini [thinks otherwise], for another purpose" and "Jaimini [thinks so], because of primacy. Furthermore, the fact that substance is more powerful than the deity when both are common [to several rites] is established through the means of proof (pramāṇa), not by its own nature.

For the nature of the substance is indeed perceptible, as is the nature of the oblation; however, *dharma* alone is to be known through scripture, and it should be understood that the nature of the deity, as well as its capacity to bestow the fruit [of action], is accessible through scripture alone. Therefore, since there is no intentionality regarding contradictory meanings, there is no contradiction in meaning. It was stated [in the *Tantravārttika*] that this is like the distinction between the six sections (*ṣaṭka*) or the distinction between chapters, with respect to the intended purport of the earlier and later sections (*kāṇḍa*). By this, the differences in purpose and subject matter are refuted.

Because the distinction between the subject matter and its results—consisting of the nature and transformation considered in the two groups of six chapters—does not constitute a ground for dividing the treatise. As for the avoidance of a difference in authorship, it has not been explicitly stated; for indeed, a difference in authorship exists in the *Pūrvavṛtti* and *Uttaravṛtti* of the Grammarians and others. Granting that there is a single treatise, [the author] says "Mīmāṃsā" in response to the question: why should the inquiry into Brahman not come first?

The specific types of connection (*saṃgati*) to be described hereafter are: the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*); the logical order (*arthakrama*), which consists of the initial inclination toward the three aims (*trivarga*) among sentient beings; the relationship between the meaning of words and the meaning of sentences (*padārthavākyārthabhāva*); the relationship between the illustration and the illustrated (*dṛṣṭāntadārṣṭāntikabhāva*); and the relationship between that which is depended upon and that which depends (*upajīvyopajīvakabhāva*). Thus, the meaning is that it possesses a specific sequence characterized by these particular types of connection that determine the priority and posteriority [of the topics].

For instance: first of all, by the injunction "one's own Veda (svādhyāya) is to be studied," the acquisition of the aggregate of syllables known as the Veda—which is denoted by the word *svādhyāya*—is prescribed through the act of study itself. Furthermore, it is understood that study has as its fruit the acquisition of the aggregate of syllables in the form of repeating after the teacher, performed by one who is engaged in specific vows and observances (*vrata-niyama*).

By presenting the injunction for one's own Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) as the authority for the previously asserted duty of studying the entire Veda along with its limbs and appendices—on the grounds that such study is useful for the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*), which belongs to a single scripture, and for the subsequent inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) which depends upon it—he dispels both the doubt regarding the non-commencement of the inquiry into Brahman caused by the [objection] that the injunction ends with the knowledge of the meaning, as well as the doubt arising from the conflicting views of opponents; he does so with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*).

For only when it is established that the injunction extends up to the grasping of the syllables is the necessity of its commencement established. Otherwise, according to the rule "having studied, one should perform the ceremonial bath" (*adhītya snāyāt*), since the knowledge of meaning is enjoined as a subordinate part of ritual action—just like the rice-grains to be pounded—the Self to be known would likewise be a subordinate part of ritual action. Furthermore, because the words "Self" (*ātman*) and "Brahman" have the same meaning in the passage "This Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*), the Vedāntas would merely refer to the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) already determined as the agent in rituals. Consequently, there would follow the consequence that this scripture—which consists of an inquiry into a Lord distinct from that [soul] who is not established by other means—need not be commenced.

Therein, he briefly sets forth five points—four accepted by the Bhaṭṭas and one not accepted by Guru Kumārila—beginning with the word "first" (*prathamam*). "First" means, indeed, from the very beginning. By stating this priority, it is implied that the fourfold qualification cannot be established through any other scripture. This priority is relative to a stage unfit for the study of other scriptures; for it is only after being initiated at the eighth year from conception that one undertakes formal study.

From this very point, it follows that the specific time limit mentioned as "eight years" is also an auxiliary element (*aṅga*) of study by way of being a prerequisite for initiation (*upanayana*). By this, the following is illuminated: the status of initiation as an auxiliary to study; the fact that study is prompted by its own injunction through the inclusion of the injunctive sentence regarding *svādhyāya*; the status of [the injunction] as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) through the mention "by means of study"; and its status as a restrictive injunction (*niyama-vidhi*) by the use of the particle *eva*. The word "Veda" is used to exclude the notion that the term *svādhyāya* refers merely to a heap of syllables.

By the term "called Veda," it is intended that the entire study [of the Veda] is enjoined; for a mere portion of the Veda is not the meaning of the word *svādhyāya*. With the intention that this injunction does not extend merely to the comprehension of the meaning, it is stated that there is the "acquisition of the mass of syllables."

The intended meaning is as follows: since the injunction [to study] extends up to the grasping of the syllables, according to the rule "having studied, one should return home" or "having studied, one should perform the ceremonial bath," the knowledge of the meaning does not constitute a subordinate part (*śeṣa*) of the ritual action. Consequently, because the Self to be known—unlike the rice grains to be pounded—is not a subordinate part of the ritual, there arises the possibility of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a performer of rituals who is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, it is established that the scripture consisting of the inquiry into the Lord, who is different from that [individual soul], must be commenced. This is the conclusion.

And this point—the meaning of the sūtra to be stated later, namely "for one who possesses merely the study"—is shown here for the sake of ease of understanding; however, neither its being the primary [duty] nor its being accompanied by the auxiliary sciences (*sāṅgatva*) is perceived here, because only the injunction for teaching is heard. To the objection that it is therefore perceived as being prompted by that [teaching], he says: "And that... The word "and" (*ca*) serves to dispel the doubt. What is its form? Does it consist of independent pronunciation or dependent pronunciation; does it consist of a single utterance or multiple utterances? This is the meaning.

How so? What is its subsidiary (*aṅga*)? Being eight years old is a subsidiary to the study [of the Veda] by way of initiation (*upanayana*). The scriptural injunction regarding study is like [the injunction]: "One desiring offspring should cause him to sacrifice for twelve days. For in that case, the act of sacrificing is not prompted by the injunction to officiate at a sacrifice (*yājana-vidhi*). Here, however, because of the accusative case-ending in the word *brāhmaṇam*, initiation is a subsidiary to the boy (*māṇavaka*); and due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of its internal connection, it is a subsidiary to the study pertaining to him. As for the verbal suffix *-ktvā* in the word *upanīya*, it is set aside by the two-fold delay; for that [suffix] is a Smṛti rule and is of the nature of a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Therefore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger than the direct statement (*śruti*). Nor should it be argued that initiation (*upanayana*) is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the teaching belonging to the initiator, on the basis of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) used when the fruit is intended for the agent; for the middle voice is prescribed by the sūtra beginning with *saṃmānana* (Pāṇini 1.3.36), which applies even when the result does not accrue to the agent.

The objection—that because "the agent's intentionality" (*kartrabhiprāyatva*) consists in the connection of the result with the agent alone, and since that [intentionality] is absent here, the result could possibly connect with both [agent and object], thereby making the result of the initiation (*upanayana*) reside in the teacher and thus be a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the teaching (*adhyāpana*)—is refuted. For even in the case of *agnīnādadhīta*, where the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed by the rule *svarita-jitaḥ* etc., we observe that the result connects with both [agent and object]. Therefore, "the agent's intentionality" does not mean that the connection of the result occurs with the agent alone.

However, since the fruit is merely connected to the agent, when that [agency] ceases, the connection of the fruit to the agent would not be established; thus, there is no connection of the fruit with the teacher. Nor is there a lack of connection between two conscious beings, because in the case of "he chooses the priests" (*ṛtvijo vṛṇīte*), the fruit is connected to both [the patron and the priests], as it pertains to what is intended by the agent.

Nor should it be argued that because the fruit is not immediate, there is no connection with the agent (*kartṛ*), and thus the condition of "being intended by the agent" (*kartrabhiprāyatva*) is absent—resulting in the non-application of the *ātmanepada*—the *ātmanepada* is prescribed by the rule beginning with *saṃmānana* even when the fruit is remote and connected to the agent; for this would imply that since initiation (*upanayana*) has the purpose of accomplishing the remote status of being a teacher (*ācāryaka*), it is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of teaching (*adhyāpana*), which contradicts the requirement of "being intended by the agent. This is not so, because although initiation is not a subordinate part of teaching, it is nonetheless related to it, just as the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) is related to the subsequent injunctions of sacrifices.

Since it is logically consistent for the act of initiation to produce the status of a teacher merely by virtue of being beneficial to him, the fruit of initiation does not accrue to the teacher; therefore, it is not a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of teaching.

*Vrata* refers to the *upākarma* and other such rites. *Niyamāḥ* refers to the rules regarding place, time, what is fit to be eaten and what is not, and so forth, as stated in passages such as "this [body] is indeed a walking cremation ground. This separate mention of "and instruction" (*upadeśaśca*) is made because of the distinction between those based on direct revelation (*śruti*) and those based on tradition (*smṛti*), and between disagreement and consensus. By the phrase "four months and a half," the time for the study of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) is established. To the question of what is accomplished by this primary injunction together with its auxiliary injunctions, he says: "Thus"; that is, when the injunction along with its auxiliaries has been defined.

The passage beginning with "one of good lineage" (satsaṃtāna) conforms to such sūtras as "one endowed with noble birth and learning" (abhijanavidyāsamudeta). [This refers to] one who has been initiated by a teacher (ācāryopanīta).

The meaning is that the qualification of the teacher (*guru*) serves the purpose of the student (*māṇavaka*) by means of the initiation (*upanayana*), just as in another view the qualification of the student serves another purpose. "Qualities of the self" refers to non-anger and so forth. The phrase "of one endowed with specific vows and observances" is stated as an illustration. Through these two words, the expectancy of "how" is fulfilled. Through the subsequent two words, the expectancy of "of what nature" is also satisfied, since its nature as being dependent on another and consisting of repeated utterance is established. By that, its status as the first [of the Vedas] is also established.

Even though repetition is not explicitly heard [in the scriptural injunction], its accomplishment through repetition is established—just as in the case of threshing and other such acts—because that which yields a visible result must not be abandoned.

And study (*adhyayana*) is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the Vedic text (*svādhyāya*), because from the injunction "the Vedic text is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*), it is understood that the Vedic text is the object (*karman*). ... Having perceived the purposes [of the Vedas] at first glance, a person who has completed his study of the Vedas spontaneously engages in the hearing of Mīmāṃsā—which consists of the investigation of Vedic sentences resulting in the determination of the specific nature and modes of those [purposes].

First, in order to establish the injunction for refinement (*saṃskāra*) which was previously promised in the passage beginning with "first of all," he says: "And study" (*adhyayanam ca*). To the question "Why?", he replies: "Because it is the Veda to be studied" (*svādhyāya iti*). The meaning is that since the Veda is understood to be the object (*karman*) [of the action], the refinement of the person does not occur through an unseen potency (*apūrva*). Anticipating the objection, "Why should it not be like 'he offers the groats' (*saktūn juhoti')?", he teaches its true nature by saying: "It is a refinement. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "The state of being refined"; the sense is that it is not useless like the groats.

To the question "Why?", he says: "By virtue of its nature (*dharma*)," etc. By the mention of these four, the fact that the composition known as the Veda possesses a consistent meaning is indicated. "Even by its own form" means even without the knowledge of its meaning or its practical application. "Even by its own form through recitation, etc. means even by the mere mass of syllables when being recited.

It is established that knowledge is a supplement to ritual performance (*anuṣṭhānaśeṣa*), that recitation (*japa*) extends until the meaning is perceived, and that it must be done with words sanctified by formal study (*adhyayana-saṃskṛta*) and not by means of understanding them from books and so forth; thus, its status as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is proven. Anticipating the dilemma—whether the requirement that study extends to the comprehension of meaning follows from the inherent force of the words themselves or from the logical necessity of the purpose—the author concludes the discussion on the injunction for study by refuting the first alternative: "Thus... He uses the term "as if [reciting] mantras" (*mantravat*) with reference to both those mantras that are incorporated into specific observances (*vrata*) and those that are not.

The [mantras] beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us" are those not included [in the primary injunctions]. The *niyamas* (observances) are those previously mentioned. The word "only" (*mātra*) is used to exclude the knowledge of the meaning; the sense is that this much alone is conveyed by the words, and the purport (*tātparya*) culminates therein. For the sentence concerning the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) does not extend as far as the application (*viniyoga*) in subsequent sacrifices; such is the intended meaning.

Now, if the injunction were to terminate merely in the acquisition of the syllables of the Veda, then—since there would be no evidence for the Vedic study having the purpose of conveying meaning—the meaning would be unintended; consequently, the injunction would not culminate in human welfare (*puruṣārtha*), and, due to the absence of any motivator, the Mīmāṃsā inquiry would not be worth undertaking. Having thus dispelled these three types of untenability which form the basis for the view that the comprehension of meaning is the ultimate goal, as well as the doubt regarding the commencement of the inquiry into Brahman caused by that [view], he demonstrates the unity of the treatise through the relationship of a single subject matter and its commentary, beginning with the words "adhyayana" (study).

By the words "by its very nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*) and so forth, the objection that [the Veda] has no intended meaning is refuted. Furthermore, even in your own view, there is no direct culmination in a purpose; however, with the intention that if [purpose is established] through a traditional succession (*paraṃparayā*), it exists in our view as well, he refutes the charge of being devoid of purpose by stating: "The word [Veda] has a purposeful meaning. Meanings that possess purposes such as heaven and liberation are [actions like] sacrifice, meditation, and so forth. First, there is the statement of the nature of the scripture; subsequently, there is the immediate comprehension (*āpātapratīti*) caused thereby.

Even at the time of initial comprehension, the purposeful nature [of the subject matter] is reiterated in order to establish that comprehension as being indeed for the sake of a purpose. The reason for this is stated as "because they have been grasped"; the meaning is "grasped through the study of the text together with its auxiliary sciences" (*sāṅga-adhyayana*); "having seen them as being understood" means "having seen their state of being understood. The *svarūpa* (essential nature) is the primary part (*aṅgin*), while the *prakāra* (manner) is the auxiliary (*aṅga*). The *viśeṣa* (distinction) is the difference from the form presented by the opponent (*pūrvapakṣita*).

The body of the treatise (*śāstra*) consists of investigation (*vicāra*), which is distinguished from grammar and other such fields; its fruit is the final determination (*nirṇaya*). The meaning is that, since he has already studied the Vedas and is a human being—and thus a sentient being—he engages [in study] out of natural inclination (*rāga*) alone, and not by means of an injunction (*vidhi*). By this, the objection that the treatise should not be commenced due to the absence of an impeller (*pravartaka*) is refuted. Furthermore, since the word "study" (*adhyayana*) has the same meaning in both *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, it is pointless to postulate a difference in their relative strength or weakness. And there is indeed a *Śruti*: "Having studied the Veda and having performed the ceremonial bath (*abhisamāvṛtya*)."

Even for one who has attained desire (*rāgaprāpta*), the injunction regarding hearing (*śravaṇa*) provides an opportunity, just as the acquisition of wealth suitable for oneself and so forth does. The suffix *-ktvā* denotes having the same agent and priority in time, but it does not denote immediate succession. Hearing is possible even for a *snātaka*, because an opportunity exists just as it does for a teacher. Nor is there an obstruction to practice due to tasks such as fetching water, since those duties cease once the obligation imposed by the injunction to study has ceased. Wealth, fame, and the like are the fruits for the teacher.

The performance [of a rite] follows the words of a well-wisher only as far as the completion of hearing [the injunction]. However, this does not imply independence from *mīmāṃsā*, for there is dependence upon it both through the desire to know the source (*mūla*) and through the desire to explain it oneself. Nor does performance based on the words of a well-wisher contradict the principle regarding those who are not Śūdras (*apaśūdra-naya*), because [the Veda] is not taught to him by Brāhmaṇas according to such rules as "one should not give instruction to a Śūdra"; furthermore, in the case of sacrifices, the eligibility of the three higher castes depends upon the study of the mantras to be recited, which itself requires the initiatory rite (*upanayana*).

Therefore, the occurrence of activity [toward the scriptures] arises from passion (*rāga*). It is intended that the unity of the treatise is established because of the unity of the explanation provided by the word consisting of the investigation of Vedic sentences.

In that regard, once the nature of the injunctions for ritual action (*karma-vidhi*) has been determined, and having observed that the fruits of actions are meager and unstable, one qualifies oneself for the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā*, which consists of the investigation of the Vedāntas—the fruit of which is the definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) of that [Self].

"Let it be so. To the question, "How is there a fixed order of priority (paurvāparya-niyama)? he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*). "Having been determined" (*nirūpite*): the very nature of ritual action (*karman*) has been determined. The sense is that, through the injunction of repetition and so forth, the fact that its fruits are limited and unstable is established as a consequence. Alternatively, ritual action has been determined, but not the Supreme Deity who is to be propitiated (*ārādhya-paradevatā*). For when knowledge of That exists, the fruits are infinite—this is the sense. The word "immortality" (*amṛtatva*) is used to exclude incidental fruits such as those expressed in "he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food."

Terms such as *svādhyāya*, *mīmāṃsā*, and "possessing a purposeful meaning" (*prayojanavadartha*) are common to both parts [of the Mīmāṃsā system]. However, terms such as *upaniṣad* and so forth are specific to this [Vedānta] part alone. Thus, the three points—the unity of the system (* aikaśāstrya*), the rule of sequential order (*paurvāparyaniyama*), and the necessity of commencing the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicārārambhaṇīyatva*)—have been established.

Accordingly, the Vedānta texts demonstrate that the fruit of mere ritual action is perishable, whereas the knowledge of Brahman yields an imperishable fruit—as in passages such as: "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct, being favored by Him, one attains immortality. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.6) and others.

He states that there are statements which produce an initial understanding with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*). The meaning is: "in the manner that the Sūtra has been explained. The citation of other passages concerning perishable results is for the purpose of establishing the credibility of other matters as well, by showing a correspondence with a determined meaning in some instances. "World" (*loka*) is so called because it is perceived; thus, finitude is stated by way of its result. The statement "it is finite" (*antavat*) refers exclusively to ritual action (*karman*), for "without having known" (*aviditvā*) is the subject under discussion. He declares that [action] is not a means to a permanent result with the words "For not" (*na hi*).

The phrase "that is indeed eternal" (*dhruvaṃ tat*) is a segment of the statement. He explains this with the words "for they are like rafts" (*plavā hi*). These [verses] are devoted to showing that the fruits of ritual action are perishable. Now, that which pertains to both [knowledge and action] is: "having examined" (*parīkṣya*). A *brāhmaṇa* is one who has studied the *brahman*, i.e., the Veda; the suffix *-aṇ* is used here in the sense of "one who has studied that. The word "who" (*yaḥ*) is to be supplied, as it is followed by the word "he" (*saḥ*). "Uncreated" (*akṛtaḥ*) refers to the Supreme Person (*puruṣaḥ*). The particle "iti" is to be supplied. The word "only" (*eva*) indicates a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhiḥ*). "A learned scholar of the Vedas" (*śrotriyaṃ*) means one who has heard the Upanishads. "Established in Brahman" (*brahmaniṣṭhaṃ*) means one who has attained direct realization of Brahman.

Tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*) are merely causes for immediate attentiveness conducive to hearing [the scriptures], but they do not constitute the total abandonment of the outward and inward senses' inclination toward sense-objects; that [abandonment] will indeed be defined later. "The Imperishable is Truth" (*akṣaraṃ satyam*): by this, its distinction from both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) is established, meaning it is changeless in both its essential nature and its attributes. "He spoke" (*provāca*): the *liṭ* (perfect tense) is used here according to the Vedic rule *chandasi luṅ-laṅ-liṭaḥ*. Now follow the passages concerning infinite and stable fruits. The attainment of infinity is established by the sentence "one who knows Brahman" (*brahmavid*). For the context is "whence words turn back."

The passage beginning with "no more" (na punaḥ) refers to the cessation of death and its effects. Indeed, immediately after the words "neither disease nor suffering," the phrase "he who sees" (na paśyaḥ) is heard. The object of the word "sees" has been stated as "that one" (tadekam). "Sovereign" (svarāṭ) means not subject to karma; for he is independent. The phrase "him thus" (tamevam) indicates the cessation of other means. The fact that the knowledge of difference is a means is shown by the word "separate" (pṛthak). "Delighted" (juṣṭaḥ) means made an object of love.

But surely, from the mere study of the Veda together with its auxiliary sciences (sāṅgavedādhyayana), one already understands that ritual actions have results such as heaven, and that heaven and the like are perishable; therefore, please consider that an inquiry into dharma (dharmavicāra) must likewise be undertaken.

Satisfied with the mere statement of the cited passage, he objects: "But surely... For the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-vicāra*) is indeed for the sake of knowing that its fruits are perishable. Since that [knowledge] is established through the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-adhyayana*), one who desires infinite fruit should desire to know that very thing—this is the objection. "If this is so"—that is, if you are satisfied with the mere statement of the cited passage; the implication is that you are satisfied even with the entire Brahman [portion]. "True"—this is an admission regarding superficial comprehension (*āpāta-pratīti*), but it is not an admission regarding independence from inquiry (*vicāra-nairapekṣya*).

Since the words "possessing food" (*annavān*) and so forth denote results that are small and unstable—such as the attainment of space (*ākāśa*), vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the like—and since [the texts] state, "He perishes along with them," due to such qualities as impermanence, doubt and other [defects] do not cease. You, however, desire to know other passages whose meaning is unclear and have not been cited; the meaning is that you should look even at the earlier portion [of the Veda], such as "Those who have drunk Soma become immortal. If satisfaction were achieved by the cited passages, it would likewise exist in the latter part; if there is no satisfaction by those not cited, it would likewise be absent in the former part.
It is stated that since the cognition of contradictory meanings such as "finite" and "infinite" is equal in both cases, the status of being an object of investigation is likewise indistinguishable.

The Shorter Prima Facie Argument: Now, it must be stated that whatever is necessarily required by the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is precisely what has preceded it. Therefore, since that [inquiry] is the primary subject of the treatise, something that is required by it must be stated as having preceded it.

Thus, it has been stated that action (*karman*) must be investigated for the purpose of its abandonment by way of its results. Now, in order to establish that it must be investigated for the purpose of its adoption by way of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), the author raises an objection by means of its being invariably unnecessary: "But surely... (*nanu ca*). The first particle *eva* is intended to exclude [the possibility of] a required duality; the second, however, excludes the prior occurrence of that which is unnecessary. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Not as a duty" (*na dharmaḥ*). To the question "Why?", he says: "Having studied... (*adhīte*).

The meaning is that for those who study only the Vedānta, there is a mere superficial understanding (*āpātapratīti*) regarding that very point. Alternatively, even for one who has studied the entire [Veda], because a requirement for what follows arises by the power of past merit (*sukṛta*), the meaning of the word "studied" (*adhīta*) is that the portion required has also been studied. He raises an objection with the words "the ritual action" (*karma*). Among the constituent parts of the Sāman known as *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratihāra*, *upadrava*, and *nidhana*, the second is the *udgītha*. The word "substratum" (*āśraya*) is used to exclude the notion that this meditation is merely an auxiliary part of the ritual action.

This word, containing a reason within it, responds with reproach to the [objection] regarding impossibility: "one who is ignorant. The meaning is that you do not know the knowledge which is the primary subject to be established. To the question "What is that?", he says: "In this... The distinction consisting of the knower, the known, and the knowledge is manifold through various sub-divisions; that [distinction] is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). The avoidance of infinite regress is indicated by the word "beginningless" (*anādi*). The term "ocean of suffering" (*duḥkhasāgara*) is used because [this distinction] is to be discarded through the elimination of birth, old age, and so forth, which have their cause in the perception of distinctions born of ignorance.

*Mithyājñāna* means erroneous cognition or false cognition. It is described as "false" because it is something to be removed by knowledge (*jñāna*). *Ātmaikatvavijñāna*—the meaning is that the realization of the oneness of the Self, like the realization of the oneness of the moon, removes the delusion of its difference, whereas ritual action (*karman*) does not. *Kva*—"nowhere. The meaning is: nowhere among the arising of knowledge, its means, its auxiliary factors, or its fruits; on the contrary, the intention is that [action] is a cause for the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of duality. Since cognitions such as those regarding the *udgītha* are based on the Upaniṣads, they are required for the knowledge of Brahman.

Therefore, he states that the contemplation of That (Brahman) is directly relevant in the *Śārīraka* [Mīmāṃsā] by saying "the Udgītha," etc. To the question "Why is there contemplation here?", he says "in knowledge. The two words "tu" (but/however) serve to exclude the two aforementioned doubts. As for the word "ataḥ" (therefore): it means that what is required is not merely what is contextually incidental (*prāsaṅgika*), but rather what is required for the primary subject matter (*pradhāna*).

"Certainly; and what is required by that [knowledge] is precisely action and knowledge, because liberation is heard of as resulting from knowledge conjoined with action. And [the author] will state later: 'And there is a requirement for action, because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth, like the horse. ... Thus, the distinction [between them] cannot be known. Therefore, that alone is the prerequisite."

On this point, the followers of Bhāskara say, "Certainly. And the tradition identifies them as *siddhāntins* (proponents of the established conclusion), because they are alike in their acceptance of [the ritual] as a subordinate member (*aṅga*). This is because the passage beginning with "But previously, the prescribed action... belongs to their own text. By saying "Certainly," they express agreement that what is invariably required has been accomplished; however, there is disagreement regarding the phrase "not the action. To the question "What is invariably required? he says: "That. The implication is: "It is precisely what you do not accept. To the question "Why? he says: "Action," referring to the scriptural text beginning with "By sacrifice," and so forth.

"Conjunction" (samuccaya) means mere connection. The particle "ca" [is used] in the sense of a conjunction that conveys [the meaning]. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And when there is dependence. The intended meaning is that the comprehension of the sentence-meaning does not occur through the comprehension of the word-meanings alone. He concludes with "Therefore" (ataḥ).

Relying on the view of those who advocate for equal conjunction (*samasamuccaya*), the *pārśvastha* (the bystander) objects with the words "Certainly" (*bāḍham*) and so forth; this is the traditional interpretation (*nirvāha*). In that case, "conjunction" (*samuccaya*) is intended as a coordination where [knowledge and ignorance] are of equal importance. The scriptural authority is such passages as, "Knowledge and ignorance" (*vidyāṃ cāvidyāṃ ca*), etc., where the particle "and" (*ca*) signifies the conjunction of the things to be established. The meaning is that it will later describe their status as auxiliary (*aṅgabhāva*), since their status as auxiliaries prior to the arising of knowledge is already accepted. The subsequent portion is as before.

Although the priority of ritual action (*karma*) is not accepted in the system of Yādavaprakāśa, nevertheless, by relying on his own acceptance that action is required in both ways, the objector standing at the side attributes this priority [to it]; thus, there is no contradiction with the concluding section of the text.

This is not tenable; for liberation consists precisely in the cessation of ignorance through the knowledge of Brahman as pure consciousness, which is opposed to all particularity. Since liberation is indeed the cessation of ignorance, how could [the aforementioned] be a means [to it]?

The opponent replies: "This is not so. When the question arises as to how it is improper, [the author], intending to refute every possible manner in which the requirement of action might be conceived, considers the following alternatives: Is it intended that by the word "conjunction" (*samuccaya*) a connection in the sense of equal primacy (*samapradhānatayā*) is meant; or, having intended that the word "conjunction" refers merely to a general relation, is it desired to express a connection with it in the capacity of a subordinate factor (*aṅgatayā*)? With this distinction in mind, regarding the first alternative, there would be a duality of both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).

He refutes [the objection] with two verses, beginning with "sakala" (all-inclusive), etc. "All-inclusive differences" refers to differences of the same kind (*sajātīya*), of different kinds (*vijātīya*), and internal differences (*svagata*). Their "antidote" is like a rope [is the antidote] for snakes and the like. By the suffix *-mātra*, the exclusion of differences consisting of the form of differentiation (*vyāvṛtti-rūpa*) is intended. The meaning is that there is no duality of means, because the cessation of the obstacles to what is desired to be accomplished through action is established as being accomplished through knowledge by such passages as, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death."

The sense is that cessation itself is not something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because once an obstacle has ceased, there is the attainment of that which is eternally attained. In response to the inquiry "What follows from this?", he explains what was stated previously—that action is contrary to liberation and is, in fact, its very opposite—by means of the verse beginning with *varṇa*. The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) refers to prohibited actions and so forth. Regarding the phrase "consisting in the cessation of the perception of difference": since the cessation of the ignorance of the cause entails the cessation of the ignorance of the effect, it possesses that nature. "How indeed? means "not in any way whatsoever."

And the Śruti texts—such as "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death"—declare that actions have impermanent fruits and are thus opposed to liberation, while knowledge alone is the means to liberation.

Regarding the point that the meaning of the Śruti is not sublated by reasoning, he says: "And the Śrutis... First, the contradiction regarding the nature of the thing itself was stated; by the phrase "as having impermanent results," the contradiction is shown by way of the result. By the word "finite" (*antavat*), it is meant that even for many [actions] performed over a long period of time, there is a finitude. With the words "just as... (*tadyathā*), the contradiction by way of the result is demonstrated.

The fact that knowledge is the means, the absence of any distinction between the attainer and the attainable, the fact that the cessation of obstacles alone is what is to be accomplished, and the negation of other means, are established by such scriptural passages as "one who knows Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7) and others. Thus, the sense is that the scripture "Knowledge and ignorance" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.4) possesses a clear meaning supported by reasoning and is in accordance with many other scriptural texts.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that knowledge depends upon rituals such as sacrifice—and that "having become composed, one should see the Self in the very Self."

Now, [the author] refutes the view that the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifices and the like intend for knowledge to be dependent upon ritual action, by means of the word "yat" (that which). The meaning is as follows: whatever has been stated as being required by ritual action—whether by way of equal primacy (*samapradhānatayā*) or as a subordinate auxiliary (*aṅgatayā*)—is intended for the purpose of desire (*icchārtham*) through the medium of mental purification (*manaḥśuddhi*), because it is the cause of the latent impressions of duality (*bhedavāsanā*) and because of the hearing of the verbal suffix *saN* (indicating desire). If the intention were to refute the presentation of equal conjunction (*samasamuccaya*), then the word "fruit" (*phala*) would refer to liberation (*mokṣa*).

Regarding the doubt that the phrase "they desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*) might—like the expression "he wishes to kill with a sword"—be intended to exclude the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) and instead intend only the exclusion of other [means], the author first refutes its being a means for the arising of knowledge by way of being a preliminary procedure (*itikartavyatā*), stating: "In the case of the desire to know. The sense is that there can be no combination (*samuccaya*) because cessation (*śama*), which is of the nature of withdrawal, is incompatible with rites such as sacrifice, which are of the nature of engagement.

The word "only" (*eva*) was used in the Śruti with the intention that there is no option [between karma and śama, etc.], because the latter is not equal [to karma] due to the delay caused by the investigation of reasoning, which disrupts the natural flow of the word *vividiṣanti*. For through the suffix *-ktvā*, there is a rapid comprehension. To the question, "Even if the desire for knowledge requires [the means], why is karma abandoned and śama, etc., accepted? he says: "Internal" (*antaraṅga*). The requirement of karma for knowledge is mediated by way of the desire;
whereas even when the desire has arisen, śama and so forth are required for the arising of knowledge—this is the sense that they are internal.

Thus, for one whose afflictions have been worn away by specific actions performed over hundreds of previous births without regard for their fruits, this very prior occurrence is known through the very nature of the object itself.

Now, setting aside the doubt that ritual action (*karma*) might have occurred previously for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), [the author] refutes its status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the arising of knowledge with the words "Thus, therefore," and so forth. This is rejected on the grounds that it is merely possible, not because it is accepted [as a fact]. "Thus" means that, by the aforementioned arguments, [action] is untenable as a constituent factor (*itikartavyatā*) whether through conjunction (*samuccaya*) or option (*vikalpa*). The word "another birth" (*janmāntara*) is used to refute the notion that such knowledge must be accomplished in this very life for the sake of the desire [to know].

The word "hundred" (*śata*) is used to dispel the doubt that [the means] might need to be practiced in this very life because they depend on perfection over many births; the sense is that a cause is indeed to be inferred from its effect. To the question of how that which bestows heaven and so forth can have the sense of "desire," he says: "not aimed at" (*anabhisaṃhita*). "One whose impurities are rubbed away" (*mṛditakaṣāya*) means one whose sins are rubbed away. "Being alone" (*sadeva*) is the statement regarding the cause. "Truth" (*satyam*) and so forth are the purificatory statements. "Partless" (*niṣkalam*) and so forth are for the sake of clarifying the exclusion [of all else]. "This Self" (*ayam ātmā*) is the statement of identity.

The statement "That thou art" possesses abundant indicators of its intended meaning (*tātparya-liṅga*); thus, the identity [of the Self and Brahman] is established both generally and specifically. The meaning is that the sentence is the instrument (*karaṇa*), not the object (*karman*). Anticipating the objection that the injunction for meditative reflection (*nididhyāsana*) would be purposeless, he says: "the meaning of the sentence. To demonstrate that they are not purposeless, he teaches those [means]: "hearing" (*śravaṇa*), etc. [He adds] "these lead to knowledge"—meaning they bring about the accomplishment of knowledge. The word "thus" (*iti*) is used because neither a collective conjunction (*samuccaya*) nor a relationship of primary and subordinate members (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is tenable here.

"Of such a kind"—meaning, that which begins with the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence [of the Upanishads] independent of karma, once bondage has ceased. And what is that? To this he says: "And that. He states the inherent capacity of the thing itself as the reason for the fourfold means having been fulfilled: "By this. The sense is: from the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal comes the desire for the eternal and the wish to abandon the non-eternal; since tranquility (*śama*) and the other means are subservient to that, how could there be an inquiry (*jijñāsā*) without them? Let it be granted that tranquility and the rest have been fulfilled;

In response to the doubt that action might still be required, he says: "By the very nature of the object (*arthasvabhāvāt*. The meaning is that the very nature of the object is the reason for excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), and it is also the reason for excluding connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). For tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, being of the nature of cessation, are opposed to action. Furthermore, the fact that action relies upon distinctions and that knowledge is independent of action—these two natures of knowledge and action are implied by the phrase "by the very nature of the object."

This is what is meant: the root of ignorance, which veils the true nature of Brahman and is unreal... [as previously stated]... it must be said that the fourfold qualification (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) itself constitutes the prerequisite (*pūrvavṛtta*).

In response to the doubts—how can there be superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon that which is opposed to distinction; how is there no dependence on ritual action (*karman*) once that [superimposition] has ceased; how do the mind’s impurity and purity arise; and what is the nature of the object itself?—the author summarizes and demonstrates the answer by stating, "This has been said. Superimposition occurs due to the concealment of one's true nature (*svarūpa*). It is merely the perception of difference (*bhedadarśana*), not anything real. For if that were real, there would indeed be a dependence on ritual action. To the question, "What follows from this regarding the fact that bondage is removable by knowledge alone? he says: "And bondage... [etc.].

"With its root" means accompanied by the perception of distinctions based on ignorance. [Ignorance is removed] by knowledge alone, and not by action. For when the delusion of a snake is removed, the cognition of the rope does not depend upon action. Thus, the possibility of a combination [of knowledge and action] is excluded. Now, he excludes [knowledge's status as] an instrument: "and it is the remover. "Of that" refers to [knowledge] which is independent of action; "of this" refers to [knowledge] whose object is non-duality. The reason for this is that it is produced by a [Vedic] sentence; the result is the cessation of bondage. If so, where [does it reside]? To this he says: "only in the desire to know."

The sense is that [the requirement for knowledge] applies only when it is established by scripture (*śruti*). To the question "And how is that so?", he says: "And that... He says "Thus this... in response to the objection that it is not heard in scripture in such a way; the meaning is that this was stated with the intention of showing its utility through an indirect sequence (*praṇāḍyā*). He concludes the subject at hand with "Therefore": the meaning is that, therefore, because the knowledge of ritual action is not required for the purpose of abandoning [ignorance] or for the purpose of acquiring [liberation]. On this point, the commentators say: "Because of contradiction, because of being non-authoritative, because of the utility for the purification of the mind, because of the scriptural statement that knowledge alone is the cause, and also by implication (*sāmarthyataḥ*)."
"There is no combination of knowledge and action because [knowledge] has tranquility and the other limbs as its constituent parts;
Thus ends the brief prima facie argument (*laghupūrvapakṣa*). Now, the brief established conclusion (*laghusiddhānta*):

Here it is said—what was stated, namely that liberation is indeed the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) and that this occurs solely through the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavijñāna*), is accepted. However, it must be investigated what the nature of that knowledge is which is intended to be enjoined by the Vedānta texts for the purpose of removing ignorance... because the cessation of ignorance is not observed by means of that [knowledge] alone.

He states, "In this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is being declared," by saying "here" (*atra*). He replies by accepting the refutation of the duality of the probandum and the probans, saying "that which" (*yat*). To the question "In that case, where is the disagreement?", he says "ignorance" (*avidyā*). What is the nature [of the disagreement]? Is it my stated knowledge, which is fit to have ritual action as its constituent part (*karmāṅgaka*), or is it yours, which is unfit for that? Thus, the disagreement concerns the specific mode of the means of realization (*sādhana-prakāra-viśeṣa*). He states both the opponent's view and his own view, saying "or from the sentence" (*kiṃ vākyāt*). This is not, however, an alternative within the opponent's own position.

He states that your view is untenable with the words "not at all" (*na tāvat*). It is not a refutation of either the object to be refuted or the head. When asked why this is so, he provides the reason for the futility of the injunction with the word "of that" (*tasya*): for the comprehension of meaning by one who is already proficient [in language] upon hearing a word does not depend on an injunction. He further provides the reason for the contradiction with perception with the word "already" (*tāvat*). These two points of refutation were also stated by Āpastamba: "The attainment of security once [the truth] is understood is contradicted by the scriptures."

If [it were held that] "in the Buddha there is the attainment of peace, and one would not experience suffering even here," then there would be a contradiction with many other scriptures regarding worship, constant mindfulness, vision, devotion, lifelong persistence, renunciation, the specific path, and so forth—this is what is intended by the term "by scriptures. Specifically, "contradiction" (*vipratiṣedha*) means a prohibition by more powerful [scriptures], and not merely an obstruction by those of equal strength.

Nor should it be said that as long as the latent impression of difference (*bheda-vāsanā*) has not been eliminated, the sentence does not produce the knowledge that sublates ignorance; therefore, the knowledge intended to be enjoined by the Vedānta sentences is something other than the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, being denoted by terms such as "meditation" (*dhyāna*) and "worship" (*upāsana*).

Having restated the two defenses proposed by others, he refutes them with the words "na ca" (and not). To exclude the possibility that this refers to knowledge arising at the present moment, he says "avidyānivartakam" (that which removes ignorance).
