Since one might argue that even later on, if it were through the words [of scripture], then it would have occurred already today, he says "bhede" (in the case of difference). The claim that even Vyāsa and others did not attain knowledge is difficult for the intellect of a listener to grasp; therefore, he speaks of the persistence of what has been sublated: "jāte 'pi" (even when [knowledge] has arisen). He uses the term "sarvasya" (of all) because there is a single fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) common to all.

"It is not a defect"—that is, the failure to remove the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) is not a defect. To the objection that [if so] it would then be a cause of bondage, he says: "even though it has not ceased. By "having its root cut"—meaning by having the root called ignorance (*avidyā*) severed—the removal of the contradiction with the scriptures is also established by implication, since hearing and the other means are conducive to the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence; this is what is intended. He refutes the position that [the effect] does not arise: "when [the cause] exists," etc. The "collection" (*sāmagrī*) consists of a sentence in the form of a series of words whose meanings have been mastered and which is aided by logic.
Fearing that there might be a deficiency in that collection due to the presence of an obstacle, he says: "even when [the cause] exists," etc.

The meaning is that when the sublater (bādhaka) arises, the sublated latent impression (vāsanā) is not an obstacle. He refutes the persistence of what has been sublated with the words "even though" (*satyapi*). He clarifies what is intended by "by you" (*bhavatā*)—namely, by you who maintain the falsity of everything—with the word "difference" (*bheda*). Regarding the two alternatives—whether the latent impression persists even when the knowledge of unity (*aikyajñāna*) arises, or whether the cognition of difference persists even upon its cessation—he first refutes the first with the words "even upon the arising of knowledge" (*jñānotpattāvapi*).

The sense is that if [the world] were to perish by itself, then the delusion regarding its creation would likewise be such [i.e., self-perishing). He refutes the second [position] with the words "vāsanā" (impressions). "Chinamūlam" means having its root—namely, that called "vāsanā"—severed. "Bāliśabhāṣitam" (the talk of fools) implies the following sense: liberation would occur without knowledge; that [knowledge] would occur without hearing [the scriptures] and so forth; the delusion of the world would occur even without ignorance; and that [ignorance] would occur without a substratum. Then, how is it that the cognition of two moons persists? To this he says: "dvicandra" (two moons).

The darkness (*timira*) is ultimate (*pāramārthika*), not false, because it is not sublated by knowledge. To the objection that, if so, instruction would be useless, he says: "powerful" (*prabala*). The word "powerful" and so forth is used to exclude fears and the like produced by a magician. Alternatively, its purposefulness lies in its leading to activity through the realization of reality and direct perception (*aparokṣya*). Thus, the disparity has been shown: while in the opponent's position there exists both the sublation [of the darkness] and the arising of an effect without a cause, in our own position neither of these two exists.

He refutes the non-arising [of the knowledge of the means to liberation] by means of the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokita), beginning with "Moreover" (api ca). If it were to be removed by way of an unseen [instrumental cause], it would indeed be true; however, this is the refutation regarding its removal by way of a seen [instrumental cause]. Therefore, by the method of exhaustion (pāriśeṣya), he states that the knowledge of the means to liberation is distinct from the cognition of the sentence-meaning, beginning with "Therefore" (ataḥ).

And thus the Śruti passages: "Having understood, one should exercise wisdom"; "Having discerned, he understands"; and in the passage, "He who knows what he [the teacher] knows—him I have told this"—it continues, "O Venerable One, instruct me further in that deity which you worship."

"And so it is. This means that it is not only understood through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), but is also explicitly stated in scripture. Multiple sentences are cited in order to demonstrate that [the term] has a single meaning even when there is presence or absence of connection with specific prefixes and verbal suffixes, and to demonstrate that general terms reach their specific application according to the "goat-sacrifice" maxim (*chāgapaśunyāya*). The word *nicāyya* [is derived from] the root *cāyṛ*, meaning "to see. The word "iti" refers to the essential form [of the term]; the word "evaṃ" refers to the manner [of its usage], such as its connection with prefixes and so forth.

In passages such as "one should practice wisdom" (prajñāṃ kurvīta), it might be understood that mere knowledge (jñānamātra) is what is enjoined, rather than a specific kind of knowledge; to this he says: "here. Here—meaning in the collection of cited statements. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), phrases such as "meditate upon the Self" (ātmānaṃ dhyāyatha) are included. The meaning is that, according to the "logic of the goat and the animal" (chāgapaśunyāya), the injunction culminates in a specific form, namely meditation (dhyāna). If so, what is expressed by the two words ending in the suffix -lyap (gerundives) and by the phrase "to be sought" (anveṣṭavya)? To this he says: "the sentence-meaning" (vākyārtha).

He says "it should be heard" (*śrotavyaḥ*) regarding the point that a general term, such as "hearing" (*śravaṇa*), must culminate in a specific [practice]. He states that meditation (*dhyāna*)—which was not previously established—is what is enjoined, because the injunctions for hearing and so forth would otherwise be purposeless; this is expressed by "therefore" (*tasmāt*). He indicates that the aforementioned meaning is based on a Sūtra by saying "he will state" (*vakṣyati*). He explains the meaning of the Sūtra with "this very thing" (*tadidam*). This refers to what was under discussion at the conclusion of the third definition—that which is expressed in the Śrutis by a general term—and this is what is meant by "this very thing. He provides the reason with "by knowing" (*vidi-iti*).

He illustrates three instances with the words "the mind" (*manaḥ*). In passages such as "not that" (*na sa*), there is no intervening word; here, at the beginning, the act of worship (*upāsanā*) is heard, as in: "Now, he who worships another deity... In some cases the specific term occurs at the beginning, in some at both the beginning and the end, and in others at the end. In some cases the general term occurs at the end, in some in the middle, and in some at the beginning—such is the division of the three examples. This sentence is to be understood as being like the *Rātrisattra* injunction.

For in that case, the nights specified in the injunctive statement (*vidhi-vākya*) are restated in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) by the words "these nights," and stability is presented as their fruit. Similarly, here too, the meditation specified in the injunctive statement is restated in the explanatory passage by the verb "knows" (*veda*) in the phrase "he who knows thus," and its fruits—namely, "shining" and "blazing"—are presented by the words "it shines" and so forth. As for the words "that which": "he who" refers to the knower, Raikva; "that which" refers to the object of knowledge, Brahman; "that" means both of these have been declared to you.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Instruct me. It has been stated previously that when something indicated by a general term in one context is expressed by a specific term in another similar context, [it constitutes a particular case]. Here, however, the statement is made through a cross-reference within each respective context. Both of these points are intended as reasons in the preceding Sūtra. The statement is made in one place for the sake of brevity. This [passage beginning with] "tad idam" and so forth is the commentary on the Sūtra.

For if it were not the case, one would have said, "meditation (*dhyāna*) is intended to be enjoined as the means to liberation," and not "knowledge (*vedana*)," otherwise there would be a discordance between the sequential statements and the context.

And meditation (*dhyāna*) consists of an uninterrupted stream of mindfulness, like a continuous flow of oil—this is "constant mindfulness" (*dhruvāsmṛti*). ... ... ... ... ... ... "Worship (*upāsana*) would be constant mindfulness, because of the scriptural definition and because of the [resulting] vision. Thus, it is described that this very realization, which takes the form of worship and is repeated again and again, constitutes "constant mindfulness" (*dhruvānusmṛti*).

He qualifies the previously mentioned meditation with the words "and meditation. The "steadiness" (*dhruvatva*) of the memories means their non-interruption by heterogeneous memories. Because it is heard in scripture to be a means to liberation—as in the injunction "one should meditate upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*)—it is understood that this very prescribed meditation is "steadfast memory," due to the identity of their results; this is the meaning. He states another intended distinction of the author of the Sūtras, who is pointing out certain specific features, with the words "And that... "Having the same form" means having the nature of a clear manifestation.

To the question "Why?", he says: "It is severed. "The knot of the heart" (*hṛdayagranthi*) means ignorance; or else, "the heart" (*hṛdaya*) refers to the Self residing in the heart, and its "knot" is the connection with *prakṛti*. He explains the meaning of the word "to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*), which was not previously expanded upon because it is common to both the stages of the means and the experience of the fruit: "In this way. And "this being so" means: when there is another decisive statement. To the question "How can memory take the form of direct perception?", he says: "It becomes."

The sense is: "I see [it] in every tree," as it were. He states that this meaning has also been expressed by those who know the purport of the Sūtras—namely, with the words "in the sentence" (*vākya*). "Elaborated" (*prapañcita*) means by way of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). "Because it is heard regarding that" means because of its usage in connection with the intermingling [of parts], and so forth.

He explains the statement with the words "in all [the Upaniṣads]. The sense is that this is not restricted to the Chāndogya alone. By the phrase "enjoined as a means to liberation," there is the exclusion of other interpretations such as the hearing of [scripture] for the sake of some other purpose. To dispel the suspicion that the stated meaning might be a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he says "repeatedly" (*sakṛt*). "Established" (*siddham*) means the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). The word "not once" (*asakṛt*) is used to exclude the mere repetition of two or three times. He shows the explicit mention in the sentence of what was intended by the Sūtra: "meditation" (*upāsanam*). "Of that very thing" means of that which is the means to liberation; because it is denoted by the word "meditation," it must involve repeated practice.

This remembrance (*smṛti*) has been established as being of the nature of vision (*darśana*). And this nature of vision is the attainment of direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*). ... ... ... ... ... "For I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me. Thus, remembrance is of the nature of immediate realization (*sākṣātkāra*); by that very means, it is stated that the Supreme Self is attained.

He says "seyaṃ" (this very [meditation]) because another intended distinction was already stated by us; or rather, the meaning is that it was stated by the author of the *Vākya* itself through the force of the same logic (*tulyanyāyatayā*). "This very [meditation]" means that which is repeated many times and is constant. He uses the word "darśana" so that the term "vision" (*darśana*)—as in the expression "one who sees far" (*dīrghadarśin*)—should not be taken as referring to cognition in general; rather, its meaning is the attainment of a form identical to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The sense is that, because of its co-occurrence with words expressing other specific types of cognition such as "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*), it is logical that the term "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) refers specifically to a particular cognition characterized by immediacy (*aparokṣya*). He states that there is indeed a scriptural passage referring to another specific [cognition] with the word "thus" (*evam*); the sense is that this is so according to the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-naya*). "Instruction" (*pravacana*) means reflection (*manana*); this is a metaphorical application of the cause to the effect.

Regarding the doubt as to how memory (*smṛti*) is qualified here, and how meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth are understood to be non-means, he states the meaning first perceived with the words "by this" (*anena*). The sense of the word *kevala* is like [the statement]: "Fire is not to be piled on the earth. To the question "What follows from that?", he shows the worldly convention with the words "dear" (*priya*). To the question "What even from that?", he says "of whom" (*yasya*). "Of whom" means of the worshiper; "this" refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

He shows the *smṛti* (traditional text) with its underlying meaning as an authority for the point that only one who possesses love for the Supreme Self becomes an object of His love, in order to explain the choice [of the Lord] which is the effect of being most beloved: "As follows. "This one" refers to one who has love for the Blessed One. "Of those ever-united"—the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of aspiration (*āśaṃsā*). To explain this, he says: "For He is dear," etc. He demonstrates that constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) is distinguished by means of *śruti* (revelation) supported by worldly tradition and *smṛti*: "Therefore," etc.

The meaning is that the distinction among cognitions, being devoid of form (*nirākāratayā*), is indeed determined by the object itself through its being extremely dear when remembered. "Extremely dear" means extremely favorable.

This very recollection of the eternal (dhruvānusmṛti) of such a nature is designated by the word "devotion" (bhakti), because the word "bhakti" is a synonym for "meditative worship" (upāsana). ... ... ... ... "That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by means of undivided devotion."

To the question, "How then can devotion (bhakti) be said to be a means [to liberation]? he says: "In this way" (*evam*). For lexicographers state that "service" (*sevā*), "devotion" (*bhakti*), and "worship" (*upāsti*) are synonyms. Having established that the knowledge of the means to liberation is of the nature of devotion because it has the same meaning as many scriptural passages (*śruti*), he now establishes that very point through the identity of meaning between *Śruti* and *Smṛti*: "For this very reason" (*ata eva*). "For this reason" means: because devotion in the form of meditation (*upāsana*) is the knowledge of the means to liberation.

The passage from the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* has been cited to demonstrate that the word "Śiva," situated between [the words] "the Great Lord" (*mahān prabhuḥ*) and "the Supreme Person" (*puruṣaḥ*), refers to the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) as understood from the preceding and following context, because it shares the same meaning as the *Puruṣasūkta*. Furthermore, the verse beginning with "But by devotion alone... (*tato māṃ tattvataḥ*) has been quoted to establish the meaning of the statement through its explicit denial of other means, and to show explicitly that the attainment of knowledge, vision, and realization is accomplished through devotion.
Finally, the verse beginning with "That Supreme Person... (*puruṣaḥ sa paraḥ*) has been cited to demonstrate the identity of the means, based on the recognition of the identity of the object.

Sacrificial rites and other such actions are the means for achieving this kind of constant mindfulness (dhruvānusmṛti), as indicated by the scriptural mention of "sacrifices and so forth" being like the horse [in the case of the chariot]. Thus, it is stated that the perfection of knowledge occurs precisely through the performance of duties prescribed for one's stage of life (āśrama) when one is endowed with such discipline.

"Let it be so; what follows from that regarding the dependence on karma? To this he says: "Of such a form. "Of such a form" means characterized by the many previously mentioned qualifications. The sense is that the various distinctions of states are accomplished by karma. "Of the constant recollection (dhruvānusmṛti)"—the meaning is not of the desire to know (vividiṣā). For one who desires the ultimate goal engages in the intermediate goal, and for one who desires knowledge performs the practice for the sake of desiring that [knowledge]; thus, the sense is that there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya). He says "even granting" (*yadyapi*) as a concession.

"For its arising"—that is, for the arising of the desire to know (vividiṣā). He shows the sūtras regarding the lifelong persistence of both knowledge and ritual action, as well as the fact that the remaining duties of the stages of life (āśramas) are auxiliary to knowledge, by stating: "And he will say."

Now, wishing to avoid [the charge of] invalidity and the contradiction with [the requirements of] tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, he says: "In the statement" (*vākye*). By the phrase "of the constant remembrance" (*dhruvānusmṛteḥ*), the word "that" (*tat*) found in the statement is explained. The particle *eva* (only) is for the purpose of excluding sacrifice and the like, as well as tranquility and the like, taken individually. The compound is a copulative (*dvandva*) denoting mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*); by this, the exclusion of optionality (*vikalpa*) is intended. For that [optionality] involves eight defects due to the partial sublation of understanding, performance, the unseen merit (*apūrva*), and the fruit. "Possibility" (*sambhava*) means reasoning (*yukti*). "Etymological derivation" (*nirvacana*) means scripture (*āgama*).

Who are these [obstacles], and how is there no contradiction with tranquility (*śama*) and the other [qualities]? To this he says: "Discrimination" (*viveka*). The word "iti" refers to the statement of the Commentary, as well as the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*). That modification (*vikāra*) which makes one incapable of remaining without experiencing sense objects is "attachment" (*abhiṣvaṅga*). Through the absence of attachment, the non-existence of anger and the like is established as a result; for from desire (*kāma*) comes anger. "Support" (*ārambana*) means an object of focus, a virtuous basis. There is no lack of distinction between the means and the end here, because contemplation over time is an auxiliary to yoga.

The author of the Bhāṣya is the teacher Dramiḍa. Therefore, it is understood that he has demonstrated the entire etymological explanation. Regarding the term "Smārta": since the Vedic [text], namely the verse beginning with "atha muniḥ," is of obscure meaning, the Smārta [text] is presented here for its clear meaning. Regarding "according to one's capacity" (śaktitaḥ): for that which is impossible is not prescribed. Regarding "of those who know Brahman" (brahmavidām): this refers to those who already know Brahman, not to those who merely desire to know it. He provides an explanation of the words denoting action [in the verse] with the passage beginning "tam etam."

Covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is the notion of ownership regarding what belongs to another, or the constant recollection of harm done by others, or fruitless brooding. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to other scriptural passages such as "humility, lack of hypocrisy, non-violence, forbearance, and uprightness. An object of grief (*śokavastu*) is an object that serves as the cause for sorrow. By the word "and so forth," an object that serves as the cause for fear is indicated. Grief and fear are fluctuations of the mind caused by the knowledge of past or future undesirable things. The word "and" (*ca*) is placed out of its logical order.

"And born from that" means born from seeing the misery of one's kinsmen, which is to say, misery itself. "Lack of radiance"—meaning the incapacity for its own functioning—is the explanation of the word *dainya* (dejection); or it is an adjective qualifying *dainya*, meaning "that which is opposed to radiance. Alternatively, it may be construed as a separate sentence: "The lack of radiance produced by the unfavorable conditions of place and time, and by the recollection of objects of grief, is the depression of the mind. To the question, "What is being stated? he says: "Misery born from that."

"Dejection" (*avasāda*) is said to be the depression of the mind produced by defects in place, time, and so forth; this is merely the definition of dejection stated in the aphorism (*vākya*). However, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) states "the opposite of that. "Strength" refers to mental strength. Regarding the phrase "born from the opposite of that": it is born from the excellence of place and time, from knowledge of objects that cause joy in the past or future, and so forth. Because it is characterized by exaltation (*uddharṣa*), its opposite has already been established [by implication] and thus was not explicitly mentioned.

Regarding how contentment—which is declared to be a limb of yoga in such passages as "study, purity, and contentment"—is to be abandoned, he says: "Excessive... (ati). Once the individual words have been explained, he states the meaning of the sentence: "In this way... (evam). The separate mention [of contentment] is due to its distinction from the forms of engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*). The intention of the particle *eva* in the phrase "by that which is intended by you alone" (*tvadabhimatenaiva*) is as follows: there is a contradiction between the tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, which consist in the withdrawal from what is not prescribed, what is prohibited, and what is optional, and the sacrifices and so forth, which consist in engagement in what is prescribed.
And so says another Śruti passage: "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together... [standing] upon the knowledge of Brahman, he crosses over death by means of ignorance."

And pride has been shown [in the opponent's view]. Now, establishing his own position by citing another scriptural authority (*śruti*) and refuting the systems of Śaṅkara and Yādavaprakāśa, he explains the scripture beginning with the words "and knowledge" (*vidyā ca*), starting from the passage "And thus another scripture... The phrase "another scripture" means a scripture distinct from those concerning sacrifices and the like which are devoid of [knowledge], and a scripture accepted as having that [liberation] as its primary purport by those who advocate for the equal combination (*samasamuccaya*) of both paths.

The meaning is that even what has been stated by others as their own accepted means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is, in fact, intended to convey the very point I have stated. Regarding the question "What here denotes the object? he says: "In this [context]. That is, in passages such as "But let the ignorance of action also be heard" (*śrūyatāṃ cāpyavidyāyāḥ*). By these two words, there is the exclusion of both prescribed ritual action (*vihitakarman*) and ignorance (*ajñāna*). He connects the sense of the sentence with the words "by ignorance" (*avidyayā*). The intention is that it is an obstacle to the arising of knowledge, but not an obstacle to the desire to know the fruit (*phalavividiṣā*).

The meaning is that prior karma does not possess the quality of contradicting both subsequent and prior sins in the same way that knowledge (vidyā) does. Regarding the words "having crossed" (*tīrtvā*) and "having reached and remained" (*prāpya sthitaḥ*), the sense is that these are inappropriate because they involve an awkwardness (*asvārasya*) and require an unnecessary ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), since other possible interpretations exist.

By means of the two terms "action" (*karman*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*), the *Smṛti* passage—"When the impurity has been ripened by actions, knowledge then arises"—is recalled for the purpose of extracting the meaning of both the word "death" (*mṛtyu*), which commonly denotes either that which opposes the fruit or the means [to it], and the sentence regarding sacrifices and so forth, which commonly denotes either the cognition of the meanings of roots and suffixes or the cause of the desire for such cognition. For in this *Smṛti*, the statement "knowledge then arises" refers specifically to knowledge as something to be accomplished through action; it does not refer to liberation (*mokṣa*) or the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

He demonstrates that the word *avidyā* denotes action (*karman*) by providing a reason—namely, "crossing over death. The term "well-known" (*pratītā*) means "by the natural force of common usage. The meaning is that the negative particle (*nañ*) signifies the opposite of *vidyā*, i.e., something other than that. The underlying intention is that it does not refer to unenjoined action or knowledge. To clarify what has been stated, he says, "as it has been said": "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is that which arises from scripture (*āgama*), while "wisdom" (*vidyā*) is that which is born of discrimination (*viveka*) and so forth. The phrase "to cross over" (*tartum*) serves to exclude the sense of the root *tṛ* as "attaining."

Furthermore, action—consisting of merit and demerit—is an obstacle to knowledge; because it obstructs the arising of the knowledge of Brahman and results in undesirable fruits, it must be understood through the Mīmāṃsā of Action (Karma-mīmāṃsā). Therefore, that very [Mīmāṃsā] which is required by the inquiry into Brahman (Brahma-jijñāsā) should be stated as having preceded it.

One might object that it is improper to say that action (*karman*) in its entirety is to be discarded, for it is heard in scripture that only evil (*pāpa*) is to be discarded by merit (*dharma*). Anticipating this, he says: "By knowledge" (*jñāne*). To the question of how there can be a designation by the word "evil" for action consisting of both merit and demerit, he says: "Brahman. The usage "neither good deed nor bad deed, all evils" (*sarve pāpmānaḥ*) is also intended here. He then says: "And of this," [referring to the fact] that *rajas* and *tamas* are indeed opposed to it.

Since the status of these two is established by valid authority (*prāmāṇika*), the designation of the relationship between the door and that which possesses the door (*dvāra-dvāribhāva*) is indeed appropriate; to this he says: "And of sin... (*pāpasya ca*). "Leading downward" (*adho nayanam*) refers to causing aversion toward spiritual practice (*upāsti*), which is stated therein as the cause for falling into *saṃsāra*. He shows that *rajas* and *tamas* have such a nature with the word "rajas. The word "evam" indicates their being the most authoritative [sources].

To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And therefore" (*ataśca*). The particle *ca* has the sense of exclusion (*tvartha*), intended to remove doubt; or it has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). To the question "By what is there removal?", he says: "That" (*tat*). [This refers to] that which is performed—*not merely known*. He shows the scriptural passage (*śruti*) which clarifies that the thing denoted by the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is a quality (*dharma*) that removes, and that the thing denoted by the word "death" (*mṛtyu*) is a sin (*pāpa*) that is to be removed: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Thus, in this way" (*tadevam*).

"By that"—by means of the words of Śruti, Smṛti, reasoning (upapatti), the Sūtrakāra, and the Vākyakāra. "Thus"—for the purpose of removing what is opposed to its own production. To the question, "What follows from this regarding the inquiry into Brahman’s dependence on the inquiry into ritual action? he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ). "Therefore"—because the knowledge of Brahman depends upon ritual action. "Required"—the meaning is: for the sake of abandoning [what is harmful] and for the sake of acquiring [what is beneficial]. "That very same [dependence]"—the sense is: that which has been rejected by you.

Moreover, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities and so forth will not be accomplished without hearing the Mīmāṃsā; these [auxiliaries], which bring about the excellence of that [discrimination], are all the more appropriately connected right here [in this system]. And it is universally accepted that they depend upon the comprehension of the nature of ritual action (*karma*).

Thus, the status of the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) as a prerequisite has been established. Now, [the author] refutes the claim that the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) stated by others is a prerequisite—beginning with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). The term "Mīmāṃsā" refers to both parts [of the Vedānta system]. The "fruit" (*phala*) consists of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*); the "instrument" (*karaṇa*) consists of sacrifice and so forth, as well as meditative worship (*upāsana*); the "procedure" (*itikartavyatā*) consists of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, as well as the sevenfold means; and the "qualified candidate" (*adhikārī*) is one who desires enjoyment or one who desires liberation.

Just as the determination of the meaning of a sentence follows from the determination of the meanings of its constituent words, so too the determination of the aggregate of human goals and their means follows from the determination of each specific object dependent upon its respective category (*adhikaraṇa*). Thus, there is a distinction: the superficial cognition of the eternal and the non-eternal, which arises from the study of the Vedas along with its auxiliary limbs, is common to both heaven and liberation; therefore, it is not the cause for the desire for liberation born of detachment from other things. Other scriptures, such as those of the Vaiśeṣikas, however, are causes of a cognition that is contrary to the eternal and the non-eternal, because they assert that space, atoms, and so forth, are eternal.

Furthermore, [the knowledge of the Purāṇas and so forth] is seized by the wrong occasion, because it is already encompassed by the rule for the first study of the Veda. The Purāṇas and similar texts serve as supplements to the meaning of the Śruti (Veda) that has been heard; they do not independently determine [matters such as] the eternal nature of the Self. For if that were the case, the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtra) would be rendered useless, since the nature of Brahman would have already been determined by them. As for tranquility (*śama*) and the rest, they will be discussed later in the passage: "One should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that what occurs later cannot be a prerequisite for what precedes it.

Thus, the sequence between the *Karma-mīmāṃsā* and the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* has been stated on the basis of the nature of the Vedas as that which is to be explained. Now, he states that the inquiry into ritual action (*karmacintā*) must precede [the inquiry into Brahman] on the basis of the nature of Mīmāṃsā as an explanatory science—using the words "of these" (*eṣām*). "Of these" refers to tranquility (*śama*) and the other [qualifications]. "Application" (*viniyoga*) means the making known of their status as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*). "Pertaining to the third book" (*tārtīya*) means established in the third chapter (*adhyāya*). This is for the sake of illustration. The underlying sense is that [the inquiry into Brahman] depends upon all the logical principles (*nyāya*) stated in the earlier section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*) in various places.

Now he states the reason for the excellence [of this meditation]: "the Udgītha, etc. "Prosperity" (samṛddhi) means the state of having unimpeded results. To exclude the notion that something might be incidental (*prāsaṅgika*)—meaning being present in the mind through similarity and so forth even in the absence of a requirement from either one or both—he first states the dependence of the cognition of the Udgītha, etc., upon the contemplation of Brahman: "the vision of Brahman" (*brahmadṛṣṭi*). He states the dependence of this [meditation] upon the knowledge of Brahman: "those also" (*tāny api*). The word "those" (*tat*) refers to the ritual actions that produce the knowledge. "All the more" (*sutarām*) means by virtue of the requirement of both.

Since the former [section] concerns the view of Brahman as a constituent part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), while the latter concerns the nature of meditation (*cintyatva*)—even though both are common to the purpose of the success of ritual action (*karmasamṛddhi*)—it was stated "right here" (*ihaiva*). This was said with the intention that, because Brahman was not meditated upon in the former section, it is impossible there to contemplate the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth which consist of the view of Brahman. Granted that such is the connection (*saṅgati*), he says "of these" (*teṣām*) to address the question: "Even so, what [is the point]?"

Since the inquiry into the Udgītha-vidyā is directly relevant [to the present topic], the reflection on ritual action required by it constitutes a supporting reason for its being a prerequisite. However, the study of only a single part [of the Veda] is not according to the rule. If, even for one who has studied the entire Veda, the requirement [for this inquiry] arises only later due to the power of past merit (*sukṛta*), why would that requirement not likewise arise in the very chapter concerning the fruits (*phalādhyāya*)? If it is argued that the latter requires the introductory characteristics such as *samanvaya*, then here too the requirement for the reflection on the earlier portion is equal.

It has already been stated that the initial impression of [the Vedas] being infinite is equal even in the former case. Therefore, because the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) comes first according to the order of study, because the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) depends upon the principles established therein, and because it requires an investigation into the *udgītha* and other such elements, the inquiry into ritual action alone is what must have preceded.
Thus ends the *Laghusiddhānta* (the Short Exposition of the Conclusion). Now follows the *Mahāpūrvapakṣa* (the Great Prima Facie Argument).

As for what they say: "Brahman alone, which is pure consciousness devoid of all distinctions (*aśeṣaviśeṣapratyanīka-cinmātra*), is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Everything else—consisting of the manifold variety of knowers, objects of knowledge, and the resulting distinctions of cognition—is superimposed upon that very [Brahman] and is therefore illusory (*mithyā*)... because the scriptures, whose purpose is to teach the true nature of reality, declare that Brahman alone as non-dual pure consciousness is real, while everything else is false."

Thus, among the reasons stated by the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*), those reasons other than the capacity of the thing itself (*vastusāmarthya*) have been refuted by examining the statements concerning the means (*upāya*). However, since the capacity of the thing itself must be refuted after having been set forth in detail by examining the statements concerning the goal (*upeya*), it was not refuted previously. Therefore, it is now set forth in detail, beginning with the words "As for what they say... and ending with "...all the Vedāntas are commenced."

Regarding what they say: by the use of the word "api" (also) and the plural number, both the primacy of this point and the consensus of many authors are indicated. He asserts that pure consciousness alone is real and everything else is false through the two passages beginning with "aśeṣa" (without remainder). "Aśeṣaviśeṣaḥ" refers to the knower and so forth, as well as that which is of the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). "Pratyanīkatvam" means, in reality, the unfitness for inherence in that [consciousness], as well as its capacity to remove [the world] by being known. By the word "cit" (consciousness), its insubstantiality (*tucchatva*) is excluded.

Nor do [the terms] "knower" and "knowable" [apply]. The word "only" (eva) implies that [the world] with attributes is merely conceptual. Pure consciousness has been asserted as the reality; now, in order to establish that everything other than it is false—so that the intellect may remove the root of bondage—the author states its falsity by means of the word "that" (tat). The sense is that the negations such as "not here, not manifold" (neha nānā) have as their object that which is other than that [pure consciousness]. He shows the referent of the word "manifold" (nānā): "the knower," etc. By the phrase "produced by that" (tatkṛta), he excludes the notion that [the world] is inherent in its own nature.

"Differentiation" (*bheda*) refers to internal variety. The word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to birth, old age, death, and so forth. "Everything" means that there is no object whatsoever that is not grounded in that [substratum] and is ultimately real. The word "only" (*eva*) serves to exclude a plurality of substrata and to highlight the suspicion of contradiction regarding its nature as self-luminous.

He states the proof for the two propositions asserted [in the previous verse] with the words "sadeva" and so forth. The causal statement (*kāraṇavākya*) characterized by the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparyaliṅga*), namely "sadeva," is intended to exclude difference from the dissimilar, the similar, and internal difference. To clarify the meaning of the particle *eva*, he cites another causal statement: "atha parā. "Invisible" (*adreśyam*) means not within the range of perception or inference; that is, not an object of the eye or of the other senses. "Nameless" (*agotram*) means without a name. "All-pervading" (*sarvagatam*) means resting as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Now, the purificatory statement is "Truth" (*satyam*). Through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with other purificatory statements that share the same meaning as the causal statement, the intention is to show that [the text] aims at the featureless (*nirviśeṣa*). He says "partless" (*niṣkalam*) to clarify that the statement beginning with "Truth" aims at exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). "Parts" (*kalāḥ*) means limbs or components. "Peaceful" (*śāntam*) and so forth means free from the six waves. "Of whom" (*yasya*) is the negation of being an object of knowledge. "Not of sight" (*na dṛṣṭeḥ*) is the negation of being a knower. Bliss (*ānanda*) is the exclusion of what is not happiness.

Now, he states the falsity of everything else: "All this is the Self. This grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is intended for the purpose of sublation, as in the case of "the rope itself is the snake. By the phrase "in that very [Self]," the previously asserted fact that Brahman is the substratum of the superimposition of all things is indicated. He clarifies the sublation with the words "not here. He says "the ignorant one who perceives duality" by using the term "from death"; here, "death" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). To the question, "In that case, might there not eventually be a cessation [of this perception]? he replies: "For where indeed... Here, "where" means "when."

*Tat* means "then. The two words *itarena* (by the other) and *kaḥ* (who? are to be supplied. He establishes this by means of an illustration with the word *vācā* (by speech). He shows the result of the cognition of the distinction between the aforementioned death and its effects with the words *yadā* (when). Now follow the two sūtras beginning with *na sthānataḥ*, which concern the reality of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and the falsity of everything else.

Now, he shows the statement from the Purāṇas regarding both meanings with the words "pratyastamita" (completely subsided). "Pratyastamitabheda" means devoid of distinctions consisting of the similar, the dissimilar, and those inherent within itself. "Sattāmātra" (pure existence) means devoid of distinctions in the form of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). He sets aside its insignificance by saying "ātmasaṃvedya" (self-cognizable); the meaning is that it is self-luminous. The reason for this is "jñāna" (knowledge). "Atyantanirmala" (absolutely stainless) means eternally untouched by distinctions such as being an experiencer of suffering or being a knower. "Artha" refers to objects such as gods and so forth.

The statement "there is nothing else" declares the unreality (*apāramārthya*) of the world. To explain that, there are two verses beginning with "that which is this. He states that the cessation of the aforementioned delusion occurs through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) in the words "But those who... He introduces the section on the identity of the individual soul (*jīvaikya*) with the words "Of that... He says "one-fold" (*ekamaya*) meaning "one" (*ekam*). He dispels the doubt regarding a difference in the self based on the etymological grounds of the words "Self" (*ātman*) and "Supreme" (*para*) with the words "If... He provides an illustration with "as in the case of the bamboo... He instructs with "I am that... Practice according to the instruction is shown by "he abandoned..."

The cessation of the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is expressed as "non-difference" (*vibheda*). Regarding both meanings, there is the statement from the *Śrī Gītā*: "I am the Self" (*aham ātmā*). To clarify that the word "being" (*bhūta*) refers solely to the body, he says "the field" (*kṣetra*). The falsity of anything other [than this] is stated as "that does not exist" (*na tad asti*). That it has no other purpose is stated as "the very nature of reality" (*vastu-svarūpa*).

Falsehood (mithyātva) is defined as the state of being removable by a knowledge of a thing as it actually exists, preceded by its being perceived. And the defect (doṣa) is beginningless ignorance (avidyā), which is indefinable as either existent or non-existent, and which effects the concealment of one's true nature and various forms of distraction.

Falsity does not consist in absolute non-existence, because that would entail the uselessness of the treatise due to the absence of anything to be negated by its teaching; nor does it consist in appearing elsewhere than where it exists, because that would entail the truth of things even in other locations. To this, he says: "falsity" (mithyātva).

"Being perceived" (*pratīyamānatva*) excludes the non-existent (*asat*). "As it actually exists" (*yathāvasthita*) excludes the existent (*sat*). "Preceded by being perceived" intends to express that it is preceded by a necessary rule (*niyama*), as in the expression "one who drinks water" (*abbhakṣa*). "Being removable by knowledge" (*jñānanivartyatva*) means being removable by knowledge alone. The word *vastu* is used to eliminate the suspicion that it might be a *karmadhāraya* compound.

This being the case, there is an exclusion of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of that cognition which removes the real rope—[the latter] being strengthened by a capacity that is itself removable by a hammer or similar instrument, yet removable by a false cognition and removable by true knowledge. Nor is there an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of the snake-in-the-rope, because even that [snake] is fit to be removed by a cognition of the rope as it actually exists. He illustrates this with the words "Just as. [Objection: But surely, since the rope and such things are insentient (*jaḍa*), they do not manifest their own nature, and thus superimposition (*adhyāsa*) occurs upon them.

But how can that [superimposition] occur in the case of a self-luminous reality? To this he says: "defect" (*doṣa*). A defect alone is the cause of superimposition; whether its manifestation occurs by itself or through another, it is useful for superimposition upon a substrate, for even when the substrate is manifest, that [superimposition] takes place—this is the sense. By extending to the subject of the illustration what was shown regarding the definition of falsity and its being produced by a defect in the example, he simultaneously dispels two doubts. He removes the doubt as to how there can be the superimposition of many things on one thing by saying: "the other" (*para*).

The sense is that this is due to the difference in the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), just as [the appearances of] a snake, a ghost, or a hole [are superimposed] upon a rope. He dispels the doubt as to how there can be error in the Omniscient One by using the word "Supreme" (*para*). The meaning is that omniscience and other such qualities belong to the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇabrahman*), but not to the Supreme One. By the words "defect" (*doṣa*) and so forth, he extends the two points previously stated. "This" refers to what is being perceived. The word "Deity" (*deva*) and so forth is an elaboration of its manifold nature.

What is the defect (*doṣa*)? If it were real, it could not be removed by cognition; if it were unreal, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the requirement of further defects. If it is postulated as residing in Brahman while it is unobscured (*atirohita*), then either the non-arising or the non-cessation of error would result. If it resides in Brahman while it is obscured (*tirohita*); if that obscuration is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), there would be either non-cessation or the cessation of its very nature. If it is extrinsic (*parataḥ*), there is an infinite regress. Since various superimpositions (*adhyāsa*) are observed to have various defects as their roots, he says "And the defect... in order to dispel many such doubts.

These doubts are answered by the terms "ignorance" (avidyā), "indescribable as being or non-being," "beginningless" (anādi), and "that which causes the concealment of one's own nature and various diverse distractions."

"For they are indeed obstructed by untruth; untruth is the covering for those who are truly real. ... ... ... ... It is understood that Brahman itself, its true nature obscured by beginningless ignorance—which is indefinable as being or non-being—perceives a manifoldness inherent within itself.

He states the authority for such ignorance with the words beginning "by untruth" (*anṛtena*). "Obstructed" (*pratyūḍhāḥ*) means "impeded. To explain the word "obstructed," he says "of them" (*teṣām*); the plural number is used as in the expression "Aditi [released] the bonds" (*aditiḥ pāśān*). By the phrase "neither being was nor non-being" (*nāsadāsīt*), its indeterminability is shown. For "darkness" (*tamaḥ*) is primordial nature (*prakṛti*) in its subtle state, and not ignorance (*avidyā*) in the form of a false appearance; regarding this, he says "but [it is] illusion" (*māyāṃ tu*). He states that it is the cause of many delusions with the word "Indra. He states that it is difficult to remove without wisdom (*dhī*) with the word "mine" (*mama*).

He states its beginninglessness with the word "beginningless" (*anādi*). The word "beginning" (*ādi*) refers to the collection of Śruti and Smṛti passages previously cited regarding its essential nature. Dispelling the suspicion that it possesses attributes based on words such as "Indra" or "Maheśvara," he states the meaning of those passages as "without attributes" (*nirviśeṣa*). The sense is that because of the uniformity of meaning with the passages concerning the essential nature, even in those passages concerning defects, the attribute-less reality is intended as the locus of those defects. In the phrase "inherent" (*svagata*), a relationship with itself as the substrate is understood. The word "since" (*yataḥ*) is used for the purpose of completing the sentence.

As it has been said: "The Blessed One is of the nature of consciousness (*jñānasvarūpa*), since he possesses all forms and is not a [mere] substantial entity... [omission] ...Moreover, that which belongs to the sphere of conventional transaction (*saṃvyavahāra*)—even therein, you have taught that [the world] is dependent upon the worlds (*bhuvana*)."

He says "Just as... to show that even by a recollection (*smṛti*) concerned with defects, the non-differentiated reality is known through sentences that, as it were, refer to its own nature. The word "reality" (*vastu*) here refers to the gods and so forth, which will be mentioned later. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is called "cognition" (*vijñāna*) because it is by means of this that things are known diversely. He explains, by way of contrast, that the perception of difference is the effect of ignorance: "When... [the text continues: "Pure" means having its own essential form, devoid of the perception of difference created by ignorance. "Ignorance" (*avidyā*) is "mental construction" (*saṅkalpa*), because by means of it differences are imagined on all sides.

It will be stated that [the world] arises from the tree of ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding "entities" (*vastu*)—that is, those possessing the attributes of gods and so forth—"diverse entities" (*vastubhedāḥ*) refers to the distinctions in the forms of gods and so on. The two verses beginning with "The entity exists" (*vastvasti*) will be explained in the section on the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). He concludes the negation of difference based on dissimilar classes (*vijātīya-bheda*) with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He negates difference within the same class (*sajātīya-bheda*) with the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). He negates even internal difference (*svagata*) with the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*). "Pure" (*viśuddha*) means stainless and free from the vision of the distinctions of ignorance. "Always one" (*sadaika*) means devoid of increase and decrease.

He says "this is not the ultimate view" with the word "sat. This refers to knowledge (*jñāna*); "residing in the world" means it rests upon the world as its substratum. The meaning is that the reason why this exists as the locus of all worldly transactions (*saṃvyavahāra*) is said to be ignorance (*avidyā*).

And they declare that this ignorance is ceased through the realization of the oneness of the self with Brahman, which is pure consciousness without distinction; and by this realization of the oneness of Brahman and the self, the cessation of bondage—which is false in nature and has a cause—is logically established.

To the question, "What then follows from this regarding the independence of knowledge from karma?", he says: "And of this... (*asyāśca*). The phrase "not again" (*na punaḥ*) is employed to demonstrate the cessation of ignorance. The phrase "that one" (*tadekam*) is used to show that the object of knowledge is unity. The phrase "when" (*yadā*) is for the sake of attaining fearlessness (*abhaya*). "Ātmyam" means the body. "Niruktiḥ" means name. "Abhayam" means for the sake of the absence of fear; it is an *avyayībhāva* compound. He says, "it is split" (*bhidyate*), so that even that which is considered by others to be a cause of bondage may be removed by knowledge.
Here, in order to eliminate the perception of difference, he says: "Brahman. To negate other means, he says: "that very [Self].

To show that the cessation of ignorance is not perceived here, he says: "in this case. To the question "How so?", he says: "just as. "Pramāda" means lack of attention; the meaning is that its cause is avidyā (ignorance).

To the objection that the identity of the self with the attributeless Brahman has not been understood, he says: "True. The attributelessness [of Brahman] is established by the purificatory texts (*śodhaka*). By means of that, the scripture declares the identity with the Self: "Now, he who worships another [deity]" (*atha yo 'nyām*). The notion of difference is negated; then it shows the instruction: "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*). Likewise, it addresses the deity: "Thou indeed" (*tvaṃ vā*). It reflects upon itself: "Therefore, I am that" (*tad yo 'ham*). He states its status as a Sūtra: "He will say... (*vakṣyati*).

He states the words of one who knows that intention with the phrase "And thus" (*tathā ca*). "Because of its accomplishment" means because it is superimposed upon that [Brahman]. He shows the corroborating evidence for this with the words "And by this. The phrase "of the false form" contains a reason. "Along with its cause" means together with ignorance (*avidyā*). The point is that the delusion of a snake is indeed to be removed by the knowledge of the rope, not by ritual action (*karman*).

But surely—how can the cessation of all distinctions, which contradicts direct perception, be effected by the cognition produced by the scripture? ... ... ... That whose validity might be established otherwise is sublated; that which cannot be established otherwise and has no other scope sublates the other—this is the determination of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator in all cases.

He objects with "But surely... [The word] "entire" (*sakala*) is used to exclude cases such as the double moon or dreams. The sense is that, because it depends upon perception for the sake of establishing the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga*), the subject (*dharmin*), and so forth—just like the argument for fire being non-hot based on its being a substance, or like the scriptural statement regarding the identity of the sacrificial post and the sun—the Śruti would not cause one to understand what is contrary to that [perception].

Setting aside this [objection], he addresses the first alternative—asking whether you think that sublation (*bādhyatva*) of perception is impossible, or whether the sublation (*bādhakatva*) of the indirect [cognition] is impossible—with the words "Or how? (*kathaṃ vā*). The point is that the status of being a pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsatva*) did not appear at the time of the cognition; rather, the subsequent sublation is equal [to that of other cases]. He raises the doubt that the indirect [cognition], being the root [cause], cannot be a sublater with the word "therein" (*tatra*); the word "but" (*tu*) is used to exclude the notion of equality.

With the intention that [the scripture] has its root in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it is rooted and not indirect, it was stated: "of a scripture whose root is direct perception. He says, "between two equal [arguments]," in order to lead one to accept another decisive factor, lest there be a reversal even when they are equal. Therein, he raises an objection stated by the opponent: "between the former and the latter. He replies, "it is the same here also," with the words "in the case of scripture. Since the presence of a faulty reason and its absence—qualified by the absence of the relation of root and rooted—are the decisive factors for those two, he says, "this has been stated," regarding the phrase "when they are equal."

The meaning is: while [the two cognitions] are equal, there is the state of being produced by a defective cause and the absence thereof. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the distinction between perceptual and non-perceptual [cognition], as well as priority and posteriority, is intended. To the question "Why?", he says: "As in the case of a flame. The word "otherwise" (anyathā) is to be supplied; the meaning is "because of the consequence of non-connection" (ayoga-prasaṅga). To the question "With respect to what object is perception sublated?", he says: "For in that case... (tatra hi). Then, what is the determining factor? To this he says: "And thus... (evaṃ ca). The meaning is: when that which was stated by you is untenable.

"Of two means of valid cognition" (*dvayoḥ pramāṇayoḥ*) means: of two perceptions, of perception and inference, of two inferences, of perception and scripture, of inference and scripture, or of two scriptures—this is the meaning. "Non-establishment otherwise" (*ananyathāsiddhatvam*) means not arising due to sublation by a means of valid cognition regarding a contradictory object; and that [non-arising] is due to being "without scope," which consists in the non-attainment of another object and the absence of inclusion within the category of a means of valid cognition. "In all cases" (*sarvatra*) means in the case of contradiction between two similar or two dissimilar [cognitions], such as perception and so forth. The syntactical connection is: "thus this has been stated."

Therefore, by that very logic of sublation (*apacchedanyāya*), since the statements concerning the absence of attributes (*nirguṇavākya*) are superior and more powerful because they depend upon [the prior mention of] attributes, nothing is lost. [The Brahman is] that which is produced by the scripture (*śāstra*)—which is without beginning or end, possesses an uninterrupted tradition, is free from even a scent of possible defects, and allows no room for [contradiction]—consisting solely of self-luminous consciousness (*cinmātra*) that is without distinctions, eternal, pure, liberated, and awakened. Thus, nothing is deficient.

To the question, "What follows from that regarding the superiority of the scripture? he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). By the phrase "for this [scripture] is without beginning or end," the *smṛti* is recalled as a mark (*liṅga*) proving its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*), as indicated by the words "without beginning" and so forth. Since there is no possibility of defects, it does not fall into the category of invalid means of knowledge. He demonstrates the contradiction with the [opponent's] position through the words "devoid of distinctions" (*nirviśeṣa*) and so forth. "Purity" (*śuddhi*) is the absence of ignorance (*avidyā*). Consequently, it is "liberated" (*mukta*), meaning free from the bondage that is the effect of ignorance. It is "awakened" (*buddha*), meaning manifest; and that manifestation is intrinsic (*svataḥ*).

And that [Self] is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), because it is so heard in the scriptures; this is the meaning of the words. Bondage consists of various forms of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). To the question "What is the defect?", he says: "And it is possible. The "expansion of difference" (*bhedaprapañca*) is the collection of differences, such as the knower and so forth; and that is manifold in the form of gods and other beings. Furthermore, it is characterized by conceptual differentiation in the form of Brahmins and so forth; thus, it takes the form of manifold distinctions and conceptual constructions. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the perception of difference is indicated. The word "beginningless" (*anādi*) is used to exclude the charge of mutual dependence between those two.

It is beginningless in its continuity, like the sequence of seed and sprout. The term "called ignorance" (*avidyākhyā*) is used to exclude [defects] such as cataracts; for if one were to infer a defect everywhere based on a localized cataract or the like, it would follow that even the Veda is defective simply because it is a verbal statement. The point is that the non-perception of a capable object (*yogyānupalabdhi*) is equal in both cases. Alternatively, the word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to the causal ignorance (*kāraṇāvidyā*).

He objects with "nanu" (is it not so?). He states the absence of the grounds for sublation mentioned immediately above with "anādi" (beginningless). The word "api" (even/also) indicates a contradiction. He demonstrates the contradiction that serves as the basis for accepting the relationship between the sublated and the sublator with "jyotiṣṭomena" (by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice). Accepting sublation while refusing to admit a perceptible cause, he replies with "satyam" (true). The resolution is achieved through the sequence of priority and posteriority, which takes the form of the distinction between having scope (*sāvakāśatva*) and lacking scope (*anavakāśatva*).

When the *udgātṛ* and *pratihartr̥* priests suffer a ritual interruption (*apaccheda*), it is prescribed that the sacrifice be concluded without fees (*adakṣiṇa*) or with the giving away of all one's possessions (*sarvasva-dakṣiṇa*) as a contingent rite (*naimittika*). A conflict arises between these two when they occur within a single performance (*ekaprayoga*). In that case, if they occur simultaneously, there is an option (*vikalpa*). However, if they occur in a sequence (*paurvāparya*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) maintains that the earlier rule prevails; for the earlier rule arises without its opponent having yet appeared, whereas the later rule arises precisely because it encounters an opposing factor. [The Siddhāntin replies: Because the opposing factor is not present at the time of the earlier rule’s arising, the earlier rule can indeed arise without being sublated by the later.

However, since the arising of a subsequent [rule] is impossible without subverting the contradiction inherent in its immediate predecessor, it arises only by subverting that predecessor; thus, its superiority is established on the grounds that the occasional scripture (*naimittika-śāstra*) is indeed enjoined upon the appearance of its occasion (*nimitta*). As it has been said: "For the arising of a subsequent [rule] is not established without the subversion of the preceding. By this logic—the sequence being established through the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) and the order of purpose (*arthakrama*) consisting of the worldly beings' initial inclination toward the three aims of life (*trivarga*)—the meaning is that there is a subversion of the former.

Since such a sequence of priority and posteriority is absent, this [method of sublation] cannot be maintained in the scriptures concerning the meditation on the qualified (saguṇa) Brahman; to this he says: "In the Vedānta. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of its being devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva). The meaning is: because we observe a sublation that constitutes the fruit of the *apaccheda* (simultaneous contradiction) maxim. He intends that the meditation on the qualified is prior, since it is heard to have worldly fruits such as eating and so forth (*jakṣaṇa*). He raises an objection regarding how this applies to the statements concerning the supreme nature and the qualified Brahman: "But surely... He refutes this: "It is devoid of qualities."

Regarding which are the statements concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa-vākya*) and how they possess efficacy, he says: "This has been stated. "Immutable" (*kūṭastha*) means changeless. "The others" refers to passages such as "He who is all-knowing," and so forth. "By virtue of depending on qualities" means that negation depends upon that which prompts the possibility of what is being negated. "Nothing is deficient" implies that because the statements concerning qualities serve the purpose of meditation (*upāsana*), they are not rendered useless.

Alternatively, intending to show that even such passages as "He who is omniscient" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9) are for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*), he says: "In the Vedānta. He raises an objection: "But surely," [arguing] that because there is no sequence of prior and subsequent, there can be no sublation of attributes, and for that very reason, there can be no assumption that they are for the purpose of meditation. He replies, with the word "Nirguṇa" (devoid of attributes), having in mind the sequence consisting of injunctions and prohibitions. Everything else is as explained previously.

But is it not the case that in the passage "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite," qualities such as truth and knowledge are perceived? No, it is said in reply: ... ... ... ... ... Thus, these three words—being synonymous yet non-interchangeable—are more purposeful insofar as they convey that a single reality possesses a nature that is opposed to everything else.

Having understood the statement beginning with "Truth" (*satya*)—which was cited as referring to the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman—to instead refer to the qualified (*saguṇa*) Brahman, the opponent objects: "But surely... (*nanu ca*). "Truth, knowledge, etc. means "truth-ness, knowledge-ness, etc. The phrase "of two and one" (*dvyekayoḥ*) means "of duality and unity"; for the sense is that [the suffix *tasi*] is used there, whereas otherwise, the plural form "of two and many" (*dvyekeṣu*) would have resulted. He refutes this: "No" (*na*). The meaning is that if this is merely a superficial cognition (*āpātadhī*), we have no objection; but if it is valid knowledge (*pramiti*), he will demonstrate why it is not so.

To the question "Why?", he says: "By virtue of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*). He raises an objection: "Multiple [referents]" (*aneka*). The sense is that, as in sentences with different grammatical substrata (*vyadhikaraṇa*), the multiplicity of word-meanings does not contradict the unity of the sentence-meaning. Having rebuked him for being ignorant of the specific modes of expression in both coordinate and non-coordinate sentences, he replies: "Because there is no denotation" (*anabhidhāna*). The sense is that "the beloved of the gods" (*devānāṃ priyaḥ*) refers to a goat—that is, an ignorant person. To the question "How so?", he says: "The state of having a single referent" (*ekārthatvam*).

However, there is no unity of the primary meaning understood from a collection of words with distinct referents; rather, that [unity] occurs in sentences with coreferential terms—this is the sense. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "In the qualified [sentence]. With the following alternatives in mind—whether the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) occurring in a sentence with coreferential terms refer only to the qualifiers, or to the qualified object, or only to the essential nature (the substrate)—in the first case, there is no unity of meaning because the objects in the form of the qualifiers are multiple; in the second case as well, that [lack of unity] is the same.

Furthermore, there is no identity of meaning due to the difference between the meanings of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Moreover, there would follow a distinction in the qualified by virtue of the distinction in the qualifier; for a qualifier is, by nature, a differentiator. In cases such as "Devadatta is dark-complexioned and young," identity is established through the force of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, Brahman is not within the scope of such perception.

Nor can the identity of the qualified (viśeṣya) follow from the identity of the subject-term (dharmin) ending in the singular number, because such is not observed in cases like "the cow is spotted, hornless, and full-horned," where its plurality is established by the force of perception. If this is argued, we say no; for even by a person who does not perceive the cows, the plurality of cows is understood through this sentence. Therefore, since Brahman is imperceptible, the distinction of the qualified resulting from the distinction of the qualifiers is unavoidable. These and other objections have been stated in the passage beginning with "by the distinction of the qualifiers" (viśeṣaṇabhedenetyādi).

The word *artha* denotes even the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). If there were sequential denotation, then just as with the qualificand, because of the connection of the qualifier prescribed by another word with the qualifier [itself], there would be a mutual inherence (*samavāya*) between the two qualifiers. If, on the other hand, there were simultaneous denotation, then because the identity is conveyed in the qualifier just as in the portion of the qualificand—by virtue of having the same case-ending—there would be identity of the qualifiers and an absence of distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*). These and other such objections stated elsewhere are intended here. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And therefore... (*tataśca*).

By refuting the [first] two positions, the third position is effectively accepted; explaining that, he raises an objection with the words "In this case" (*evam*). "In this case" means: if the [sentence] were intended to have as its purport merely the thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*), then either one of the two terms would be redundant, or there would be a loss of the defining characteristic of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); however, since these points will be resolved later, he says "denoting a single object" (*ekārtha*) with the intention that this objection should not be raised prematurely in the middle of the work when it can be resolved by many arguments. The phrase "even though they denote a single object" is a restatement of the reason for the objection.

He avoids [the charge] that there is identity [of meaning]. The determination of the intended sense (tātparya) is established by means of the common case-ending. And the avoidance of the loss of the definition [of a word] is what is intended by the word "and" (ca). "Possessing meaning" (arthavattva) means being purposeful. It possesses meaning because it excludes many things to be set aside. It is stated that non-synonymy, achieved through those factors which serve as the grounds for application, and conformity with the definition of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), are both established without contradicting the fact that they share a single referent.

Why, then, could that [sentence] not have as its primary purport the essential nature (*svarūpa*) by means of an indication through the method of positive concomitance (*anvaya-mukha*), just as it does for the two words [“That” and “Thou”]? [Objection: Because there are many exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), there is no single referent; and because the things to be excluded (*vyāvartya*) are infinite, their exclusion cannot be accomplished by a few words. Furthermore, from what are they excluded, and what are those [things]? [If the exclusions were identical to the properties], there would be the consequence of having common properties (*sadharmakatva*). [If] the exclusions themselves were not properties, there would be synonymy (*paryāyatā*). Anticipating this, he says: "This has been stated."

Since the removal of suspected defects regarding that which has been stated as the cause is required, the phrase "by way of definition" (*lakṣaṇataḥ*) and so forth was stated with the intention that [the words] have their own nature (*svarūpa*) as their primary meaning by means of excluding what is other than that. All this is accomplished by these three words; the sense is that the exclusion of infinite things to be excluded occurs through the form of the efficient cause (*prayojaka*). The exclusion, however, is the result. But since the words themselves pertain to the essential nature (*svarūpa*), a single unified meaning is intended. To the question "By what [means] and from what [object] is there exclusion?", he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*).

The exclusion of being subject to modification was stated precisely because its exclusion from insubstantiality follows from its being the cause [of manifestation]. The explanation of the term "insentient in nature" (*jaḍarūpa*) is "having its manifestation dependent on another" (*anyādhīnaprakāśa*). Regarding the phrase "possessing those same attributes," he says: "And not... The statement regarding its nature as either existence or non-existence is made with respect to specific disputants. To the question "What then?", he says: "But rather... He provides an illustration: "Just as... The meaning is that it is not a separate attribute (*dharmāntara*), because it is not perceived, and because if one were to accept it, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

To the objection that [the terms] would then be synonyms, he says "of the very same" with the intention of presenting a counter-argument: "whiteness is excluded from blackness, excluded from yellowness," and so forth. It is "more meaningful"—that is, in comparison to the example and in comparison to the "possessor of qualities" (saguṇa) intended by the opponent. For whiteness is directly perceived; therefore, the statement serves no purpose. For the function of a purifier is the removal of suspected defects, not the communication of an association with qualities.
The second quarter of the first chapter.

In the first chapter (*pāda*), a person who has studied the Vedas [is the subject]; in the second, those whose marks are clear; in the third, those whose marks are clear; and in the fourth, those who follow the manner of establishing each respective [topic].

The sequential summary of the topics of the first *pāda* is provided for the following purposes: to ensure that the subject matter of the first *pāda*, which follows upon each respective *adhikaraṇa*, remains present in the mind for the sake of its connection with the subsequent three *pādas*; to establish the necessity of commencing the three *pādas* by showing that the sentences constituting their subject matter do not fall within the scope of the logical principles already stated; and [to show] that the four *sūtras*—which serve to establish the commencement of the entire treatise—are, by implication, connected to the first *pāda*.

It has been stated that because the *janmādi-sūtra* (the first three aphorisms) begins with the first [pāda], its sequence of primary meanings is for the sake of establishing the commencement of the treatise (*śāstra*). Furthermore, there is a specific thematic connection (*viśeṣasaṅgati*) between the *janmādi-sūtra* and the first pāda, because it concerns the characteristics such as birth (*janma*) belonging to the Reality that is distinct from both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*). Indeed, the subject matter of the first pāda is the existence of that Reality which is distinct from the conscious and the unconscious. Alternatively, "the commencement of the treatise" may refer to the meaning of the four aphorisms (*catussūtrī*) by way of subsequent connection (*anuṣaṅga*).

He states the meaning of the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) with the words "having studied" (*adhīta*). He states the meaning of the section on the origin and so forth (*janmādyadhikaraṇa*) with the word "infinite" (*ananta*). The phrase "the sole cause of great bliss" expresses the resultant meaning of the injunction "seek to know That. Everything up to the end of the word "abrūmahi" is of clear meaning. The purposefulness of each respective term should be understood in accordance with what has preceded.

He states the meaning of the [first] quarter: "Thus, in this way" (*tadevam*). By the term "transcendent" (*atipatita*), the sublation of the apprehender of the subject (*dharmigrāhakabādha*) by fallacious arguments (*kutarka*) is intended. The existence of a cause distinct from both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) has been stated as the subject matter following from the quarter. Regarding the phrase "henceforth" (*ataḥ param*): the meaning is that the exclusion of any other connection for the stated fact of Brahman being the cause is now being established.

"Jīvādi" (the soul, etc.): the sense is that [terms] such as "unmanifest" (*aspaṣṭa*) and so forth do not constitute marks of Brahman (*brahmaliṅga*). "Tattat" (this and that): the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*); the meaning is "the more clearly evident seeds of the prima facie argument. The statement "jīvādi" is made because the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) are perceived in the first section of the second book (*dvitīyādhyāya-prathama-pāda*). The intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*) arises from the doubt that the passage might refer to the soul due to the natural tendency toward the whole (*avayavin*). Marks of the soul are observed here, such as identity with all things, connection with the mind and breath, abiding in the cavity of the heart, minuteness (*aṇutva*), and so forth.
Because the teaching is established as being everywhere. (1.2.1)

This is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Now, indeed, [the person] consists of resolve... It is determined that even the word *brahman* occurring in the concluding passage refers only to the individual soul (*jīva*), used there for the sake of honor.

"Because of the teaching that is well-known everywhere. He states the subject matter with the words "this" (*idam*). Only what is required for the first interpretation is taken up—namely, the passage beginning with "atha khalu"—but not the entire section beginning with "sarvam" and so on. The portion ending with "bhārūpaḥ" is taken up because the passage beginning with "bhārūpaḥ" constitutes the subject matter of the second sūtra. This is the first interpretation, following other commentaries. It is clear that the passage beginning with "sarvaṃ khalu" has the Supreme (Brahman) as its subject matter. Other [commentators] have explained this sūtra as having the passage beginning with "atha khalu" as its subject matter.

Since the preceding statement has the Supreme as its object, and since the subsequent statements are supplementary to it, they too must be understood in that way; thus, there is no suspicion that they refer to the individual soul (*jīva*), and the present section (*adhikaraṇa*) need not be commenced. To this, he says: "In this [case]. The meaning is that because the subject matter concerns the object of another injunction for meditation, it does not share the same scope as the preceding one; therefore, the suspicion that it refers to the individual soul is appropriate. Regarding the phrase "of the meditation already set forth," the word *kratu* refers to meditation (*upāsana*).

However, this does not refer to the ritual actions previously enjoined as auxiliary to the meditation on Brahman, because the connection with a fruit is seen through the phrase "according to one's resolve" (*yathākratuḥ*). And in that context, "resolve" (*kratu*) means meditation (*upāsti*), since this is identical in meaning with the passage "in whatever way they meditate upon Him. The sense is that even though meditation on Brahman was previously enjoined, because the individual soul (*jīva*) abounds in various resolves, the injunction of other forms of meditation upon it is appropriate. The passage beginning with "In that [context]" (*tatra*) and so forth is clear.
