Because the specific relationship characterized by the status of being an instrument and the object of an instrument is not explicit, there is an "indistinctness of the mark" (*aspaṣṭaliṅgatā*).

Regarding the doubt that the previously mentioned Brahman itself might be connected as the object of meditation in the phrase "one should perform the sacrifice," such that the attributes like "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) would qualify it—anticipating the dilemma of whether the word *brahma* requires a verb of injunction, or whether the word *brahma* is to be construed with what follows because the phrase "one should perform the sacrifice" requires an object of meditation—the author first addresses the first alternative, stating: "Nor all... The meaning is that [the word *brahma*] has no further expectancy, as its purpose has already been fulfilled by another [function].

He provides the second response: "And not that [the Self] is for the sake of ritual" (*na ca sa kratum*), meaning that because it is self-sufficient through its own sentence-meaning which serves no other purpose. Regarding the word "vibhakti": there is no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) between the accusative ending, just as there is none with the nominative ending, since they are alike in not being in the genitive case; however, the modification (*vipariṇāma*) is more appropriate for the proximate word whose meaning serves no other purpose. "Mutual expectancy" (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) refers to the expectancy of the injunctive word for the words "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth.

This being the case, we reply: "Because of the teaching of that which is well-known everywhere. That which possesses the qualities of consisting of mind and so forth... [the text] denies that knowledge depends on the mind and that stability depends on the vital breath (prāṇa) in the case of Brahman.

He states the final conclusion: "Thus. [The reason is: "Because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere"; the sense is that this applies everywhere, including those passages containing both general and specific terms. In the passage "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), only a general connection with the mind is shown; in "with the heart" (*hṛdā*), a specific connection is indicated. In "not with the eye" (*na cakṣuṣā*), a specific connection is shown as a qualification of the mind. He shows the state of having the vital breaths as its body (*prāṇaśarīratva*): "Likewise. *Prāṇa* means the sustainer; for one who sustains is indeed the embodied one (*śarīrin*). He addresses the contradiction regarding the concluding summary: "Thus. He addresses the lack of contradiction regarding the negation: "without vital breath" (*aprāṇa*).
Alternatively: "All this, indeed, is Brahman, [like] water... ... "...by beginningless ignorance, it exists in the form of gods, animals, humans, and stationary beings."

He states his own interpretation [of the connection between the words]: "Or rather" (*athavā*). The sense is that the previous interpretation is not superior because: (1) it requires the supply of an unstated proposition (*adhyāhārya-pratijñātva*); (2) it contradicts the natural consistency of the unity of the two occurrences of the word *brahman* at the beginning and end; (3) the hearing of the phrase "one who is thus peaceful" (*evaṃvit śāntaḥ*) shows that peace is to be accomplished through hearing and reflection (*śravaṇa-manana*); (4) no other meditation is seen as a means to that [peace]; (5) the status of being a mere prayer (*āśaṃsāryatva*) results from the lack of natural consistency in the word "peaceful"; and (6) it does not conform to the grammatical construction (*vṛtti*). Regarding the phrase "in this very [context]": [it refers to the present passage].

The meaning is that there is no difference between the means for peace (*śāntyupāya*) and the means for liberation (*muktyupāya*). Demonstrating the natural sense of the word *śānta*, he states the meaning of the sentence as "consisting of all" (*sarvātmakam*). "Material cause" (*upādāna*) refers to the injunction (*vidhāna*); "restatement" (*anuvāda*) is like the oblation in the passage "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*). He states the meaning of the sentence as "therefore" (*ataḥ*). Having thus accepted that they have the same object, he raises a doubt with the words "in that case" (*tatra*). The beginninglessness of ignorance and karma follows the analogy of the seed and the sprout. He states the impossibility of this for the Supreme (*para*) with the words "but for the Supreme" (*parasya tu*).

To the question "How is the word *brahman* [applied here]?", he says: "The inward" (*pratyak*). He establishes this with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). He shows the application of the ground for its usage (*pravṛttinimitta*) with the words "The inward" (*pratyak*). He explains the nature of being the cause (*kāraṇatva*) with the words "Of the ignorant one" (*aviduṣaḥ*). Brahman-hood resides in the pure [Self], while causality resides in the bound [Self]. To the question "How then can there be a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between Brahman-hood and omnipresence?", he says: "This very [Self]... (*tadayam*).
To this, it is replied: "Because of the teaching of that which is well-known everywhere. ... As the author of the Vṛtti said: "In the words 'All this indeed,' the Lord Brahmā is the Self of all. (1)

He states the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) with the words "herein" (*atra*). [The reason is] "because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere. The meaning is that the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) does not refer to the denotative term (*vācaka*), but rather to the denoted object (*vācya*). For it is that which is well-known which serves as the reason (*hetu*). By stating it as a reason, there is a teaching of birth and so forth by way of their being well-known. The sense is that by the particle *khalu*, the identity (*tādātmya*) is stated as something well-known. He clarifies what has been said with the words "of Brahman. He demonstrates the well-known nature [of this] with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*).

To exclude the possibility that the passage beginning with "from which words turn back" refers to the individual soul (jīva), he says: "Bliss" (ānanda). He clarifies that the word "bliss" refers to the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) by stating: "in the preceding section. He states another scriptural passage: "He is the cause. Intending to show that identity resulting from being the cause is also established by implication, he says: "Therefore. The meaning is that since other Śruti texts teach identity through the state of being the cause, the identity mentioned here is logically consistent.

To the question, "How can there be identity with that which is distinct from both consciousness (cit) and unconsciousness (acit)? he replies with the word "ataḥ" (therefore). The meaning is that its nature as the Self is established because the scriptures themselves declare it to be "That-ness" (tat-tvam). [Objection: The state of being the body is indeed present, but not in the causal state; therefore, how can there be a statement of oneness at that time? To this he says, "For [it is] the Supreme Brahman. The intention is that this is established both by the inherent power of the reality and by explicit scriptural declaration. To the question, "What is it like? he says, "being thus."

What was stated [in the verse beginning with] "yad uktam" and so forth is clear. Regarding the phrase "jīva-karma": the sense is that Brahman possesses both agency (*kartṛtva*) and material causality (*upādānatā*), whereas "karma" refers merely to the cause of inequality (*vaiṣamyamātra-hetu*). "Therefore" (*ataḥ*) is the conclusion. He states the traditional authority for his own position with the words "imam eva. In the sentence "sarvaṃ khalu," the meaning is that Brahman, which is described as being the self of all, is the Lord (*īśaḥ*), the Supreme Self (*paramātma*). || 1 ||
And because the intended qualities are applicable [to Brahman]. (1.2.2)

Furthermore, the qualities about to be described are appropriate only in the case of the Supreme Self... [the phrase] "sitting silently" (joṣamāsīna) means this. These intended qualities are appropriate only in the Supreme Self. || 2 ||

"And because the intended qualities are appropriate. "Intendedness" (*vivakṣitatva*) means being the object of the desire to speak; that is, being the object of speech occurring immediately thereafter—this is why it was said, "those which are about to be mentioned. He explains the term *manomaya* in accordance with the general and specific statements, using the words "by the purified," etc. By the word "one," he intends an exclusive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), as in the case of "one who subsists on water. He clarifies this with the word "discrimination" (*viveka*). He states the result [of this] with the words "by this," etc. To the question "Why?", he says "because it is impure," etc.

The non-cessation of the pervader follows from the cessation of the pervaded. To the question, "How is the establishment of being the locus (*ādheyatva*) and so forth [known]? he says: "Being the locus," etc. *Bhā* means radiance; that which has this as its attribute is *bhārūpa*. He states that this possession of the attribute is by way of its form (*vigraha*), saying "luminous" (*bhāsvara*). With the intention of recognizing what was stated in the passage, "In space alone is that woven warp and woof," he says "all else," etc. "He illumines"—the meaning is "for himself. "Or all," etc.; the meaning is "to be worshipped by all actions."

Intending that a prohibition has as its object that which is distinct from what is enjoined, he says "therefore" (*tataḥ*). Regarding the question "from where?", the meaning is that he states it here. For this very reason—the sense being that it is not due to a lack of capacity in speech—he explains that [point] with the words "perfectly complete" (*paripūrṇāḥ*). He concludes with "these, then" (*ta ete*). || 2 ||
But because of the impossibility [of its origination], it is not the embodied soul. (1.2.3)
When this ocean of qualities is thoroughly reflected upon... the meaning is that in this context, no sense of identification with the body arises. || 3 ||

He states the impossibility [of the soul being the agent] even in the case of one who is liberated by way of negative concomitance: "But because it is not possible, it is not the embodied soul. The word "worthy" (yogya) is used for the purpose of showing that [the agency] is impossible even in the case of the liberated one; the mention of the bound state is by way of illustration. || 3 ||
And because of the designation of [the Self] as both the object and the agent of action. (1.2.4)

"Having departed from here, I shall become that... and "The supreme Brahman is to be attained and meditated upon"—from these [statements], it is understood that this [Brahman] is indeed other than the attainer. || 4 ||

"And because of the designation of the object and the agent. This [sūtra] is intended to establish their distinction; the difference between the object to be attained and the attainer is stated in the sūtra. To the question, "What follows from that? [Does this mean] a difference of the object of meditation mentioned in 'All this indeed,' etc., from the individual soul (jīva)? he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ). ||4||
Because of the distinction in the word. (1.2.5)
"This is my Self within the heart... the golden person"—thus it is to be meditated upon as the primary object; thereafter, it is to be meditated upon as the transcendent. || 5 ||

He states the reason for the supreme goal: "Because of the distinction of the word. This refers to the use of different case endings intended in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā within the section on the same [meditation]. || 5 ||
For this reason also, [the Self] is other than the embodied one—on account of Smṛti as well (Sūtra 1.2.6).
"And I am seated within the heart of all... [the scripture] Smṛti shows that the Supreme Self is the object of worship. (6)
And because of Smṛti: Smṛti has been shown regarding the two residing in the heart and the distinction between the worshippers. || 6 ||

"If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the object of meditation] because of its having a small abode and because of being designated as such, we say no; for it is to be perceived as such, and it is like the ether. 1.2.7.
"Having a small extent" means having a small abode. ... Therefore, for the purpose of meditation, [the text mentions] having a small abode and being minute. || 7 ||

"If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the Supreme Lord] because of its having a small abode and because of the designation of such [smallness], we say: no, because He is to be perceived as such, and because [the smallness] is like that of space. The meaning is: because there is a statement implying smallness, and because that [smallness] is explicitly stated. He states the difference of the Supreme [Self] from that [smallness] with the words "But rather... He asks why it is not the opposite, and answers with "For thus... The phrase beginning with "Now then" (atha khalu) is stated to avoid breaking the context. Regarding the essential qualities (svarūpaguṇān), that is, the qualities not mediated by limiting adjuncts: since all-pervasiveness is mentioned both before and after, the smallness mentioned in between is merely adventitious (aupādhika).
If it is argued that [the individual soul] attains enjoyment [of the world], we say no, because of the difference [between the two]. 1.2.8.
Just as with the individual soul, so it is with the Supreme as well... "Of these two, one eats the sweet pippala fruit; the other looks on without eating. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.6) || 8 ||

If it be argued that [the soul] attains enjoyment [in the heart], we say no, because of its distinctness. "Existing within the body" means residing in the heart. "Distinctness" (vaiśeṣya) means difference (viśeṣa). || 8 ||
Thus concludes the section on the universal establishment [of Brahman as the Self].
If the Supreme Self were not the enjoyer, then... "The Eater [is the Self], because of the inclusion of both the moving and the unmoving. (1.2.9)
In the Kaṭhavallīs it is recited: "For whom both Brahman and... [and so forth]; the nature of being the withdrawer of the universe belongs to the Supreme Self alone. || 9 ||

He states the intermediate connection with the words "yadi" (if). [The Self is the eater] because of the mention of the moving and the unmoving. Since the word "eater" is not explicitly heard, it is said to be "indicated. In the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), he states two reasons for its being of the nature of the destruction of the moving and the unmoving, beginning with "so 'dhvanaḥ" (he [is the end] of the path). The intention is that the words "brahman" and "kṣatriya" are intended to illustrate the entirety of the moving and the unmoving. To the question, "How is the state of having death as a condiment (*upasecanatva*) equivalent to being the food of the moving and the unmoving? he replies: "For a condiment... (9).
And because of the context. (Sūtra 1.2.10)
And this context concerns the Supreme Brahman alone; for, apart from His grace, its inherent difficulty of comprehension is recognized as having been previously introduced. || 10 ||
And because of the context. To explain what is stated in this context, he says: "Who indeed... (Ka itthā).

Now, it might be argued: "This [eater] is not indicated by the rice of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas... To this, he states the objection regarding what follows: "Now, it might be argued" (*atha syāt*). The sense is that there is no interruption of what is immediately contiguous. Here, it is stated that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of drinking the *ṛta* is stronger than the context (*prakaraṇa*).

To the question, "How can there be the state of being a consumer for the first [principle], or how can the second possess either intellect (*buddhi*) or vital breath (*prāṇa*)," he says: "For [it is] eating... The intention is that, like the previously mentioned state of being an eater, its being the destroyer of the world cannot be asserted [of the second principle]. Regarding the phrase "just as": the meaning is that the instrument is metaphorically designated as the agent. To the question, "What follows from that regarding the state of being a consumer for the first? he says: "That alone..."
To this it is replied: "The two selves have entered the cave, for that is seen [in scripture]. (1.2.11)

Neither the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), nor the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul, have entered the cave; or rather, the agency in drinking is possible for the individual soul and the Supreme Self in the form of the instigated and the instigator. 11.

"Because of the perception of that [Brahman], both selves have indeed entered the cave. This means that the entry into the cave is seen even for the *jīva*. He states that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) which would interrupt the context is not established: "And thus," etc. He provides an alternative interpretation as the primary option: "Or rather," etc. Even the causal agent possesses agency. || 11 ||
And because of the qualification. (1.2.12)

In this context, it is the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) alone who are designated as "shadow and light," being distinguished by their respective states of ignorance and omniscience.
And because of the qualification; the ellipsis is "we are able to worship. The sense is that this is also because it has the same meaning as the passage cited here.

Now, it might be argued that since [the text] taught this doubt regarding a person after death... and also instructed on the specific details required for that [knowledge], everything is consistent; therefore, it is established that the Supreme Self alone is the Eater. ||12||

Although the objection and its resolution will be stated in the fourth chapter (*pāda*), they are mentioned here for the sake of easy comprehension, because the objection is present in the mind [of the student]. Now, as for the phrase "it might be so": he says "for thus" (*tathā hi*) to address the question of what the two boons are and how their acceptance is appropriate. Regarding the word "here" (*atra*): the meaning is that the question is asked with the desire to know that which is connected to liberation, namely, knowledge. Regarding the phrase "its means" (*tadupāya*): from the manner of the reply, it is understood that the means and other factors have been inquired about. By the term "without remainder" (*nirleśa*), the purpose of purifying the cause and so forth has been stated. "Specifics" (*viśeṣān*) refers to the *praṇava*, the fire-vidyā, and others. || 12 ||
Thus ends the section on the eater (attradhikaraṇa). || 2 ||
[The intermediate state exists] before rebirth. 1-2-13.
The Chandogas recite this: "This person who is seen in the eye... for he indeed shines in all worlds. This is because these qualities are logically possible only in the Supreme Self. || 13 ||

Because of the intermediate birth; because of the statement regarding its being difficult to perceive in the words "Who, indeed, knows that which is so difficult to see," there is a connection [of the text] with the doubt that "he who is seen here" is not the Supreme, though this is established by the sense and not explicitly stated. The expression "he who is this" refers to something well-known. The word "is seen" expresses immediate perception (*aparokṣatva*), [referring respectively] to reflections and so forth, which are immediate, conceptual, and those well-known from scripture.
"In the final conclusion, 'of these'—the meaning is 'of those that are without limiting adjuncts' (nirupādhikānām). || 13 ||
And because of the designation of "place" and so forth. (1.2.14)
The stabilization, control, and so forth [of the vital breath] in the eye and other locations are possible because they are perceived by yogis. || 14 ||

"And because of the designation of place and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), [qualities such as] being the sustainer and being the object of knowledge are meant. He states the sublation of the two arguments for the prima facie view—which were established by the statement of the proving reasons—with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 14 ||
And because [the Self] is designated as being distinguished by bliss. (1.2.15)
Furthermore, because the Supreme Person is the substratum of the eye... since it is the very Brahman under discussion that is denoted here, this substratum of the eye is the Supreme Self. 15.

And because of the very mention of [the fruit] as being distinguished by happiness; regarding the statement "there is a contradiction with being a subordinate member (*aṅga*) and so forth," he says: "Nor... In order to dispel the doubt that there might be no contradiction with the fruit of the principal (*aṅgin*), he says: "...contradictory to that. "It is said," and so forth. "In both cases"—that is, in the opening and the conclusion. By means of four reasons, the relationship of principal and subordinate has been stated.

Having encountered an opposition to the fruit [of the teaching] through such statements as "Brahman is the vital breath" (*prāṇo brahma*), he says: "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). And he says "no" (*na ca*) to that [objection]. The intention is that [the word] "we protect" (*paripālayāmaḥ*) implies the *parasmaipada* (active voice) of the root *bhuj*. [Objection: "But surely... Since the place (*sthāna*) and the quality (*guṇa*) will be explained later, those two are not things to be enjoined; therefore, the Supreme Self is not mentioned here for the purpose of enjoining them. This is the meaning of the phrase "not for that purpose" (*anaya-param*). He refutes this with: "That is said... (*tadabhi*). This is clear. || 15 ||
But is it not so—that [the term *kham* here] is the same as in such scriptural statements as "Brahman is Ka," "Brahman is Kha," and "Brahman is Manas"?

He raises a doubt regarding the immediately preceding sūtra with the words "nanu ca" (but surely). The sense of "yāvatā" is "on the contrary. Regarding the phrase "vacanasārūpyāt" (due to the similarity of the expression): because the word *brahman* is mentioned later [in the sequence], the meaning is that one should perceive the specific object as *brahman*. The underlying intention is that there is no concluding statement (*nigamana*) using the word *brahman*.
Regarding this, he says: "And for this very reason, it is Brahman. (1.2.16)
Since that which is "ka" there is the very same as "kha," and that same thing is designated here as the support of the eye, the Supreme Self is the support of the eye. || 16 ||

And for this very reason, that [ether] is Brahman. The masculine gender in "saḥ" (he/that) follows the concluding statement (*nigamana-vākya*). The phrase "yadeva kam" is an adoption of the meaning, not an adoption of the sentence; whereas "yadvāvakam" is the actual sentence. Here too, there would be an injunction for mutual meditation (*anyonya-dṛṣṭi-vihiti*). To the question, "How can that which is denoted by the word 'kha' (ether/space) be Brahman?", he says: "This has been stated. And to the doubt, "How is there the discrepancy between being known and being unknown, and how is the ether characterized by bliss?", he says "Of this, this... in order to explain that.

Since it is impossible to distinguish between what is known and what is unknown if the intent were merely a figurative meditation (*dṛṣṭividhi*), and since the instruction is given for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), and because it is illogical for another figurative meditation to follow as a subsequent response regarding the ignorance of something other [than the truth], the mutual exclusion being established, he states the meaning of the sentence: "Of Brahman. Therefore—the meaning is that, because it cannot be a figurative meditation, the concluding sentence is in accordance with the introductory statement concerning Brahman, whose nature is infinite bliss.

He states the removal of that very doubt by which the Sūtra was introduced, with the words "Therefore, what... He connects the meaning of the Sūtra with the primary subject matter under discussion, saying "And that very same... (16).
And because the path of one who has heard the Upaniṣads is described [in the scripture]. 1.2.17.
"Of one who has heard the Upaniṣads"—that is, of one who has realized the true nature of the Supreme Person... for this reason also, this Person in the eye is the Supreme Self. || 17 ||
And because of the designation "one who has heard the Upaniṣads. The specific mention of "one who has heard the Upaniṣads" is for the sake of explanation. || 17 ||
And because of instability and impossibility, it is not the other. (1.2.18)
Because reflections and the like do not necessarily abide in the eye, therefore the person in the eye is the Supreme Self. || 18 ||

"Because of non-abiding and impossibility, it is not the other. By these two words, the exclusion of the meaning of the first two sūtras is shown according to the sequence established in the intellect. The word "pratiṣṭhita" (established), like the phrase "one who is devoted to knowledge" (*vidyāniṣṭa*), has the intention of signifying mere mastery (*vaśīkāra*). The meaning is that the connection with the eye is possible through an intermediate medium, just as one sleeps in a palace by means of a couch. He concludes the meaning of the section with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). || 18 ||
Thus concludes the section on the "Intermediate" (antarādhikaraṇa) — 3.
Having established the nature of the Supreme Self in the section beginning with "And because of the designation as 'His own' and so forth," he now further supports that very point.
He states the intermediate connection with the words: "In the case of the locus," etc.:
"On account of the designation of its attributes in the cases of the internal ruler (antaryāmin), the divine (adhidaiva), the worldly (adhiloka), and so forth" (Sūtra 1.2.19).
And because the Kaṇvas, the Mādhyandinas, and the Vājasaneyins [teach this], and because of the negation of another seer in the passage, "There is no other seer than He."

[The Lord is the Inner Controller] because His attributes are designated in relation to the internal, the divine, the worlds, and so forth. He clarifies the subject matter with the words beginning "the Kāṇvas," etc. The terms "Veda" and "sacrifice" refer to the presiding deities. To the question, "How can there be a suspicion that the Inner Controller is a living soul (jīva) when He is the controller of all sentient and insentient beings? he states the argument of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "the remainder of the passage. To the question, "What follows from that regarding the Inner Controller's status as a living soul? he says, "Thus, of the seer. To the question, "What then? Does it mean the direct perception of form and so forth? he says, "none other."

The meaning is that it is not elsewhere that [the functions] are to be negated, because they are possible in living beings; rather, it is elsewhere [than in the Supreme Self] that they are to be negated as being dependent on instruments, since they are incompatible with the Supreme. And by the repetition of the word "yat" (which), plurality is indicated. The word "sa" (he) refers to the genus, while "yaḥ" (who) refers to the individual instance. The intention is that the functions such as abiding and so forth should be understood according to their natural sense in relation to the Self.

This being the position reached, it is stated in reply: The Inner Controller (antaryāmī), who is taught as the Self of the individual soul (jīva) with respect to the internal, the divine, the worlds, and so forth, cannot be the inner self (pratyagātman). || 19 ||

"In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), [the terms] are marked by their respective words. The sense is that they do not have [independent] meaning as their primary purport, because it would result in the fault of redundancy with the word *adhi*. He states the purpose of mentioning the two words: "The Kāṇva [recension]," etc. To the question, "Let there be an answer to that; what follows from it?", he says: "This very [fact]," etc. Since [the meaning] is impossible in anything else, he cites other scriptural passages: "For thus," etc. He cites a passage from the same context: "And thus," etc. Regarding the objection that "the eye does not see" is contradictory, he says: "And not in the case of seeing," etc.

He states the underlying reason (*anugatanimitta*) with the words "but rather" (*api tu*). Even though [the organs] are not mentioned by name, they are dependent on a controller due to the force of pervasion; to this he says "and that" (*sa ca*), meaning that [dependence] is conditioned by an adventitious attribute (*sopādhika*). He counters the reasoning stated by the opponent with the words "none other than Him" (*nānyo'taḥ*). He explains what was said with the words "whom the earth... (*yaṃ p�ṛthivī...*). Regarding the phrase "another seer" (*anyaḥ draṣṭā*): by the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word "other" (*anya*), another seer possessing the aforementioned characteristics is negated; thus, the meaning is the negation of another seer in the form of a controller.

He states—"This [is] yours"—intending that even the mention of a case-ending expressing distinction (vyatireka-vibhakti) is intended here as a reason for the aforementioned difference, on account of the specific word used. || 19 ||
And [the self] is not the one mentioned in the Smṛti, because its attributes are not predicated [of it], and because of the mention of the body. 1.2.10.
The Smārta [view] holds that the Pradhāna is the primary cause... and its absence in the inner self (pratyagātman) has been demonstrated by two Sūtras. || 20 ||

And [the soul] is not that which belongs to the Smṛti, because its characteristics are not mentioned; nor is it the embodied [self], because [the Smṛti] is irrelevant. To the question "For what purpose is this rejection of the Smṛti's [view] introduced?", he says: "This has been stated. He says "of these" to show that there is no tautology between the two sūtras. || 20 ||
And he states another reason for its independence: "For both [schools] indeed study this [text] separately. (1.2.12)
Both [schools], the Mādhyandinas and the Kāṇvas, establish that the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, who is distinct from the individual self (pratyagātman) and free from all evil, is thus proven. || 21 ||

For both [schools] indeed study this [Self] as distinct; the meaning is that the distinction is established by the statement of a distinguishing attribute, namely "by way of being the object of meditation. Since there is no exception [to this], the natural consistency of the negative designation and so forth is established. || 21 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin). 4.
[The Being] characterized by qualities such as invisibility is Brahman, because of the mention of its attributes (1.2.22).
The followers of the Atharvaveda study [this]; therefore, here the word "akṣara" denotes the insentient subtle element of matter (bhūtasūkṣma). || 22 ||

The one possessing qualities such as invisibility [is Brahman] because of the statement of its attributes. The masculine gender indicates that the intended subject of the Sūtra is that which is "higher than the high Imperishable" (akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ). The connection [of this Sūtra with the previous topic] is indicated by the fact that [the attributes] are like those in passages such as "the unseen seer" (adṛṣṭo draṣṭā). For here, invisibility is not associated with being a controller—as it is in the case of the "seer"—which might lead to the suspicion that the reference is to Pradhāna; rather, the sense is that grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is naturally established through the similarity of the case endings in the phrase "higher than the high Imperishable."

Invisibility is a common attribute, and the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is consistent with [the view that the subject] refers to a conscious being; to this he says, "This has been stated. The sense is that when an internal factor is present, an external factor should not be accepted. He states the consistency with the illustrative example: "presided over by that" (tadadhiṣṭhitam).

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), he says "tathā hi" [to address the point] that this sentence would have the aforementioned subject matter. Regarding the claim that "the Imperishable (*akṣara*) is not the Supreme Self because of the hearing of its being 'higher' (*para*)," he says "paścāt. The sense is that there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) due to the natural force of the expectation for the fifth case (*pañcamī*) and the natural force of the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). He states the reason for the contradiction in meaning with the words "tasya. For that of which the connection with the attribute "higher" is heard is indeed the Supreme (*para*).

Therefore, the sense is that it is appropriate for these two instances of the word "Brahman" situated in the context of the "Supreme" to have different referents, just as in the case of the two words "Brahman" in the section concerning the Supreme. || 22 ||
For this reason as well, [the Self] is neither Pradhāna nor Puruṣa; and because of the designation of distinctions and differences, it is neither of the other two. (Sūtra 1.2.13)

It distinguishes [the Self]... or, because there is an absence of any emission capable of being designated by another name—just as in the case of the "Great One" (mahat) and so forth—the state of being the Imperishable (akṣaratva) is somehow established. || 13 ||

"And because of the distinction and the designation of difference, those two are different from each other. To the question "In what way does [the scripture] distinguish [the Self] by means of its attributes?", he says: "From the Pradhāna. He explains the designation of difference with the words: "Likewise. To establish both points, he says: "For thus... He also states that the status of being the Supreme Object is established even by the words expressing the qualifying attributes: "And only the knowledge of the Supreme..."

Because the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) Brahman includes all other objects of knowledge within itself, and because the knower (*veditṛ*) of that [Brahman] includes all other knowers within himself, it is said that [these two] are the foundation of all knowledge. To eliminate the notion that the two knowledges have different objects, he explains: "by one desiring to attain Brahman. The expression "the two knowledges are to be known" is used in the same sense as "he performed austerity" (*tapo 'tapyata*) or "he cooks the rice-porridge" (*odanapākaṃ pacati*). To the question, "If the object is the same, what is the difference [between the two]? he says: "and the higher. To provide the reason for the difference in the causal apparatus (*sāmagrī*) in those cases, he says: "therein..."

To the objection that the first [means] alone is sufficient, he says: "Of those two. To the objection that the other [means] are useless because they are mentioned in scripture, he says: "And that. To the question "What is the use of the first?", he says: "The means for that. [The phrase] "supported by the sevenfold means" means accompanied by the sevenfold means. In order to clarify what has been stated, he says: "And it is said. He refers to the passage beginning with "the supreme [knowledge] arising from scripture therein," etc., when he says: "In that regard. To the objection that this is not perceived as arising from scripture through the treatises on Dharma and so forth, he says: "Of that which possesses its auxiliary limbs."
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that "then" (*atha*) means "it has been said. He explains the sentence beginning with "by austerity" (*tapasā*) by [the words] "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*).

The meaning of the word *satya* has been stated as "the class of enjoyers. To dispel the suspicion of tautology, he says: "He who is omniscient. The intention is that this is like [the injunction] "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*). Regarding "the enjoyed and the enjoyer," the intention is that the etymology of "food" (*anna*) is "that which is eaten and which eats. Regarding "in the mantras," etc., he says "omniscience" in order to exclude the sense of being intent upon the world of the four-faced Brahmā; the intention is that this is because of its consistency with the preceding passage beginning with "this is the truth" (*tad etat satyam*). [This refers to] those persons in whom...

He explains the second of the two reasons from the Sūtra with the words: "Even the designation of difference. The term *aśnute* (it pervades) is intended in the sense of the rule regarding the *prokṣaṇī* waters. || 23 ||
And because of the presentation of form. (1.2.24)
"Agni is the head, the eyes... [and so forth]. All this originates from the Supreme Self alone, who is the inner self of all beings; therefore, it is the Supreme Self. || 24 ||
And because of the presentation of form; this is for the sake of clarity. He concludes the meaning of the section with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 24 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the one possessing qualities such as invisibility (Adṛśyatvādiguṇaka-adhikaraṇa). 5.
Vaiśvānara [is the Self], because of the distinction of common terms. 1.2.25.

The Chāndogas recite this: "This very Self, Vaiśvānara... [etc.]. This [passage] makes known that the fruit of the knowledge of the Vaiśvānara-Self is the realization that the Vaiśvānara-Self is the Supreme Brahman. || 25 ||

Vaiśvānara [is the Supreme Self] because of the specific nature of the common term. The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt that the form presented might be seen as belonging to someone other than the Supreme. Since the term is common to both, the doubt is raised as to whether its determination is possible or not. "The banner of the days" refers to the sun. Regarding how the terms *ātman* and *brahman* [are used here], he says: "In the sentence."

In the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), [the word] "is qualified" (*viśeṣyate*) does not mean that the meaning of the genitive case contained within the compound is the meaning of the suffix *ghañ*. Rather, the meaning is that it is the genitive used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The inclusion of the word "qualified" (*viśeṣya*) is intended to indicate that when a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix is joined [with another], the genitive has as its cause the sense of the object. Alternatively, "is qualified" is a statement regarding the meaning of the suffix *ghañ*. Furthermore, the compounds are *karmadhārayas*. The sense is that they function as the result because they are being qualified; this is not the literal (grammatical) meaning. To the question "What, then, are the properties (*dharmas*)?", he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
Or, there are two *kiṃ* words because of the desire to know whether the dharma is one or many, or because of the intention to qualify the two terms [dharma and adharma]. (25)
For this reason as well, Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Self: "That which is remembered [in the Smṛti] would be an inference. (1.2.26)
From heaven down to the earth, through the analysis of its constituent parts, [it is seen that] this is indeed the form of the Supreme Person; thus, Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Person alone. || 26 ||

"It would be an inference based on what is being remembered. [Objection: Since this is due to hearing a word expressing a mark (*liṅga*), the word ["iti"] is redundant; to this he says: "The word 'iti'. As for why the instruction regarding the head and so forth was not given collectively, he says: "For thus... Because it is the embodiment of the universe and because it is its illuminator, the sun is "Viśvarūpa" (the Universal Form). The rest is clear. || 26 ||

Again, anticipating the doubt that there is still no definitive conclusion, he provides a rebuttal: "If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the subject of the passage] because of [its association with] sound and so forth, and because of its being established within, we say: No; for it is taught as being seen thus, because [those qualities] are impossible [in the case of the individual soul], and they also read this very one as the Puruṣa. (1.2.27)

"Because of the words [of the Veda] and because of their being established within," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the establishment of the three sacrificial fires and the state of being the locus for the oblation of the vital breaths are included, as these are closely proximate due to being situated within this very scripture. The phrase "of the Vājasaneyins" is used because they are distant; the sense is that they are mentioned explicitly. He concludes the point under discussion by means of the sequence of the stated reasons with the word "therefore."

"Not so," and so forth. The meaning is that because of the hearing of both the marks of the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) and the marks of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the text is intent upon a qualified meditation (*viśiṣṭopāsti*). To the question, "How is there a presentation of a qualified [object]," he replies—given that such a presentation is established, the text is indeed intent upon qualified meditation—"by means of the word 'fire' and so on. Furthermore, the idea is that the word *puruṣa* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth by virtue of the context and other factors, but not by its own inherent power. || 27 ||
For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor an elemental being. (1.2.28)
Precisely because of what has been stated, there is no possibility of even the great elements (mahābhūta) being [the object of] Vaiśvānara. || 28 ||

For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor a living being. The sense is that even though, like the gastric fire, it lacks spatial limitation, the reasons for applying terms such as "Self" (ātman) and "Brahman"—namely, being the cause of all—do not hold true [for these other entities]. || 28 ||
Jaimini [maintains] that there is no contradiction even with direct perception. 1.2.29.
The word "Agni," which is used in grammatical apposition with Vaiśvānara, denotes the Supreme Self alone, as it is qualified by attributes that are unique to the Supreme Self. || 29 ||

"Jaimini [maintains] there is no contradiction even in the direct [sense]. The word "directly" (sākṣāt) is to be explained as "without mediation" (avyavadhānena). To the question of by what quality the word Vaiśvānara is applied, and by what quality the word Agni is applied in that same manner, he says: "This has been stated. (29)
"But he who [meditates on] this very one as measured by a span, as the all-pervading... [is so because it is] due to manifestation; thus says Āśmarathya. (1.2.30)
For the purpose of manifesting [himself as] a lay follower (upāsaka)... it occurs precisely because of the manifestation of one who is free from pride. || 30 ||
He states the concern regarding the subsequent sūtra: "But he who... etc.

"Because of manifestation," says Āśmarathya. Here, the doubt that the limited size [of Brahman] might belong to either the third element (fire) or the third deity is refuted. By the words "the heaven and so forth," terms such as "measured by a span" (*prādeśamātra*) and others are explained. (30) He states the doubt concerning what follows: "The head and so forth. The human-like form [of Brahman] is due to specific parts beginning with the head... because of remembrance; thus says Bādari. (1.2.31)
"Likewise, for the sake of worship," says the teacher Bādari... [but] because it is to be abandoned by those seeking liberation (mumukṣu), it is not accepted here. || 31 ||
Bādari [holds that] it is for the sake of recollection; the anthropomorphic form is for the purpose of meditation, and that [meditation] is for the purpose of liberation—this is the meaning. || 31 ||
If Vaiśvānara is indeed the supreme Self, how then [is it so]? "On account of meditation [on the Self], Jaimini [says this is] so; for thus he shows. (1.2.32)
"Of this very Vaiśvānara, the Supreme Self... thus indeed all his evils are burnt away. (32)

"Jaimini [holds that it is] attainment, for thus he shows. "Attainment" (*saṃpatti*) means the attribution of something to what it is not. He explains the portion of the sūtra beginning with "thus" (*tathā*) as follows: "for thus" (*tathā hi*). The meaning is that [the scripture] shows the very result of the performance of the *agnihotra*—its being for the purpose of propitiating the Supreme Self. || 32 ||
And they record this [Self] in this [body]. (1.2.33)

This Supreme Person, characterized by qualities such as being the support of the heavens and so forth... therefore, it is established that the Supreme Self, the Puruṣottama alone, is Vaiśvānara. || 33 ||
Thus concludes the section on Vaiśvānara—6.
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.

The subsequent sūtra is intended to address the doubt that the heaven and so forth cannot be the body of another [the Self], because it is stated that the limbs of the meditator are the heaven and so forth.

And they enjoin this in this [context]. Explaining the word *enam* (this), which is implied therein, he clarifies what was stated: "This is the meaning. This is clear. Regarding the phrase "and the result": the sense is that when something without a fruit is in proximity to something with a fruit, it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that. For the sake of ease of understanding, he states the previously mentioned point—which is consistent with the meaning of this sūtra—by saying "thus" (*evam*). "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 33 ||
Thus ends the section on Vaiśvānara (6).

Thus concludes the second quarter of the first chapter in the *Śrutapradīpikā*, composed by Śrī Sudarśana Sūri—the ornament of the Harita lineage, son of Vāgvijayin, who acquired the secondary name Vedavyāsa by the divine command of Śrī Raṅgarāja, and who grasped the heart of the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śrī Bhagavadrāmānuja through service at the feet of the venerable Varadācārya.
The third quarter of the first chapter.
The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word. (1.3.1)

The followers of the Atharva Veda recite: "In whom heaven... ... And the status of being the substratum for the instruments of the individual soul, beginning with the mind, is logically possible only for the Supreme Being who is the substratum of all. || 1 ||

"The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman] because of the word 'dog' (śva). The connection with the preceding section has been stated previously. The internal connection arises from the doubt that the quality of being the support of heaven, earth, and so forth might be seen in something other than the Supreme. This topic was not examined in the *Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa* because it contains clear marks of the individual soul (*jīva*). "The followers of the Atharvaṇa," and so forth, is clear. The sense is that the state of being a supporter occurs either by way of its own nature or by way of its action (*karman*).

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), it is said: "the word 'self' (*ātman*). The intention is that since there is no usage [of this term] with respect to space, the directions, and so forth, it is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*). By the words "in many ways" and so forth, the disparity between cause and effect regarding birth has been stated. He says "Smṛti also... in order to clarify this. || 1 ||
For this reason also, the Supreme Person [is the cause]: "And because He is designated as that which is to be approached by the liberated. (1.3.2)
This person who has become the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth... it is taught that this person who has become the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is indeed the Supreme Brahman. || 2 ||

"And because of the designation of that which is to be approached by the liberated. To address the doubt that the word "liberated" (mukta) does not appear in the scriptural passage, he explains: "in saṃsāra. The state of having shaken off merit and demerit is mentioned to exclude the dissolution at the end of a cosmic cycle (pralaya). The explanation of the term "unblemished" (nirañjana) is: "by those who are free from contact with primordial matter" (prakṛti). || 2 ||

By means of words and other indicators that are unique to the Supreme Brahman, [the text] refers to the Supreme Brahman itself... [This is established by the Sūtra: "But it is the Supreme [Brahman], because of the inference from those words and because of the denial of the individual soul. (1.3.3)

Just as in this section, because there is an absence of a word expressing a primary subject (pradhāna), the compound is an avyayībhāva according to the rule "that which is indeclinable when there is an absence of meaning" (Pāṇini 2.4.83). || 3 ||

"Thus" refers to the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that has been stated; the meaning is that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) will now be explained. [The rule] "there is no inference from that word" applies to living beings as well. The inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) is for the purpose of [the rule] "that which is indeclinable when there is an absence of meaning," and not for the purpose of including the [specific] aphorism (*sūtra*). || 3 ||
For this reason as well, this [Self] is not the inner Self (pratyagātman): because of the designation of difference. (1.3.4)
When a person, immersed in the same tree... then he becomes free from sorrow. || 4 ||
On account of the context. (1.3.5)
And this is the context of the supreme Brahman... we have here merely dispelled the suspicion that there might be a break in the context. || 5 ||
Because of the context. To the question, "In that case, what is the purpose of this section? he says: "The channels," etc. (5).
And on account of abiding and eating. (1.3.6)
"The two birds, united and friends... From this, it is established that the Supreme Self is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth. || 6 ||

"And by reason of abiding and eating. Because it is more venerable or because it is fewer in number, "abiding" (sthiti) is placed first in the Sūtra; however, in the Commentary, it is explained according to the order stated in the Śruti. He concludes the meaning of the section with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 6 ||
Thus ends the section concerning Dyubhvādi (the Heaven, Earth, etc.). 1.
Bhūman [is Brahman], because it is taught as being superior to the state of perfect serenity (saṃprasāda). 1.3.7.
The Chāndogyas recite this: "Where one sees nothing else... Since the inner self (pratyagātman) has thus been determined, the remainder of the passage must be interpreted in accordance with that.

[The word] *bhūta* [is used] because of the instruction regarding the supreme serene being (*saṃprasāda*). It has been stated that [the passage] refers to the Supreme because there is no interruption in the context of the Supreme. In that case, the connection [of the present section] arises from the doubt: "Since there is no interruption in the context of the individual soul (*jīva*), does this not refer to the individual soul? It is recited [in the sūtra], but it is not a member of the *ākṛtigaṇa* class. Regarding the word *bahoḥ*: it means that the word *bahu* undergoes the substitution of the word *bhū*, and there is the elision of the vowel at the beginning of the suffix. Regarding the word *atra*: the meaning is that because [the word] "that is small" (*tadalpam*) functions as a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) with respect to the quality of smallness, it does not have the property of referring merely to the quality of number.

Since the word *bahu* is seen to apply commonly to both number (*saṃkhyā*) and magnitude (*vaipulya*) in such passages as "There are many persons, O King," whether few or many, this determination of its meaning is now made: the determination that *bhūman* is the subject (*dharmin*) occurs through its being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the subject, accompanied by the non-mention of another thing possessing that same attribute. [An objection is raised: "Censure and its absence would be based on being possessed of breath (*saprāṇatva*) or being devoid of breath (*niṣprāṇatva*), and not caused by being living (*sajīvatva*) or being lifeless (*ajīvatva*). To this he replies: "In the case of those without breath" (*aprāṇeṣu*).

The meaning is that the state of being subject to injury distinguishes [the Self] from both "another" (para) and from the fivefold-functioning vital breath (prāṇa). To the question, "Let the individual soul (jīva) be what is denoted by the word 'prāṇa'; how then can it possess the quality of plenitude (bhūmatva)? he replies: "And this very one... and so forth.

Having raised the doubt that the word "but" (*tu*) indicates a different context (*prakaraṇāntaratva*), he says: "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*). The intention is that this is like the statement, "But indeed, he is an Agnihotrin who speaks the truth. When it was said, "When I know," a person possessing knowledge produced by the scripture concerning the individual soul (*jīva*) was mentioned. To the question, "Since sorrowfulness was established for the soul at the beginning [of the section], how can there be such vast happiness?", he says: "Being free from ignorance" (*avidyāviyuktam*). To the question, "How is it possible for him to abide in his own greatness (*mahiman*) and so forth?", he says: "In accordance with that" (*tadanuguṇatayā*).

This being the case, it is replied: "The Bhūman [is Brahman], because of the instruction regarding abundance... it is understood that the Self under discussion is other than that which is indicated by the word 'prāṇa'."

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), he says "of that which is denoted by the word 'Truth'" because the word *bhūman* is not heard in the text as something distinct from the word *prāṇa*. The meaning is that "Truth" is the *bhūman*, due to the non-interruption of the context. To the question, "Let Truth be the *bhūman*; what of it? How does that establish its being the Supreme Self? he says "Truth."

Regarding the statement "he speaks beyond," although this may be an instruction on the superiority of the Truth (satya), the identity [of Brahman] with the vital breath (prāṇa) is not heard as being its counter-correlative; furthermore, since—as in the passage "the Truth and the Infinite" (satyam cānantam ca)—it is possible for the individual soul (jīva) also to be denoted by the word "Truth," the fact that the Truth is something other than the soul is not established. To this, he says: "This has been stated."

Although Prāṇa is not explicitly heard as the correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the "excess" (*ādhikya*) of Truth, nevertheless, when an excess requires a correlate, Prāṇa—being the most proximate [to Truth] like Name and the others—is fit to be that correlate. Thus, the meaning is established: the Supreme Brahman, which possesses an excess over that [Prāṇa] and is indicated by the word "Truth" in such passages as "Truth, Knowledge," is distinct from it. To the question, "What follows from the fact that the 'Full' (*bhūman*) is the Supreme Self? he says: "The word 'Truth'... [and so on].

It was stated that there is a difference in meaning because of the teaching [of the latter] as something additional. Now, one raises the doubt: "How is it that the teaching itself is additional?"—this is expressed by the words "The word *praṇa*. He replies: "He, indeed... (sa vā). He sets aside [the objection] with the meaning "as something additional. The sense is that the subsequent section is intended to state what is additional to what was previously specified. [An objection is raised: "There is no perception of a different person who speaks beyond [the first], because of the recognition of the previous speaker. To this he says: "For this very reason" (*ata eva*). "For this reason" means: because of the natural force of the word *tu*. [The opponent asks: "What follows from that? To this he says: "Therefore, of this... (*ato'sya*).

He raises an objection with reference to the illustration of the *agnihotra*, saying "But surely" (*nanu*). He refutes it, saying "This is not so" (*naitat*). To state the dissimilarity between the illustrations, he indicates the perception of another subject (*dharmyantara*) by means of the word "but" (*tu*), saying "by the word 'but'. He states the dissimilarity: "But this... (*eṣa tu*). However, the natural force of the word "but" is undermined because there is no perception of a different substance or deity—which would be the cause for a different *agnihotra* based on it being a different *agnihotrin*.

The point here is that there is no violation of natural consistency (*svārasya-bhaṅga*), because the object of meditation is established by means of the distinctness of the excellence of "speaking beyond" (*ativāditva*) as the cause for the distinctness of the meditative act itself. However, if the word "Truth" (*satya*) were intended to refer to another object of meditation, the natural force of the word "but" (*tu*) would be lost; yet, since that [object] is established, it can indeed refer to another object of meditation. To this he says: "And the word 'Truth'... The meaning is that, due to its well-known usage in scripture and the capacity of the word "but," the aforementioned defect does not apply. Regarding the objection that the unique excellence of "speaking beyond" belonging to one who rests in *prāṇa* violates natural consistency, he says: "For the excellence of speaking beyond..."

The meaning is that this word is not conventional (*rūḍha*), but rather etymological (*yaugika*). "Only those who propound the Supreme Brahman" (*parabrahmavādina eva*)—the sense is that this is because the full significance of the word's components (*avayavārtha*) is present. The emphatic particle *eva* is intended to highlight the natural force (*svārasya*) of the words *tu* and *ati*. For this very reason—that is, precisely because the word *ativādin* is etymological—the intention is to request the student to provide an explanation of the verbal form (*ākhyātanirdeśa*). And as for the phrase "and the teacher"—the sense is that if [the student] were intent merely on speaking the truth, there would be a lack of natural force in the word *jijñāsitavya*. He states the teaching with a further distinction: "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*).

As it has been stated: in response to the question, "Is there, O Blessed One, anything greater than breath? [the answer is given] because Brahman, which is denoted by the word *satya*, is taught as the *bhūman*; therefore, the *bhūman* is the supreme Brahman.

And it has been said: "iti. The meaning is that there is the hearing of the word *tu* (but) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the soul's origination. [The question] "What is the basis for the absence of a question? is answered with "asti" (it exists). [It is] "that which serves as the means for the direct realization of Brahman. The meaning of the passage beginning with "When indeed one knows" is: "when one realizes [Brahman], then one speaks the supreme truth (*satyam ativadati*). The intention is that this refers to the context of "speaking the supreme truth" (*ativāda*).

The phrase "the nature of happiness is knowledge" is supplied by the force of the context, as it is experienced through the spontaneous words of the wise. In this sentence, there is a negation of other specific [qualities]. To the question, "How can there be a vision of the object of rule within the vision of the Ruler?", he says: "Therefore, sovereignty... The word *guṇa* (attribute) signifies that which does not exist separately. Regarding the statement "for happiness is a particular attribute of the Self," he says: "For that alone is happiness. There are two examples for the case where [happiness] takes the form of suffering due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and for the case where it is not favorable due to ignorance of its connection.

Other kings are "self-ruling" (svārāj) only in a relative sense; thus, the presence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and their subsequent removal have been demonstrated. He states that the one characterized by sovereignty and other attributes is of the nature of bliss—describing it as "unsurpassed" (niratiśaya). For it is heard in scripture: "He made himself his own Self; He is indeed Bliss. He concludes the meaning of the entire section with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 7 ||
And because it is consistent with the nature of Dharma. (1.3.8)
Since those attributes which are traditionally taught belong to this "Bhūman," it is established that the Supreme Self is distinguished by being the Bhūman. || 8 ||

And because of the attainment of the nature of *dharma*. By means of the "I-grasping" (*ahaṅgraha*)—that is, by the cognition that the referent of "I" (*aham-artha*) and the word "I" extend up to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). To the objection that, in that case, there would be the cognition of something as what it is not, he says: "of the referent of 'I'. The fact that the Supreme is the Self of all is established by the Supreme Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), Brahman, and others; he states that this is also understood in this very context by saying: "of the Supreme Self. The phrase ending with "Supreme Self" expresses the meaning; thereafter, the mention of "we" (*vayaḥ*) is for the sake of the suffix *-maya*. "This very [thing]" refers to this alone.
The word "vijānataḥ" means the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhyanta). He concludes the discussion regarding the locus with the words "tasmāt. || 8 ||
Thus ends the section on the "Fullness" (Bhūmā). 2.
[The Imperishable] is the Supreme, because it supports everything up to the ether. 1.3.9.

The Vājasaneyins record this in the dialogue with Gārgī: "He said, 'That indeed is the Imperishable... [That] which is the nature of the object as it is understood through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not need to be depended upon at the time of its presentation. || 9 ||

"Because the Imperishable (akṣara) supports that which has the sky as its limit. The connection [of this sūtra] arises from the doubt that the state of abiding in one's own greatness, which was described for the Infinite (bhūman), might also be seen elsewhere than in the Self. By the very words "neither short nor long," the possibility of it being a phoneme (varṇa) does not arise; therefore, that is not what is proposed as the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) here. Regarding the phrase "by another means of knowledge": the Vedic [cognition] is delayed compared to inference, because the Veda depends upon perception and inference—this is the sense.
The sense is that the Veda depends upon linguistic usage (vyutpatti), and linguistic usage depends upon perception and inference.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is clear. He refutes the reasoning of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "That is not so. The meaning is that there is no dependence on other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) for the comprehension [of Brahman] because it is expressed by the Word (*śabda*). To the question, "How can there be no dependence, given that [the Word] depends on linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) and so forth? he replies: "The relation... (verse 9).
If that is so, let the individual soul (jīva) be the one designated by the word "syllable" (akṣara); for it [the soul] is also [the ruler] because of its presiding over [the elements]. (1.3.10)
And this support of the sky's limit belongs to that Imperishable; therefore, the Supreme Person alone is the Imperishable as the Ruler. 10.

He raises a doubt regarding the immediately preceding sūtra with the words, "If that is so. And [the Lord is the ruler] because of His command; for since even the individual soul (jīva) possesses a slight degree of power to govern, he says "supreme" in order to exclude that possibility—the meaning being that His command is unimpeded. And because there is the exclusion of any other [possible ruler]. (1.3.11)

"Being otherwise" means being different, namely, having the nature of *pradhāna* and so forth. ... It is established that that through the knowledge of which there is the attainment of *saṃsāra*, and through the knowledge of which there is the attainment of immortality—that is indeed the Imperishable, the Supreme Brahman. || 11 ||

And because of the exclusion of other existences. "Not seen" means not seen by those who are supported by Him. It is seen by Him as their supporter. Since such a seer is the subject under discussion, there is nothing else that is unseen by the Supreme Self, who is the supporter, nor is there any other seer of this [Self] as its supporter—this is the meaning. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the absence of any other supporter or seer distinct from the conscious and the unconscious is intended.

In this interpretation, the explicit statement (*kaṇṭhokti*) regarding the exclusion of the sentient and the insentient is established; furthermore, there would be the intention of the sentence to express all the attributes that effect such an exclusion. In the other [interpretation], however, the exclusion is established by implication (*arthasiddha*); only the absence of any other sustainer or seer would be explicitly stated (*kaṇṭhokta*). The subject-sentence (*viṣayavākya*), "There is nothing else," would thus be followed by the words of the Sūtra. The portion ending with "excluding" (*vyāvartayan*) expresses the meaning of the Sūtra; what follows is the statement of the resultant meaning.
Intending that the word "and" (ca) from the Sūtra is intended to include what has not been explicitly mentioned, he states its meaning: "Furthermore... (kiṃ ca).
Thus ends the section on the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa). 3.
On account of the designation of the object of the act of seeing, it is He [the Supreme Self]. 1.3.12.

The followers of the Atharva Veda study this in the *Satyakāmapraśna*: "But he who [meditates on this]... Since it is thus established that [the Self] possesses four faces, qualities such as being undecaying (*ajara*) and so forth must be interpreted in some way or another [as applying to the individual soul].

"On account of the designation of the object of seeing, that [is Brahman]. The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt that, just as with the word "ether" (*ākāśa*), the words "interior space" (*antarīkṣa*) and "Brahma-world" (*brahmaloka*) cannot be explained otherwise [than as referring to Brahman]. In this section, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) posits a difference in the objects of meditation (*dhyāna*) and seeing (*īkṣaṇa*), while the author establishes their identity as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). He refutes opposing views with the words "here," and so forth. "Meditation" is clear. "In both cases" refers to [the passage concerning] the "Supreme Person."

The meaning is that the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) stated by the opponent are not tenable, because there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the subject indicated by the word "Person" (*puruṣa*) as qualified by the word "other" (*para*) as being one and the same in both instances. Since "otherness" (*paratva*) is dependent upon a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), and since the very same counter-correlative specified later as "than the Person who is the mass of living beings" (*jīva-dhana*) is understood through syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*) to serve as the counter-correlative in the earlier instance as well—and because no other counter-correlative is mentioned—there is no room for suspicion of a difference in the subject matter.
Furthermore, the status of the Four-faced One (Brahmā) as a collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) is relative to the gods and others.

This being the position, we reply: "He [is the Supreme], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing. ... It is entirely consistent that it teaches the Supreme Brahman alone as the goal to be attained. Therefore, the object of the act of seeing is the Supreme Self. (Sūtra 1.3.12)
In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), it refers to the Supreme Self alone; the intention is that if it referred to the Four-faced One (Brahmā), the masculine gender would be inappropriate.

"Even for the Four-faced One (Brahmā)" means that because his knowledge is produced by instruction, he remains subject to karma; this is the sense. "And not... and so forth: the sense is that the lack of elegance is equal [in both cases]. Since there was previously no distinction between the *prakṛta* (material) and *aprākṛta* (non-material), and since at that time the mention of "three worlds" would be inappropriate, one might argue that the world mentioned immediately after the two material worlds must itself be material; to this he says: "This indeed... [is] "everything is consistent. In our view, the fact that the word *antarikṣa* (intermediate space) is used merely for the sake of illustration is precisely what lacks elegance;
however, for the opponent, everything is lacking in elegance—this is the meaning.
Thus ends the section on the object of the act of seeing. 4. The small [ether] is [Brahman], because of the subsequent [scriptural statements]. 1-3-13.

The Chāndogyas recite this: "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman... If that were the case, it would not be possible for the heaven, earth, and all else, as delimited by the heart, to possess inexhaustibility.

The section on the "Small" (*dahara*) follows from the subsequent [sections]. The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt that, whereas the previous [section] declared the one dwelling in the city (*puriśaya*) to be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), this [section] might declare him to be the non-Supreme Self (*aparamātman*). Since it is certain that the one denoted by the words "ether" (*ākāśa*) and "intermediate space" (*antarikṣa*) is other than [the Supreme], there is a co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) between the section on the Imperishable (*akṣara*) and the section on the locus of the act of perishing (*īkṣatikarma*); however, because that [otherness] is absent here, there is no such co-occurrence between the section on the Imperishable and the section on the "Small. Furthermore, since the term is used for the Supreme as well, the word "excellent" (*prakarṣa*) is employed to exclude that [Supreme].

Because of the scriptural mention of the qualities of Brahman, such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*), the small ether (*daharākāśa*) is Brahman; regarding this, he says: "In that... This point will become clear through the passage beginning with "Now, it might be argued" (*atha syāt*).

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): there is indeed no hierarchical relationship of superior and inferior among the attributes of the Supreme Self. Therefore, he states that its status as "subsequent" is established by way of the sentence—namely, "from those occurring in the sentence. The particle *hi* is used to dispel the doubt regarding the dative case-ending (*caturthyanta*).

But surely—even if the small ether were the supreme Self, its being comparable to the external ether would not be possible... Therefore, for these reasons, the small ether is indeed the supreme Brahman.

Now, it might be argued as follows: because of the lack of intervention, and because of the primacy indicated by the nominative case in the designation "the locus of space" (*ākāśādhikaraṇatva*), that which is referred to by the word "this" (*eṣa*) must be sought [as the primary object]. Therefore, qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth are its [the Self's] qualities, and not qualities of the small space (*daharakāśa*). The author refutes this: "It might be so. In the meditation on the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), the cognition of the qualities is incidental; however, in the meditation on the qualities, there is no inclusion of the possessor of qualities. Here, a prescription for the simultaneous presentation of both is not enjoined, since no word is observed that presents both together.

For the word *tat* (that) has as its object only that which is contained within [the preceding]; since the word *tat* refers to the object indicated by the word *yat* (which), he says here: "In this [context]. The word *tat* does not refer to both [the individual and the aggregate], because the word *tat* is a reference (*parāmarśin*) to what was indicated by the word *yat*, and because that [word *yat*] has as its object only that which is contained within [the aggregate]. To this he says: "That which is this... The sense is that there is a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*), a singular number, and the form *tat* [is used for all three genders] according to the rule: "The pronouns beginning with *tyad* are always [retained when combined] with others; when not neuter, they may optionally take the singular [number]."

"Regarding the phrase 'the small ether' (*daharākāśa*) and so forth: the meaning is that when a scripturally authoritative matter has been stated, it is appropriate to avoid the exhaustion of laborious efforts to provide an alternative interpretation. He replies: "He who is attentive. The word "this" (*eṣaḥ*) in the phrase "this is the Self" (*eṣa ātmā*) does not refer back to what is separated by the sentences beginning with "as large as... (*yāvān vā*); rather, its meaning is that it refers back to the immediately preceding "ether" (*ākāśa*). He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "it does not age with his aging" (*nāsya jarayaitajjīryati*) in the words "of that" (*tasya*). The rest is clear. (13)
For it is seen so from both motion and sound, and there is also an inferential mark. (1.3.14)

For this reason as well, the small ether is Brahman: "Just as [people] go toward a treasure of gold..."—this is sufficient evidence for its being the Supreme Brahman, since all creatures who do not know [it] go toward it.

For the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is seen from both the context (*gati*) and the word (*śabda*). Regarding the term "Niṣāda": the meaning is that, according to the principle that "it is more reasonable for the syntactical connection of the heard [word] itself with its offspring to be established than to assume the meaning of an unheard case-ending or to postulate another substratum," [the Niṣāda is the subject]. He states another meaning for the mere word "context" with the words "Or rather. "As the inner self" is stated because of the identity of their nature (*dharma-ekya*). || 14 ||
For this reason also, the small ether is the supreme Brahman: "And because its greatness, consisting in supporting [the worlds], is perceived in this. (1.3.15)
Now, that which was introduced as "the Self" [in the preceding passage]—its greatness is perceived within this small space (daharākāśa); therefore, the small space is the Supreme Brahman. || 15 ||
And because this greatness of support is perceived in this [ether]: "Support" (dhṛti) means upholding; it is the sustaining of things in their unmixed state. || 15 ||
And because of common renown. (1.3.16)
And the word "ether" (ākāśa) is well-known to refer to the supreme Brahman; the intention is that the established usage for the elemental ether is weaker [than this]. || 16 ||
And it is well known; regarding the claim that the elemental ether possesses a preeminent degree of such renown, he says: "It is free from evil," and so forth.
Thus, first of all, the small ether is the elemental ether...
[if it be argued] "it is that [ether], because of reference to the other," [we reply] no, because of impossibility. (1.3.17)

As has been stated, on account of the supplementary statement, the "small ether" [is Brahman]; for qualities such as being free from evil and so forth are not possible in the individual soul (jīva). || 17 ||

Stating what has already been said, he speaks of what is about to be said with the words "Now" (*atha*). If it is argued that "He" (*sa*) refers to the other [the individual soul] because of the reference to it, we say no, because of impossibility. Regarding the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*): since the word "this" (*eṣa*) in the phrase "Now, this which... refers to what is under discussion, the meaning is that the individual soul (*jīva*), though previously mentioned, is the subject here. The rest is clear. || 17 ||
If it be argued that [the soul's nature is acquired] from the north, we reply: "But [its] true nature is manifested. (1.3.18)

From the subsequent passage of Prajāpati, we shall demonstrate later that it is the individual soul alone [that possesses the power of knowledge], with the exception of the activity of creating the world. || 18 ||

If [it is argued that] from the subsequent [text], "But one whose nature has become manifest," [the conclusion follows]: why should the statement of Prajāpati not be about the Supreme Self? And even if it were about the individual soul (jīva), what would that have to do with the subject under discussion? To this he says: "This has been stated. Regarding the phrase "of the one to be attained": the implication is of the Supreme Person as the object to be attained by the individual soul, and not because He is the primary subject matter of the context. This is the sense. As for the phrase "if it be so": the construction is "this has been stated. He states the intended meaning of the word "but" (tu): "even for one whose nature has become manifest. || 18 ||
If this is so, then in the passage concerning the "small [space]," "Now, that which is this serene being...
the reference has another purpose. (1.3.19)

Just as the quality of being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and the support of the world belong to the small ether itself, so too the fruit mentioned in the Prajāpati passage is indeed the fruit of the Dahara-vidyā. || 19 ||

And the reference has another purpose. To the question, "If the meditation on the small [space] alone bestows liberation, for what purpose is there an injunction for the worship of the individual soul (jīva)? he says: "And in the Prajāpati discourse... To the question, "How can a subordinate element have its fruit stated? he says: "All... (19).
If it be argued that this is because [the scripture] has a limited scope, that has already been answered. (1.3.10)

The scriptural mention of small size in the phrase "small in this" refers to the Self whose essential nature consists of manifested qualities such as freedom from evil; thus, the "small ether" is not the elemental ether. || 20 ||

The reason based on the concluding portion has been answered. Now he replies regarding that which pertains to the introductory portion. If it is argued that "because of the limited scope of what is heard," that has already been addressed. There may be a further suspicion arising from the greater weight of the introduction; however, the resolution follows from the even greater weight of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*).
