To indicate the connection of the two subsequent sūtras with the primary subject matter, he says: "Therefore—" Knowledge and the other qualities culminate in the fruit of the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*). 20.
And for this reason it is so: "And because of the imitation of that. (1.3.12)
Of that small ether (daharākāśa)... the small ether is the Brahman which is to be conformed to. || 21 ||
And because there is conformity with that; this is clear. || 21 ||
It is also recorded in Smṛti. (1.3.22)

Furthermore, since it is understood that even the transmigrating soul possesses the nature of light in its state of liberation, and because the Supreme Brahman is likewise known to have the nature of light, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) does not arise; thus [the opponent's position] is untenable. Moreover, there is a discordance with the literal meaning of the words of the Sūtra. || 22 ||

It is also recorded in tradition. He refutes the claim made by others that this constitutes a separate section (*adhikaraṇa*) by restating it with the words "some say. He states that the present discussion begins for the purpose of refuting the notion that light (*tejas*) is elemental (*prākṛta*); thus he says, "The light [is Brahman], on account of the feet" (*jyotiścaraṇa*). It has been stated that there is no excess of doubt; however, this is not appropriate as the meaning of the word "after" (*anu*) in the sūtra, because in this system of philosophy, the mere form of a word is not intended as the primary subject matter.

The sense is that it is inappropriate for the word *tasya* from the Sūtra—being devoid of the words *yadeva vidyayā*, *hi*, and *iti*—to have as its purport the citation of the Śruti passage beginning with *tasya bhāsā*. || 22 ||
Thus ends the section on the "Small One" (daharādhikaraṇa). 5.
[The person within the small lotus] is known from the word itself. 1.3.13.

In the Kaṭhavallīs it is heard: "The Person the size of a thumb... And the lordship over all that has been and is to be is not possible for the individual soul (jīva), which is dependent on its karma. || 23 ||

"He is measured by the word alone" (ŚB 5.9.1). Because of the mention of "smallness" (*alpa*), the small dimension of the Supreme is stated. The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt that a specific [dimension] of the individual soul (*jīva*) is heard in scripture. To the objection that the small dimension is stated even for the Supreme, he says: "And not... This is a hypothetical deliberation (*kṛtvā-cintā*), because elsewhere the small dimension of the Supreme is indeed heard. Regarding how there can be lordship (*īśānatva*), he says: "Lordship... For the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), the natural force (*svārasya*) of the first-mentioned "measured by a thumb" (*aṅguṣṭhamātra*) prevails over the natural force of the later-mentioned "lordship."
In the final conclusion: [the knowledge of Brahman arises] from the word alone, not from an inferential mark (liṅga). The meaning is: "from the word *parāyaṇa* itself. || 23 ||

How, then, can the Supreme Self be of the size of a thumb? To this he says: "But [the size of a thumb is] with reference to the heart, because the qualification [of the scripture] is for human beings. (1.3.24)
This [section] which stands for the purpose of meditating upon the Supreme Self shall be concluded further on. || 24 ||

"But with regard to the heart, [the measure applies] because the qualification belongs to humans; and this applies to the individual soul (jīva) as well. The meaning is that since both [interpretations] would be inconsistent, it is more logical to accept the consistency of one. Regarding the objection that being "measured by a thumb" is not universally applicable, he says: "Of humans. Having understood that the incidental matter is inconceivable, he says: "That much stands for now. (24)
Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] even beyond that [the gods may attain knowledge], because it is possible. (2.3.25)

In order to establish that the Supreme Brahman is measured by the size of a thumb... therefore, because of the absence of both capacity and interest, the gods and others have no qualification [for this knowledge].

"Bādarāyaṇa [holds that there is eligibility] even for those above that, because of the possibility. He states the connection by way of context with the words "of the Supreme" (*parasya*). The meaning is that the connection arises from the doubt as to whether the term "human being" excludes only animals, or whether it also excludes gods and others. "Due to the absence of capacity" is also an indication of the absence of desire (*arthitva*). "Conclusion" means performance. "Even though" [is said] because [such things] lack the nature of engagement or withdrawal, and because they lack the nature of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), like Brahman.

The meaning is that there is no intention to establish [the existence of] a physical body. This is because [the texts] are intent on something else—namely, praise (*stuti*) and the manifestation of what is to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*). To the objection that the establishment of a physical body and so forth follows from the fact that ritual action (*karman*) is defined by its constituent substance (*dravya*) and deity (*devatā*), and thus requires them, he says: "And the injunctions for ritual action... It is for this very reason—that is, precisely because of the absence of a body.
This being the case, we reply: even though that [is so], Bādarāyaṇa [holds]... therefore, because they possess bodies and so forth, the gods indeed have the qualification [for knowledge]. || 25 ||

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), he explains the [conditions of] desire (*arthitva*) and capacity (*sāmarthya*) through the passage beginning with "desire" (*arthitvam*). To the question, "Which are the statements that declare [the gods] to possess bodies, and how is that established by them?", he says, "For instance" (*tathā hi*). By the scriptural text concerning the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*), as well as other scriptures and the *smṛtis* which corroborate them, the fourfold nature of those [gods] is intended. The sense is that there are also such [texts] as "Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra," and so forth. To the question, "What follows from this?", he says, "The gods, etc. (*devādi*).

He shows this even in the section on meditation (upāsana) with the word "likewise" (tathā). He states that its establishment [as authoritative] is due to its being a supplement to injunctions (vidhiśeṣatvena) with the words "the injunction of ritual action" (karmavidhi). And he says "not by means of what is non-existent" (na ca asatā); the sense is that since Vedic sentences have the purpose of determining reality, it is not proper to regard them as being like mere enticements for children and the like. In response to the objection that because statements such as "Water is indeed peaceful" (āpo vai śāntāḥ) and "The sacrificial post is the sun" (ādityo yūpaḥ) express meanings contradicted by other means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara), they cannot be authoritative in all cases, he replies: "In that case, regarding other means of valid cognition... (tatra pramāṇāntare).

For the purport [of a text] resides in what is required by an injunction (*vidhi*). To the question, "How is the corporeal form of the deity and so forth required by an injunction? he says: "Of the ritual injunction" (*karmavidheḥ*). The sense is that one must avoid abandoning what is heard in scripture (*śruta*) and instead assume what is not heard (*aśruta-kalpanā*). Regarding the phrase "not understood at the time of learning" (*vyutpatti-samayānavagatam*): the sense is that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) which holds that the literal meaning is primary, the assumption [of a figurative sense] would be cumbersome. This was stated here for the sake of ease of understanding regarding what will be discussed under the aphorism *phalam ataḥ* (JS 3.2.38). The unique purpose here is that its establishment [as having a corporeal form] occurs through praise (*stuti*) and manifestation (*prakāśana*). The term "mixed" (*saṅkīrṇa*) serves to exclude the possibility of an eternally inferred scripture (*nityānumeya-śruti*). || 25 ||
If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe the attainment of various [results] from a single [action]. (1.3.26)
If it is admitted that gods and others possess bodies and so forth, then there is the simultaneous assumption of multiple bodies by those possessing power, such as Saubhari and others. || 26 ||

If it is argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe multiple modes of manifestation. It is not the case that there is a failure to perceive those possessing bodies; for, as with mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth, invisibility is possible—this is the intended meaning. || 26 ||
If it be argued that [the world] is sound, we say no; because it originates from this [Brahman], as is known through both perception and inference. (1.3.27)

The term "contradiction" (virodha) carries over [from the previous sūtra]. Let there not be [the charge that] Vedic words are meaningless, nor does it follow that the Veda has a beginning in time. || 27 ||

If it is argued that [the Veda] is non-eternal because it is a sound, we say no, because it originates from this [Brahman], as established by perception and inference. "Non-eternality" here means the state of not being currently uttered. How can there be the production of word and meaning, and how, consequently, can the objection be resolved? To this he says: "This has been stated. Even though the individual forms (ākṛti) are non-eternal, the resolution is achieved through continuity (pravāha-nityatā), just as in the case where cattle, rice, and so forth remain essentially the same despite the non-eternality of individual instances. || 27 ||
And for this very reason, it possesses eternality. (1.3.28)

Precisely because words such as "Indra" and "Vasiṣṭha," which denote gods and sages, [are eternal], and because the Vedas are eternal, it is logically established that these [beings] are the authors of the mantras. || 28 ||

The impermanence [of the Veda] by way of its meaning has been refuted. He now refutes the impermanence by way of its words; for this very reason, it is eternal. To the question "How so?", he clarifies what was stated with the words "by these very [means]": the status of being a composer of mantras consists in the vision [of them] even without having studied them, by way of [their] syllables and accents being unerring.
He states the doubt regarding the subsequent sūtra: "Now, it might be argued... and so forth.

Now it may be argued: "In the case of the production of Indra and others during occasional dissolutions (naimittikapralaya) and so forth, there is no contradiction even though there is recurrence [of creation], because their names and forms are the same; this is known from scripture and tradition. (1.3.19)

Even though the entire world undergoes dissolution and re-creation, it is established that even gods and others possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, because they are endowed with both the desire for liberation and the capacity for its attainment.

"And because names and forms are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of recurrence, as seen from scripture and from traditional teaching (smṛti). [The phrase] 'from the very same as previously mentioned' means that by the word *tat-tat* (this-that), it is established that creation is preceded by the recollection of those respective objects, resulting in the identity of names and forms; this is the intended meaning. That [objection] is untenable because of the absence of one who could remember the object preceded by the memory of the word; to this he says: 'For thus...'. 'Remaining as mere potentiality' means that the capacity for being an enjoyer and so forth exists, but not the actual performance of its effects; this is the intended meaning. 'In all cases' refers to the identity of names and forms, the eternity of the Veda, and its meaningfulness."

To the question, "If the production and so forth of sound are admitted, how can there be the eternity of the Veda?", he says: "And this very [point]... The meaning is as follows: because the eternity of the phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth is subject to deviation in the case of human speech; and because the pronunciation based on the sequence of those phonemes—which are accepted as eternal and all-pervading—is non-eternal; therefore, eternity consists in being pronounced successively with a sequence identical to that of the preceding one. Anticipating the objection that in the case of pronunciation following recollection, the cognition of another would be dependent on something else, he says: "...thus they are... (*ityān*).

"By itself" (*svayam eva*) means independently of a teacher. By the two restrictive particles (*avadhāraṇa*), the initial and subsequent utterances by persons such as ourselves are excluded. The phrase "let them be many" (*bahu syām*) indicates that such utterance is dependent upon one's own independence. Although in all the cited *śruti* and *smṛti* passages there is no mention of the Veda being the specific instrument for creation, its establishment [as such] follows from the fact that, even if not explicitly stated in some, it must be understood from other sources.

Once the existence of God is established through the proof of the non-interruption of the tradition, His eternity is established; and once the authority of the Veda is established, the existence of God follows. Thus, one should not suspect a circular argument (*cakraka*), because the authority [of the Veda] is intrinsic (*svatastva*) and because any grounds for sublation (*apavāda*) have been refuted by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible. This is just as the circularity was avoided in the case of the authority of the entire Veda. || 29 ||

Thus ends the section on the deities (Devatādhikaraṇa). 7. Jaimini [maintains] that there is no eligibility [for the knowledge of Brahman] for gods and others, because it is impossible [for them] in the case of the Madhu-vidyā and similar meditations. (Sūtra 1.3.30)

There is also eligibility for gods and others in the knowledge of Brahman, as indicated by such passages as: "Having become one with the waters alone, he satiates himself by beholding this very nectar through the mouth of Agni," and so forth. || 30 ||

Jaimini [holds that there is] no entitlement [to these meditations] because they are impossible in the case of the gods and others. The entitlement of the deities to meditations in general has been established; now, their lack of entitlement to the specific instances of those meditations is being determined because their fruit has already been attained—this is the connection. Due to the contradiction between the action and the agent, and because the fruit has already been attained, there is an absence of both capability and desire. He clarifies this pair [of reasons] with the words "In the Madhu-vidyā," meaning that [the gods] cannot be the objects of meditation (*upāsya*). || 30 ||
And [the same applies] to the states in the luminous realm. 1.3.31.
"The gods [meditate upon] that light of lights..."; therefore, there is no qualification for Vasu and the others among these [beings]. || 31 ||

And because of the context of the luminaries. It has been stated that "the gods alone" [are meant], since the present discussion concerns the qualification of humans; therefore, the sense is that [the subject] is indeed the luminaries (jyotis). This is the intended meaning. || 31 ||
The sūtra of the established conclusion: To this [objection] it is replied—“But Bādarāyaṇa [maintains] existence, for it indeed exists” (1.3.32).
[The opponent argues: "Even for Āditya, Vāyu, and others, there is a state of eligibility for those [meditations], because Brahman alone is to be perceived everywhere. (Sūtra 32)

Bādarāyaṇa, however, holds that there is indeed [the existence of the Lord]; for, having stated the literal meaning [of the text], he refutes the arguments of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with two passages beginning with "asti hi. He says "atra hi" because this refutation is possible only when it is established that the fruit of meditation culminates in Brahman and the attainment thereof. To the objection that the meditation on the sun is perceived as being in both states (rising and setting) and not as having the Supreme Being whose body is that sun as its object, nor as having the attainment of Him as its fruit, he says "na ha vā. [In the passage] "upaniṣadam veda," he means "he performs the meditation," just as one says "he cooks the rice until it is soft. He concludes with "ataḥ."

The resolution of the contradiction between the object and the agent—arising from the collection beginning with Vāyu being the object of meditation and the individual being the meditator—and the possibility that the mere attainment of the state of being Vāyu and so forth constitutes the fruit in another cycle of creation (kalpa), have both been explained by others; however, [the author] demonstrates that these are not authoritative by establishing the authority of his own intended meaning. Thus, stating that his own view is traditional and indicating that the views of others are non-traditional, he says: "Therefore, it is said... (32).
Thus ends the section concerning Madhu (1.3.29–32).
Now, 1.3.33: *Śugasya tadanādaraśravaṇāt tadādravaṇāt sūcyate hi* (The grief of this [Gārgya] is indicated by the hearing of his disregard for that [instruction], and because he ran toward him).
Whether or not there is eligibility for a Śūdra even in the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) ... therefore, eligibility for a Śūdra is indeed possible.

The connection [of this section] is indicated by the mention of Śuka’s lack of respect and by its subsequent narration; for there is a doubt that if the desire [to know] and the capacity [to perform rites] were the sole determinants of eligibility, then even Śūdras and others would possess such eligibility. The meaning is that while they lack eligibility for rituals such as sacrifices, they do not lack eligibility for meditation (*upāsana*). This is established by logic in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the non-Śūdra) within the Karma-kāṇḍa. The primary argument is stated with the word "tathā" (so).

This being the position reached, it is said: there is no eligibility for a Śūdra... because they are joined with such a birth due to the power of previously commenced karma (prārabdhakarman), their state of being established in Brahman [is possible].

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), he states the reason for the incapacity characterized by the lack of comprehension of the nature of Brahman and so forth with the words, "And as for the incapacity... He addresses the claim that the qualification of Śūdras for the injunctions regarding meditation (*upāsanā*) should be inferred with the words, "For just as indeed... For the assumption of [the capacity for] performance is made in cases such as the *rathakāra* (chariot-maker) regarding sacrifices and the like; however, such an assumption is not logical here. Furthermore, there would be the additional burden of assuming that study (*adhyayana*) is also a prerequisite; the same applies to meditations—this is the meaning. Thus ends the section on "Itihāsa."
The meaning is that just as there is no fullness of meaning through mere exposition alone without something to be explained, so it is here.
The Fourth Quarter of the First Chapter.
"If it be argued that for some [the soul] is also inferential, we say no; because [the text] shows that it is understood as being presented through the metaphor of the body. (1.4.1)

It has been stated that [Brahman] is the object of inquiry because it is the means to liberation, which is characterized as the supreme human goal. [Objection: If it is argued that in the branches of certain Vedic schools, Pradhāna is also traditionally taught as a cause, based on inference; |||
If it be argued that for some [the Self] is also inferential, we say no; for [the scripture] shows that it is grasped as presented in the allegory of the body.

The connection with the previous section has already been stated: that the respective words refer to the possessor of the attributes (*liṅgin*). The intermediate connection is as follows: in the final section of the third chapter, it was argued that the distinction of the individual soul (*jīva*) [from Brahman] is untenable because everything other than that [Brahman] is subsequently negated. The statement beginning with "it has been said" (*uktam*) here expresses the meaning of the three chapters in accordance with the Sūtras. Indeed, by the phrase "even that which is inferential" (*ānumānikam api*), the exclusion of any other possible connection has been demonstrated. Furthermore, in the *Śrībhāṣya*, this is indicated by the two words "sole" (*eka*) and "firmness" (*sthema*) in the expression "for the sake of the firmness of Brahman as the sole cause."

The phrase "each respective word refers to that which possesses the mark" is indicated by the words "primordial matter," "spirit," and so forth. It is stated [as a question]: "Is it so, or not? This formulation of a doubt arises because the proponent's (siddhāntin) position is that the word *avyakta* does not denote primordial matter (*prakṛti*). Otherwise, one would have to doubt whether [the unmanifest] has Brahman as its essence or not. He states that this doubt is not based on the Sūtra itself with the words: "This very [point]."

To this, the reply is: "No. By the word "Unmanifest" (avyakta), that which is non-Brahman in nature is not intended; therefore, there is no possibility whatsoever of the Pradhāna established in the Sāṃkhya system being referred to here.

"Rūpyate" means "it is illustrated"—that is, an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). "Arranged as an illustration" means "imagined" (*kalpita*). To the question, "Which things are illustrated, and how?", he says: "The Self," and so forth. What is the illustrative statement? How is it known that there is here a mention of those things that have been illustrated? And for what purpose is this? Furthermore, in that context, how is it that the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) refers to the body? To these questions, he says: "This has been stated," and so forth. "Of everything" means even of correct determination (*samyag-adhyavasāya*).

The body’s state of being subject to control consists in its being nourished by *sāttvika* food; as for how the Supreme Being is included within the category of the instruments of worship, he says: "He indeed... By the statement "There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the ultimate limit," there is an exclusion of any other [higher] connection (*anyayogavyavacchitti*). He states that the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) refers to the body by means of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*), saying: "Thus, in this way... The implication is that while the identity with Brahman was stated elsewhere by accepting the word's reference to *pradhāna*, here, however, it does not have the meaning of *pradhāna* at all.
Nor is there here a recognition of the procedures established in the Tantras; rather, the meaning is that one should proceed to the station of Viṣṇu by means of such a charioteer. || 1 ||

He refutes the identification with the *tantra* [of the body] with the words "And not... (*na ca*). The portion ending with "grahaṇam" (the grasping) is connected with what precedes. The fragment of the Sūtra beginning with "darśayati ca" (and he shows) follows. That very [state] is "subordination," which is indeed "otherness. The lengthening of the vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Otherwise, one would have to say "vāṅmanase," and not "vāṅmanasī. Therefore, although the Vedic nature is the same, the point is that conformity to the context is superior. The subduing of the self within the Supreme Brahman is its being directed toward Him.
In the phrase "tat" [in the rule *vyatyayena tad*], the word "tat" is to be explained as having the intended meaning of the sūtra beginning with *suptiṅupagraha*. || 1 ||
How can the unmanifest term denote the manifest body? To this he says: "But that [body] is subtle, because it is worthy of that [designation]. (1.4.2)

For the subtle element of the primary matter (bhūtasūkṣma), which is unmanifest (avyākṛta), having attained a particular state... [is like a chariot], because it is fit for activity as a means to accomplish the purposes of the Person (puruṣārtha). || 2 ||

He raises a doubt regarding the immediately preceding Sūtra with the words "avyakta" (the unmanifest). [The Sūtra states: "But that [is] subtle, because it is so worthy. This means that the designation of the cause is applied to the effect. To the question "Why is it not the reverse? he replies: "Because it is so worthy. This means because it would contradict the sense [of the context]. || 2 ||

If it is admitted that the subtle elements are unmanifested (avyākṛta), [then they must exist], because [the manifest world] depends upon them, just as [an effect exists] because it has a cause. (1.4.3)
Because [the world] is dependent upon the Supreme Person who is the ultimate cause... and because the Supreme Self is the support of all things, He is the Supreme Lord. || 3 ||

He raises a doubt regarding the immediately preceding Sūtra with the words "If... (*yadi*). [The Sūtra] states: "Because it is dependent on that, it is purposeful" (*tadadhīnatvādarthavat*). To the question, "How is the objection concerning the approach and non-approach of the Pradhāna refuted by the statement of its being 'purposeful'? he replies: "This has been said" (*etaduktam*). Regarding the phrase "abiding in its own nature" (*svarūpasthiti*): since the performance of an effect depends upon the persistence of existence (*sattā*), when its dependence on that [Brahman] is stated, the dependence of both [existence and the performance of effects] on Him is also established—this is the sense. The scriptural passage concerning His majesty (*mahimavādaśruti*) is: "He whose body is the earth," and so forth. (3)
And because [the Lord] is not mentioned as being an object of knowledge. (1.4.4)
If that which is established by the Tantra were unmanifest here, then there would be no apprehension of what is established by the Tantra here; therefore, it is not so. || 4 ||
And because there is no statement that it is an object of knowledge. This is clear. || 4 ||
If it be argued that [the Self] speaks, we say no; for the wise one [is meant], according to the context. (1.4.5)
"Soundless, touchless, formless, and imperishable..."—it is precisely the transcendence of the individual self (jīvātman) mentioned previously that is being stated here. || 5 ||
If it be argued that [the Self] speaks, we say no; for it is the intelligent [Self] that is meant, according to the context. This is clear. || 5 ||
And thus there is both the presentation and the question regarding these three alone. (1.4.6)
For in this context, [the discussion concerns] the means, the goal, and the attainer; therefore, there is no mention here of the "Unmanifest" (avyakta) as it is understood in the Tantras. || 6 ||

The fact that [the Upaniṣad] is devoted to the Supreme Intellect (*prājña*) does not contradict its being devoted to the Pradhāna, because it lacks exclusive devotion to the Supreme Intellect alone. To this he says: "And thus there is the presentation and the question of all three. The phrase "thus there is the presentation" is to be explained as follows. He explains the word "thus" there by saying "as objects of knowledge. "Serving as the means to liberation" means that they serve as means to liberation by way of being constituent parts (*aṅga*). "This which... refers to the question regarding the three, based on the manner of the answer. *Dharma* is the means (*upāya*); *adharma* is that other than *dharma*, the end to be attained (*upeya*).

"Done and undone" refers to the present. Regarding "austerities" (*tapāṃsi*): the subsequent sections [of the verse]—"those whose chief wealth is knowledge" and "those who are devoted to Brahman"—indicate that austerity is knowledge. This is because we observe the word *tapas* being used to mean both knowledge and Brahman in such passages as "whose austerity consists of knowledge" and "they revere austerity as faith. "The state" (*padam*) means that which is to be attained. || 6 ||
And like the Great [Self]. (1.4.7)
Just as in the passage, "The Great Self is superior to the intellect," it is established that the [Self] proven by the Sāṃkhya system is not what is being referred to. || 7 ||
And as in the case of the Great [Self]. This is clear. || 7 ||
Thus ends the section concerning those who rely on inference (Ānumānikādhikaraṇa). 1.
It is like the cup, because there is no distinction. 1.4.8.
Here too, the procedure established by the Tantras is refuted... because it is heard [in scripture] that many [goddesses] of identical form possess the power of creation independently.

"Like the cup, because there is no distinction. Previously, it was stated that the word denoting the cause refers to the body of the effect. Here, however, the connection [of the sūtra] arises from the doubt that, since no word denoting an effect is heard, the "cause" must refer to *pradhāna* alone. An inquiry has been conducted by others as to whether [the passage] refers to *pradhāna* or to fire, water, and food (*tejo-'b-anna*). In this regard, intending to show the lack of internal consistency within its own sentence, and in order to demonstrate the lack of consistency in other scriptural passages, [the author] says "atrāpi" (here too) in order to cite a collection of sentences concerning *pradhāna*.

*Adhyāsitā* means presided over (*adhiṣṭhitā*). *Tanyate* means it is impelled in the form of a collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) for the sake of individual creation (*vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*). Now, in order to cite the collection of supreme scriptural passages concerning that Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), he says: "Of which [Brahman] they consist," and "And others. The intention here is that the identity with Brahman is established because these sentences have the same meaning as other scriptural passages. "From the state of being that" (*tattvabhāvāt*) means from the manifestation of that [Brahman]. "Primordial nature and so forth" (*prakṛtyādayaḥ*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest are included. He states the subject matter: "Śveta... [etc.]. Regarding "independently" (*svātantryeṇa*): in the phrase "creating" (*sṛjamānām*), the suffix *śānac* denotes the agent; the sense is that the independent one is the agent (*kartā*).

This being the case, it is replied: "Like the cup; because there is no distinction. ... Therefore, by this mantra, the *ajā* (the unborn) is not denoted as something whose nature is not Brahman. || 8 ||

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the proposition (*pratijñā*) must be supplied. "Camasa" means an instrument for measuring. The meaning is that the mere scriptural mention of "being unborn" (*ajātvamātraśravaṇa*) is not in contradiction with the fact that [the world] has Brahman as its self, provided that [Brahman] is established by valid means of knowledge. And as for the phrase "not of this" (*na cāsyāḥ*): because it lacks a qualifying term (*nirupapadatvāt*), there is no perception of it being an independent act of creation; such is the meaning. || 8 ||

He states that there is indeed a specific reason for the perception [of the Self] as consisting of Brahman even during the waking state: "But [the soul] begins with light, for thus it is studied by some. (1.4.9)

The word "tu" (but) has the sense of restriction... because it is precisely that [conventional] cognition [that occurs], there is not even a trace of the apprehension of an independent *prakṛti* established by the Tantras in this mantra. || 9 ||

He introduces the immediately following sūtra with the words, "consisting of Brahman" (*brahmātmaka*). Regarding the statement, "But [the creation] begins with light, for thus some read," he says, "of everything," because there is no perception of origination in this mantra. The intention is that it is like the subordinate status (*aṅgatva*) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. The phrase "by another" does not refer to a separate mention, because the context of creation has been interrupted; rather, it functions as a qualifier. The intention is that the creation continues in what follows, as in, "From whom [all] was born, than whom nothing else exists."

And this [objection] having been raised, [it is answered] by the passage beginning with "even here," because the identity of Brahman and the Self is demonstrated within one's own Vedic school alone. || 9 ||
How, then, is there no contradiction? [The Sūtra says: "Because there is instruction regarding a conceptualization beginning with light, as in the case of honey and so forth. (1.4.10)
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of removing a possible doubt. ... ... The conceptualization of "goat-ness" as being fit for connection [with the sacrifice] is utterly contradictory. || 10 ||

He raises a doubt regarding the immediately preceding Sūtra with the words, "How then? [The Sūtra states: "And because there is instruction based on metaphorical conception, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of *tu* (but). The terms "conception" (*kalpanā*) and "light" (*jyotis*) follow the usage of the Veda, just as in the expression "from the state of serene confidence" (*saṃprasādāt*). He explains the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "honey" (*madhu*): the meaning is that there is no contradiction due to the difference in states, just as there is between the conception of rising and setting and the conception of being honey, and the absence thereof.

In order to refute the interpretation of the two sūtras proposed by others, he first restates the meaning of the first sūtra—introduced by the words "others, however" (*anye tu*)—and then analyzes it with the question "What? (*kim*). The statement regarding the "middle head" is for the purpose of establishing the oneness of the unborn (*ajā*). The phrase "each one" (*pratyekam*) means that there is no oneness of the aggregate; rather, the meaning is that there are three aggregates. He analyzes the second [sūtra] with the words "the second. The alternative is whether the states consisting of fire, water, and food are what is denoted by the word *ajā*, or whether it is their essential nature (*svarūpa*).

In the second [alternative] as well, the lack of intrinsic consistency in the scripture has been stated. He points out the lack of intrinsic consistency in the Sūtra itself: "tejo'banna" (fire, water, and food). For the opponents have explained that the term beginning with "light" (jyotis) denotes fire, water, and food. He refutes the third among the initial alternatives: "in the third as well."

Now, having restated the meaning asserted by others regarding the third sūtra, he refutes it with the words "yat punaḥ" and so forth. [The opponent's view is rejected] because a secondary (gauṇa) sense cannot be accepted when the primary sense is possible; because there is no purpose [for such an interpretation]; because it contradicts the literal meaning; because there is an absence of words denoting the metaphorical object (*rūpaka*) and the metaphorical subject (*rūpin*), unlike the expression "the self as the charioteer" (*ātmānaṃ rathinam*); because there is an absence of appropriate qualifiers, unlike the statement "the cow is without beginning or end" (*gauranādyantavatī*); because there would be a lack of naturalness (*asvārasya*) if one intended merely to express that [the Self] is the means for accomplishing a purpose; and because that [secondary sense] lacks the inherent consistency found in other words of the passage.
The meaning is that the fabrication [of the term] from goat-skin is improper; however, the meaning we have stated is the very natural interpretation for those who follow Vedic injunctions. || 10 ||
Thus concludes the section on the cups (Camasādhikaraṇa). 2.
"Not even because of the inclusion of a number [is there a plurality of Brahmas], because of their distinctness and because of the excess. (1.4.11)
The Vājasaneyins record: "In whom the five five-people... Here, the number five is specified as qualifying the "five people," just as in the expression "the seven seven-sages. || 11 ||

"Nor [is it so] because of the inclusion of a number, due to their being manifold and because of excess. The nature of *prakṛti* as having Brahman as its essence has been established; that [position] is here shown to be untenable. The connection [of the sūtra] arises from the doubt that, if [the passage] refers to the Supreme Self, there would be an excess in the number. From two words meaning "five," the number ten would result. How can there be a relationship of qualifier and qualified between two words denoting equal numbers, and how is the doctrine of the Sāṃkhya system established? To this he says: "This has been stated."
The sense is that the cognition of twenty-seven principles, including the self and space, is logical because it is accepted that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are distinct substances.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), "multiplicity" (*nānātva*) is intended to mean distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), otherness (*anyatva*), and not plurality (*bahutva*). This is because *vinā*, *nā*, *ahiruk*, and *pṛthak* are recited as synonyms. When time functions as a qualifier of another entity, there are twenty-six [categories]; when another entity is intended to be expressed independently, there are twenty-seven. Regarding the phrase "in five": for a collection is indeed the state of being grasped by a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); the meaning is that this is not the case here. The verbal refutation has been stated [by the opponent] with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). The substance-ness (*dravyatva*) of existence (*sattva*) and the other qualities is unestablished, because they possess the nature of qualities (*guṇatva*). 11.
Who, then, are those five people? To this he says: "The vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth, because of the remainder of the passage" (1.4.12).
"The breath of breath, and the eye of the eye..."—thus it is understood that the five persons (*pañcajanāḥ*) are none other than the five [vital functions] beginning with breath. 12.
He raises a doubt regarding the subsequent sūtra with the words "But who [are they]? [The answer is: "The vital breaths and so forth, because of the remainder of the passage. This is clear. 12.
Now, it might be argued: "For the Kāṇvas and the Mādhyandinas... for some, there is [the meditation] 'with light' when food is absent" (1.4.13).
In the reading of certain Kaṇva reciters... it is established that there is no comprehension of the principles (tattvas) as established in the Sāṃkhya system of Kapila. || 13 ||

He raises the doubt regarding the immediately preceding Sūtra with the words, "Now, it might be argued. [The objection is: "In the case of some [schools] where food is absent, how can there be a mention of the four [elements] in the supplementary passage? To this he replies: "Of them... What is the meaning of the term "by light" (*jyotiṣā*), and how is the understanding of the sense organs [to be explained]? To this he replies: "This has been stated... The phrase "by light" is a reference to the actual form of the word; for it is not possible to indicate [the sense organs] by means of the word "light" alone. This [objection] applies equally even to our own established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The explanation of the eyes and other organs by their own specific names is intended to indicate the section on the sense organs (*indriya-prakaraṇa*) and the force of the natural meaning of the three terms. Their number as five is based on the specific enumeration. The determination that the thread is the material cause (*upādāna*) follows from the qualities of luminosity (*jyotiṣṭva*), the number five, and the remaining connection with the mind (*manoyoga*). He states the conclusion: "Thus, therefore" (*tadevam*). He concludes by stating the purpose of the two-fold refutation: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 13 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the inclusion of the number [five]. 3.
And because of the statement as it was declared regarding space and the rest, by way of being the cause. 1.4.14.
Again, the proponent of the doctrine of primordial matter (pradhāna) as the cause objects... [omitted] ...therefore it is determined that Brahman alone is the single cause of the world. || 14 ||

The theory of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause has been refuted. The connection [of this section] arises from the objection that "that is incorrect. Furthermore, regarding space and the other elements, it is stated that they proceed from a single cause as previously described. "From one" means from a single-natured source. The phrase "as in the case of Brahman" is a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), he states the thesis—which has been brought to fruition by the word "and" (*ca*)—as "from the Omniscient One. He says "origin and so forth" (*janmādi*) in order to exclude the sense of being "designated as such" (*vyapadiṣṭatva*) that appears in the scripture with the phrase "as it has been designated. [The term] "in ether and so forth" refers to ether and the other elements. 14.
But surely—“In the beginning this was non-existent... [is not the case], because of the subsequent reference (samākarṣa). 1.4.15.
Even in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," [it is shown that this is not the case]; therefore, it is established that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. || 15 ||

Because of the drawing together [of all things]. With the intention of referring to such passages as "by the wise Brahman," the qualities of being "wise" (*vipaścit*) and so forth are stated; this is clear. To the objection that it is also logical for the Pradhāna to enter into the effects, he says: "entered within. To exclude the suspicion that it might have been manifested by another, he explains: "that very same [Brahman] as undivided. (15)
Thus concludes the section on being the cause—4.
On account of the mention of the world [in the word "Self"]. 1.4.16.
The Sāṃkhya again objects: even though... these conscious attributes are established in this very [pradhāna], it is pradhāna alone, thus presided over, that is the cause of the world.

"Because of the mention of the world. He states the connection [between this and the previous section] with the words "Even though," etc. "Not something else" means "not the Lord. Since the previous section (the *Īkṣati-adhikaraṇa*) was raised as an objection against the present one (*Ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa*), the objection here is effectively established. For agency consists in possessing the karma that is the cause of the production of those respective things; therefore, if it were said that he is "the maker of men," the statement "of whom this is the karma" would be redundant. Furthermore, he says "This is the meaning" regarding the point that the nature of a bound soul is not to be taught [as the Supreme Self].

The state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) is the state of having performed action (*kṛtimattva*). The pure nature [of the Self] is unknown; rather, its connection with karma is merely a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*); this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "from this Self the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) [proceed]," in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the word *prāṇa* refers to the vital breath consisting of the five functions. Regarding the phrase "in this *prāṇa*," he offers an alternative interpretation to avoid the charge that the word *prāṇa* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇikatva*): "Or else... Having raised the possibility that it refers to the Supreme Self, he says: "of the word *prāṇa*..."
This being the position, we reply: "Because it denotes the world. ... It is well known that the Supreme Brahman alone is taught here as the object to be known. (16)

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), he makes his formal declaration with the words "here," etc., stating the qualifying attributes that justify the natural sense of the terms "agent" and so forth within his own position. He says "of the person" (*puruṣasya*) because the state of being unknown belongs to the essential nature that is devoid of connection with karma; the meaning is that when a word denoting a connection with karma has as its referent a nature devoid of that [connection], it functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). He states another reason for the term's referring to the world with the words "of whom," etc. He explains the purpose of the separate mention with the words "those which among these," etc.

Regarding the phrase "from the origination of the world": the point is that a potter’s status as the maker of a jar does not belong to one who merely possesses the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) for the employment of the jar. Regarding the word "well-known" (*prasiddham*): because of the use of the relative pronoun *yat*, the meaning is that the well-known cause—just as in the passage "from which indeed these [beings arise]" (*yato vā imāni*)—is restated as a basis for the injunction concerning that which is to be known. || 16 ||

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [meant here] because of the characteristic marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), that has already been explained. (1.4.17)

Now, as for what was said—on account of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the mention of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa)—the mention of the vital breath is a fit mark for the purpose of meditating upon Brahman whose body is the vital breath. || 17 ||

Now, having restated the reason found in the subsequent passage, he replies: "If it be argued that [Brahman is not the subject] because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), that has already been explained. To the question—how was it resolved in the Pratardana-vidyā, what is the portion to be extended there, and how does that apply here—he says: "This has been stated," ending with the words "are to be described. By this, the portion to be extended is stated; the meaning is that it is not the fact of being for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanārthatva*) that must be extended. For this very reason, there is no mention of the mark of the individual soul being for that purpose. || 17 ||

Regarding how, then, those [passages] containing the marks of a living being can have Brahman as their ultimate purport, [the Sūtrakāra] says: "But Jaimini [holds them to be for another purpose], on account of the question and the answer; and thus also some [readings]. (1.4.18)
The word "but" (tu) [is used] because of the mention of the individual soul (jīva); it is established that the causality of the sentence is not perceived anywhere in the Vedānta. || 18 ||

He states the doubt regarding the subsequent sūtra: "of the marks of the individual soul" (*jīvaliṅgānām*). But Jaimini [holds that it is] for another purpose, on account of both the question and the explanation; and thus some [also maintain].

The word "tu" (but), and so forth: it does not intend to provide another interpretation according to a different school of thought; rather, its meaning is that it serves to exclude the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). The two questions, "Where is this? and "Or where [is he]?", concern the states of dream and deep sleep. "The vital breaths" refers to the individual souls (*jīvas*). Regarding the phrase "of the channels": the sense is that since the preceding sentence, which deals with the dream state, mentions the channels prior to the statement "when one has fallen asleep."

"Taking consciousness by means of consciousness"—this means taking knowledge along with the mind, [referring to] the mind as it ceases its activity toward each sense organ. Because there is no co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the Supreme Self and its attributes, the scriptural mention of the individual soul (*jīva*) is not stated for the purpose of meditation. He concludes the resolution of the marks pertaining to the individual soul with the words "therefore. He concludes the failure to establish that the Vedāntas have as their ultimate purport both primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*) with the words "consequently. || 18 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the world-denoting nature [of the term "Self"], based on the connection of the sentence:
*Vākyānvayāt* (Sūtra 1.4.19).

Here too, since [the scripture] speaks of the very *puruṣa* established in the *Kāpila-tantra*—being intent on making known the principle of *puruṣa* as established in that *tantra*—it follows that *prakṛti* alone, presided over by him, is the material cause of the world, and not the Lord (*īśvara*).

Because of the connection with the sentence (*vākyānvayāt*). The objection that the statement of the essential nature devoid of karma by means of a word denoting one who is subject to karma is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), and thus the [prima facie] view that the passage refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) has been refuted. Here, however, the connection [of the discussion] arises from the doubt: "Since the word *ātman* is heard here as common to both the bound and the liberated, and since the marks of the liberated are heard, it is appropriate that the passage refers to that [Brahman]. Alternatively, the connection arises from the doubt: "In the previous [section], the connection with karma was not to be interpreted otherwise because the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) was heard. The sense is that the word *vijñātṛ* (the knower) refers to the individual soul because it is supported by the mark of the soul in the phrase "the knower" (*vijñātāram*). This is clear.
This being the case, we reply: "On account of the connection of the sentences. All these qualities are possible only in the Supreme Self; therefore, He alone is the subject to be established here.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), [the term] *samañjasaḥ* means "natural" (*svārasika*). With the intention that this naturalness consists in having the same meaning as other scriptural passages of the same class, he says, "that very [Self]" (*tameva*). Regarding the point that naturalness arises from having the same meaning as the passage concerning Prajāpati and others, he says, "the Supreme Person" (*paramapuruṣa*). The meaning is that naturalness consists in having the same meaning as the principal passage which refers to the ultimate reality. Thus, the naturalness of the opening statement has been shown.

He demonstrates the consistency of the subsequent statements which assert causality and teach oneness with the words "tathā" (thus), and so forth. In this context, the word *etat* (this) is used in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) in place of the word *idam* (this) found in the Śruti. He shows that [the teaching of oneness] would otherwise be untenable due to the individual soul's lack of oneness, by saying "for that which is denoted by the word *idam*," and so forth. The meaning is that because the gross and subtle bodies composed of consciousness and non-consciousness do not exist [in the soul], oneness with the world as an effect is impossible. For this very reason—namely, because everything has the Supreme Self as its essence.
As for what was stated—that one who follows after those dear things such as husband, wife, son, wealth, cattle, and so forth... it is taught that he is to be seen as none other than the Supreme Self.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yat tu" and so forth: [the opponent asks] how there is a lack of syntactical connection (*ananvaya*), or how that [lack of connection] is undesirable. To this, he says: "The Self, indeed... (*ātmā vai*). The meaning is that the suitability of the Self as the object to be seen (*draṣṭavya*) is understood from the natural sense of the preceding sentence. He demonstrates the lack of syntactical connection if [the Self] were taken as the individual soul (*jīva*) by means of the passage beginning with "ātmanaḥ. In the Śruti, the word *priya* refers to being worthy of enjoyment. "For the sake of desire" (*kāmāya*) means for the sake of pleasure (*prīti*). It does not mean that the husband and others are subordinate to the Self, such that the husband and others would possess the status of being objects of love.

The meaning is that the fitness of the husband and others for enjoyment is not due to their being causes of pleasure for him, but rather due to their being causes of pleasure for himself. "Vākya-bheda" means a split in the great sentence (mahāvākya). "So 'yam" and so forth; "being himself unsurpassed bliss"—the point is that for one who brings bliss to those dependent on him, his own state of unsurpassed bliss is established as a matter of course. This is also because it is clearly stated as such in other Śrutis. The intended meaning (tātparyārtha) has been stated by the passage ending with "upadiśyate."

Thus, the meaning is this: "Verily, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear... the Self, indeed, is to be seen"—by the method previously stated, the two occurrences of the word "Self" (ātman) in both passages refer to one and the same subject. || 19 ||

To the question, "How is this [text] verbal (śābda)? he says: "The meaning of this is as follows. Even if the reference is to the individual soul (jīva), the syntactical connection (anvaya) is possible. If it were argued that because of His sovereignty He takes up wives and so forth for His own pleasure, He would not act for the sake of experiencing non-eternal bliss such as that of a wife, but rather for the sake of experiencing His own nature which is eternal bliss; in response to this doubt, he states the second resolution: "Even if the reference is to the individual self (jīvātman)."

The meaning is that because [the bliss of the individual soul] is even more excellent than that of the individual soul (jīva), one would be motivated toward attaining the Supreme Self; this is the more appropriate sense. To the doubt, "In that case, this alone would be the resolution," he says: "But in this [case]," etc. This means according to the manner of the sūtra to be cited later, namely, "Because of the designation of the Supreme Self itself. The impossibility of a difference in meditative absorption (samādhi) is intended as the reason. For this very reason, the idea that the first occurrence of the word *ātman* refers to the Supreme Self through an intermediary (sadvāraka) is unsatisfactory.
Therefore, the two occurrences of the word *ātman* in the preceding and following sentences have as their object Brahman without an intermediary (advāraka). ||19||

To demonstrate that even according to another opinion the word *jīva* can denote the Supreme Self, he says: "Āśmarathya [holds] that it is a sign for the fulfillment of the initial proposition. (1.4.10)
Since the proposition that all cognitions are [identical with] a single cognition is established, the term "living being" (jīva) denotes the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 20 ||

He introduces the immediately following sūtra with the words "according to another opinion": "Āśmarathya [holds that] there is a mark for the establishment of the proposition. This means: because the unity produced by the causal relationship—which serves to support the proposition—is established. || 20 ||
Auḍulomi [holds that the soul] will attain this state only when it is about to depart [from the body]. (1.4.21)

As for what was stated—that because the individual soul (jīva) is an effect of Brahman, it is one with Brahman, and thus the Supreme Self is denoted by the word "jīva"—this is the view held by the teacher Auḍulomi. || 21 ||

"Audulomi [holds that the soul departs] because it is about to attain such a state. Since this view is not inconsistent with what preceded it, [the author] states the refutation of the previous opinion intended by the Sūtra, beginning with the words "As for what was said," and so forth. This is clear.
"Because of the abiding [of the Self in all beings], so says Kāśakṛtsna. (1.4.22)

As it has been said: "Because the individual soul (jīva) attains the state of Brahman upon departing... it is established that neither the Person (puruṣa) nor the primordial nature (prakṛti) presided over by him [is the cause]. || 22 ||

"Because of the abiding [of the world in Brahman], thus says Kāśakṛtsna. This is clear. He states the difference from the view of Kāśakṛtsna with the word "thus" (*evam*). The sense is that [Bādarāyaṇa] accepted [this view] because no other opinion is mentioned and because this [view] possesses consistency (*sāmañjasya*). Specifically, he accepted it by saying, "Thus indeed does Bādarāyaṇa [hold]. This is the intention.

In this context, [the author] states "this here" (*ayam atra*) to address what word denotes the living being (*jīva*) and how, by that means, there is the designation of the Supreme (*para*). "For the sake of encouragement" (*protsāhanāya*) means that activity would be more intense due to the knowledge that one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is attainable. "Having unified" (*ekīkṛtya*)—the sense is that the prefix *sam-* implies unification. As for the passage beginning with "where indeed," the statement "by what, whom? (*tat kena kam*) is a negation of a seer who is not that [Self], as well as the object of sight and its instruments.

The statement "by whom this [is known]" has as its primary purport that it is difficult to comprehend without his grace. The statement "the knower" has as its primary purport that such grace is difficult to obtain without the aforementioned means. He concludes with the word "therefore. || 22 ||
Thus concludes the section on the syntactical connection of the statements (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa) – 6.
And the material cause [of the world], because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. (1.4.23)

Thus, when the Sāṃkhya system without a Lord has been refuted, the Sāṃkhya with a Lord [is considered]: [the Lord] is not the material cause; rather, the material cause is primordial matter (pradhāna) itself presided over by Him.

"And [Brahman] is the material cause (prakṛti), because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. He states the connection [of this sūtra] with the words "In this way. He states the presumptive implication (arthāpatti) of the scripture with the words "Even though it is not so heard. He states the supporting reasoning for the scripture with the words "In this very manner. To the objection that even if there were a difference in kind (*vaijātya*), either a scorpion or cow-dung could be the material cause of a scorpion, and likewise either *prakṛti* or God (*īśvara*) could be the material cause of the world—since scripture speaks of each one as a cause—he replies with the words "And the accomplishment of the effect."

To the question, "How can that which is established by scripture be abandoned? he says: "In this way. A statement supported by reasoning is more powerful than the other; the other, however, is like the statement regarding the identity of the sacrificial post and the sun—this is the meaning.

This being the case, it is replied: "And [the cause] is primordial matter (prakṛti), because that would not contradict the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. ... It is designated by such passages as, "The unborn, one, ignorant mother of transformations," and so forth.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), it is stated—"and the material cause" (*upādānaṃ ca*)—in order to exclude the nature of the Pradhāna. By stating "and" (*ca*), the sūtra expresses the meaning of the sentence as a whole: "not the efficient cause" (*na nimitta*). Up to the words "it would be already known" (*vijñātameva syāt*), the terms expressing the reason are explained. Anticipating the objection that the proposition (*pratijñā*) is untenable according to the Vaiśeṣika doctrine, and thereby resolving it, he states the meaning of the sentence: "the cause itself" (*kāraṇameva*).

In order to dispel the suspicion that there might be another [intended] meaning, he restates the opponent's argument—"that which..."—and refutes it with "that is incorrect. To exclude the possibility that [the word] refers to the instruction or its object, he explains the base and the suffix: "by means of this, one is instructed. Although the lack of natural appropriateness is equal in either case, he states "of this" (*etasya*) because the sense is more fitting; for the status of being an instructor (*śāsitṛtva*) is indeed unique [to the Lord]. Anticipating the objection that the suffix might have an agentive sense, he says "the accomplisher" (*sādhaka*); the intention is that this follows the maxim: "The grammatical relations (*kārakas*) are determined by the speaker's intention."

Even in the causal statement, he demonstrates the identity of the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*) with the words "Being alone" (*sadeva*). By the word "primordial matter" (*prakṛti*)—that is, by the term denoting primordial matter—he shows that the two statements, "All this indeed" and "But where [it is] one," refer to having that [Being] as their essence through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). If there is nothing apart from Brahman, then the defects of modification (*vikāra*) and lack of ultimate purpose (*apuruṣārtha*) would apply to Brahman; to this he replies with "This has been said. If so, what is the difference between the states of effect and cause? To this he replies with "At certain times. What follows from this for the subject at hand? To this he replies with "Thus at all times."

But is it not the case that "the Great merges into the Unmanifest, and the Unmanifest merges into the Imperishable"? Therefore, Brahman alone is both the efficient cause and the material cause of the world. || 23 ||

He raises an objection by way of its arising, even regarding that which is in a subtle state, with the words "But surely... (nanu ca). This is because a subtle state is possible even for the unmanifest state. [The opponent holds that] Brahman, characterized by consciousness in that state, is the unmanifest cause. He refutes this with "This is not so" (naiṣa). He states the proof for this: "When darkness... (yadā tamaḥ). For this very reason—because consciousness, which is denoted by the word "darkness," exists at that time. If the substance of the Supreme Self were to become [merely] the state of darkness through the abandonment of its specific conditions, like [the abandonment of] the state of being earth and so forth, then the term "dissolution" (laya) would be heard [in scripture].

Nor has it been heard [otherwise]. Therefore, the meaning is that darkness resides within it. Even though there is a distinction between entities, the use of the singular word is appropriate because [the distinction] is unmanifest, as in the case of wood containing fire, or as in the case of a pregnant woman. By the phrase "this has become darkness," it is made clear that dissolution (*laya*) is simply the attainment of another state, not the destruction of the substance; this is further clarified by the passage beginning with "and water in the state of fire."

With the words "But that which... and so forth, the refutation of the opponent's argument regarding the superiority of scripture supported by reasoning is stated. Regarding the phrase "of clay, etc.": the meaning is that if [Brahman] were merely the efficient cause, or merely the material cause, or if it required many auxiliary factors, there would be limiting adjuncts such as non-omniscience, lack of omnipotence, and unreality of resolve. || 23 ||
And because of the teaching regarding covetousness. (1.4.24)
For this reason as well, both are Brahman alone: "He desired... for creation is taught as being preceded by volition (saṅkalpa). || 24 ||
And because of the teaching on covetousness; this is clear. 24.
And because both are directly recorded [in scripture]. (1.4.25)

It has not been refuted [by us] merely by means of propositions, examples, desires, or instructions that Brahman alone is both the material cause and the instrumental causes; therefore, Brahman is both. || 25 ||
And because both are explicitly mentioned. He states the purpose of the statement in the form of a question and answer: "For here... (25).
Because of the act of self-creation. (1.4.26)
"He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate'... He made himself thus by himself"; thus [the Self] is both the efficient cause and the material cause. || 26 ||

Regarding "because of being made by itself": its own status as an agent is contradictory. Anticipating the objection that there is a contradiction between the established [status] of an agent and the task to be accomplished (sādhya) of an effect for a single entity, he resolves it by means of a distinction in form—namely, "undivided. Because the effect is non-different [from the cause], he states the identity of the efficient cause (nimitta) and the material cause (upādāna) with the words "by itself."
"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite; Brahman is bliss... [because of] transformation. (1.4.27)
Because its nature is transformation; for that which is being taught here, [transformation] is both logically established and observed, owing to its beginninglessness.

He raises a doubt regarding the immediately preceding Sūtra with the words "truth, knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*). Regarding the phrase "because of transformation" (*pariṇāmāt*), he anticipates the objection that this would constitute a contradictory reason and therefore says, "because of the nature of transformation" (*pariṇāmasvābhāvyāt*). To the point that it is indeed the very nature [of Brahman] that constitutes the cause of contradiction, he replies, "not here" (*nātra*). In response to the expectation of how this is so, he explains by stating, "for it is exactly thus" (*evameva hi*).

Showing that, like the creation of the sequence of principles (*tattva-krama*) and like the qualities (*guṇa*) useful for it, the state of being mediated by another (*sadvārakatva*), though not explicitly stated, is to be understood from elsewhere, he declares that the Śrutis concerning the Pradhāna culminate in the Supreme with the words "Without remainder" (*aśeṣa*). The phrase "even as its own body" (*svaśarīratayā api*) is an explanation of the word "one" (*eka*). He states the authority for this stated meaning with the words "In the same way" (*tathaiva*). It is called "darkness" (*tamas*) because it is an obscuration; it is called "death" (*mṛtyu*) because it is the root of evil. He uses the term "non-distinction" (*avibhāga*) to exclude identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*).
Thus, because it cannot be designated as distinct from itself, [the world] is by the Supreme Self... Therefore, Brahman alone is both the efficient cause and the material cause of the world. || 27 ||

He states the meaning established by the cited scripture with the words, "Thus from itself. Then, in response to the doubt as to what follows regarding the contradiction under discussion, he takes up the sentence from this very section which reveals the contradiction, in order to explain it later without conflict: "Truth, Knowledge... He explains the words to be interpreted with the word "here," [noting that] the verbal root *tap* means "to contemplate" (*ālocana*).

He states the meaning of the sentences within that context as supported by other scriptural passages (*śrutyantara*) with the words: "Thus, this is the meaning. He explains the meaning of the constituent sentence among the cited passages with: "That very [Self]... He explains how the contradiction is resolved with: "In this way... And he states the absence of the defect of being an effect with: "In the Supreme Self," etc. He provides the authority for the sport-creation of one whose desires are fulfilled with: "All [beings]," etc. He states the meaning of the scripture cited by the opponent clearly with: "From this," etc.

This Sūtra is opposed to those who maintain that [the world] is illusory. Even in the view of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*), transformation occurs through the aspect of the object of experience (*bhogyāṃśa*); whereas in our own view, it occurs through the aspect of the qualification (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*). Thus, the lack of natural elegance (*asvārasya*) is equal [in both cases]. However, there is a distinction: [our view] possesses the further advantage of being in greater conformity with the logical consistency of other scriptural passages (*śruti*). || 27 ||
For it is indeed proclaimed as the source (yoni). || 1-4-28 ||
Furthermore, Brahman is both the efficient cause and the material cause of the world, as is understood from the supplementary passage: "Just as a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web]. (Sūtra 1.4.28)
For the womb is indeed sung [in the scriptures]; this is clear. || 28 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the primordial nature (prakṛti).
By this, all [objections] have been explained—yes, they have been explained. (1.4.29)

By this—that is, by the collection of logical arguments stated in the four quarters [of the chapter]—[the objections] are explained. The repetition of the word "iti" is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter. || 29 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the explanation of all [scriptures]—8.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
And the chapter is completed.

By this, all [sections] have been explained; they have been explained. To exclude the notion that these are merely a supplement to the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), he says: "In the [fourth] quarter" (*pāde*).

The additional doubt is that the causality of Hiraṇyagarbha, Rudra, and others—such as Indra—is possible. The resolution is that since there is no difference in the scriptural testimony regarding their being created by and subject to the dissolution by the Supreme Self, the *Atharvaśiras* and other such texts refer to the Supreme Self as having them as His body. He states the purpose of the repetition of the word [“Self”] with the words: “They have been explained. (29)
Thus concludes the section concerning the explanation of all [scriptures]—Section 8.

This is the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Śrutapradīpikā*, composed by Śrī Sudarśanasūri—the ornament of the illustrious Harit lineage, son of Vāgvijayin, who bore the secondary name Vedavyāsa by the divine command of Śrī Raṅgarāja, and who attained the heart of the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śrī Bhagavadrāmānuja through service at the feet of the venerable Varadācārya.
And the chapter is completed.
The first quarter of the second chapter.
If it be argued that this leads to the fault of leaving no room for the Smṛti, we say no; because that would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis. (2.1.1)

In the first chapter, [it was shown that Brahman is] beyond the scope of means of knowledge such as perception; regarding this, the following objection is raised: "If it be argued that there would be the defect of rendering the Smṛtis irrelevant."

If it be argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis, we say no, because that would lead to the fault of leaving no room for [other] Smṛtis [that are not contradictory]. He restates the subject matter of the first chapter for the sake of connection and for the sake of easily grasping the initial meaning: "In the first," etc. He states the subject matter of the second: "Immediately thereafter," etc. "Entire" (samasta) is intended to signify the variety of arguments to be refuted by each respective section. The meaning is that in the first chapter, Brahman’s status as the cause was established by excluding non-connection and connection with others; in the second, however, contradictions are resolved.

He states what is to be established in the second [section] and so forth, beginning with the word "first. He raises an objection with "how? and answers with "true. In sentences such as those concerning the *audumbarī* post, since the meaning of the Veda is determined independently of logic (*nyāya*), it is appropriate to disregard Smṛti that contradicts it. Here, however, because there is a diversity of Śruti texts and the meaning of the Veda is subject to doubt, it is not possible to reject Smṛti on the grounds of contradiction; therefore, investigation is appropriate—this is the meaning.

What is the proof for Kapila’s status as a great seer (*maharṣi*)? Even if that were granted, why should it not be like the Lokāyata and other systems taught by Bṛhaspati and others? To this he replies with the words "this has been said," because [Kapila's system] has been determined by the previously stated primary principle and thus does not depend on *smṛti*.

By the phrase ending with "abhyupagacchatā" (by one who accepts), the exclusion of the Lokāyata and other such systems is stated. "The Seer" (*ṛṣim*) is a statement regarding his authority (*māna*). "Smṛtyupabṛṃhaṇam" means reinforcement in the form of *smṛti*. By the words "by those of little learning" (*alpaśrutaiḥ*) and so forth, the dependence upon that [scripture] is shown. The sense is that there is no independence from *smṛti* on the basis of logic (*nyāya*), because logic is weak when in conflict with a scriptural statement. "Of the whole" (*sakalāyāḥ*) excludes the *smṛtis* of Manu and others, because they possess room for interpretation (*sāvakāśatvāt*). It is improper for this [text], being composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*), to lack such room for interpretation. He states that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not in accordance with the Sūtra: "This very... (*tadidam*).

To this, the reply is: "No, because it would result in the consequence that there is no room for other Smṛtis. For other [Smṛtis]... since there is the possibility of establishing the meaning of the Śruti through the Lokāyata system composed by him (Cārvāka). || 1 ||

He introduces the section on refutation with the words "In that regard, the reply. In order to establish His state as the supreme cause—so that He may be worshipped through all ritual acts and proven to be the self of all deities who constitute the effects—the state of dissolution is described prior to creation in accordance with the *Subāla Upaniṣad*: "It existed" (*āsīt*). This world was "consisting of darkness" (*tamobhūtam*), meaning it was in a state of darkness, just as [the term] is used in the sense of water being in the state of fire. It was "unperceived" (*aprajñātam*), meaning it was beyond the range of direct perception of its excellent form. Why? Because it was "without marks" (*alakṣaṇam*).

The meaning is that [the cause] is devoid of characteristics such as sound, touch, and form. To the objection that the cause must also possess specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) in order for the qualities of the effect to be established, he says: "uninferable" (apratarkya), meaning beyond the scope of logical reasoning; "unknowable" (avijñeya), meaning impossible to know by means of analysis; and "it becomes one with darkness," meaning it exists in an undifferentiated state, as stated in the scripture.

He dispels the doubt that [the world] is identical in essence [to Brahman], as it were, while remaining dormant—as if in deep sleep, having entered an extremely subtle state unfit for distinct empirical usage. He states the difference from ordinary sleep with the word "from all sides" (*sarvataḥ*). Then—when the time for creation has arrived—"Self-existent" (*svayaṃbhūḥ*) excludes the existence of any other cause. "The Blessed One" (*bhagavān*) is a designation of a specific deity, based on both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), denoting the perfection of attributes necessary for the act of creation.

In order to manifest this individual effect (vyaṣṭi-kārya), He—possessing knowledge in the form of His own volition directed toward the objects of the Great Principle (mahat) and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which are the primordial elements of the gross elements (mahābhūta)—appeared, impelling the quality of darkness (tamas) for that purpose, with the unmanifest state of Prakṛti as His body. His state as the Imperishable (akṣara) is also established by implication.

In order to dispel the suspicion of contradiction regarding His being free from defects and so forth—which might arise from the notion that He undergoes transformation of His own essential nature (svarūpa)—He says, "from the body, which is Himself" (śarīrāt svāt). The word *ap* (water) is intended to indicate the causal principle of the egg (the cosmic egg); for it has been stated that [the Lord] possesses the power residing in the great elements and so forth. "Vīrya" refers to the capacity to produce the egg generated by the process of triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa); for it has been said that "in its absence, He was unable to create living beings. The seven verses beginning with "This existed" (āsīdidam) should be considered here. The passage beginning with "I am the whole" (ahaṃ kṛtsnasya) is clear.

The Smṛtis of Manu and others have their scope, and Kapila is a trustworthy authority (*āpta*). It has already been stated that supplementation (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) is required. To the question, "How can one discard that Smṛti and adopt another? he says: "This is the meaning. "An established fact" (*bhūtārtha*) means an accomplished reality (*siddhārtha*). The sense is that, as with a matter of action (*kāryarūpa*), a contradiction is difficult to maintain; therefore, the abandonment of one of them is inevitable. By the term "most trustworthy" (*āptatama*), what is intended is the quality of speaking exactly as one has seen, accompanied by seeing things as they truly are.

In the case of Kapila, there is only the status of being a seer (*ṛṣi*); here, there is merely authoritative attainment (*āpti*). However, because both [status and attainment] exist in the case of Manu and others—as evidenced by the statement, "Whatever Manu said is medicine"—they are the most authoritative (*āptatama*). Thus, the three points of distinction have been stated: that [the Purāṇas] were composed by many, are endowed with logic, and so forth. He states another reason as well: "and they provide supplementary elaboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*)."

The passage beginning with "na ca" and so forth is clear. For while the rites that are auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*) consist in the worship of the Blessed Lord, those [rites] whose fruits are heaven and the like lack that character; therefore, they do not have as their ultimate purport (*tātparya*) Brahman, who is the object of worship. To this he says: "Nor [are they] for the sake of this world. This is self-evident.
