Regarding what was stated, beginning with "it has been said," etc.: even if one accepts the authority of the Śruti, since the contradiction with the meaning of the Śruti is the reason for its disregard, this applies equally to the systems of Kapila and the Lokāyata; thus, the meaning is that they must both be abandoned. || 1 ||
Now, it might be argued: [the knowledge of Kapila exists] by virtue of his own greatness of yoga... and because it is not perceived in others. (2-1-2)
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of the word "tu" (but/however)... it is established that the meaning of the Vedānta as described cannot be shaken by that [objection]. || 2 ||

He raises the doubt regarding the subsequent sūtra with the words, "Now, it might be argued" (*atha syāt*). The sense is that since Manu and others were intent upon the promulgation of Dharma, there was no occasion for Yoga; furthermore, [the teachings] of others are not perceived. The certainty that a single perception is erroneous arises from its conflict with the perceptions of many. However, devotion to the practice of Dharma is the cause of mental purity, which is the reason for the strength of the perceptions of Manu and others. The absence of that [devotion], due to mental impurity, leads to error—this is the meaning. ||2||
Thus concludes the section on Smṛti (Sūtra 1).
By this, Yoga is also refuted (Sūtra 2-1-3).
By this refutation of the Smṛti of Kapila... it is not proper that the Vedānta be supplemented by it. || 3 ||

By this, Yoga is refuted. Having stated the literal meaning, he states the intended meaning in response to the doubt with the word "Yoga. By the phrase "not having Brahman as its self," the disparity in principle is stated; by the phrase "consisting of meditation," the disparity in practice is stated. || 3 ||
Thus ends the section on the refutation of Yoga (Sūtra 2.1.3). Now, Sūtra 2.1.4:
"Not so, because of its being of a different nature; and that [different nature] is established by scripture."
Furthermore, the proponent of the contradiction with memory, relying upon reasoning, says: "This is not so, because even there, the causal relationship pertains only to the insentient portion. (4)

"It is not so, because this [Smṛti] is of a different character, and its validity is due to the Word [of the Veda]. It has been stated that the Vedas must be supplemented by the Smṛtis of Manu and others; however, those [Smṛtis] are contradicted by reasoning (*tarka*). The connection [of the present sūtra] arises from the objection that the supplementation should be performed solely by the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, which is supported by reasoning. He explains the word "not" (*na*) in the sūtra with the word "that which" (*yat*). The word "of this" (*asya*) is what is to be explained. He explains the phrase "because of its being of a different character" (*vilakṣaṇatvāt*) with the words "according to your own view" (*bhavadabhimata*).

He explains the portion of the sūtra beginning with "tathātva" by saying "not merely. To the question "What follows from that?", he says "For that which... [is sublated]. Regarding the point that reasoning (tarka) is sublated by scripture (śāstra), he says "And necessarily... "Independent" means not depending on other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). For reasoning is not itself a means of valid cognition; therefore, the meaning is that it is required because it serves as an auxiliary (aṅga). "In some cases" refers to those instances where the object is not clear in itself.

He states that reasoning (*tarka*) has no effect whatsoever upon the means of valid knowledge (*māna*) with the words "For reasoning... (*tarko hi*). The word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "But of the scripture" (*śāstrasya tu*) indicates a difference in the object to be established (*sādhya-vaiṣamya*). The word "especially" (*viśeṣeṇa*) indicates a difference in the means of establishment (*sādhana-vaiṣamya*). [Objection: There is no perception of consciousness during deep sleep, yet its capacity [to manifest] is admitted both by the Vedists and others. How then can there be a requirement for a determination through cognition regarding jars and the like based on the statement that Brahman is the material cause? To this he replies: "For between two dissimilar things... (*vilakṣaṇayor hi*). The sense is that it is like the identity of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sun. The doubt that dissimilarity is unestablished is raised and refuted by the passage beginning with "What then? (*kiṃ punaḥ*). The charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) is addressed by the passage beginning with "But surely... (*nanu ca*). || 4 ||
Now, it might be argued: "Even for those things regarded as insentient... [the designation of a presiding deity] is due to the distinction and the conformity [of the individual soul]. (2.1.5)

The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of removing the suspicion that has been raised... [namely,] that the world's having Pradhāna as its material cause is what is propounded by the Vedāntas—thus [ends the objection]. || 5 ||

He raises a doubt regarding the immediately preceding Sūtra, saying: "Now it might be [objected]... The phrase "But the designation is based on the presiding deities (abhimānin)" is intended to remove the doubt raised [in the previous Sūtra], and not for the purpose of refuting a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa); this is the sense. This is clear. || 5 ||
This being the case, it is replied: "But it is seen. (Sūtra 2.1.6)
By the word "tu" (but), the position is reversed: [the transformation] is observed in cases such as honey, cow-dung worms, scorpions, and so forth. || 6 ||

But it is clearly seen; moreover, the similarity (sālakṣaṇya) asserted by the opponent is easily refuted, because the state of being an effect belongs precisely to that which is qualified by both consciousness and non-consciousness. Thus, the rule of similarity asserted by the opponent is now broken. || 6 ||
If it be argued that [the world] does not exist, we say no, because [that statement] is a mere negation. (2.1.7)

If the cause is [inferred] from the world which is its effect... and even though there is a difference in their characteristics, there is indeed a unity of substance, just as between a bracelet and gold. || 7 ||

If it is argued that [the object] does not exist, we say no, because it is a mere negation. The meaning is that identity of substance is not negated; rather, what is negated is the rule of similarity and fitness for recognition. || 7 ||
Here he raises an objection: "Because of the consequence that [the world] would likewise [cease to exist] upon dissolution, [the doctrine] is inconsistent. (2.1.8)

“Also because of [the world] being preceded by dissolution” (apīti)—that is, because creation and so forth are preceded by dissolution—there is an inconsistency in the Vedānta statements regarding the doctrine that Brahman is the cause. || 8 ||

He introduces the subsequent Sūtra with the words "In this regard" (*atra*). [The objection is: "If [the individual soul] were to merge [into Brahman], there would be the undesirable consequence that [Brahman] would likewise [be affected by the soul's qualities]; thus, [the doctrine of creation, etc. is inconsistent. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in "creation, etc.," maintenance is included. He raises an objection regarding the final position (*siddhānta*) with the word "Now" (*atha*). It was stated that [the body] is the locus of activity (*ceṣṭāśrayatva*), as in the phrase "having five functions" (*pañcavṛtti*). The term "abode" (*āyatana*) refers specifically to the means of accomplishment. For this very reason, it was said: "of the mere means for experience. He refutes the definition favored by the proponent of the final position with the words "Now, if it is thought" (*atha matam*). He states the fallacy of under-extension (*avyāpti*) with the words "by being a body" (*śarīratayā*).

He states the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) with the words "sāla" (the sal tree). He states the partial pervasion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśavyāpti*) with the words "of the sentient being" (*cetanasya*). Regarding "action and so forth" (*kriyādiṣu*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), qualities (*guṇa*) are included. || 8 ||
To this, the reply is: "But it is not so, because of the existence of examples" (2.1.9).
There is no such inconsistency; for by these two sūtras, the point established in the section [beginning with] "Because of the designation of the other" (1.1.31) is recalled. || 9 ||

But it is not [the case] because of the existence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). To the question, "In the absence of anything to be abandoned (*heya*), what would be the illustrative example?", he says: "This has been stated. Anticipating the objection that [the qualities] are secondary (*amukhya*), he says: "And yet... [The qualities] such as divinity belong to the waters alone, not to the Person (*puruṣa*); to this he replies: "The subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*)... Regarding the passage "He meditated" (*so 'bhidhyāya*), since the distinction between consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) is not clear there, he says: "From the subtle element..."

The meaning is that [the definition] is established by the statement beginning with "this was" (*āsīdidam*), as it is the subject under discussion. Regarding the passage beginning with "and in the world," etc.: you have stated that the definition of "living being" (*ceṣṭāśrayatva*, "being the locus of movement") applies even to worms, insects, moths, and so forth; however, you did not state "having two feet" (*dvipāttva*) and the like. For when a common, inclusive definition is possible, it is improper to accept one that is non-inclusive. Thus, the meaning is that since a definition applicable to all worldly and Vedic usage is possible, it is incorrect to resort to a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*) in some instances by accepting a non-inclusive definition.
Therefore, the sense is: because a common definition serves as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*), whereas what you have stated is not common.

He states the inclusive definition (*anugatalakṣaṇa*) with the words "of which" (*yasya*). The triad beginning with "being the locus of activity" (*ceṣṭāśrayatva*) is not inclusive; however, this triad of definitions is inclusive. That substance which can be entirely controlled for its own sake by a conscious being is the body of that conscious being; that substance which can be entirely sustained for its own sake by a conscious being is the body of that conscious being.

The distinction is as follows: that substance which belongs to a conscious being and whose sole nature is to exist as a remnant is its body. [The term] "svārthe" means in its own object; "śakye'rthe" means in a possible object. "Sarvātmanā" means by way of persisting as long as the substance exists. In place of this, the word "eka" (one) appears in the third [case]. The third case is mentioned separately because it does not depend on the words "svārtha" and "śakya. By the phrase "of whom" (*yasya*), it is shown that the body, like a father and so forth, is an entity possessing a correlative.

It has been stated that "it is to be governed" (*niyāmyam*) so as to avoid the undesirable consequence that the father and others would [themselves] possess a body merely by virtue of that much. By saying "substance" (*dravyam*), there is an exclusion of action and so forth. By saying "in its entirety" (*sarvātmanā*), there is an exclusion of [limited objects] such as jars. The term "for its own sake" (*svārthe*) is used to exclude the impossibility [of governing for one's own sake] in the case of humans and others, since it is impossible for them to travel through the sky and so on. By saying "capable" (*śakyam*), there is an exclusion of non-pervasion in cases such as a diseased body. By saying "of the conscious being" (*cetanasya*), there is an exclusion of knowledge as a quality (*dharmabhūtajñāna*); for that [knowledge] is not governed by that which is qualified by knowledge.

In the second and third [sections], there is the exclusion of light (*prabhā*); but in the third, by the word "one" (*eka*), there is the exclusion of houses and so forth. Anticipating the objection that defects inherent in being a body might apply, he says: "The subsequent... (verse 9).
And because of the defects in one's own position. (2.1.10)

Not only [is the doctrine of Brahman as the cause untenable], but even if it were accepted, it will be elaborated upon by the statement beginning with "because of the absence of an object" (arthābhāvāt) and so forth. || 10 ||
And because of the defect in their own position; that is to say, because [the Sāṃkhyas] do not admit it, since they maintain that [the Self] is eternal and immutable. || 10 ||
Also because reasoning is not firmly established. (2.1.11)
Furthermore, because everything is non-abiding... the non-abiding nature of reasoning is understood from the mutual contradiction of reasonings. || 11 ||
Also because of the non-establishment of reasoning. This is clear. 11.
If it is argued that the object of inference is otherwise, even so, there follows the consequence of the impossibility of liberation. (2.1.12)

Now, for the purpose of providing logical reasoning (*tarka*) that serves as an elaboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the Vedas by clarifying the meaning of the Vedas for the Śākyas and others existing today, the *Sāṃkhya-smṛti* is not to be respected. || 12 ||

If it is argued that [the objection] is "otherwise inferable," even so, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-liberation (*anirmokṣa*). The meaning is that a counter-argument is possible for a future [objection] by means of another future argument, just as [a past object is countered] by a past one. To dispel the suspicion of Sāṃkhya approval—which arises from the syntactical disparity (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the word "Veda" and "scripture" (*śāstra*)—he says: "named Veda. This is because of the context: "The Veda is the eternal eye... the established state is 'the scripture of the Veda'. (12)
Thus concludes the section on "Having Different Characteristics" (2.1.12).
By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned are also explained. (2.1.13)
The "remnants" (śiṣṭāḥ) are those left over; since there is no [contradiction] because a lack of contradiction is observed, the refutation is that it is indeed non-established. || 13 ||

By this, those [doctrines] not accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) are also explained. He explains [the term] as "the learned" in order to exclude a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*). For it is only when it is a *karmadhāraya* that the Sāṃkhya doctrine's status as being "not accepted by the learned" is established. This refers to its lack of definiteness, its nature of being both true and false, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the fourfold variety and the uniformity [of these defects] are included. (13)
Thus ends the section concerning what is not accepted by the learned (Śiṣṭāparigrahādhikaraṇa). 4.
"If it be argued that there would be no distinction because of the attainment of the state of being an enjoyer, [we reply] it would be as in the world. (2.1.14)

The Sāṃkhya again objects: "As for what was said—that if there were a transformation of its own nature (*svarūpapariṇāma*), Brahman itself would incur the state of being both the enjoyer and the enjoyed, and thus there would once again be an inconsistency."

"If [it is argued that] there would be no distinction because of the attainment of the state of being an enjoyer, [the answer is: it would be as in the world. In the preceding section, the body was cited as an illustration. The connection [of this section] arises from the emergence of a doubt regarding the state of being an enjoyer caused by that [body]. Now, as for the words "But surely... and so forth: it was stated previously that the state of being an enjoyer occurs in proximity to [the Self], like [someone staying] in another's house due to some other business. Here, the meaning is that the state of being an enjoyer is not denied when one possesses ownership of the body. By the phrase "even though modifications such as old age and so forth are impossible," the portion of the previously mentioned illustration that was set aside is addressed.

He states the portion that has not yet been refuted: "In the case of the body," and "It may be as in the world. The defect regarding the causality of Brahman when it possesses a body has been refuted. Now, he answers by way of non-acceptance the defect regarding the causality of Brahman alone, with the examples of clay and gold.

He refutes the aforementioned point restated by the words "But that... with the phrase "that is incorrect. Regarding the expression "and the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)," the word *upādhi* refers here to the limiting adjuncts consisting of power (*śakti*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). This word *ayaṃ* (this) is like the word *vāda* (discourse). To the objection that a non-distinction between the limiting adjunct and that which is limited by it might be suspected, he says: "of two different natures" (*vilakṣaṇayoḥ*). To the claim that the objection and its resolution are appropriate regarding a modification of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), he says: "the essential nature" (*svarūpe*). Why? He says: "not an action" (*na karma*). Having [provisionally] accepted [the opponent's view], he refutes it: "the essential nature" (*svarūpe*).

If it is argued that over time there is a confusion of jars, bowls, and so forth, this same defect applies even to the analogy of foam and waves. Furthermore, whatever defense is offered for that [analogy] must also be applied to the modification of the essential nature (*svarūpa-pariṇāma*). He states the impossibility of avoiding the defects of transformation and its lack of purpose for man, which were mentioned in the previous section, with the words: "In the essential nature... (14).
Thus ends the section on the identity of the enjoyer (Bhoktrāpatti-adhikaraṇa). 5.
"Its non-difference [from Brahman], on account of words such as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa) and others. (2.1.15)
In passages such as "If it be said that it is non-existent, no, because it is a mere negation," its indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva) is established through both perception and sublation.

"The non-difference from that [cause] is established on account of the words concerning 'origination' (ārambhaṇa) and so forth. He states the connection [of the sūtra] with the words "asat" and "saty api. "By way of being useful for the effect"—that is, by way of being useful for effects such as the fetching of water. "And not..."—the meaning is: if the pot were not present in the lump of clay, then the potter would have to take up yarn [instead], since there would be no distinction in the absence of the pot in either case.

"Why is it that the pot exists in the lump of clay and not in the threads? If it is argued that "only the lump of clay is fit for the existence of the pot," then [the author] replies with the intention that "that very thing is fit for its production," using the word "kāraṇe" (in the cause). This is clear. The phrase "they say" means the proponents of a certain school within the Siddhānta.

Intending to explain the meaning of the passage beginning with "a mere modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*), he says: "Therefore, as... The intended reason is the persistence [of the cause] within the modifications (*vikāreṣu*). He states the meaning of "one alone, without a second" (*ekamevādvitīyam*) with: "in that same way. To establish the contrary [case] regarding the effect's being distinct from both existence and non-existence, he says: "from the existent. He states that being other than both existent and non-existent is the positive concomitant reason (*anvayihetu*) for its falsity (*mithyātva*) with: "and it is indefinable. He shows the probative property in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) with: "and of that..."

Furthermore, if the causal substance such as clay were to produce its effect [as being non-different from itself], there would be no distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), or between the bound and the liberated, nor between the disciple and the teacher, nor the differentiation between knowledge and ignorance.

He states the difficulty of defining "the effect" as a supporting argument (*anugrāhaka-tarka*) in order to show that the property of "being subject to exclusion" (*vyāvartamānatva*) is free from adventitious conditions (*nirupādhika*), beginning with the words "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). The meaning is: if [the effect] were real, it would be easily defined. Anticipating the objection that the aforementioned argument contradicts perception, he says "Nor... (*na ca*). The term "ruca-kādi" refers to states such as the *rucaka* (necklace) and so forth. Regarding the claim that "recognition has for its object the inherent cause" (*samavāyin*), he replies "Beyond that" (*tadatirikte*). This means that two distinct individuals are not perceived. The phrase "like threads in a cloth" was stated according to the process of the production of a cloth.

"Nor indeed" means that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of recognizing [the cause] as being qualified by its effect. "Therefore" means that because nothing is perceived apart from the cause, there is no sublation by perception (*adhyakṣabādha*). For that very reason, there is no presence of a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*), because there is no sublation even in the subject (*pakṣa*); this is the intended sense.

If everything were false, how could clay and so forth be real? To this he says: "This very [world]," etc. And he states that it is explicitly stated [in scripture]: "This," etc. Anticipating the objection that there is a similarity with the identity of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sun, he says: "Nor is there any scripture [to that effect]. Considering the two alternatives—that the [scripture] has another purpose, or that there is a contradiction with perception due to the absence of such a cognition—he first sets aside the first: "As has been stated. He sets aside the second: "And of perception," etc. Admitting [the objection], he says: "Even if there is a contradiction. The "defect" is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of duality. With reference to the rule of the "later [annulment]" (*apaccheda*), he says: "The latter," etc.

The existence of its own nature is the arising of knowledge. By the word "etcetera," the production of the causal complex [is meant]. Regarding "in valid cognition" (pramitau), it means "in the state of being a validly cognized object. For, by virtue of delimiting the object, it makes the object known through the state of having been known (*jñātatā*), just like memory; this is the meaning.
In this regard, some, while indeed accepting the non-duality of Brahman, argue that because the stream of delusion among individual souls (*jīvas*) is beginningless, no cause for it need be sought.

Now, in order to establish the distinction between the worldly and the Vedic [realms] as previously stated, he introduces the view that ignorance belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*) with the words "here" (*atra*). To whom does it belong? That is, what is its locus? Regarding the phrase "in that which is non-substantial"—meaning that which is illusory (*mithyā*)—he states that there would be "non-applicability," meaning a lack of proof. He addresses the objection that, due to its non-difference from Brahman and its inherent purity, the connection with ignorance could not belong to the individual soul just as it does not to Brahman, by saying "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*).

The meaning is that even though [the Self] is pure by its own nature, impurity arising from limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*) is possible; thus, the connection with ignorance (*avidyā*) is established, and consequently, the conceptual nature (*kālpikatva*) of birth, old age, and so forth is established. "Impurity" (*aśuddhi*) means the state of being subject to defects. To show that this impurity is removable by knowledge, he says, "impurity also... Having raised the objection of mutual dependence—that the connection with ignorance arises from the delusion of impurity, and the delusion of impurity arises from that [connection with ignorance]—he says, "of the individual souls" (*jīvānām*).

If it is argued that this [world] is merely a mental construction (*kalpanā*) of Brahman by those who do not know the true nature of non-duality (*advaya*), then it follows that Brahman itself is subject to ignorance (*ajñāna*).

He refutes the position that ignorance belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*) with the words, "This very [point]. He intends the following alternatives: does the soul's status as the locus of ignorance belong to its non-imagined (*akalpita*) essential nature, or to its imagined form, or to its essential nature as qualified by its imagined form? Having thus set forth the options, he refutes the first horn of the dilemma with the words, "Of the soul. He refutes the second with the words, "By something other than that. To the objection—"For the soul is the locus of ignorance; how then can that which is insentient (*jaḍa*) be its locus?"—he replies, "Certainly not."

He raises a third objection with the words "imagined" (*kalpita*). He refutes it with "that is not so" (*tan na*). To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of its own nature" (*svarūpasya*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "The form of the locus of ignorance" (*avidyāśrayākāra*). The meaning is this: if it is the locus of ignorance, then being qualified [by that ignorance] means that the locus of ignorance is precisely the qualified form; thus, there is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

He states the refutation regarding the oneness of ignorance: "In that case, in one [ignorance]... He raises the objection of multiplicity: "...with respect to each [individual]... He will say "he will be bound"—that is, he will become bound. He refutes this: "That is not so. Because it would entail the loss of non-duality (advaita), its inherent nature is not admitted. He asks: "Of what is this [the cause]? The meaning is that ignorance, which is supposed to create the distinction between individual souls (jīvas), is not capable of being the support even prior to the creation of those distinctions, because the souls themselves are not yet established. Regarding the phrase "in the case of seeds and sprouts":...

In that regard, there is no dependence on the produced for the producer by way of its being a producer; this is the distinction. "Inability" means the impossibility of establishing [the position]. Regarding the phrase "destruction of what has been done," etc.: by the word "etc.," the contradiction with scriptural statements such as the eternity of the soul (*jīva*) is indicated.

Having stated the refutation regarding the beginninglessness of the stream [of existence] based on the postulation of the property called "living being" (*jīva*), he extends that same refutation to the beginninglessness of the stream of the postulation of the property "jīva-ness" by saying, "for this very reason. He explains the rejection of the position involving the postulation of a property by saying, "in the stream of ignorance. He states a single refutation common to both positions by saying, "until liberation," meaning [the refutation applies] to the living being as characterized by the state of being a *jīva*.

He refutes the rebuttal based on the difficulty of the situation with the words "as for what was said. Because it is of the nature of pure knowledge—that is, because its form is pure consciousness (śuddhajñapti). By the aforementioned [arguments], such as mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya) and so forth. "Non-liberation" means that liberation would not occur as long as the state of the individual soul (jīva) conditioned by ignorance persists.

It has been refuted by an examination of the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*). Now, he refutes it by examining the example itself with the words "as for what was said. He refutes it by showing the impossibility of the appearance of a defect with the words "furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). The phrase "of another" (*anyasya*) is stated in accordance with the example of the head.

He refutes [the opponent's position] by examining the locus of the error that is the effect of ignorance, beginning with "Furthermore" (kiṃ ca). Who is the imaginer? Who is the locus of the error? [The opponent claims] it is the Self (ātman). The meaning is that this results in the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya), because the establishment of the individual soul (jīva) as the locus of an error regarding itself is dependent upon the very establishment of that soul.

Furthermore, if the ignorance of Brahman is not admitted, what [is the basis for the world]? Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no existence apart from Brahman, the world is non-different from it.

And what [is the reason]? It is clear. For this very reason—the meaning is that he accepts the connection with ignorance (*avidyā*) for the sake of creation preceded by observation (*īkṣā*) and for the sake of seeing the individual soul (*jīva*). *Māyā* is the cause of another's delusion; *avidyā* is the cause of one's own delusion—such is their doctrine. "Seeing the individual soul" means seeing the individual soul as something not ultimately real. He raises an objection: "Now," etc., [suggesting] that the cause of deluding others is itself the cause of the vision of that which is to be deluded. The response begins with "Then," and so forth; this is clear.

He refutes [the opponent's position] by following the reasoning that it lacks the status of being a cause for the perception of what is not the human goal (*apumartha*), stating: "And in its refutation... The point is this: even if it is a cause of suffering, the mere appearance of a non-entity (*avastu*) is what constitutes the non-human goal, because it is to be refuted; therefore, since *māyā* is the cause of that, it possesses the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*). The sense is that it would not be possible without ignorance. The sense is that it is false (*mṛṣātva*). The sense is that it is eternal—because, due to the absence of anything that is a non-human goal, there would be nothing to refute it. And he refutes it by showing the impossibility of the distinction of its locus, stating: "By being the locus of *māyā*..."

As for the passage beginning with "yat tu" and so forth: for this very reason—namely, because [the multiplicity] is conceptual (*kālpinika*), which is the reason that accounts for all systematic arrangements even when the substratum is one—it is said that the multiplicity of causes exists only if the effect is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), but not if it is not ultimately real; thus he says, "paramārthikī. To the question "What follows from that?", he says, "apāramārthikī tu."

And as for the "application" (*prayoga*): the first two [reasons] are stated against the proponent of the doctrine of the ignorance of the living being (*jīva-ajñāna-vādin*); the final two are stated against that proponent of difference (*bheda-vādin*). [The properties] such as insentience (*jaḍatva*) and so forth are independent of one another. "And in the case of difference" constitutes the three negative concomitants (*vyatirekin*). Non-difference is the probandum (*sādhya*). By means of the phrase "of that which is delimited as a real entity," and so forth, he brings forward two other types of delimitation following from the delimitation of a real entity. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And thus," etc. [Regarding the word] "origination" (*utpatti*).

The meaning is that there would be a contradiction with the scriptural teaching of immutability. He concludes the demonstration that all systematic arrangements are possible through a single ignorance with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). He concludes the position of the doctrine of Brahman’s ignorance with the words "Hence" (*tasmāt*). Regarding the phrase "non-difference of the world," the meaning is that there is no difference in the sense of ultimate reality; the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) here is non-existence [of such difference].
To this it is replied: Brahman is merely self-luminous and devoid of distinctions; for in your own view, the Self is pure consciousness, distinct from the referents of "I," "you," and so forth.

The Vaiśeṣika replies to the proponent of Brahman-ignorance (brahmājñāna), saying: "To this it is said. Regarding the phrase "of that which is partless": the sense is that even if there were concealment, it would be impossible to maintain that an insentient (jaḍa) portion remains. "Contrary to its own statement" means contrary to the statements establishing [the self's] eternality and so forth. "As stated" means by the proponent (siddhāntin) in this treatise. He states the distinction between falsity (mithyātva), non-eternality (anityatva), and difference (bheda): "In whatever place... If non-eternality were what was to be proved, it would result in proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā).

The meaning is that in the case of falsity (*mithyātva*), there are [logical fallacies] such as being contradicted by the presence of a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*), being sublated (*bādhitatva*), and inconclusiveness (*anaikāntyāt*). Regarding the phrase "place, time, etc. (*deśakālādi*): the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes action (*kriyā*) and so forth. It should not be argued that because there is no limiting condition in the form of another place or time during errors regarding place and time, there is no co-extensiveness (*samavyāpti*) with the probandum (*sādhya*); for the meaning is that even in those cases, action and the like do serve as limiting conditions. "Worthiness of being sublated" (*bādhārhatva*) is the probandum (*sādhya*); "being sublated" (*bādhitatva*) is the logical mark (*liṅga*); thus, there is no lack of distinction between the probandum and the reason. This is like the relationship between "worthiness of being burned" and "being the effect of a burner. "From what is present" (*samavahitāt*) means from what is combined or associated.

Another cause—such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), the will of God (*īśvara-saṅkalpa*), and so forth—is excluded because [the subject] does not depend on these; that is, because it does not depend on mere entities, since it possesses the quality of being unmodified (*avikṛta*). This is what is under discussion here.

He states the object to be favored [by the argument]: "And of the cause," etc. The reasoning stated by the opponent is a mere sophistical rejoinder (*jāti*), because his own statement—which asserts the destruction of the relation between cause and effect—is admitted to produce valid cognition. And if that is not so, then all the more there is no destruction of the cause-and-effect relation. The aforementioned auxiliaries are place, time, and so forth. Regarding the question "How is there recognition of the gold?", he says: "Previously," etc. And as for "and whatever else," by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he includes the principle that even in the case of contradiction, scripture is more authoritative.

Regarding what was stated [in the verse] beginning with "And that which was said," etc.: concerning the argument that "there is no reconnection due to the difference of bodies," he says, "Saubhari. Concerning the argument that "it is because of the difference of internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*)," he says, "Nor is it so. The meaning is as follows: if the self residing in a single body is one, then the proof establishes what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). If, however, there are selves residing in multiple bodies, then there is a contradiction with the evidence that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakabādha*). This is because all bodies are not products of ignorance (*avidyā*). The intention is that since even the body that serves as the concordant instance (*sapakṣa*) is not a product of ignorance, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*).

And by the passage beginning with "and because of volition," the point that "I alone am all that which possesses volition, because of being volitional" has been restated in substance. He refutes this by pointing out the lapse of time (*kālātyayāpadeśa*)—namely, "that too. He states the refutation of the argument itself with the words "as for what [you say]..."

Furthermore, for one who asserts that everything other than undifferentiated pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is false, the effort toward hearing [the scriptures] and so forth for the sake of liberation is fruitless. For the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*), however, because Brahman possesses all things—both sentient and insentient—as its body and thus exists in every mode, no limitation exists either intrinsically or extrinsically.

He states the counter-argument with the words "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*). The meaning is that there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the world] being fruitless and so forth, because it is an effect of ignorance. If it is argued that, since it has karma as its cause, it must likewise be fruitless even in your own view, we say no; for since the scripture is free from such an equal defect, it is easy to provide a rebuttal by means of sublation (*bādha*) by that scripture. This point will become clear later.

The destiny of those who speak falsely is twofold: [they may claim] that Brahman is what is to be established by the words of another, or that Brahman is not to be established because the Vedāntas are intent upon negating difference. Regarding these, he adduces an undesirable consequence for the position that Brahman is to be established: "Furthermore, [if it were] without attributes... By "inferences" (anumānaiḥ) is meant by "reasonings" (tarkaḥ), according to the well-known definition: "Reasoning (ūha) is logic (tarka), which is the statement of inference. By "refuted" (nirastān) is meant that their capacity to prove the object desired by themselves has been refuted.

"Of that which is not such"—meaning, devoid of both object and agent. If the reading were "of that which is such," it would imply that for that [world] which possesses an agent and an object, non-distinctness (nirviśeṣatva) is intended; in that case, such [non-distinctness] would not be established.

Previously, it was stated that [the cause] is fruitless because of ignorance (*avidyā*); that is not so, because truth arises from the untrue. To this, he says: "As for that which... He states its non-establishment in the view of others: "That too... He states its non-establishment even in his own view: "By us also..."

Having accepted the view that there is sublation (*bādha*), he refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "due to a defective cause" (*duṣṭakāraṇa*). He says "and that is not so" (*sā ca na*) with the words "furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). Regarding the claim that the Madhyamaka statement is rooted in a defect, he says "as for its being rooted in a defect" (*doṣamūlatvaṃ tu*). Thus, the syntactical connection is: "...therefore, it will not be established. He demonstrates the lack of establishment (*asiddhi*) with the words "in the world" (*loka*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says "without distinction" (*nirviśeṣa*). The meaning is that because both the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) and the state of possessing distinctions (*saviśeṣatva*) are absent, [the self] cannot be the cause of manifestation and so forth, either as a substratum (*āśrayatayā*) or as an instrument (*karaṇatayā*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is intended.

"There is no distinction [between the two cases] other than the intensity of that [delusion]. This is the intended meaning: if the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) were false, then the defect of infinite regress (*anavasthā*)—due to requiring another substratum—would be equal [to the case of the defect itself being false]. And the resolution [of that regress] through its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and beginningless continuity (*pravāhānāditva*), as well as through its self-sustaining and other-sustaining capacities (*svapara-nirvāhaka*), is likewise [applicable here]. Furthermore, the over-extensions (*atiprasaṅga*) resulting from the non-dependence on logical justification (*upapatti*) have already been shown previously. Moreover, the dependence on the reality of the defect is of the nature of a justification necessitated by its being non-ultimate (*aparamārtha*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "yattu" (as for that which...): "infinitude" (*ānantyam*) means the absence of any finite number. "Due to infinitude of essential nature" (*svarūpānantyāt*) means due to the infinitude of the essential nature which is devoid of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as space and time. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "space, time, etc.," agents (*kartṛ*) and so forth are included, since limitation is observed even by means of agents and the like. If one were to take as the subject (*pakṣa*) a self delimited by a house or the like, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). If delimited jars are taken as the corroborative instances (*sapakṣa*), their distinctness is shown to be conditional (*sopādhika*). Otherwise, the instance would be deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*).

As for what was stated regarding the sublated object (*bādhitaviṣayatva*) in the phrase "of the selves" (*ātmanām*), and regarding "in the case of difference" (*bhinnatve*): the delimitations of space and time are devoid of deficiency or excess, because they are delimitations, just like the delimitation of a real entity (*vastu*). The meaning is that for that which is delimited by reality, its being delimited by space and time is uncontradicted. The passage beginning with "by reality" (*vastutaḥ*) and so forth is clear.

He states the refutation regarding the non-acceptance of the distinction between ignorance (*avidyā*) and Brahman with the words "If... The sense is that, just as the silver in front would indeed be real if the nature of the mother-of-pearl were unreal. If it is argued that ignorance is unreal in relation to its counter-correlate, then even a jar would be unreal; consequently, like a cloth which is distinct from it, there would follow the delimitation of the object and the defects resulting therefrom. Now, he states the refutation by way of the general non-acceptance of distinction with the words "In the reality of difference."

The meaning is that if the distinction—that one's own position is faultless while the opposing position is faulty—is real, then difference is real; if it is unreal, then difference is unreal. Regarding the infinity [of Vaiśeṣika categories], he states his own intended method: "In the case of infinity. He provides the justification for that in the opponent's (the Siddhāntin's) own view: "But for the proponent of difference. "By itself" refers to the exclusion of jars and the like; "by another" refers to the exclusion of knowledge as an attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*).

The meaning is that "the state of being capable of co-referentiality with all things" consists in the non-limitation of the entity itself and the absence of any other entity distinct from it. Furthermore, the infinity of qualities is like the non-limitation of a ten-coin necklace in relation to a six-coin one; what was mentioned previously is also included within this.
Thus, because the effect, being distinct from its cause, is real, the entire world, which is the effect of Brahman, is indeed other than Brahman.

This being the prima facie conclusion (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: "The non-difference from that [cause] is established on account of such terms as 'originating' (*ārambhaṇa*) and others... ... Differences in the effect are observed, such as the various states of childhood, youth, and old age, as well as differences in cognition, terminology, and so forth."

Now, concluding the Vaiśeṣika position, he introduces the established conclusion (rāddhānta): "Thus, therefore" (*tadevam*). [The Sūtra states: "Its non-difference [from Brahman] is due to such terms as 'originating' (*ārambhaṇa*). To the question "From what is its non-difference? he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Non-difference (*ananyatva*) means oneness (*aikya*). Contradiction is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). The two sentences concerning the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) constitute the subject matter of the *Prakṛti-adhikaraṇa*. With the intention that this sentence establishes the identity of cause and effect by refuting the Vaiśeṣika view, it is said [in the commentary] "to those who establish that" (*tad-upapādayadbhyaḥ*), indicating its relevance to this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*). The term "vāc-ādibhyaḥ" is not used to avoid the interpretation of a single compound (*ekapada*); rather, he says "the word *ārambhaṇa*" to avoid interpreting it as a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound.

He establishes that the cited statements have no other purpose than that [Brahman] with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*). He explains the illustrative sentence with "Just as one... (*yathaika iti*). He states that the sentence beginning with "by speech" (*vācā*) serves to support that [point] with "In this regard" (*atra iti*). Since a name is not actually produced from clay, it is explained as being for the sake of touch (*sparśārthatayā*). The meaning is that in the phrase "by means of a jar" (*ghaṭena*), there is a non-exclusive indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*) of "speech. The meaning of "for the sake of accomplishment" (*siddhaye*) is that it functions as a reason by way of its purpose. "By that very same" (*teneva*) means by that which was introduced in the preceding sentence.

Explaining the meaning of the word *sparśa* (touch/contact), he states what was said in the *Saṃgraha* in brief: "Water," etc. A distinction such as "pot," "cloth," "it sits," or "it lies down" is observed to arise from a difference in cognition and from a difference in state (*avasthā*). To the question, "What is the determining factor here in regard to its being based on a difference in state? he says: "Therefore," etc. He explains the sense of the particle *eva* (only): "But not," etc. He states that distinctions such as cognition and so forth are otherwise established by way of generality: "Therefore," etc.

Even though the body is momentary, the examples [cited]—such as the words "child" and so forth—are not devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*), because they extend up to the conscious self (*cetana*); furthermore, the body is the object of uncontradicted recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

As it has been said: "Because of the conventional usage that 'the jar is destroyed while the clay itself remains'... Thus, by means of the arguments concerning origination (*ārambhaṇa*) and the like, the non-difference of the world from the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate cause, is established.

He resolves the contradiction between existence and non-existence with the words "as it has been said. He explains the diversity of effects with the words "this and that. He dispels the futility of the operation of causal factors with the words "the conjunction of configuration. The use of the past-participle suffix (*kta*) refers to the first moment; this is the intended meaning of the word "conjunction" (*yoga*). Therefore, the expression "it does not arise" is not a denial of the arising of its causal capacity. For that very reason, the statement that the jar is "terminated" when it exists as shards is likewise logical.

He refutes the objection raised by the words "of the configuration" (*saṃsthānasya*) and so forth, by means of a counter-objection: "Even for the proponent of the theory that the effect is non-existent" (*asatkāryavādinaḥ*). Just as the urging of the production of production is an utterance of the *nityasama* fallacy, so too is the objection regarding the production of a state (*avasthā*) by way of its production; the meaning is that a particular state is itself of the nature of production. But for us, however—those things which are incapable of separate existence, perception, or causal function do not require a separate production and so forth, just like [the nature of] production itself.

However, the meaning is that for those very things [the potsherds] which are so worthy, there is a dependence on a separate origination and so forth. He resolves the objection regarding the difference in number with the words: "in the state of being potsherds."

Now, regarding the sentences introduced by words such as "as in the case of the Sūtra" (*sautrādi*), he states the meaning of the sentence that serves as the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "tathā" (so). By the particle *eva* in the phrase "Being alone" (*sadeva*), the non-existence of the effect is excluded. The syntactical connection is: "In the same way... it has been established," because it is consistent with the meaning of the sentence beginning with "How could [the effect arise] from the non-existent? (*katham asataḥ*).

In order to strengthen the fact that the words have the meanings already stated, he states the meaning of the subsequent passages and declares the establishment of non-difference: "Thus it thought" (*tathā tadaikṣata*). By the two terms "plurality" and "the thinker," the meaning of the words "one" and "without a second" is made clear. He raises an objection regarding the statement concerning the resolve for the creation of individual entities (*vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*): "The word *sat*... The meaning is that if the word *sat* refers to Brahman, this grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is improper; if it refers to the world (*jagat*), then [Brahman's] capacity for seeing and so forth would be inconsistent.

He explains the illustrative statement—"the three," etc.—in order to make known that identity (tādātmya) is based on pervasion (vyāpti). The word "entire" (kṛtsnam) excludes the possibility of deficiency; the sense is that there is nothing additional established by other means of knowledge. The term "acidvastu" (non-sentient entity)—the word *devatā* (deity), which is in grammatical apposition with the word *idam* (this), refers by implication (*lakṣaṇayā*) to the non-sentient object to be presided over—this is the sense. The word "entity" (*vastu*) indicates the ultimate reality of the non-sentient; its ultimate reality is established by the statement "he created it" (*asṛjata*), because it is said to be something created.

Regarding the phrase "consisting of its own self" (*svātmaka*): the intention is that the word *ātman* in the expression "by this living self" (*anena jīvenātmanā*) denotes one's own self. To the question "To whom do name and form belong?", he says "this" (*etat*); the intention is that name and form are indeed present right here. Regarding the word "variegated" (*vicitra*): the meaning is name and form as individual manifestations (*vyakti*) such as gods and so forth. By this, there is an exclusion of name and form as collective aggregates (*samāṣṭi*), such as the term "fire" (*tejas*) or the property of "fiery-ness" (*tejastva*). For name and form as collective aggregates have already been manifested previously.

In order to dispel the suspicion that the word *ātmanā* (by itself) might be a qualification of the individual soul (*jīva*), he shows that the word *jīvena* (by the soul) is a qualification of the Self (*ātman*). Furthermore, in order to exclude the idea of entering into the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of souls, he qualifies the act of "entering" and demonstrates that even the individual soul possesses name and form—using the phrase "by this. Here, the pronoun *etad* (this) refers to Consciousness as qualified by the individual soul. The term *ātmatayā* means "as the controller. To avoid the misconception of identity between the essential natures of the individual soul and the Supreme, he clarifies their relationship as being "of his own self," meaning "by me, who am like a lion."

He clarifies this by means of another scriptural passage: "having created. For this entry occurs at the stage of the effect (*kāryadaśā*), and not at the stage of the cause (*kāraṇadaśā*); to this he says: "That very [Self]. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "By this. The sense is that the words *sat* and *idam* do not refer exclusively to Brahman or exclusively to the world. The suffix *-tara* has the meaning of "primacy" (*mukhyatva*). This is clear. He states the non-difference [of the cause and effect] through sentences from other contexts mentioned by the word "etcetera": "Likewise," and so forth.

In this regard, the truth is as follows: Brahman alone, having the conscious and unconscious entities as its body, is the mode (prakāra) of those [entities]. Furthermore, although there is non-difference of everything from [Brahman] in its nature as pure existence (*sadātman*), it was already stated previously that because [Brahman] is omniscient, it would follow that it perceives the natures of all things, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a confusion between all virtues and defects. Therefore, non-duality is precisely in the manner described above. || 15 ||

For the effects of *tamas* and so forth are most clearly differentiated; yet, because scripture speaks of the unification (*ekībhāva*) of *tamas*, and because scripture speaks of the origin and dissolution of both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), there can be no fixed distinction of natures due to the absence of plurality prior [to creation] and the consequent lack of the relationship between body and embodied being. Furthermore, this would contradict such sūtras as "Because of the designation of difference" and "Its non-difference [from Brahman]. To this, he says: "In this regard, this...

The sense is that the existence of the conscious and unconscious as the bodies of [Brahman] even at that time is established through the otherwise inexplicable nature of scriptural texts concerning the body-soul relationship—texts which are appropriate for resolving contradictions regarding the eternity of the Supreme Self, its being the material cause, the eternity of the individual soul, its plurality, and its diversity.

He refutes the meaning stated by the proponents of falsehood regarding this Sūtra with the words "But those who... He sets aside the view of Bhāskara with the words "And those who..."; up to the end of the phrase "due to connection with limiting adjuncts" (upādhisaṃbandhāt), the attachment of defects belonging to consciousness (cit) has been stated. With the phrase "the form of the rejectable" (heyākāra), the attachment of defects belonging to non-consciousness (acit) is stated. To the objection that there is no association with the rejectable in the essential nature [of Brahman] because power (śakti) is a transformation of the form of non-consciousness, he replies: "Power... (śakti).

He refutes what was stated by Yādavaprakāśa with the words "But those who... and so forth. "Viplava" means modification (*vikāra*). "Always" (*sadaiva*) implies even during the state of being a cause; for the Śruti says, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving... from Him [proceeds] this," and "From Him, the Self-born. The word "Bhagavat" refers to the Lord (*Īśvara*), such is the sense. He states the contradiction with logic with the words "Nor is it the case that... Because it possesses distinctions—that is, because it possesses the distinction of having the form of a controller. [The opponent claims: "There is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for the suffix is prescribed when there is primary denotative power (*śakti*). To this he replies: "Nor [is it the case] as in 'cook' (*pācaka*)."

"Of some only"—the sense is that otherwise, the employment of the qualification would be purposeless. To the objection that the meaning of [words] such as "cook" (pācaka) is seen to be a power (śakti), he says: "The cook."

He states the refutation regarding the position that "existence" (sattva) is a property (dharma) that persists [in all things] with the words "And not... He instructs [the opponent] on non-existence as a consequence with the word "contradictory" (virodhi). He states the refutation regarding the position that it is a substance (dravya) with the words "Substance itself... Regarding the claim that the existence of action and so forth consists in their connection with a substance, he says "In actions and so forth... He concludes the meaning of the aphorism with the words "Therefore... (15).
Now, it might be argued: "Even when a single entity enters into different states...
because [the substance] is perceived even when [the quality] exists. (2.1.16)

Furthermore, since the effects such as earrings and the like exist [within the cause], it is understood that the differences in terms such as "intellect" (*buddhi*) and "word" (*śabda*) are based solely on differences in state. Therefore, the effect is non-different from the cause. || 16 ||

He states the doubt regarding the subsequent Sūtra with the words, "Now it might be said. [The Sūtra] reads: *bhāve copalabdheḥ* (And because of perception when there is existence). The meaning of the passage beginning with "clay" has been stated here. What is intended is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is because connection (*pratisandhāna*) would otherwise be untenable; for there is no connection with the jar in the water contained within the jar—this is the meaning. He raises an objection with the word "cow-dung. [The Sūtra replies: "Not even there. The sense is that even by you, who maintain the persistence of the inherent cause (*samavāyin*), the connection with the primordial cause must be asserted. This is clear. || 16 ||
And because there is existence of another [entity] here as well. (2.1.17)
And because another effect exists within its cause, as it is said in the Veda: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. || 17 ||

"And because of the existence of another. In the previous sūtra, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) was stated as the cognition of the identity of the substance; here, however, there is such a designation (*vyapadeśa*). For the commentary (*bhāṣya*) states, "it is designated" (*vyapadiśyate*). Alternatively, this is called recognition (*abhijñā*) in the form "this is that."

"If it be argued that [the soul is not eternal] because of the designation of its non-existence, we say no; for [the existence of the soul is established] by means of another attribute, on account of the supplementary statement and the logical reasoning, and from another scriptural passage. (2.1.18)

As for what was stated regarding the existence of the effect in the cause, it has been very clearly stated [in the scripture]: "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest; it became manifest through name and form. || 18 ||

"If it be argued that [the term *sat*] does not apply because of the designation of non-existence, we say no; for [existence] is established through another attribute (*dharmāntara*) based on the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), from reasoning, and from other words. It has been stated that these are attributes of substance, beginning with the words 'for existence is the fitness for empirical usage' (*vyavahārayogyatā hi sattvam*). He states the meaning of the word 'antara' (other) with the word 'tatra' (therein). He provides the resolution for those passages where the remainder of the passage is not explicitly heard with the phrase 'because of having the same purport' (*tadaikārthyāt*). This is clear. (18)
Now, regarding the non-difference of the effect from its cause, there are two illustrations: ...
... "and like a cloth" (2.1.19).
Just as threads themselves, by undergoing a particular kind of interconnection, assume another name, form, and function such as "cloth," so too does Brahman. 19.

He states the function of the two preceding sūtras with the words "now" (*idānīm*). "Now" means once non-difference has been established; the sense is that, therefore, there is no deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*). "Two examples" refers to the worldly and the Vedic. "And like a cloth": the state of many things being one is thus demonstrated. || 19 ||
And as in the case of the vital breath and so forth. (2.1.20)
And just as the single air within a body [exhibits] various specific functions... thus the non-difference of the world from the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate cause, is established. || 20 ||

And as in the case of the vital breath and so forth. The fact that a single entity can exist in many states has been demonstrated. He concludes the meaning of the section with the words "iti" (thus). || 20 ||
Thus ends the section on "Origination" (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa) — 6.
Because of the designation of [the Self] as something other [than Brahman], there follows the contingency of faults such as not performing what is beneficial, and so forth. (2.1.21)
By those who establish the non-difference of the world from Brahman... therefore, this [notion] that Brahman is the cause of the world is inconsistent. || 21 ||

"Because of the designation of the other, there would follow the defect of not performing what is beneficial, and so forth. The connection and so on are clear. "And so forth" (ityādayaḥ): by the word "and so forth," the experience of pleasure and pain is included. (21)
This being the position reached, it is replied: "But [the soul is] distinct, because of the designation of difference. (2.1.22)

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the [opposing] position; [for the Lord is known] through such passages as, "The inner Self of all beings... the divine, unique God Nārāyaṇa, free from evil," and so forth.
In the final conclusion: "But it is more [than that], because of the designation of difference. (Sūtra 22)
And like a stone and so forth, that [creation] is untenable. (2.1.23)

The scriptural testimony (*śruti*) has been shown. Now, the presumption based on the meaning of scripture (*śruty-arthāpatti*) is stated: "And as in the case of stone and so forth, that [identity] is untenable" (*aśmādivacca tadanupapattiḥ*). Regarding the example "stone and wood": although grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is equal [in both cases], the admission of the exclusion of the non-sentient (*acid-vyāvṛtti*) is due to the impossibility of identity; the sense is that this is equally applicable to the sentient as well. The sūtra "On account of persistence" (*avasthiteḥ*) is a supplement to this section. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), what is intended is [the passage] beginning with "But not because of the existence of examples, for in both cases... and so on.

The reconciliation of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with consciousness has been established; now he states the reconciliation of the coreferentiality with the world: "Therefore, all this... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19]. To the objection that there is no such settled state because of the statement regarding non-differentiation (*avibhāga*), he says: "Only Being... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1]. To the question "How is that so?", he says: "But the non-differentiation... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.12].

Regarding the passage beginning with "ye punaḥ": the fault in the case of the object being separate has already been stated. He states the refutation regarding the object being conjoined with the words "na ca" (nor). The meaning is that the nature of the object of inquiry as non-imagined (akalpita) is what has been introduced as the subject matter.

Regarding the statement "the difference [of nature] at dissolution has also been stated," he says: "at dissolution. He restates it by speaking of it as a supplement (*śeṣatvena*) to this. If one asks, "What then is the meaning to be established there? he says: "For there... It is not merely the impossibility of an effect and a cause of different natures that is being established there, because it serves as an illustration for the refutation of the theory of non-existent effects (*asatkāryavāda*); thus he says: "non-existent" (*asad*). The meaning is that this is a restatement of the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* (Topic on the Origin) made by way of incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*).

Here, the primary sense of the scriptural texts concerning difference has been described in a manner that does not contradict the scriptural texts concerning non-difference. By the sūtras "In absorption" (*apītau*) and "But [the soul is not affected] by the defects residing in the non-intelligent, because [the Lord] is designated as other [than them]," the defects pertaining to the non-intelligent and the defects pertaining to the intelligent have respectively been refuted. The three sūtras beginning with "The grammatical coreferentiality [of the individual and the universal] is established on account of the persistence [of the universal]" constitute the remainder of this section. || 23 ||
Thus concludes the section on the designation of the other (the individual soul). 7.
"If it be argued that [Brahman is not the material cause] because we observe the withdrawal [of the world into Him], we say no; for [the case is] like milk. (2.1.24)

For the Supreme Brahman, who is omniscient and whose resolve is infallible, there is no requirement for external means such as the addition of an acidulant to milk and other substances in order to bring about the state of curds and the like; rather, such means are required only for the sake of purification or for the sake of a particular flavor. || 24 ||

For the distinction [of the Lord] has been stated by means of attributes such as having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*); in that context, the non-limitation (*asaṅkoca*) of His true resolve is now being determined—thus the connection is clear. Regarding the phrase "in milk and so forth": the meaning is that the rays of the sun are merely the cause of the initial melting, but they are not the cause of the water’s transformation into the form of ice. || 24 ||
And [the Lord is] like the gods and others in the world. (2.1.25)
Just as the gods and others [are perceived] in their respective worlds, it should be understood that this is for the sake of easily grasping Brahman, whose power is known through the Vedas. || 25 ||
Also, as in the case of gods and others, [the power of mantras] is evident in the world; this is the clear meaning. || 25 ||
Thus ends the section on the observation of withdrawal (Upasaṃhāradarśanādhikaraṇa) – 8. [Sūtra 2-1-26:
"Either the entire [Brahman] would be consumed, or there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning its partlessness."
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone... [and so on]; therefore, the causality of Brahman is not tenable. || 26 ||

The meaning is that it has been stated in this manner through a particular turn of phrase: "There would be the consequence of [the whole] being affected in its entirety, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts stating that [Brahman] is partless. The connection [of the objection] arises from the doubt as to whether, like the milk previously cited as an example, [Brahman] possesses parts or not. The word "existent" (*sat*) implies that limitation occurs only so long as there is sublation; since such sublation is absent here, the single term is non-contracted, and the sense is that it cannot tolerate even a distinction in terms of parts. The word "part" (*avayava*) refers to a constituent portion (*aṃśa*).

The core meaning is that its nature as a distinct region qualified by various conscious and unconscious entities is not possible. Regarding the phrase "or this": the sense is that its partlessness (*niravayavatva*) is established because the division of parts such as earth and so forth is denied. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), terms such as "without parts" (*niṣkala*) are included. The term "partless" (*niravayava*) is an explanation of the word "one" (*eka*). The meaning of the sentences contained up to the word "was" (*āsīt*) has thus been stated.

He states the established conclusion: "In the state of causality. It is undivided, one, and partless. Because it is denoted by the word "one," it is partless; for this very reason, it means that the distinction between consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) has been eliminated. As for the phrase "even though": the meaning is that since the portion belonging to the embodied self (*śarīrin*) would be fully contained within a single body, it could not exist elsewhere. || 26 ||
To this objection, he provides the following resolution: "But on account of scripture, because [the world] has its root in the Word. (2.1.27)
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the aforementioned objection. ... Brahman does not admit of either proof or refutation by means of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). 27.

"But because of the fact that [Dharma] has scripture as its source. The phrase "but because of scripture" (śrutestu) refers to the subject matter (*dharma*). The phrase "because of having scripture as its source" (śabdamūlatvāt) refers to the substratum (*dharmin*). The meaning is this: when a substratum, which is not within the scope of other means of knowledge, is cognized by its own means of knowledge as being of a different class from other substrata, then the concomitance of properties belonging to a different class [from those of other substrata] is also cognized by that same means of knowledge; thus, there is no contradiction with the means of knowledge. "Inference based on general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭam*) is that which is connected through similarity in some form or another. || 27 ||
And likewise in the self; for [the world] is indeed manifold. (2-1-28)
Furthermore, the meaning is that this objection—which applies to [an entity] connected with other things—does not apply to the Supreme Brahman, which is distinct from all things. || 28 ||

And likewise in the case of the self, for there are indeed various [entities]; and "the non-attachment to that" is the way the portion of the Sūtra is joined by supplying the ellipsis. The entities are qualified by the word "various. Because its meaning is clear, the statement from the Purāṇa is primary. Having raised an objection, the connection is: "as has been stated. || 28 ||
And for this reason as well, there are defects in our own position. (2.1.29)
In our own position—that is, in the doctrine of a primal cause such as Pradhāna—even though [the atoms] are conjoined, they would not be capable of initiating a gross effect. || 29 ||
And because of the defect in one's own position:
the meaning is that only for that which is inferred in accordance with [one's own] perception does the defect observed in the world necessarily follow. || 29 ||
And [the soul] becomes endowed with all [powers], upon seeing Him. (2.1.30)
"Supreme [Brahman] is of a nature entirely distinct from all other things... 'He has swallowed up all this; He is speechless and indifferent,'" and so forth. (30)

And [the Lord] is endowed with all [powers] because of the vision of Him. It has been stated that, by the force of the scriptural texts concerning His partlessness (*niravayavatva*), one must postulate both a distinctness of nature from the substrate (*dharmivaijātya*) and a connection with extraordinary powers (*vilakṣaṇaśaktiyoga*). Here, however, there is this difference: those [texts] state it explicitly. By the phrase "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā*), the establishment of a distinctness of nature from the substrate follows from His being undeserving of evil. By the phrase "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), they demonstrate the connection with all powers, since it results in the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), which is a quality of the substrate distinct from what is graspable by the defiled mind; thus it has been stated. || 30 ||
If it be argued that [the Lord] does not [act directly] because He is devoid of instruments, that has already been answered. (2.1.31)
Although Brahman alone is distinct from everything else, [it is described by such scriptural passages as]: "Without hands or feet, swift, a grasper," and so forth. || 31 ||

If it is argued that [the Lord cannot be the cause] because He is devoid of instruments (*vikaraṇatva*), that has already been answered. Even though [the Lord] does not depend on such things as a staff or a wheel, His dependence on a body and so forth is here refuted. "Effect" refers to the body. In the Sūtra, the mention of "instruments" is for the sake of illustration. (31)
Thus ends the section on the consequence of total dissolution (Kṛtsnaprasaktyadhikaraṇa). [Sūtra 32:
Not so, because [the world] has a purpose. (2.1.32)
Even though Īśvara was indeed one alone prior to creation... [the status of] Brahman as the cause is not tenable. || 32 ||
It is not [the case that the treatise is useless], because it possesses a purpose; the connection and so forth are clear. //32//
This being the case, we reply: "But as in the world, there is mere sport. (2.1.33)
For one who has attained all desires and is perfectly fulfilled, it is faultless to say that his sole purpose is divine play (līlā). || 33 ||
But for the world, it is mere sport; the word "mere" (kevala) excludes any wagering. 33.
"Neither partiality nor cruelty [can be attributed to the Lord], because He has regard for [other factors]; for thus [the scripture] shows. (2.1.34)
Although the Supreme Person is distinct from everything else, the attainment of the state of being gods and so forth occurs through His own power and by His own action alone. || 34 ||

"Partiality and cruelty [cannot be attributed to God] because He has regard [for other factors]; for thus [the scripture] shows. Because it is common [to all], the primary cause is not the efficient cause, such as the earth and so forth; this is because it was stated that [the causes] have become the primary causes. Uncommonness constitutes primacy, just like the potency of a seed. (34)

"If it be argued that [the distinction between soul and matter] does not exist because there is no differentiation of karma, we say no; for [the cycle] is beginningless, and this is both logically established and perceived. (2.1.35)
Prior to creation, there are no such things as individual souls (*kṣetrajña*). Because of its connection with manifold creation, Brahman alone is the cause of the world. (35)

"If it is argued that [the inequality of the world] does not arise from the non-differentiation of karma, we say no; for it is justified by beginninglessness, and it is both logically established and observed. He explains the meaning of the word "api" (also/even): "Even though that [beginninglessness] exists," and he explains the meaning of "ca" (and): "it is unearned (*akṛta*)."
And because all phenomena arise [from it]. (2-1-36)
Since [theories of] primordial matter, atoms, and so forth are [refuted as being] causes, it is established that Brahman alone is the cause of the universe. || 36 ||
Thus ends the section concerning "having a purpose" (prayojanavattva)—10.
Thus concludes the first quarter of the second chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
"And because of the production of all dharmas. This sūtra is a supplement to the entire section concerning the feet [of the Lord]. Thus ends the section on "Having Purpose" (10).

This concludes the first quarter of the second chapter in the *Śrutapradīpikā*, composed by Śrī Sudarśana Sūri—the ornament of the Hari clan, son of Vāgvijaya, who bears the secondary name Vedavyāsa by the divine command of Śrī Raṅgarāja, and who has grasped the heart of the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Bhagavān Rāmānuja through his service at the feet of the venerable Varadācārya.
The second quarter of the second chapter.
And because the origination [of the world] is not possible, there is no inference [of a creator]; and because of [the nature of] activity. (2.2.1)

It has been stated that the Supreme Brahman is the cause of the birth and so forth of the world. Therefore, it is concluded that the world, which consists of the three *guṇas*, has as its sole cause the *pradhāna*, which is the state of equilibrium of the three *guṇas*.

"And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, there is no inference; and because of activity. While restating the meaning of the five quarters, he states the connection with the words "It has been said," etc. In our own position (*svapakṣa*), the objections raised by the opponent regarding the cause have been refuted; in the opponent's position (*parapakṣa*), the objection regarding the cause is now stated—this is the connection. By this, the suspicion that the third quarter belongs to the second [section] is dispelled, since that [second section] concerns the effect (*kārya*).

He states the reason for the priority of the refutation of the Kāpila [Sāṃkhya] system with the words "In that regard" (*tatra*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the acceptance of the twenty-four principles (*tattva*) is meant. Anticipating the charge of redundancy, he says "Because of seeing" (*īkṣateḥ*). He explains the summary verse regarding that [system] with the words "That which is called the root-nature" (*mūlaprakṛtiḥ*). "Supporting" (*upaṣṭambhana*) means overcoming others. To dispel any suspicion of similarity [to other systems] in some other form or aspect, he says "not deficient" (*anyūna*).
"Devoid of attributes" (*nirdharmakaḥ*) means lacking the quality of being a knower. "Practically discarded" (*nirastaprāyaḥ*) means that its refutation has reached its conclusion.

The purification of the locus has been accomplished by the words "te caivaṃ" and so forth. He explains the verse beginning with "bhedānām" as follows: "This is the meaning. To the doubt—"Let there be the state of having a cause of similar nature; how is the existence of Pradhāna established?"—he explains the term "samanvayāt" (due to homogeneity) as "consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. The world is an effect because it possesses a variegated arrangement; because it is an effect, it must have a cause of similar nature—this is the inference.

Furthermore, since pleasure, pain, and delusion are inherent in the effect, and since a limited cause would lead to an infinite regress, the fact that Pradhāna is the cause is established by the force of the property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

To this it is replied: "And because the arrangement [of the world] is impossible, there is no inference [of an intelligent creator], and because of [the nature of] activity... for the very commencement of an effect, limitation must necessarily be admitted. (Sūtra 1)

To this it is replied, beginning with "atrocyate" (here it is said). The two causal terms serve to exclude [the case of] wood and so forth that have been presided over by a conscious being. He teaches the pervasion (*vyāpti*) useful for the counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*) with the words "yadevam" (if it were thus).
