Or, they are useful for the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) regarding the contradiction of specific qualities, as in the inference of a [specific] efficient cause (*nimitta*). Showing the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in the example, he states the meaning of the sentence with the words "dārvādeḥ" (of wood, etc. and "cakārāt" (from the word "and").

The meaning is that the argument—that sattva and the other guṇas possess causality because they are present in the effect (such as pleasure) which consists of sattva and so forth, just as clay and the like are present in their effects—is seen to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) in the case of whiteness and similar qualities. The intention is that the inherent sense of the term "guṇas" remains unimpaired.

The world, being insentient, does not have consciousness as its cause when it is not presided over by an intelligent being, because it is an effect; whatever is an effect has an insentient cause presided over by one who is cognizant, just like a pot—this is the inference. Or rather, there is the undesirable consequence that [the world] must have an insentient cause presided over by an intelligent being. [Objection: But in this way, the refutation of the inference for God (īśvara) is contradicted. For once a conscious agent is established through [the reason of] being an effect and so forth, a specific [agent] is established as a presider who is independent of [physical] instruments and the like prior to the creation of those instruments. [Reply: Not so.

From the perspective of the commencement of an effect, a cause that exists in an even state is unestablished for that which exists in an uneven state; even if it were established, your desired conclusion would not follow—this is stated by way of a concession (*abhyupagama*). Alternatively, it is because that which is insentient (*acit*) and unguided cannot initiate activity, just like a piece of wood or similar objects.

And as for the passage beginning with "yacca" and so forth: "ata eva" means precisely because of multiplicity. He demonstrates the acceptance of multiplicity with the word "sāmye. To the question "What follows from that?", he says "ataḥ. Regarding the point that "there would be no fixed order (*vyavasthā*) because of being unlimited," he says "na ca. To the question "How so?", he says "aparimitatve hi. The meaning is: the commencement of a large effect by many [atoms] occurs because they possess conjunction through their conjoined sides; and that [conjunction] is due to limitation; and that [limitation] is due to inequality; and since limited and unequal things must have a cause, and the causes of those [inequalities] are likewise of this same nature, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Where, as in chariots and the like, the state of being presided over by a conscious agent is clearly evident, [if it were argued that] "it is like milk and water," then that [argument] applies there as well. (2.2.2)

As for what was stated regarding the Pradhāna being uncontrolled by the Intelligent One (Prājña), [it is replied: its being controlled by the Intelligent One has not been refuted, because of such scriptural texts as, "He who dwells in the waters," and so forth. || 2 ||

He introduces the immediately following sūtra with the words "yatra" (wherein). The meaning is that he says this because, if you seek to establish the lack of superintendence by the Intelligent [Self] through the analogy of milk and so forth, then that very point has already been made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣīkṛta*).

"If it is like milk and water," [the author replies] "even there"; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the spinning of a wheel is excluded. "Vibration" (*spanda*) means becoming otherwise, not physical movement. "Pratipratī" means with respect to each individual object, due to the specific manifestation of qualities. Anticipating the objection that this contradicts what was stated previously, he says: "In the summary" (*upasaṃhāra*).
And because there is no establishment of a distinction [between cause and effect], since [the effect] is independent [of the cause]. (2.2.3)
And for this reason as well: [the Lord] does not depend on the presiding of a Lord whose will is true... "I incessantly hurl the inauspicious ones into wombs that are indeed demonic," so it is said.

"And because there is no persistence of difference, owing to independence. [The phrase] "desires have been attained" means that all desires have been attained, just as one says "he who subsists on water" (*abbhakṣa*). The meaning is that there is nothing further to be attained. The reason for this is His perfection through qualities, manifestations (*vibhūti*), and so forth. He states the favorability of these manifestations and the rest with the word "limitless" (*anavadhika*). "Of the faultless one" (*niravadyasya*) means of Him who is not subject to karma. "Of the stainless one" (*nirañjanasya*) means of Him who is devoid of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*. Therefore, the meaning is that because of the absence of desire and the like, there is no creation and so forth. [The prefix] *pari-*...

There is no loss of its independence because it awaits a specific transformation, for that [transformation] is dependent upon its own volition; indeed, independence consists in the capacity to act according to one's own will.

He refutes the objection raised with the words "nanu" and so forth by stating "anabhijña" (unacquainted). He says "śāstraṃ ca" (and the scripture) in order to exclude the *Kapila-āgama*. He says "tathā cāha" (and thus it has been said) to indicate that this was spoken by those who are experts in the scriptures. "Bibharti" means he accepts [it] as an object of propitiation. He says "tathā ca bhagavatā" (and likewise by the Blessed One) in order to make known that evil consists in the form of such transgression.
That Blessed One, the Supreme Person, has attained all desires; therefore, primordial matter (pradhāna), when not presided over by the Wise One, is not the cause. || 3 ||

How is the objection answered by these statements? [The objection: How can a compassionate being engage in what is harmful? Furthermore, if his punishment and favor are dependent upon karma, there is a loss of independence; if he were independent, there would be no connection of living beings with their fruits, because it is logical that the connection with the fruit belongs only to the independent agent. To this, he says: "That Blessed One... [sa bhagavān iti].

The Lord has demonstrated through the words "ubhayaliṅgatvam" (the possession of both genders/attributes), "tatkṛtavailakṣaṇyam" (the distinction caused by that), "sāpekṣatvavyudāsaḥ" (the rejection of dependence on other factors), and "phaladānānuguṇajñānādimattvam" (the possession of knowledge and so forth conducive to the granting of fruits). He dispels the objection that such great effort would be inconsistent with His being mere sport (*līlā*) by saying "svamāhātmye" (in His own majesty). To the objection that if He were independent, He might ordain merit and demerit in a contrary manner, he says "etāni" (these). The meaning is that the beginningless regulation of those [factors] is dependent upon His beginningless independence.

If all activity were dependent upon His will, there would be no connection with the fruits [of action] for living beings; to this he says: "In taking that up. He who impels one already engaged is the "sanctioner" (*anumantṛ*). Thus, dependence on another has been shown. He shows the scope for the independence of living beings by saying: "But the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*)... The meaning is that the Lord is indifferent regarding the initial activity and the corresponding will and knowledge [of the individual]. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Therefore, [there is] independence," etc. By the word "etc.," mercilessness is also indicated.

And there would be an impossibility of living beings attaining the fruits [of their actions]. He teaches the nature of compassion with the words "For compassion... To exclude the notion that it is merely an inability to endure the suffering of those who depend on one, he says "...for its own sake. He states the fault of compassion when misplaced with the words "And that... To the objection that it would then have no scope, he replies with "...in His own teaching... The construction is "I give with love," because the suffix *-ta* in *satatayuktānām* has the sense of a benediction (*āśaṃsā*). Otherwise, there would be a redundancy in the phrase "to those who worship Me."

In general, because [the soul] depends upon the Lord through its being supported, its instrumentality, its receiving a body, its being permitted [to act], and its receiving the fruit [of action], there is total dependence on Him. However, regarding specific activities, the individual soul possesses independence; thus, it is connected with the fruit [of those actions]. Nor is there a loss of the Lord's sovereignty over everything, for even that [soul's] independence is dependent upon Him. Nor is there any contradiction, since we observe that the independence of ministers and others is dependent upon the king. Furthermore, ministers and others are indeed connected with the fruits [of their respective actions].

The Lord is indifferent at the initial commencement [of action], and thereafter He becomes a permissive witness (*anumantṛ*). Furthermore, He acts as an instigator (*prayojayitṛ*) toward those who produce excessive joy or displeasure, while maintaining indifference due to His absolute sovereignty (*svātantrya*); and this is not a fault, because it is established by the very nature of the subject (*dharmigrāhakatva*). Moreover, His permission is like a judicial punishment (*daṇḍakalpā*), as seen in the case of kings and others. If compassion were not a virtue, then restraint would not be a fault; for we observe that these two—compassion and restraint—take on opposite forms when they fall upon an inappropriate object. Therefore, the reason [adduced against the Lord's existence] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

If it is argued that a king’s punishing those who deserve punishment is a virtue because he is subject to the authority of the scriptures (*śāstra*), then compassion (*dayā*) must likewise be accepted as a virtue in God (*īśvara*), who is not subject to the scriptures, provided He acts in accordance with the scriptures. Since the scope for compassion has already been demonstrated, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. He concludes with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*): this means that since the doctrine of Brahman as the cause is free from defects, the defect resides only in your own position.

Now, it might be argued: "Even though [the material cause] is not presided over by an intelligent being... and because of its absence elsewhere, [it does not produce effects] like grass and so forth. (2.2.4)
This is not tenable. [The argument regarding] grass and so forth... has been elaborated upon right there in order to demonstrate the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). || 4 ||

He states the doubt regarding the subsequent sūtra: "Now, it might be argued" (*atha syāt*). The mere proximity of non-conscious matter (*acit*) is sufficient for the exclusion [of other causes] such as mere wood and so forth; there is no necessity for the presence of a person possessing specific volition (*saṅkalpa*). For even when a cow is asleep, one observes that the grass and other things she has eaten turn into milk. Nor can that [example] be made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣīkārya*). The sense is that since the effect is possible through that much alone, it is improper to postulate anything further.

And because it does not exist elsewhere, it is not like grass and such; by the two words "unused" and "discarded," the status of grass and the like as examples for the transformation of either the solitary Intellect (citi) possessing mere proximity or the non-intelligent (acit) alone is refuted. Furthermore, it is intended that the presiding over [matter] by a specific conscious being endowed with a specific volition is undesirable to the opponent, as is elaborated upon by the phrase "not presided over by the Prājña."

The sense is that an additional doubt has been resolved here: namely, that there exists an illustrative example for transformation occurring through the mere proximity of consciousness—which lacks the capacity for volition and so forth—acting as the differentiator of mere wood and other materials. "In that very [example]" means in the example of the cloud itself. || 4 ||
If it is argued that it is like a man and a stone, even so [the objection remains]. (2.2.5)

Now, it might be argued: although its nature consists solely of consciousness... [there would be] an absence of bondage due to its eternal liberation, and consequently, an absence of liberation (apavarga). || 5 ||

If it is argued that it is like a person and a stone, even so, the word "perception" (*darśana*) has been explained by the word "experience" (*upabhoga*). If it is claimed that there is no need for movement toward proximity due to omnipresence (*vibhutva*), then the consequence of constant creation (*nityasarga*) has already been stated.
And because the status of being the principal is untenable. (2.2.6)

For it is due to the relationship of primary and subordinate among the qualities (guṇas), based on their relative increase and decrease, that... and for this reason, the Pradhāna is not the cause when it is not presided over by an intelligent being. || 6 ||

And because the status of being the principal member (*aṅgin*) is untenable. Thus, up to this point, the contradiction with the specific [conclusion] of the inference stated by the opponent has been explained.
And otherwise, in the case of inference, there would be a lack of the capacity for knowledge. (2-2-7)
Since it is by means of a mode other than those modes already refuted that [the argument proceeds], the Pradhāna is not established by inference in any way whatsoever. || 7 ||

He extends [the argument] to other inferences as well, stating: "And otherwise, in the case of inference, there would be a lack of the power of a knower. For only when there is the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is it possible for activity to occur through volition (*saṅkalpa*) without depending on another presiding agent. Since that [state of being a knower] is absent [in the case of atoms], the consequence is the eternal creation [of the world]; such is the meaning. || 7 ||
Even if it were admitted [that there is a cause], it would be so because of the absence of an object. (2.2.8)
Even if one accepts the establishment of Pradhāna through inference, liberation will never be achieved because the proximity of Prakṛti is eternal. || 8 ||
Even if this were accepted, it would be because of the absence of an object; for it has been stated that enjoyment and liberation are impossible for that which is eternal and immutable. || 8 ||
And because of contradiction, [the Sāṃkhya doctrine] is inconsistent. (2.2.9)

Moreover, this doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas is contradictory. As previously stated, because it is impossible for Brahman to have a connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) if this [agency] were its very nature, there is a lack of consistency. 9.

Nevertheless, in anticipation of the suspicion that this might be accepted, the following sūtra states: "And because of contradiction, it is inconsistent. The form that is the opposite of being for the sake of another is the state of being a controller—namely, independence. As the nature of the witness, one is the synthesizer.

The seer [is known] through the senses and so forth. Because of the reversal of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and the rest—that is, because an insentient entity consisting of the three qualities and their effects cannot possibly be a presiding controller—and because of the engagement for the sake of isolation (*kaivalya*); for indeed, one who is to be abandoned cannot be the agent of that abandonment. He demonstrates the contradiction regarding the stated points with the words beginning "being a witness" (*sākṣitve*). And as for the phrase "he [is]": since this is a property of consciousness, it does not belong to *prakṛti*; and since it is a modification (*vikāra*), it does not belong to the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "the *puruṣa*'s perception of its own self": this refers to a perception whose agent is the *puruṣa*. The meaning is that he does not superimpose [this state] by way of being its own agent.

He states, "Even those who... [referring to] the refutation of the Sāṃkhya position by way of seizing the opponents by their own throats. Because it is eternal and immutable, superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and so forth are untenable. This is because [the opponent] admits its visibility and subliability (*bādhyatva*); the meaning is that modifications in the form of the experience of ignorance and the knowledge that sublates it are impossible. This very point—its immutability, faultlessness, and so on—is intended as a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning its having both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgaka*). Alternatively, because of its connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it would possess suffering.
The meaning is that because of its vastness, it would possess a nature opposed [to suffering] in the sense of being an adversary to suffering; thus, there would be an inconsistency. || 9 ||
Thus concludes the section on the impossibility of the arrangement (racanānupapattyadhikaraṇa):
"Or [the world] may be like the large and the long, from the short and the spherical" (2.2.10).
Since the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause is rooted in fallacious reasoning, everything accepted by it is entirely inconsistent; such is the meaning of the Sūtra. || 10 ||

"Or [the production of] the large and the long from the short and the spherical; since the nature of atoms is inferential, their refutation is appropriate. For the production of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) occurs from three dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), and not from a dyad and an atom; regarding this, he says "from atoms. The inclusion of "large and long" is for the purpose of illustrating even the "minute and short," because it will be stated later: "like the production of the large, the long, the minute, and the short. [This is so] because the [existence of] mustard seeds and mountains themselves is not established.

If [the whole] possesses parts, then because of the infinity of those parts, the property called "heterogeneity" (vaiṣamya) cannot be established. If, desiring to avoid that [consequence], one asserts partlessness, then the very subjects—the two wholes consisting of the mustard seed and the mountain—would be unestablished; this is the meaning. "What shall we do? means: which view should be adopted? The Vedic [proponent] implies: [this is] within the scope of sublation by reasoning. "Incoherent" (asaṅgatam) means: incoherent with the [preceding] section. He demonstrates both the lack of connection and the tautology through two passages, beginning with "Brahman," etc. (verse 10).
"What else here is inconsistent? To this he says: "In either case, there is no karma; therefore, that [bondage] is absent. (2.2.11)
For in the doctrine that the atom is the cause... therefore, there is an absence of the state where the arising of the world is preceded by motion inherent in atoms. || 11 ||

He states a doubt regarding the immediately preceding sūtra: "What is here? [The answer is: "In neither way is there karma; therefore, there is an absence of it, because it belongs to the self. The meaning is that they belong to different loci (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*). "Maturation" (*vipāka*) refers to the state fit for the fruit. || 11 ||
And because of the admission of inherence, there would be an infinite regress due to its being on the same footing [as the categories it relates]. (2.2.12)

And because of the admission of inherence, [the Sāṃkhya doctrine] is inconsistent... it would be more reasonable to assume that, having admitted inherence, this is its very nature—thus [ends the commentary on verse 12].

Furthermore, because of the acceptance of inherence (samavāya), there would be an infinite regress due to parity; how then could parts and so forth require a further establishing factor? To the question of how this [inherence] can be self- and other-establishing and thus avoid such parity, he says: "This has been stated"—[verse 12].
Whether inherence is eternal or non-eternal...
[it is not so], because it exists eternally. (2.2.13)
Because inherence is a relation, and because the world exists eternally, [the doctrine of primordial matter] is inconsistent. || 13 ||
And because [the effect] exists eternally; therefore, due to this eternity, the postulation of atoms and Īśvara as its causes is untenable—this is the sense. || 13 ||
And because they possess form and other qualities, the opposite [of the soul's nature] follows from observation. (2.2.14)
Furthermore, you postulate that atoms—whether earthy, watery, or fiery—possess qualities such as color and so forth; for this reason as well, [your theory] is inconsistent. 14.

Furthermore, because they possess form and other qualities, the opposite is observed. Regarding the claim that this specific distinction of atoms—namely, their dissimilarity to jars and the like due to their eternity and so forth—is what sets them apart, he says: "Not indeed" (na hi). || 14 ||
Now, with the desire to avoid this fault, [the opponent might argue that] atoms [are not joined], because there is a fault in both ways. (2.2.15)
Not only does the aforementioned fault arise from the admission that atoms possess form and other qualities, but since there are faults in both ways, the position is untenable. || 15 ||
And because there would be faults in both ways; the sense is that, since "otherwise" has not been stated, there is no other head. || 15 ||
And because of non-possessiveness, there is absolute lack of concern. (2.2.16)
The contradiction of the Kapila school with scripture and logic... [is such that] those seeking the supreme good must treat it with absolute disregard. 16.

And because of non-possessiveness, there is absolute indifference. He states the term "absolute" (*atyanta*) to indicate what is excluded by it—namely, the follower of Kapila (*kāpila*). The contradiction with the *Śruti* has been stated as a defect [in that system]. || 16 ||
Thus ends the section on "The Great and the Long" (Mahadīrghādhikaraṇa) — 2. [Sūtra 2-2-17: "Even if the composite were caused by both [atoms], that [composite] would not be attained."
The Vaiśeṣikas are proponents of the theory that atoms are the cause [of all things]... and it has already been established previously that this [atom] is indeed cognizable. || 17 ||
Even if both [types of] causes were accepted together, that [result] would not be attained;

for there is a commonality in the acceptance of the absolute fourfold nature among atoms. To distinguish the various types among the Buddhists who maintain the doctrine of atoms as the cause, he shows their classification with the words "And those... Since two [of them] are introduced as proponents of atoms, the connection with the other two follows from their belonging to the same category—this is the sense.

Regarding the term *citta*: *citta* is the stream of consciousness (*vijñānasantāna*); *caitta* refers to passion and the like. Vācaspati and others maintain that even the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is included within *citta* and *caitta*, because it is an object of consciousness. In the *Bhāskarīya*, however, it is held that the four aggregates other than the aggregate of form are included within *citta* and *caitta*. The aggregate of form consists of the elements, the sense organs, and their objects. The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is the stream of cognition (*jñaptisantāna*) mounted upon the conceit of being a grasper in the form of "I."

The aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is a particular state of the mind produced by the experience of pleasure and pain arising from the agreeable and the disagreeable. The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-pratyaya*). The aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists of attachment, aversion, and so forth. "Attainment" (*tatprāpti*) means the attainment of the state of being an aggregate. "Activity" (*vyāpāra*) refers to motion, as they are said to "operate. The word "what" (*kiṃ*) is used in a derogatory sense. "Touches" (*spṛśati*) means it establishes a connection with the sense organ. When? Never. He demonstrates this very point with the words: "for having touched" (*spṛṣṭvā hi*).

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "How so? He states that it is improper for cognition (*jñāna*) to be the self, saying: "It is only the object of the 'I' (*ahamartha*). The term "caused by both" does not mean being caused by both external and internal factors, because it is impossible for the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) to constitute a composite whole (*saṅghāta*). Therefore, this is a statement of something distinct [from the preceding]. || 17 ||
If it is argued that [the formation of a body] is possible because of mutual causality, we say no, because this is not the cause for the existence of a composite organism. (2.2.18)
Since ignorance and the other factors are established as being mutually causal, it is also impossible to conceive of the continued existence of formative forces [independently]. 18.

If it is argued that [the world] is established because of mutual conditionality (*itaretarapratyayatva*), we say no, because it lacks the cause for being a composite entity (*saṅghātabhāva*). This is the correct reading. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of being an object of knowledge (*jñānaviṣayatva*) and conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is intended. To the question—"What are ignorance and the rest? How do they have mutual causality? And how, by that, is the establishment of a composite entity possible?"—he says: "This has been stated," and "And this... [as follows].

The meaning is this: this cycle—wherein the aggregate arises from ignorance and so forth, and ignorance arises from the aggregate—is perceived; however, it is not tenable if one does not accept an aggregate that serves as the cause for ignorance and the rest. Regarding the example of "mother-of-pearl": the meaning is that the delusion of silver in mother-of-pearl is certainly not caused by a conjunction of two pieces of mother-of-pearl. He states what is intended by the Sūtra with the words "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*); if it is argued that [the delusion] is due to a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), he replies to that with: "The substratum of the latent impression" (*saṃskārāśrayam*). || 18 ||
And because the preceding ceases when the succeeding arises. (2.2.19)
Furthermore, on the view of momentariness, the production of the world... [is impossible]; for no object whatsoever can possibly become an object of cognition. 19.

And because the preceding [moment] ceases when the succeeding one arises, it is also illogical to claim that a pot-moment is the cause of another pot-moment situated in the same spatial continuum. The point is that if [the pot] were moved to another location, it would follow that it arises from a pot-moment [already existing there]. He states "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*) to show that the fault mentioned regarding arising applies equally to cognition as well. // 19 //
If it did not exist, there would be a contradiction of the thesis; otherwise, there would be simultaneity. (2-2-20)
If the effect were to arise even when the cause is absent, it would follow that the sensory faculty and the cognition [produced by] its contact with the object would occur simultaneously. || 20 ||

"If [it is argued that] momentariness is already established because otherwise there would be either a contradiction of one's own thesis or simultaneity—meaning, if the subsequent moment were to exist at the time of the preceding moment—the author refutes this with the words 'of the sense organ. The meaning is that it would follow that the relationship between cause and effect is destroyed. The demonstration regarding objects such as jars and so forth is for the purpose of showing that the consequence of the simultaneity of cognition and its causes applies to them as well. ||20||
Because there is no interruption of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) regarding both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). (2-2-21)
Thus, the arising of what is non-existent has been refuted; for even in that case, it is more logical to conceive of it as the attainment of another state. || 21 ||

The non-attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) [is established] because there is no interruption; this is what has been demonstrated. The meaning is: by means of the two [reasons], namely, the impossibility of its being perceived and its establishment otherwise. "In the case of certainty" implies: by means of uncontradicted recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). || 21 ||
And because there would be a fault in either case. (2.2.22)
The arising from the void accepted by the proponents of momentariness is neither of the two modes of arising and cessation described by you. 22.
And because there would be faults in both ways; furthermore, it is not perceived, the implication being that this is due to its insubstantiality.
And because there is no distinction in the case of space. (2-2-23)

There is no contradiction in external and internal objects being perceptible to the eye, despite their stability, because they possess form through the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa). || 23 ||
And because there is no distinction in the case of space; the connection [of this topic] is due to the incidental occurrence of the refutation of momentariness. || 23 ||
And because of the traditional remembrance. (2.2.24)

It is precisely the stability of the subject matter that was previously introduced... for it is not possible for others who do not know what has been commenced by another to bring it to completion. || 24 ||

"And because of recollection" (*anusmṛteśca*). "And that" (*tacca*)—the sense is that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) supported by reasoning (*tarka*) is more powerful. A common refutation against both perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumiti*) has been stated. He addresses perception with the words "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). The designation of the "indicated" (*gamya*) and the "indicator" (*gamaka*) as "exclusion conveys" (*vyāvṛttir gamayati*) follows worldly convention. For exclusion from what is not present is precisely the connection with the present time. And the difference between the state of being present and the preceding and succeeding states is stated as a proof for momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).

Because there is no contradiction in a single entity being connected with two different times—just as it may possess both blueness and lotus-ness—it does not prove momentariness. Regarding the phrase "contrary to what is intended": since pervasion (*vyāpti*) is possible even through the opposite [of the desired conclusion], it proves a contradictory meaning. "Contradictory" (*viruddha*) means "opposite. This is the sense of *prakaraṇasama* (the counter-balanced).

He states that causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is indeed contradictory [to permanence] with the words "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). He asserts that the reason—the existence of the jar-moment—is *sopādhika* (vitiated by a limiting condition) with the words "Likewise, the last [moment]" (*tathāntya*) and "the prior" (*pūrva*). For it is not the case that one thing appears while another is the object; this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), such is the meaning. The causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) consists of the sense organ aided by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Its object is the connection of a single entity with two points in time. Thus, the impossibility of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumiti*) regarding this has been stated. || 24 ||
Not from the non-existent, because it is not observed. (2.2.25)
Thus, first, for both the Sautrāntika and the Vaibhāṣika, the variety of cognitions arises precisely because the object persists at the time of its cognition. || 25 ||

"Because what is non-existent is not seen. The six sūtras beginning with "In the arising of a subsequent [moment]" are intended to refute [the theory] through observed consequences; immediately following that, there is the occasion for the Sautrāntika [position] as a rebuttal to that. Suspecting the view of the Yogācāra, he says: "And not previously," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "reflected image, etc.," by the word "etc.," the intended meaning is the falling of a shadow, such as that of a *japā* flower upon a crystal. (25)
Furthermore, he states a common refutation: "And in this way, there would be accomplishment even for those who are indifferent. (2.2.26)

In this way, even for those who are indifferent [to action], momentariness, non-existent origination, causelessness, and so forth, would result in the attainment of fruits both in this world and the next, as well as liberation. || 26 ||

And in this way, there would be the attainment [of results] even for those who are indifferent. He states that such a consequence is undesirable: "the attainment of what is desired. [For example,] ritual purification and the like lead to heaven; knowledge and the like lead to liberation. || 26 ||
Thus concludes the section on the aggregate (samudāyādhikaraṇa). 3.
[Sūtra 2-2-27: "There is no non-existence, because of perception."

It has been stated that for the Yogācāras, who maintain the doctrine of the existence of consciousness alone (*vijñānamātra*), substantial reality (*dravyatva*) is not contradictory; therefore, there is no absence of external objects. || 27 ||

"Not non-existence, because it is perceived. To the question "How is there variety?", he says: "And that... To the question "How is there the arising of a cognition of a different kind?", he says: "That which has the form of a jar... The sense is: just as the capacity of an object to produce something of a different kind is accepted, so it is here. Regarding the phrase "of cognition and object": the sense is "just as in the case of two moons."

"Thus it being the case" means "in such a manner. Is the non-ultimate reality of that which is other than knowledge established by this [very] knowledge or by another knowledge? In the first case, since there is no difference in its appearing without dependence on anything else, why should knowledge itself not be likewise [non-ultimate]? The second case is struck down by non-perception; such is the sense.

He avoids the restriction of simultaneous cognition with the words "But that which... He states that the restriction of the cause of non-difference is itself an extreme proof of difference with the words "That... and "And the relation... Here, "relation" means a direct relation. To the question of how a substance can possess a restricted mode of manifestation, he replies: "Light... (27)
As for the [objection] raised by others using the example of dream-cognition...
[it is refuted by: "And because of the difference in nature, it is not like a dream, etc. (2.2.28).
Because of the dissimilarity with dream-cognition, and because the property of being a waking cognition is inconclusive, the lack of an object is even more thoroughly unestablished. || 28 ||

He introduces the immediately following sūtra with the words, "yat paraiḥ" (as for what others [say]). And because of dissimilarity, it is not like a dream and so forth. This was stated by way of accepting the falsity of dream-objects; for the truth of those [dream-objects] will indeed be asserted by the authors of the sūtras.
There is no existence, because it is not perceived. (2.2.29)
It has been established in the examination of manifestation (*khyāti*) that it is not only for knowledge devoid of an object that there is no lack of an object. || 29 ||

"There is no existence [of the object], because it is not perceived. Regarding the phrase "in any case whatsoever": the meaning is that in deep sleep there is only the manifestation of the substratum (*dharmin*), but not the manifestation of the cognition of its attributes (*dharma*). || 29 ||
Thus ends the section on perception (upalabdhyadhikaraṇa). 4.
And because [the Pradhāna] is in every way untenable: 2.2.30.
In this regard, the Mādhyamika, who propounds the emptiness of all things, [claims that] the total emptiness of everything in every respect is untenable. || 30 ||

"And because it is impossible in every way, and because there is no purpose [for its arising]. For the fruit of arising is one's own existence (*svasattā*). Since that [existence] already exists prior [to arising], it cannot be the fruit of arising—this is the meaning. "Thus, the position being reached" refers to the view that "it exists. This was stated for the sake of providing an illustration: a jar exists in relation to itself, but does not exist in relation to its shards. Therefore, it is logical that it possesses the nature of both being and non-being. Furthermore, the jar is not non-existent in relation to itself; thus, it is neither of the two natures [exclusively].

In relation to the skull, [the jar] is not existent; nor is it "not both," for that would imply it is of the nature of both existent and non-existent. Thus, because it possesses a particular state, its absolute non-existence (*tucchatva*) is not established. Furthermore, thinking that the word "in every way" (*sarvathā*) intends the impossibility of the conceptualization of a means of valid cognition (*māna*), he says: "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*). This concludes the refutation of the Sautrāntika, consisting of three topical sections. || 30 ||
Thus ends the section on the impossibility in every way—5.
Not in one [substratum], because of the impossibility [of contradictory attributes]. (2.2.31)

The Buddhists have been refuted; the Jains as well... [in their doctrine] that atoms unpresided over by a Lord are the cause [of the world], the aforementioned defects remain exactly as they were. (31)

Because [the fourfold classification] is impossible in a single [system], and because the refutations of the followers of Kaṇāda and the Sugata are logically connected through their common acceptance of a fourfold [classification] due to its exclusivity, the refutation of the Ārhata follows immediately after that of the Saugata. "That which serves as the cause of stability" means the cause of immobility and so forth; the meaning is that it does not produce activity. Pleasure, pain, and equanimity induced by that [cause] constitute a single group, for otherwise the fourfold [classification] would be untenable.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), he states "this has been said" regarding the point that there is no contradiction because of the difference in form (*ākāra*). He states the refutation of the position that substance (*dravya*) and its state (*avasthā*) are distinct with the words "of the substance. If there is no difference between the two, the establishment of non-contradiction on the basis of a difference in form is not possible. As for the case of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*), since it was previously stated that this leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the dependence on further forms, it was not explicitly mentioned here. To the question "How is there a contradiction in the matter at hand?", he says "for instance" (*tathā hi*). Thus, the contradictions regarding existence and non-existence, permanence and impermanence, and difference and non-difference have been demonstrated.

"Only as a qualifier of the object" (*padārthaviśeṣaṇatayaiva*). This was stated with the intention of referring to the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*), and not with the intention of [time] having a single substratum like genus (*jāti*) and so forth; thus, the refutation of the atomistic nature of time (*kālāṇutva*) is the resulting conclusion. The cognition "many objects exist at one time" is a cognition qualified by time. He states the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) through deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with the words "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). || 31 ||
And thus, the self would be non-omnipresent. (2.2.32)
If your position is accepted in this way, the consequence of incompleteness follows; that is to say, the consequence of being non-whole follows. || 32 ||

And thus, there is incompleteness of the self. "Having innumerable spatial units" (asaṃkhyātapradeśaḥ) means having spatial units that lack a fixed number; the meaning is that the spatial units are indefinite. || 32 ||

Now, [the opponent might argue] that because [the soul] has the nature of contracting and expanding... [but] even through a change of state, there is no lack of contradiction, because of the [objections regarding] modification and so forth. (2.2.33)
And because the fault of [the soul] being subject to contraction and expansion would follow, it would result in its being equivalent to a jar or similar objects. || 33 ||

He raises a doubt regarding the immediately preceding sūtra with the words "Now" (atha). Nor can there be non-contradiction even through figurative interpretation, because of [the mention of] modification and so forth. "Modification" means origination and so on; by that, there is existence for a limited time, which is impermanence. || 33 ||
And because of the persistence of the final state, and because both are eternal, there is no distinction. (2.2.34)
That which is the final dimension of the soul... this doctrine of the Ārhata is indeed entirely inconsistent. 34.

"And because of the permanence of the final state, and because both [sizes] would be eternal, there is no distinction. The meaning is as follows: just as one's essential nature (svarūpa) persists in the state of liberation and was therefore existent previously, so too the final dimension (parimāṇa), since it persists in liberation, must have been existent previously; thus, the claim that the soul's size is that of the body is not established. || 34 ||
Thus ends the section on the impossibility [of multiple natures] in one [entity]. 6.
On account of the lack of consistency, [the doctrine] of the Lord [is not tenable]. 2.2.35.
"Having undertaken the Kāpāla vow, a man becomes an ascetic [who follows] the doctrines of Kapila, Kaṇāda, Sugata, and the Arhats. Thus it is said.

The connection [of this section] with the preceding one is due to its presence in the mind, as both share the commonality of being inconsistent with the *Veda* and thus lacking coherence regarding the Lord (*pati*). Although there is a similarity in their approach to the *pradhāna*, the refutation of the Sāṃkhya system is bypassed and placed immediately after the Ārhata (Jaina) system in order to demonstrate that this [Pāśupata] system is even more extreme in its heterodoxy; this is the contradiction regarding the principles (*tattva*). Likewise, the contradiction regarding practice (*anuṣṭhāna*) has been stated. He states the mutual inconsistency [with the Veda] by saying "the ring" (*mudrikā*). Wearing the ring and other such practices are mentioned in various *tantras*, but not in a single [authoritative] source.

Regarding this, it is said: "On account of the inconsistency of the Lord" (Patyurasāmañjasyāt). Because it teaches the practice of meditating upon principles that contradict the Vedas, the doctrine of Paśupati is indeed to be disregarded. 35.

Regarding this, the text begins with "tatredam" and so forth. He states the difference from the Vedic position with the words "vedāḥ khalu" (the Vedas indeed). "Have attained unity"—the sense is that this is due to the principle of all branches of the Veda conveying the same meaning (*sarvaśākhāpratyayanaya*). To extract the essential meaning of terms such as Śambhu and Śiva, he says "kevala" (solely). Just as the sentence "yasya parṇamayī" is intended to determine a specific substance, the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka is intended to determine a specific deity.

The sense is that, just as sentences prescribing the means of an oblation—such as "he offers with curds"—have meanings consistent with that [prescription], so too the passages concerning meditation have meanings that are concordant with that [deity].

Regarding the claim that there is the perception of another deity in the causal statements, he says: "In the same way. The logic of the goat and the sacrificial animal is intended here. Since this is intended by the statement "from which indeed these [beings arise]," it is indicated by the passage ending with "from the Supreme Person" that this very meaning is also intended in the Sūtra "janmādy asya yataḥ" (That from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed).)
And because the existence of a substratum is untenable. (2.2.36)
For, as has been stated in the sūtra *śāstrayonitvāt* (II.1.27), there is a defect in the view that [the Veda] is based solely on inference from those outside the Vedic tradition. || 36 ||
And because a locus [for such a claim] is untenable. To show that the fault about to be stated does not touch his own position, he says: "Of those outside the Veda. (36)
If it be argued that [the soul] is like an instrument, we say no, because of [the necessity of] experience and so forth. (2.2.37)

Just as [it would follow that] everything—including the instruments and the body—would belong to the living soul (jīva) who is the enjoyer; therefore, the possibility of [the Lord's] presiding over them is not tenable. || 37 ||

If it is argued that [the Lord] is like an instrument, we say no, because of [the resulting] experience and so forth. If He presides over the world by means of having a body, then there would be experience and the like; if not, there would be a requirement for another body. However, in the case of [His own] body, there is no such requirement, as this is due to the fact that being a body is self-sustaining both for itself and for others. || 37 ||
Either it would be finite, or it would lack omniscience. (2.2.38)

The word "vā" has the sense of "and. Since everything—merit, demerit, and so forth—of Paśupati would be entirely inconsistent, it was stated [in the sūtra] "because of inconsistency" (asāmañjasyāt). || 38 ||
Either there would be finitude or a lack of omniscience; the word "iva" (as if) indicates the sense of deception.
Thus ends the section concerning Paśupati (Sūtra 2.2.38).
Now follows Sūtra 2.2.39: "Because of the impossibility of origination."
Because it is common to the *Kapila* and other tantras, [the teaching] spoken by the Blessed One begins with: "The wise one is neither born nor does he die," and so forth. (39)

"Because of the impossibility of origination. He states the intermediate connection with the words "Kapila and others. That [objection] is raised and then refuted; thus, the two pairs of sūtras represent the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) and the established conclusion (siddhānta). To the question "How is the objection raised?", he says: "In that regard, as follows" (tatraivam). || 39 ||
And there can be no instrument for the agent. (2.2.40)
From Saṅkarṣaṇa, the mind known as Pradyumna is born... [and] thus the authority of this system is also refuted. || 40 ||

Nor is there an instrument for the agent. "Agent" refers to the individual soul (*jīva*). It is the position of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) that terms such as Saṅkarṣaṇa and others are qualifiers of the individual soul and so forth; however, it is the position of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntin*) that terms such as the individual soul and so forth are qualifiers of Saṅkarṣaṇa and others. || 40 ||
This being the case, we reply: "Or, even if [the elements] exist as consciousness and so forth, there is no negation of that [Brahman]. (2.2.41)
By the word "or," the position is reversed: ... ... just as Brahman is denoted by words such as "space" (ākāśa) and "breath" (prāṇa). || 41 ||

Or, if [the term] "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and so forth refers to [Vāsudeva], there is no negation of that [position]. He shows this to be a *siddhānta-sūtra* by means of the word "or" (*vā*). The sense is that it is like [the sūtras]: "Or rather, because the agent is common," or "Or one [is the same] because there is no difference in conjunction, form, injunction, and name. As for "and consciousness": the intention is that the words "consciousness" and so forth refer to Vāsudeva, who is the supreme cause whose nature is knowledge, in accordance with such mantras as "to Him whose nature is consciousness" and "the supreme primordial matter" (*parā prakṛtiḥ*). He states the meaning of the sentence: "Saṅkarṣaṇa."

Who are Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others? How can they possess the nature of the Supreme Brahman? In that case, how does the origin of Brahman occur? And consequently, how is the authority of the scripture established? To this, he says: "This has been stated. By the phrase "the fourfold form is worshipped," the fact that the fourfold manifestation is the object to be resorted to is established. [He worships] with their own names ending in "namaḥ" (salutation), which are the names of the Vyūhas. To the question of how they possess the nature of the Supreme Brahman, he says: "And that... [referring to the following].

The statement that a scripture devoted to the worship of the fourfold self (*cāturātmya*) is actually devoted to the worship of Brahman known as Vāsudeva is meaningful only if Vāsudeva himself possesses a fourfold nature. Not only is the worship of the fourfold self mentioned, but the worship of the *vibhava* (manifest) forms is also taught. For what purpose? He says "taddhi" (for that [is so]) to explain that Vāsudeva alone is the bestower of liberation. To the question of who these *vibhava* forms and others are, he says "vibhavo hi" (for the *vibhava* is...). This refers to the fourfold division of the *caturvyūha*.

In the statements included by the word "etcetera," one should observe the manifestations (*vyūha*), the expansions (*vibhava*), worship, fruits, and so forth. To the question, "Granted that these possess the nature of the Supreme Brahman, how is their origination possible? he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). "Unborn" (*ajāyamānaḥ*). The sense is that not only is there an absence of contradiction with the Śruti, but there is even conformity to it. He establishes the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the individual soul (*jīva*) and others: "Therein" (*tatra*). || 40 ||
And because of contradiction. (2-2-42)
For the production of a living being is indeed contradictory [to scripture]; thus, it is beyond reproach that he himself composed the Pañcarātra scripture.

A favorable indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been stated regarding Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others being the subjects [of the passage]. Now, an unfavorable indicative mark is stated regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) and others being the subjects: "And because of contradiction" (*vipratiṣedhāt*). Contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*) means a specific or various kinds of negation, as in the expression "it is contradicted by those scriptures. The difference in meaning between the two occurrences of the word *vipratiṣedha* in this section is justified by the requirements of the context, just as the two occurrences of the word *brahman* in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* differ in meaning according to their respective contexts.

Alternatively, the statement regarding its origination is contradicted by the scripture that negates such origination. He shows this negation with the words "as it has been said. Even though origination is established, since it is also seen in the Śruti, and because the method for resolving the lack of contradiction is the same, he says "birth" (janma) to show that the scripture is not in conflict with the Śruti; the meaning is that it will be explained as consisting of the expansion and contraction of knowledge caused by conjunction with and separation from a body. He concludes with "therefore" (ataḥ).

The alternative view—that those who conclude that the scripture lacks authority because of the statement regarding the birth of the individual soul (jīva) have merely attributed an unintended meaning of the scripture to an intended one and thus offered a refutation—is incorrect. He refutes the grounds for doubt other than the birth of the soul by restating them with the words "And this which... and so forth. Having accepted the point stated by the opponent, he has provided a rebuttal. Now, in order to state another meaning, he instructs [the reader] using that same illustration with the words "Or else..."; and he applies it to the case under discussion as well with the words "In the same way...".
To the question "How is this so?", he says: "Later. He demonstrates its nature as the clarification of the meaning of the Vedas by saying: "In that way."

A verse in the form of an answer to the question verses: "Having extracted the essence from the Vedāntas, the learned Lord Hari, out of compassion for his devotees, condensed [the teaching] for their ease.
[This is found] in the *Vākas*, the *Anuvākas*, the *Niṣads*, and the *Upaniṣads*.
Those whose nature is truth proclaim truth in their speech and in their sacred chants.
O Sage, this great [Veda] is the root of the vast tree of the Vedas;
the Ṛgveda and the others are its trunk, and likewise, they are its branches.
And such passages as these should be further investigated.

If the intended subject here is the meaning of the Vedas, then the Vedas themselves should be promulgated; what is the use of composing another book? One might ask: "Could this not be based on a desire to deceive, like the scriptures of the Buddha and others? To this, he says: "Therefore, that Blessed One... [and so forth].

The intended meaning is that the inference—"He is knowable through the Vedas alone because he is a person, like us"—is sublated. Regarding the point that Brahman is indeed known through the Vedānta, he says: "designated as the Supreme Brahman. He states the meaning established by the conventional designation of the word *bhagavat*: "entire" (*nikhila*). To show the absence of any desire to deceive and so forth, he says: "boundless" (*apāra*). By the term "devotees" (*bhaktān*), there is an exclusion of the followers of the Buddha’s teachings and others.

For that [Vedic revelation] was intended for the destruction of evil-doers such as the Asuras and others, and not for the protection of the virtuous such as Nārada and Śāṇḍilya; but this [work] is of that nature. Regarding the phrase "Ṛg and Yajus": the meaning is that because the Vedas are infinite, he composed other texts.

If one accepts the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the Vedas, why is there so much repetition of their meaning? Why is there the explicit statement that its purpose is to clarify that meaning? And why is it established in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts that [the scripture] is devoted to the purpose of the Vedas and was composed for the protection of the virtuous? Furthermore, the opposite of this constitutes the difference between this [scripture] and the teachings of the Sugata and others. If you argue that the mention of Nārada and others as listeners is due to a desire to deceive (*vipralipsā*), then there would be no confidence in the Veda either; for how could it not be possible that someone else composed it and merely proclaimed it to be authorless (*apauruṣeya*)?

As for the claim that others [interpret] the four sūtras as referring to some contradictory portion—[we reply that this is not so], because they have the same meaning as the statement: "The Lord Nārāyaṇa is the final goal," according to scripture and according to reason.
Thus ends the section on the impossibility of origination (Utpattyasambhavādhikaraṇa) — 8.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.

Now, having restated the meaning of the Sūtra as stated by others, he refutes it with the words beginning "yat tu" (but as for...). "Inconsistency with the syllables" [refers to] the word "vā" (or); "inconsistency with the word 'apratiṣedha'" [refers to] the word "śabda". He explains the contradiction of the intended meaning with the words "tathā hi" (for thus). Regarding the phrase "the logic of Vedānta": the sense is that one alone is not sufficient, because their purposes are different. The fruit of the Sūtra is the removal of misconceptions regarding the meaning of the Śākhā studied; the fruit of the *upabṛṃhaṇa* (supplementary elaboration) is the systematic determination of that meaning together with the contents of Śākhās not studied.

The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "this is the highest good" (*idaṃ śreyaḥ*) and so forth is figurative. That which is to be established by this [text] is Brahman, the means for attaining heaven and other such goals; "the beneficial" (*hitam*) refers to the means for liberation (*mokṣa*).

He raises the objection that its excellence as a work of Bharata is inconclusive with the words "But surely... This [work] possesses complete authority because it is entirely non-contradictory to the Vedas. If it were based on a single source, there would be a desire to know the specific truth; if it were based on various sources, there would be a desire to know the means of knowledge (*māna*). In the alternative—whether the question concerns the author's intention or the actual nature of the subject matter—the answer to the first point is: "These are cognitions. Two qualifiers of the speaker and the spoken are heard in the phrase "of the whole by himself. He states what is implied by these: "saying thus..."

He states the nature of the reflective discernment (*parāmarśa*) of the object as supported by logic: "by way of [realizing] that it does not have Brahman as its self. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore, in the Vedānta... He clarifies the stated point with another statement: "Therefore, in that very [Vedānta], this... Regarding the word "unified" (*ekībhūtāni*): their unity is stated for the sake of the meaning, because they serve as mutual auxiliaries (*parasparāṅgatva*). The single word located within the text to be explained (*vyākhyeya*) is an adjective qualifying the *Pañcarātra*.

"What, then, are the limbs? How do they constitute 'limbs'? In what respect is there a requirement for them? And how was all of that established in the *Pañcarātra*?"—to this he says: "This has been stated. "Then how is it refuted here?"—to this he says: "And in the *Śārīraka*. He explains the statement in the *Mahābhārata* which appears to grant full authority to the Sāṃkhya and other systems: "Therefore," etc.

If it is claimed that the Sāṃkhya and other systems possess complete authority (*prāmāṇya*), then that very statement itself would be invalid, because it asserts authority even for those portions that contradict the Veda. If one accepts the non-contradictory portions [of those systems], then one should not entertain such a doubt regarding the Buddha’s scriptures and others as well, since they do not accept the authority of the Veda. Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated. || 42 ||
Thus ends the section [Adhikaraṇa] 8, "The Impossibility of Origination.

This concludes the second quarter (pāda) of the second chapter in the *Śrutapradīpikā*, composed by Śrī Sudarśanasūri—the ornament of the Harita lineage, son of Vāgvijaya, who bears the secondary name Vedavyāsa by the divine command of Śrī Raṅgarāja, and who has grasped the heart of the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śrī Bhagavadrāmānuja through service at the feet of the venerable Varadācārya.
The third quarter of the second chapter.
Space [is not produced], because it is not mentioned [in the scriptural account of creation]. 2-3-1.

Because the systems outside the Veda, such as Sāṃkhya and others, are rooted in fallacious reasoning, the production of ether (viyat) that is heard [in the Vedas] is sublated by contradiction with the actual meaning—thus [it is said]. || 1 ||

"Not ether, because it is not heard [in scripture]. He states the connection: "Sāṃkhya, etc. The refutation of faults alleged by opponents regarding the cause and the rejection of their opposing positions were accomplished in the first two quarters [of this chapter]. Now, the faults alleged by opponents regarding the effect are being refuted; this is the connection. The impossibility of the self's origination was introduced [in the previous section]. Similarly, the non-origination of ether (*viyat*), which is a partless substance, constitutes the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*). The doubt is as follows: is the state of being an effect the same for both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), or is it of a different nature?
Having made uniformity the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), diversity is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of two quarters [of a verse].

Regarding this, he states the doubt concerning the first topic: "In that regard" (*tatra*). How can there be no scriptural authority (*aśruti*)? To the objection that there is indeed a scripture stating "ether was produced," he replies: "Of that which is possible" (*saṃbhāvitasya*). "Hearing" (*śravaṇam*) refers to valid cognition produced by words. For [scripture does not establish] what is impossible, as in the case of the identity between the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sun; this is the sense. A "sky-flower" is cited as an example. He establishes its impossibility through its being a partless substance and its being all-pervading: "Indeed not" (*na khalu*).

Regarding the point that mere reasoning (tarka) is sublated, he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ). The primacy of the creation of light is an implication of the scriptural meaning (śrutyarthāpatti). The sense is that the scripture which is free from [the need for] reasoning is stronger than that which is joined with it. || 1 ||
This being the case, it is replied: "But it exists" (2.3.2).
However, there is indeed the origination of space. It will be explained later that the non-origination of the self—which is an object beyond the senses—is not caused by its being partless. || 2 ||

However, there is [an objection]: incapacity does not consist in being beyond the scope of other means of knowledge (*māna*), because it would follow that sacrifices and the like could not be known as the means for attaining heaven and so forth. As for a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it does not arise merely from the perceptibility of the substratum (*dharmin*), nor does it constitute a subversion of the dharma taught in scripture, due to the faults previously mentioned; rather, incapacity arises from contradiction with a property perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as in the case of the identity of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sun. But such [contradiction] does not exist here, because omnipresence and being a partless substance are unestablished, given the scriptural declarations of its possessing ten attributes and its being composed of five elements.

But the final [argument] regarding the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth is inconclusive; the meaning is that inference is contradicted by scripture. To the question, "In that case, how is the eternity of the self established?", he says: "Of the self also... (verse 2).
Again, he objects: "Because of the impossibility of a secondary sense and because of the word itself. (Sūtra 2.3.3)

"From this very Self, indeed, ether [was produced]... because of the word "immortality" applied to the ether (*viyat*). He states the connection with the subsequent sūtra: "Again," etc. [Sūtra 2.3.1]: "Because of the impossibility of a secondary sense and because of the word. Since fire (*tejas*) comes first, there is no possibility of the creation of ether prior to that; nor is it possible after that, even according to your own view. How can the single word *saṃbhūta* (produced) apply to ether? [Sūtra 2.3.4]:
"And it may apply to one thing, just as the word 'Brahman' does."

Because it is heard in connection with that very same [subject]—in the passage beginning "From this very one..."—the repetition of the designation exists, just as there is a repetition of the action; such is the meaning. || 4 ||

And it may belong to one [word], as in the case of the word *brahman*. In that instance, the word *brahman* is employed twice; but here, since there is only one [word] due to *anuṣaṅga* (syntactic connection), how can there be both primary and secondary senses? To this he says: "And in the case of *anuṣaṅga*... The meaning is: even when there is a difference in usage (*prayoga*), the postulation of a difference in function (*vṛtti*) occurs through the repetition of the denotative act (*abhidhāna*). That [repetition] is the same in the case of *anuṣaṅga* as well; therefore, the postulation of that [difference in function] by means of it is not contradictory. "Repetition of the denotative act" means the repetition of the operation of making something known (*bodhana-vyāpāra*).
He refutes [the objection]: "There is a loss of the thesis because there is no distinction. (2.3.5)
In accordance with the Chāndogya Śruti, for other [elements]... because even ether is an effect of Brahman, it follows precisely from its non-difference from that [Brahman]. || 5 ||
He states that this is the final sūtra of the internal [position]—namely, "he refutes"—with the words: "The abandonment of the proposition [follows] because there is no distinction;
this is clear. (5)
From words. 2-3-6.
Moreover, the origination of ether is perceived in the Chāndogya; it is not possible to set aside the origination of ether established by another scriptural text. 6.

"From words": the passage beginning with "This world has that as its essence" (aitadātmyam) is cited because it aims to show that the entire effect has Brahman as its cause. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), passages such as "All these beings have Being as their root" (*sanmūlāḥ*) are included. Regarding the phrase "And not...": the meaning is that a statement concerning the production of a jar does not preclude the production of a cloth. To the objection that priority [of mention] might be the precluder, he says: "The ether" (*viyat*). The sense is that it is improper to abandon what is explicitly stated in scripture (*śruta*) and to postulate a priority that is not so stated (*aśruta*).
But as far as there is modification, there is division, as in the case of the world. (2.3.7)

The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "ca" (and). "Aitadātmyam" [means] the state of having this as its self... [this refers to] the intention that [these things] endure for a long time, like the gods. || 7 ||

"However, there is differentiation according to the degree of modification, as in the world; 'modification' means being an effect. By the word 'etcetera,' [the sūtra includes] the determination of oneness and so forth. And thus it is said: otherwise, even air would not be produced—this is the sense. (7)
By this, Mātariśvan is explained. (2.3.8)
For this very reason, [the term] *mātariśvan* is used for the wind (*vāyu*) as well, in order to refer to *mātariśvan*. ||8||

By this, Mātariśvan (the wind) is explained. There is no absence of the status of an *atideśa-sūtra* (an extended application rule), because there is no additional doubt [to be resolved]. The subsequent sūtra, "Fire [arises] from Mātariśvan," was not formulated by making a separate connection for Mātariśvan. The words "from this" (*ataḥ*) and so forth serve the purpose of carrying over [the discussion] from that point onward. Since the sūtra "But non-origination" (*asaṃbhavas tu*) has as its subject matter the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest, the sūtra concerning Mātariśvan follows immediately after the sūtra concerning ether (*viyat*). 5.8.8.
But the non-existence of that which exists is impossible, because it is logically untenable. (2.3.1)

The word *tu* (but) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Non-occurrence... [is as follows]: it is not possible for that which has been understood to have the nature of an effect not to arise. || 9 ||

"But the non-existence of that which exists is impossible, because it is not logically tenable. Indeed, it cannot be said that Brahman is unproduced. Without space and the other elements, for what would there be the impossibility of non-production, and for whom would there be this lack of logical tenability? To this he says: "This has been stated," referring to the proposition and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the determination of oneness and other such points are included.
Thus ends the section concerning ether (1).
Now follows: "Light [arises] from that, for so it says" (2.3.10).
For everything other than Brahman... [it is] thus stated: "From wind, fire. || 10 ||
"From that [fire], light [is produced]; for thus it says. He states the intermediate connection: "Brahman," etc. || 10 ||
Water also [arose] from that fire... for the scripture says, "He created water. (11) Water. The phrase "from that," etc., is to be supplied [to complete the sentence]. (11)
The earth. ||2-3-12||
"The earth arises from water... for the scripture says, 'They created food. || 12 ||
The earth [is the example]; likewise, here too, there is a logical connection (anuṣaṅga). 12.
But how can the earth be denoted by the word "food" (anna)? To this he says: "On account of the context, the form, and other words. (2.3.13)

Since the section concerns the creation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is only earth that [is intended]; thus, even though Brahman is the cause through a traditional succession (*paramparā*), these [scriptural passages] are justified. || 13 ||

In order to introduce the subsequent sūtra, he says: "Now, however" (*nanu*). [This is] because of the context, the form, and other words. "Context" (*adhikāra*) means the introductory topic (*prastāva*). || 13 ||
This being the case, we reply: "But he [the individual soul] [arises] from that very meditation on Him, because of the indicatory mark of that. (2.3.14)
By the word "but" (tu), the alternative view is excluded: [namely] that "of whom the intellect is the body," "of whom the unmanifest is the body," and so forth. || 14 ||

"But from that very meditation, on account of its characteristic mark, he [is the cause]. "On account of its characteristic mark" means that meditation itself is the characteristic mark of the Supreme. By the principle of the uniform teaching across all Vedic branches (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-naya*), he states that the power of "seeing" (*īkṣā*) is established even in the case of Mahat and the rest: "Mahat, Ahaṅkāra," etc. It is not merely because of the impossibility of seeing otherwise that these entities, having those respective bodies, possess causality; rather, their state of having those specific bodies is also directly stated in scripture, as he says: "And it is heard," etc. (Sūtra 14).
And as it has been said: "From this [Being] arises the vital breath... however, the reverse order is established from this [scriptural statement]. (2.3.15)
The word *tu* (but) serves the purpose of emphasis. ... [and so forth]—this also supports the possibility of everything arising directly from Brahman. || 15 ||

But the sequence is established by the reverse order from this. Therefore, he states the meaning of the word "and": "And that. By the phrase "would be obstructed," the loss of natural fitness is expressed. "Supporting" means that which establishes or sustains. || 15 ||
If it be argued that consciousness and the mind arise in succession within the interval because of their respective marks, we say no, because there is no distinction [between them]. 2.3.16.

Because they are the means for the accomplishment of consciousness, the sense organs are consciousness... and words such as "fire" (tejas) and so forth denote Brahman itself, which has become their very essence. || 16 ||

If it is argued that consciousness (*vijñāna*) and mind (*manas*) [arise] in succession because of their respective indicative marks (*liṅga*), we say no, because there is no distinction [between them]. He explains this term by saying "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). Here too—the sense is that it is not only in other scriptural passages (*śruti*)—there is a reading together with them; the sense is that this follows the principle of the "foremost" (*agryaprāya*). To the question "Of what is there no distinction?", he says: "from this" (*etasmāt*). The sense is that the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is indeed as follows: "from this [comes] breath (*prāṇa*)," "from this [comes] mind (*manas*). This has been explained in the *Dīpa* by virtue of its being explicitly stated.

The phrase "established by another scriptural passage" means that it would contradict the fact that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is a modification of air, arises prior to the [gross] elements. If even effects that are separated [in the sequence] arise from Brahman, one might ask how they can be designated by terms such as "fire" and so forth; to this he says: "Fire and the rest."

But if all words thus denote Brahman, [how is it that] "the designation of the moving and the non-moving, however, would be based on [Brahman], because that designation is not figurative, since it exists as long as that [Brahman] exists" (2.3.17)?

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of removing the doubt that has been raised. For it is understood in that way from the scriptural text concerning the differentiation of names and forms. || 17 ||

He raises a doubt regarding the immediately preceding Sūtra with the words "nanu" (but surely). [The Sūtra states: "But [the designation of birth and death] must depend on the moving and the non-moving; that designation is not figurative, because it occurs when those [bodies] exist. Expounding upon the refutation of the reason (*hetu*), he states the meaning of the sentence: "samasta" (all). In the first interpretation, the lack of etymological derivation and the possibility of another explanation would be explicitly stated. In the second, the scriptural authority for its extending up to Brahman would be presented. For both [interpretations], the meaning of either one is implied by the other.
Thus ends the section on fire (tejo'dhikaraṇa). Now:
"The Self [is not produced], because of the scriptural statement and because of its eternity according to those [scriptures]. (2.3.18)

The origination of the entire universe, beginning with space, from the supreme Brahman—this very origination, characterized as a change in essential nature, is denied in the case of the individual soul (jīva).

"The Self [is not produced], because of the eternity [of the individual soul] and because of those [scriptural texts]. He states the connection [between this section and the previous one]: "Of ether and so forth. Thus, it has been stated that the production of ether and the rest proceeds from Brahman, whose body is its immediately preceding cause. In that case, the connection is that there might likewise be such a production for the Self, which is partless. The doubt is whether there is production or not, as in the case of ether and the rest. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is established by means of scriptural implications and direct scriptural statements; furthermore, the word "progeny" (prajā) refers to the individual soul (jīva) in its state of association [with matter].

"In the final conclusion (rāddhānte), [it is said] 'of the Self'. The meaning of the word is "because it has been established as such" in relation to those [scriptural passages]. To the question "How so?", he removes the objection with the words "In this way. In order to explain [the point], he states the definition of being an effect: "For being an effect... He states the distinction: "To this extent..."

This is what is meant: the non-final goals (apuruṣārtha) and the transformations of essential nature (svarūpānyathābhāva) residing in the conscious and unconscious entities that constitute the modes of the objects of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the controller—all this is entirely consistent. || 18 ||

The distinction is made as follows: for the non-conscious (acit), "being an effect" consists in a change of its own nature; for the conscious (cit), however, it consists in the contraction and expansion of the intellect (dhī). If it is argued that the Supreme’s state of being an effect occurs through one of these two modes—since He is conscious, His state of being an effect would consist in a change of attributes (dharma-anyathābhāva), and by that, there would follow a lack of omniscience rooted in karma—the author says: "This has been stated. The meaning is: "pertaining to the object of experience" (bhogyagata), and not something unique to Himself. The phrase "origination and so forth" includes destruction.

He states the meaning of the word *ghaṭaka* (connector) with the words "in both states. To the question, "If it is always thus, how can there be the relation of cause and effect? he replies with "that [becomes manifest] at a certain time. The result is that being an effect consists in the attainment of another state. He explains the internal distinctions within the nature of being an effect with the word "therein" (*tatra*). Then, in response to the inquiry as to how Brahman can possess the nature of an effect, he states the common definition of being an effect: "from the causal state... (*kāraṇāvasthāyāḥ*).

Regarding the question of how the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are established, he says: "For this very reason. The meaning is that the illustrative example concerns merely the difference in states of a single reality characterized by manifold forms; however, any form contrary to what is perceived—such as hardness and so forth—is to be discarded. He states the distinction in the scope of the scriptural texts concerning origination and non-origination with the words "of such a kind" (*īdṛśa*); the word "unwanted" (*aniṣṭa*) is intended to exclude the idea that [the Lord] is the controller of states through an indirect mediation. Thus, the restriction to oneness is maintained.

"But those who..."—the meaning is: because [it is] stated in the Sūtra and because of our own acceptance. To the objection that "in that case, only that position should be accepted," he says: "To this extent... He says "of the controlling part" regarding the point that the controlling part does not possess the status of an enjoyer. ||18||
Thus ends the section on the Self (Ātmādhikaraṇa)—3. "Therefore, [the Self] is a knower" (2.3.19).

It has been stated that the individual soul (jīva) is not produced, like space and other elements; in connection with that, the nature of the soul is now being defined. ... "The agent, the conscious self, the person"—thus [it is said]: "In this very way, for this observer, these sixteen parts... (19).
