The word "immediately after" (*anantaram*) expresses the meaning of the word "from that" (*tataḥ*); for by the negation "not from this," it is understood that the [object's] own nature alone is real, not its quality. To this he says: "The meaning is as follows."
Because Brahman is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition, [the scripture] declares it to be unmanifest; for so it says: "That is unmanifest. (3.2.22)
That Brahman is not manifested by any other means of valid cognition... it is not grasped by the eye, nor even by speech, and so forth. || 22 ||

He states the connection with the immediately preceding sūtra: "Of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*). The meaning is that, having raised the objection that Brahman might be within the scope of another means of knowledge because perception grasps only pure existence (*sanmātra*), he confirms its being beyond the scope of other means of knowledge by way of refuting that objection. This has been made clear in the *Dīpa* and the *Sāra*. "For it says that it is unmanifest" (*tadavyaktamāha hi*)—this is explicit. (22)
And he states another reason: "Moreover, even in the case of propitiation, [the Lord is known] through perception and inference" (3.2.23).

Moreover, regarding "in order to propitiate" (saṃrādhane)—that is, for the sake of perfect pleasing—it is not possible [for the text] to merely restate the previously unestablished fact that Brahman possesses a distinction of two forms, the embodied and the formless. || 23 ||

"Even in the case of propitiation, [the Lord is known] through perception and inference. To the question, "Let Him be accessible through meditation; what then follows from that regarding the direct realization resulting from propitiation? he says: "In the form of devotion. (26)
And there is no difference [between the Lord and the individual soul], as in the case of light and so forth; and there is illumination in action through practice. 3.2.24.

For this reason as well, [the text] negates only that which has been previously stated as the extent [of Brahman's nature]; the meaning is that their being characterized by form, formlessness, and so forth is also perceived without distinction. || 24 ||

"And like light and so forth, there is non-distinctness; and light [is seen] in action through practice. Here, the doubt that the qualification by the manifold of the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) is merely superimposed for the sake of meditation is refuted. To the doubt that the cognition of those [attributes] as qualified by the manifold of the formed and the formless is an error, he explains the latter part [of the sūtra]: "being of the very nature of Brahman. The meaning is that because it is realized through meditation, the state of being qualified by the manifold is ultimately real (*paramārtha*), just like light, bliss, and so forth. || 24 ||
He concludes the statement regarding the twofold nature of Brahman: "Therefore, [Brahman is] with the Infinite; for thus is the mark. (3.2.25)
Therefore, by the reasons stated, Brahman is... [as follows]; for in this way, Brahman is established as possessing both characteristics. || 25 ||

Therefore, it is "endless," for such is the mark [of Brahman]. Since the statement "not this, not this" (neti neti) is intended as a negation that has no further limit, the meaning is that Brahman is established as being distinguished by an infinite collection of auspicious qualities. For those who take the position of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that Brahman possesses both marks (both auspicious and inauspicious), the concluding sūtra is not tenable, because the conclusion is reached through the establishment of that [very point].
Thus ends the section on the two-fold characteristics (ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa). 5.
But because of the designation of both [natures], it is like a serpent and its coils (ahikuṇḍalavat) — Sūtra 3.2.26.
The insentient manifold, consisting of both the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta), is nothing other than specific modes of arrangement (saṃsthānaviśeṣa) of that very Brahman. 26.

"But because of the designation of both [aspects], like a serpent and its coils. He states the connection [of this sūtra] with the words "the embodied one" (*mūrta*). The connection arises because of the context of non-conscious matter (*acit*). With the word "Pradhāna," the status of being a body is clarified by the mention of [Brahman's] lordship and so forth. By the analogy of the serpent and its coils—meaning that although there is a conjunction of a single genus through specific modifications of a single substance, as seen in examples such as a piece of rope—the material cause (*upādāna*) is [Brahman] itself, because of the existence of a relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*), just as in the case of the Lord and His power. By the phrase "just as of the individual soul" (*jīvasyeva*), the distinction of this [individual soul] from the previous [sūtra] "A part, manifold" (*aṃśo nānā*) is illuminated.

That [previous statement] has as its object the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman; this [present one], however, has as its object non-conscious matter (acit) and Brahman. Anticipating the objection of tautology, he says: "here" (iha). This is clear. || 26 ||
Or rather, it is like light and its substratum, because its nature is that of fire. 3.2.27.
The word "vā" (or) is for the purpose of excluding the alternative view. The meaning is that the very nature of Brahman itself constitutes the form of the manifold world of names and forms. || 27 ||

"Or like light and its substratum, because of its nature as luminosity; like a serpent and its coils"—this expresses the identity-in-difference between the insentient (acid) and Brahman through their relationship as effect and cause. "Like light and its substratum": the intended meaning is that identity-in-difference is expressed by way of both the individual (vyakti) and the universal (jāti). || 27 ||
Or as before. (3.2.28)
The word "vā" (or) is for the purpose of excluding two alternative views. ... Likewise, in this case, the individual soul and the insentient entity are both constituent parts of Brahman. 28.

Or as before. The term "two positions" (*pakṣadvaya*) is used for the purpose of excluding the first position. Because of the stated fault—that is, because it contradicts [the Lord's] changelessness and faultlessness. Regarding the phrase "all Śruti and Smṛti": if Brahman-hood were a genus (*jāti*), then there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between words such as "Lord" (*īśvara*) and the word "world" (*jagat*), just as in the case of "the maimed one" or "the shaven-headed one. If Brahman itself were the genus, then its being the locus of qualities such as omniscience would be untenable; this is the intended meaning. To the question, "Is partlessness observed as a property that is non-separately established (*apṛthaksiddha*)?", he says: "Thus, in this way... (28).
And because of the prohibition. (3.2.29)

Indeed, this great unborn Self... [is thus established]; and because Brahman is free from defects and is a mine of auspicious qualities, its possession of both characteristics is also proven. || 29 ||

And because of the prohibition. To the question "How [is this so]?", given that cause and effect are non-different, he says: "Therefore, it is subtle," and so forth. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the intended meaning is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). || 29 ||
Thus concludes the section on the serpent and its coils (Ahikuṇḍalādhikaraṇa). 6.
On account of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and difference, [Brahman is different from the individual soul] according to the opinion of others. 3.2.30.
Now, it is understood from this [scriptural passage] that there exists something even beyond the Supreme Brahman, which is the material and efficient cause of the world. || 30 ||

"On account of the designations of being the supreme, the bridge, the measure, the connection, and the distinction. By the word "from the supreme" (*parasmāt*), supremacy characterized as the state of being the goal to be attained is stated. However, by the phrase "of the Supreme Brahman" (*parabrahmaṇaḥ*), supremacy is stated in relation to its own effects. For stability—since if there were a deficiency in the qualities necessary for being the goal to be attained, there would be no perfection of the possession of both characteristics (liṅga)—faultlessness was established previously; here, however, the point of connection is that [Brahman] consists of auspicious qualities. To exclude the possibility of confusion, he says: "this" (*etam*). Likewise: "alone" (*kevalaḥ*) and "together with the genitive ending" (*ṣaṣṭhyantasahitaḥ*)—such is the distinction. || 30 ||
This being the case, it is replied: "But [it is so] on account of the commonality" (sāmānyāt tu). (Sūtra 3.2.31)
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position... and the root "tar" signifies "attainment," as in the expression "he attains the Vedānta. || 31 ||
But on account of the general context; he states the meaning of the root *tṛ* (to cross) with the words "this" (*etam*). || 31 ||
It exists for the purpose of cognition, like a foot. 3-2-32.

Just as this four-footed Brahman consisting of sixteen parts... [is described], so too is this [instruction] regarding the designation of speech and the other organs as the "feet" of Brahman intended solely for the purpose of meditation. 32.

"It has the sense of the intellect, like the word 'foot'. Regarding the objection that [the Lord] cannot be the object of the cause because of His infinity, he says: "He is the cause of the world. Therefore, as it is said: "Just as... The point is that since it is impossible for the Cause of all to be limited by speech and so forth, it is established that He is the object of meditation (upāsya). || 32 ||
How can that which is not measured by itself [be established] for the purpose of meditation?
... [It is so established] because of the distinction of location, as in the case of light and other such things. (3.2.33)

The meaning is that it is possible to perceive [the Self] by means of recollection, having delimited it through the various locations such as a jar, which serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of specific locations for speech and so forth, as well as the body. || 33 ||
"Because of the difference in location, as in the case of light and so forth. This sūtra concerns the subject of illustrative examples. 33.
And because of logical consistency. (3.2.34)
As for what was said, "This is the bridge to immortality" ... [and] "He reveals His own form to him," because of the scriptural teaching that there is no other means. || 34 ||

And because of logical consistency: the state of being the means to nothing else other than the goal itself—that is, the goal itself is the means—is established by both [scriptural] passages, namely "He chooses" and "He reveals. || 34 ||
Likewise, because of the negation of others. (3-2-35)

Furthermore, as for that which was stated [in the previous passage], "that which is higher than the high...," it is here also described as "higher than the highest" (*parāt paraḥ*) in its quality of being superior to the *samaṣṭipuruṣa* (the collective person). || 35 ||

Likewise, because of the negation of anything else: if the word "para" were construed with the ablative case in "than which there is nothing higher" (*yasmāt param*), the negation of equals would not be established. Consequently, the fact that the knowledge of Him alone is the means to liberation would not be established; for that was indeed asserted in the statement, "Only by knowing Him... Furthermore, the word "apara" (other) would be redundant, and there would be a contradiction with the phrase "nothing equal to Him. This is the intended meaning. Nor can the word "apara" be restricted [to mean only "unequals"], because such a restriction is not otherwise justified.

In the passage "That which is higher than that," the word *tataḥ* will indeed be explained as having the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Therefore, there is no application of the "cow and bull" maxim (where one term is redundant). He shows the immediate syntactical connection with the word *anya*, which is a synonym for *apara*, by saying "likewise. He states the lack of contradiction with other scriptural passages (*śruti*) by saying "not so. He explains that this sentence does not concern the cause by saying "for that..."

Since the term *hiraṇyagarbha* lacks the commonality [of application] found in the term *Śiva*, and since terms such as *Śambhu*, *Svayambhū*, and *Druhiṇa* are well-established [for Śiva], and because of the word *dhātṛ* in another passage, [the opponent] asserts that the four-faced one (Brahmā) is the supreme cause. To this, he replies with the words "from the waters" (*adbhyaḥ*). The meaning is: it is not so, because of the force of the context of the cause whose nature as the Supreme Person is understood from his lightning-like color, his reclining upon the ocean, and his being the Lord of Lakṣmī—all mentioned in the same passage. He states the meaning of the scripture cited by the opponent with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*).

Since it has the sense of being the cause (*hetvarthatva*), he demonstrates the logical connection (*anvaya*) with the words "That which is higher than the high" (*yad uttarataram*). Because of the consistency between preceding and following passages—such as "By that [Self] this is filled," "The Great Lord is indeed the Person"—and because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the *Puruṣasūkta* and the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka* through descriptions such as "having faces, heads, and necks everywhere," the word "Śiva" situated in the middle refers to the eternal Śiva. Otherwise, there would be contradictions with such statements as "There is no other path" and "Than whom there is nothing higher. This is the meaning. || 35 ||
By this [scriptural evidence], its omnipresence is established, on account of words such as "extent" (āyāma) and others. (3.2.36)
By this—by Brahman—the state of being all-pervasive, that is, the state of pervading the entire universe... therefore, this supreme Brahman alone is higher than everything. || 36 ||

By this [sūtra], its omnipresence is established through the words "extent" (āyāma) and so forth. This sūtra is intended as a proof for our own position. The scriptural passage "eternal and all-pervading" (nityaṃ vibhum) refers to the Supreme Person, because it occurs in the context of the verse "the Person higher than the high" (parāt paraṃ puruṣam). "All-pervading" (vibhum) means the Lord (prabhum). By the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is included a collection of co-ordinate statements concerning His support, governance, and pervasive extension.

The threefold non-limitation mentioned in the *Puruṣasūkta* and other texts, as well as the denial of anything equal or superior, is established; otherwise, the creation and dissolution whose agents are Brahmā and Śiva would not be logically possible.
Thus ends the section concerning another [agent]. 7.
The fruit [arises] from that [Brahman], because it is logical. 3.2.37.

It has been stated for the purpose of generating the desire to meditate upon the individual soul (jīva) that... for an insentient action, which perishes in a moment, cannot possibly be the means for achieving a result that occurs at a later time. || 37 ||

"Because the fruit [proceeds] from Him; because it is logical. This begins the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). The fact that He is the "fruit" has already been stated; the present section establishes His nature as the "bestower of the fruit"—this is the connection (*saṅgati*). And since He possesses auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇaguṇa*), this is included within the [third] chapter (*pāda*). He states the purpose of using the term "fruit" in common parlance: "equal," etc. In the previous section (*pūrva-kāṇḍa*), only the means (*dvāra*) was considered; here, however, its specific nature is examined—this is the distinction. He states the unsuitability of the other [cause]: "For not," etc.
And because it is so stated in scripture. (3.2.38)
Indeed, it is heard in scripture that this very great, unborn Self bestows as its fruit this very [Self] in the form of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 38 ||

Because it is so stated in scripture. "Annādaḥ" means "the giver of food. It is not merely on the basis of its capacity or incapacity that its status as a bestower of fruit is to be inferred; rather, the meaning is that this is also explicitly stated in scripture. || 38 ||
Now he states the prima facie view: "Jaimini [holds that] dharma [is the purpose], for that very reason. (3.2.39)
For this very reason—on account of logical reasoning and scripture—it is understood that [the sacrifice] is the means to the fruit by way of the *apūrva*. || 39 ||

"Jaimini [holds that the means] is dharma, for that very reason. He states the supporting argument: "In the world... He cites scripture: "Likewise... It is heard in scripture that [dharma] is a means; its being mediated by something else is to be inferred, so there is no contradiction. || 39 ||
But Bādarāyaṇa holds the former [view], because of the designation of a reason. (3.2.40)
The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude the previous position. Since they state that the fruit consisting of enjoyment and liberation arises from the Supreme Person, everything is consistent. 40.
Thus ends the section on the fruit (phalādhikaraṇa) — 8.
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.

He states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "But Bādarāyaṇa [holds the former view] on account of the mention of a reason. Anticipating the objection that the mantra and *arthavāda* passages have other purposes, he says: "of those desiring [results]" (*kāminaḥ*). The sense is that what is stated in mantras and *arthavādas* must be accepted—just as in the cases of the *rātrisatra* sacrifice, the attainment of stability, the killing of a cow, the hundred years of torment, the relationship between means and ends, the substance of sandalwood paste, collyrium, and specific sacrificial animals. [An opponent might argue: "Let the deity be the giver of the fruit; then the *apūrva* (unseen potency) may also be accepted. To this he replies: "In this way" (*evam*). The meaning is that abandoning what is heard in scripture and inventing what is not heard are both improper.

Regarding the claim that there is no fault if [the apūrva] is the expressed meaning, he says: "liṅādayaḥ" (the optative suffixes, etc.). The meaning is that there would be a double assumption (kalpanā-dvaya), namely, that the status of being expressed by the optative suffix must also be postulated. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "tadevam" (thus, in this way). To the question "What follows regarding the Lord's bestowing of the fruit?", he says: "vāyvādi" (wind, etc.). He demonstrates the possibility [of the Lord's agency] with: "loke ca" (and in the world). Intending to show that the contradiction with reasoning is refuted by the fact that it is a case of missing the proper time (kālātyayāpadeśa), he says: "vedāntāstu" (but the Vedāntas). Since it is established by the corroborating texts (upabṛṃhaṇa), the mention of praise and so forth is made. "All" means the entire collection of injunctions, explanatory passages (arthavāda), and mantras. || 40 ||
Thus ends the section on the fruit (phalādhikaraṇa)—the eighth.

Thus concludes the second quarter of the third chapter in the *Śrutapradīpikā*, composed by Śrī Sudarśanasūri—the ornament of the Harita lineage, son of Vāgvijayin, who bore the secondary name Vedavyāsa by the divine command of Śrī Raṅgarāja, and who grasped the heart of the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śrī Bhagavadrāmānuja through service at the feet of the venerable Varadācārya.
The third quarter of the third chapter.
The cognition [of Brahman] derived from all Vedānta texts is the same, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth. (3.3.1)

It has been stated that what remains to be said is for the purpose of generating the desire to meditate upon Brahman; therefore, because of this recognition, the unity of the knowledge (vidyā) exists even in other recensions (śākhā). || 1 ||

"All Vedānta texts convey the same cognition because there is no difference in their injunctions and so forth. He states the connection [to the previous section] with the words "it has been said. *Upasaṃhāra* (synthesis) is the acceptance elsewhere of what has been stated elsewhere. *Vikalpa* (option) is the application [of alternatives] to that very same [subject]. Synthesis occurs when there is non-difference; option occurs when there is difference. He states the function of the first section with the words "firstly. Regarding the word "multiple": the meaning is "that which is heard as having a single form, name, and result. The inquiry here is whether the principle stated in the section concerning different recensional branches (*śākhāntara*) applies here or not.

"No," says the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position. He states the reasoning for that: "because there is no distinction. The word "no distinction" (aviśeṣa) is intended to exclude [the idea] that "one offers the Agnihotra" and "one offers with curds" [are distinct acts]. The intention is that [the acts are distinct] because they possess differentiating characteristics, as in the cases of "he sacrifices the iḍā" and "he sacrifices the barhis. To the objection that the reasoning for the established conclusion (siddhānta) stated in the earlier section (Pūrvakāṇḍa) is sufficient, he shows an additional argument: "for this very reason. "For this very reason" means precisely because of the difference between the two knowledges (vidyā). He explains how otherwise the restriction would be untenable: "for if there were oneness of knowledge..."

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the word "one" (*ekam*) is supplied from the *Karmakāṇḍa-sūtra*. The term "from connection" (*saṃyogāt*) is not mentioned because of the primacy of the injunction (*codanā*). To ensure commonality between ritual action and meditation, and with the intention of referring to a verbal root that denotes meditation while excluding ritual action, it is stated as "a specific meaning of the verbal root. Although both "he knows" (*videt*) and "he meditates" (*upāset*) are heard in certain places, the phrase "of the synonym of *vid*" is used to establish their identity. Just as substance and deity belong to a ritual action, so too does the object of meditation belong to knowledge (*vidyā*), since the latter is defined by the former. || 1 ||

"But as for what was said [in the previous sūtra] regarding the repetition of the statement without qualification... [the reply is: 'If it be argued that [the meditations are] distinct because of the difference [in attributes], [we say] no, even in the case of a single [meditation]. (3.3.2)

Because of the repetition of the statement without distinction and because of the difference in context, since the repetition is thus justified, there is no possibility of another thing being enjoined therein. || 2 ||

He introduces the immediately following sūtra with the words: "But as for [the objection] that...": "If it be said [not so] because of difference, [we reply] even in the case of one [and the same]. In the preceding [sūtra], the reason establishing the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was stated in brief; here, however, the reason for refuting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated in brief. "That which is to be enjoined" refers to the universal; its particularization is the meditation (*upāsana*). "By way of inexplicability otherwise" means by way of the inexplicability consisting in the futility of the repetition of what is not different and the distinction of context (*prakaraṇabheda*). || 2 ||

And as for what was said regarding those who observe the head-vow (*śirovrata*): "For it is so with regard to the private recitation (*svādhyāya*), because of its inclusion in the *Samācāra*, and because of the restrictive rule, just like the *Sava* sacrifice. (3.3.3)

This is not so: the instruction regarding the head-vow (śirovrata) and so forth belongs only to the followers of the Atharva-veda who are connected with the single fire (ekāgni), and not to those using the three sacred fires (tretāgni). || 3 ||

He introduces the immediately following sūtra with the words, "And as for what was said... [The meaning is: Since the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) is of that nature, and because of its authority in the *samācāra* (traditional practice), there is a restriction regarding it, just as in the case of the *sava* sacrifices. Even though the knowledge (*vidyā*) is one and the same, the *śirovrata* (head-vow) is not applicable to followers of all *śākhās*, because that vow lacks the status of being an integral part (*aṅga*) of the knowledge. By the phrase "by the Vedic vow"—meaning by the *śirovrata*—the statement "this other vow is explained" is an extension (*atideśa*). The meaning is that because it is designated by the term "Vedic vow," it is understood to be an integral part of the study of the Veda.

He states the meaning of the phrase "of those very [people]" as follows: regarding the question of how there can be a restriction for the auxiliary of study, he says "and like the *sava*. The meaning is that it is logical for a particular ritual act to be restricted to those belonging to a specific recension (*śākhā*). "Seven suns" refers to those having the seven suns, beginning with Āroga, as their deities. || 3 ||
It shows. || 3-3-4 ||

And scripture shows that [the meditation on the form]... this is possible only through the combination of qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra) based on the unity of the knowledge (vidyaikatva) in both places. || 4 ||

And it shows [this]; the meaning is that because the Taittirīyaka passage contains an incomplete teaching, its reliance upon the Chāndogya indicates the identity of the two meditations (vidyā). || 4 ||

Thus, established by the logic of the section concerning other Vedic branches (Śākhāntarādhikaraṇa), [it is concluded]: "And there is a synthesis [of details] when the purpose is the same, as in the case of supplementary injunctions; for [the core rite] is identical. (Sūtra 3.3.5)

Thus, since meditation is the same in all the Vedāntas, the meaning is that those [qualities] must be combined because there is no distinction in their application; the word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis. || 5 ||

He introduces the subsequent sūtra with the words: "Thus, therefore" (*tadevam*). The conclusion [of the previous discussion] is based on the non-difference of the meaning, as in the case of supplementary injunctions (*vidhiśeṣa*), and because the meditation is the same. When there is a single designation for the fruit of the meditation, the word denoting a quality refers to a subordinate member (*aṅga*).
Thus concludes the section on the uniformity of all Vedānta texts (Sarvavedāntapratyayādhikaraṇa).
3.3.6: If it be argued that there is a difference [in the meditations] because of the words [used], we say no, because there is no distinction.

Thus, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth, the unity of the knowledge [is established]; otherwise, the word "udgītha" occurring in the introductory passage would have to be used figuratively to denote the agent; therefore, the knowledge is one. || 6 ||

"If it be argued that there is a difference [in the teachings] because of the word, we say no, because there is no distinction. The general principle for applying the method of "cognition of all branches" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-naya*) to the various sciences has been stated. Now, the presence or absence of causes for difference or non-difference regarding specific instances of those [sciences] is being examined; this is the connection (*saṅgati*). "Dvayāḥ" means of two kinds. "Atyayāma" means let us conquer. "Āsanyam" means proximate; that is, primary. The syntactical connection is "he overcomes" (*parābhavati*). "Saṃyetire" means they fought. "Ākhaṇam" means a lump of clay. "Ṛtvā" means having reached.

To the objection that no injunction (*vidhi*) has been heard here, he replies: "It is the object of knowledge. To the objection that there is no intended meaning (*tātparya*) regarding a fruit mentioned as a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), he replies: "The Udgītha."

The subject matter has been clarified. He states the doubt with the words "In that regard" (*tatra*). He introduces the aphorism with the words "In this case" (*atra*). "They directed [the breath] upward" (*udagāyan*) means they established the vision of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) upon the Udgātṛ priest. In the phrases "one who knows thus" (*evaṃ veda*) and "for one who knows thus" (*evaṃvidi*), the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) refers to the vision of the vital breath applied to the agent and the object. "Merely" (*kevala*) means that unity [of the action] arises from the collection of non-distinctive factors such as the injunction (*codanā*). "By any one of the others, such as difference of words" (*śabdāntarādiṣv anyatamena*) means that there is a distinction [between actions]. "That is not so" (*tan na*) means that because it conforms to the introductory context (*upakrama*), the status of being the agent is used figuratively (*upacarita*).
This being the position, we reply: "Not so, because of the difference in context, as in the case of the 'higher than the high' (parovarīyas) and other such [teachings]. (3.3.7)

The phrase "or not" rules out that alternative; for this is not the case, because the injunction regarding the vision of the golden person is distinct in purpose from the injunction regarding the vision characterized by qualities such as being higher than the high (*parovarīyastva*).

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "Or rather [it is not so], because of the difference in context, as in the case of 'the higher than the high' (*parovarīyastva*) and so on. The mention of the *udgītha* by means of the word *praṇava* is for the purpose of obtaining a specific accent for the *praṇava*. Regarding the term "of the Vājin-s": since there is no sublation, the word *udgītha* has the entire [Sāman] as its scope. Regarding the phrase "as that which is to be enjoined" (*vidheya*): the meaning is that a difference in form is established when there is a difference in what is to be enjoined. Even though it was stated "no," he explains the intent of using the word "or" (*vā*) once the exclusion is already established: "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). And "not" (*na ca*).

The method of *upakrama* (the opening statement) is not opposed to the acceptance of something additional, but rather to the sublation of what has been understood. And in this case, there is no such sublation; this is the meaning. As for the example: even when the object of meditation (*upāsya*) is one and the qualifying attributes of the vision (*dṛṣṭi-viśeṣaṇa*) are identical, the meditations (*vidyā*) differ due to the difference in the specific qualifying attributes of the vision—how much more so, then, when there is a difference in the object of meditation itself? This is the meaning. || 7 ||
If it is argued that it exists as a mere designation, then it has already been stated that even that [designation] exists.
Because of the identity of the name "Udgītha-vidyā," that [is the same]... just as in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the term "Udgītha-vidyā" refers to the many vidyās taught in the first prapāṭhaka. (8)

If it is argued that this has already been stated by way of designation (*saṃjñā*), even so, that too is clear. The explanation that the word *udgītha* refers to a part [of the rite] was already concluded previously; here, however, the doubt that there is a statement regarding the whole is being dispelled. || 8 ||
And because of pervasion, [the doctrine] is consistent. (3.3.9)

In the first chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, as well as in the subsequent sections... it is established that there is a difference between the meditations, since the priest who is the Udgātṛ is to be worshipped through the contemplation of him as Prāṇa. || 9 ||
"And because of pervasion, it is consistent. To the question, "How can a term denoting a whole be applied to a part? he says: "And in the part... He concludes: "Therefore... (9)
Thus ends the section on "Alteration" (Anyathātva-adhikaraṇa). 2.
On account of the non-difference of all [attributes], others are [to be supplied] here. 3.3.10.

In the Chāndogya and Vājasaneyaka [Upaniṣads], the Prāṇa-vidyā is the same; because the Prāṇa is recognized as the "eldest" through its association with qualities such as being the "most excellent" (vasiṣṭhatva), there is no difference between the two teachings. || 10 ||

These [sections] are distinct because of the absence of all identity. In the preceding section, *prāṇa* was introduced as a qualification of the vision (*dṛṣṭi*); here, however, an independent meditation (*upāsana*) upon that same object is described—this is the connection (*saṅgati*). The subject matter is clarified in the *Chāndogya*: "eldesthood" (*jyaiṣṭhya*) means seniority; "preeminence" (*śraiṣṭhya*) means excellence, according to the grammatical rule: "the suffix *śra* is used for what is excellent, and *jya* for what is senior. The words "most excellent" (*vasiṣṭha*), and so on, refer to the capacity of speech and the other organs for their respective functions. "They contended" (*vyūdire*) means they engaged in a dispute.

"Disputing" is the reading in the Vājasaneyi-saṃhitā. "You are the most capable of that"—the meaning is that since the efficacy of my own capacity is dependent upon you, the capacity belongs to you alone. || 10 ||
Thus concludes the section on the non-difference of all [attributes] (3). Now follows another investigation concerning the auxiliary elements of the knowledge of Prāṇa:
"Bliss and other [qualities] belong to the Principal. (3.3.11)
In this regard, since the qualities of the nature of Brahman are [present] in all higher knowledges (paravidyā), qualities such as bliss and others must be combined everywhere. 11.

In the middle [of the discussion], by way of a transition (*saṅgati*), he states that another reflection concerning the limbs of the science of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) will be undertaken, in order to introduce a different subject under consideration: "In the limbs of the science of the vital breath," etc. He explains the transition: "Just as," etc.; "of those not mentioned" means of those not explicitly stated through the stylistic turn of phrases such as "Whatever I am," and so forth.

"Bliss and so forth belong to the primary [Brahman]. Regarding 'the qualities of its own nature'—that is, the qualities that are concomitant with the realization of its own nature—[it says] 'because of non-difference. This is an elliptical construction (anuṣaṅga) of both the whole and a part, as in the case of the phrase 'now follows the instruction on words; of which words? 'Bliss and so forth' means 'bliss-ness and so forth,' just as in the rule 'dvyekayoḥ' (of two or one). || 11 ||

If that is so, then because the possessor of qualities (guṇin) is not distinct [from the qualities], there would be no attainment of such things as "having the beloved as the head," for increase and decrease occur only where there is difference. (3.3.12)
If it were being stated that the qualities of the nature of Brahman are attained, it would contradict such [scriptural passages] as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. || 12 ||

There is no attainment of [the Brahman] having "the beloved as its head" and so forth, for increase and decrease occur only where there is difference. "Increase and decrease" refer to stoutness and leanness. By the word "and so forth," the statement "neither coarse nor fine" is included.
"But surely, in this very way, [the qualities] belong only to those connected with Brahman... others, however, because of the commonality of the object. (3.3.13)
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the objection... [it is] faultless that those [attributes] which are heard in a particular place are to be combined there. || 13 ||

The others, however, [are attributes] because of the commonality of their referent (*artha*). "Referent" means the substratum (*dharmin*). "Commonality" is the rule that they are objects of cognition. He shows that truthfulness and the other qualities are invariably connected with the cognition of that [substratum] by saying, "from which indeed... (*yato vā*). "Characterized" (*upalakṣita*) means that causality is a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) regarding the portion of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) that is to be meditated upon. The sense is that [causality] is not included within what is to be made known [as an essential attribute]. "Qualified" refers to what is understood from the sentences concerning the cause. The meaning is that the portion of the qualified object, however, is defined by truthfulness and the other qualities. || 13 ||
If it be argued that "the head being dear" and so forth [are to be meditated upon] because otherwise there would follow the consequence of increase and decrease [in merit], [we reply:
no, because there is no purpose for such meditation. (3.3.14)
Because there is no other purpose [for them], these [attributes] such as having joy as the head do not persist in every cognition of the one consisting of bliss for the sake of meditation. || 14 ||

To introduce the immediately following sūtra, he says: "If... [The phrase] "for the sake of meditation" is because there is no other purpose. "For the sake of comprehension" means for the sake of establishing the knowledge produced by the scripture that is useful for meditation. "Not at all times" means not even during the act of worship (upāsanā). || 14 ||
And because of the word "Self. (3.3.15)
"The other inner self consists of bliss... it is understood that this is merely a figurative description intended for the sake of easy comprehension. (15)
And because of the word "self"; this is clear. 15.

But is it not the case that there is another inner self consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*)? [Reply: The self is indeed grasped here, as in other cases, because of what follows (Sūtra 3.3.18). 3.3.16.
"There is another inner self consisting of bliss... [This is known] from the subsequent passage concerning the one consisting of bliss: "May I be many, may I procreate. (Sūtra 16)

The grasping of the Self [is intended] as in other cases, because of what follows; for from what follows, the certainty that the Self is being grasped is the same even in the illustrative example. || 16 ||
If it is argued that [the relationship] exists because of positive concomitance (anvaya), [we reply] that it would [be established] through definitive restriction (avadhāraṇa). 3-3-17.

In the preceding cases, such as the sheaths consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*) and so forth, there is the application of the word "Self" (*ātman*) to what are not the Self; [here too] the application of the word "Self" to the lower self by means of the notion that it is the supreme Self is thus beyond reproach. || 17 ||

If it is argued that [the Supreme Self is meant] because of the subsequent context (*anvaya*), [we reply: this would be so because of the definitive restriction; however, it is not so on account of what follows later. The intention is that the introductory statement (*upakrama*) is indeed more powerful. Why? Because the introductory statement itself possesses that same [definitive] character; therefore, the subsequent passage cannot sublate it. If so, how is there a reference to the Supreme Self in the middle section? To this he says: "From the one consisting of food" (*annamaya*). Even there, the usage is not figurative based on the notion of a non-Supreme Self; rather, the usage is made precisely with the notion of the Supreme Self, solely on the basis of its being more internal than the preceding one.

Because of the perception of the internal [self] even from that [external action], the cognition of that [self] is known there; however, in the previous case, [the cognition of the self] had ceased. Even in the previous case, [the agent] was impelled by the cognition of another; thus, there is no sublation of the initial premise—this is the meaning. || 17 ||
Thus ends the section beginning with "Ānanda" (Sūtra 3.3.15).
Now, Sūtra 3.3.18: "On account of the mention of the effect, it is not something previously unknown."

Being a supplement to the previously introduced knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*), [the text] states only the encircling with water in the words "they encircle with water"; it does not prescribe sipping water (*ācamana*). 18.

"Because of the mention of the result preceded by reverence. He states the intermediate connection with the words "Previously. "He becomes a winner of clothing"—that is, he has obtained clothing. "Food"—meaning vital breath (*prāṇa*). This is for the purpose of praise, and not for the purpose of meditation (*upāsana*).

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "That which is not already established is enjoined, because it is described as being unestablished"—thus there is no distinction from the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*). To this he says: "Because it is unestablished. Even though the state of being unestablished is the same [in both cases], he says: "It is stated thus," regarding the view that because of the injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*), a different act of sipping (*ācamana*) is enjoined. Since the very thing already understood is what is unestablished, and since it is impossible to assume a different meaning, the injunction must be understood as the quality of being a garment (*vāsastva*), based on the consistency between the opening and the conclusion and because it follows both recensions (*śākhā*). It is not a different act of sipping, because of the opposite of what was stated. This is the meaning. || 18 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the description of the effect (Kāryākhyānādhikaraṇa).
Now follows: "And likewise, [the same person is meant] because of the non-difference [of the name]. (3.3.19)

In the *Vājasaneyaka*, within the *Agnirahasya*, there is the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā. Because there is no difference in the quality of "having true resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), there is no difference in form; therefore, the two are one and the same vidyā. || 19 ||

It is the same because there is no difference. The previous section was undertaken in connection with the meditation on Prāṇa. This [present section] has its connection with that preceding one. Just as qualities inherent in the cognition of the essential nature [of Brahman] are to be combined, so too are qualities such as "mastery" (vaśitva) which are included within "truthful resolve" (satyasaṅkalpatva). Since there is no difference in meaning between the additional "truthful resolve" mentioned in one place and the additional "mastery" and so forth mentioned elsewhere, there is no difference in the essential form (rūpa) [of the meditation]. || 19 ||
Thus ends the section on grammatical coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇa).
In the same way, it applies elsewhere as well due to the relationship [between the terms]. (3.3.20)

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka it is heard: "Truth is Brahman... Since there is oneness of Brahman as Truth, and because the knowledge is identical, there is a combination of both [attributes] in both places. || 20 ||

The same applies elsewhere due to the connection [of the word]. Thus, the connection with the word *evaṃ* (thus) is clear. The explanation of the word *upaniṣad* refers to its secret names. He states the meaning of the Sūtra: "Just as... (yathā) || 20 ||
This being the case, we reply: "Not so, because of the distinction. (3.3.21)

Nor is it the case that [the meditations are identical] because of the unity of the knowledge; for in both instances, the object of meditation is that which has the heart as its locus. Therefore, the distinction remains established. || 21 ||
And scripture shows this as well. (3.3.22)

And it shows [the application] between the substratum of the eye and the substratum of the sun... for when there is no natural attainment, there is a requirement for attainment through extended application (atideśa). || 22 ||

"Or rather, [the name is] not [restricted], because there is a distinction; and scripture shows this. These two sūtras are clear. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) and the established conclusion (siddhānta) are as follows: the restriction or non-restriction of the name depends on whether the place [of meditation] is included within the object of worship or not, resulting in difference or non-difference [respectively]. (Sūtras 21, 22)
Thus concludes the section on connection (saṃbandhādhikaraṇa). Now follows:
"And because of this, [the meditations on] the accumulation, the filling up, and the pervading [are also connected with the prāṇas]. (3.3.23)

In the Taittirīyaka, within the Nārāyaṇīya sections and the Khilas, there are passages intended to establish the majesty of the object of meditation, which is characterized by qualities such as being composed of mind (manomaya) and being free from sin (apahatapāpman). || 23 ||

The connection [of the section] is that, just as with the names, there is a fixed rule for the *saṃbhṛti* (accumulation), *dyu-vyāpti* (pervasion of heaven), and so forth; thus, even though they were not introduced (*anārabhya*)—that is, not mentioned in the context of a specific ritual—it is established that these are to be combined. To the objection that a dual number should have been used, he says: "It is a collective compound (*samāhāra*). Then, to the question of how the statement regarding the "small abode" (*arbhakaukasa*) being "greater" (*jyāyastva*) and so on is justified, he says: "In the case of Śāṇḍilya..."

[Objection: But if this were so, would there not then be a contradiction with the universal pervasion (*anantyānugama*) [of the Lord] in all places? [Reply: It is not so, because there is no contradiction due to the distinction between the natural (*svābhāvika*) and the conditional (*aupādhika*). For one who possesses conditional smallness, conditional greatness in that very same place is contradictory. However, even though He is infinite by nature, the cognition that He "occupies a small space" due to His grace is not contradictory. The meaning is that these [scriptural passages] are intended to demonstrate His majesty (*māhātmya*), but they do not intend to describe a specific form for meditation (*upāsya-ākāra*) that is unique to those particular Vidyās. || 23 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the collection [of materials].
3.3.24: And also in the Puruṣa-vidyā, because the others are not mentioned.
In the Taittirīyaka, the Puruṣavidyā is handed down... [therefore] there is a difference of knowledge; thus, there is no inclusion of the qualities mentioned in one place into the other. || 24 ||

"Also because the others are not mentioned in the Puruṣavidyā. The connection [of this sūtra] is as follows: just as the "supporting" (*saṃbhṛti*) and so forth, which are mentioned in proximity to the pervasion of heaven (*dyuvyāpti*), belong to that [vidyā], so too the Puruṣavidyā situated in proximity to the Brahmavidyā belongs as a subsidiary to it. The phrase "because no connection with a fruit is heard" means that since the Puruṣavidyā in its entirety lacks the nature of a Brahmavidyā, the fruit mentioned later is not appropriate for it. The intention is that it follows [the main vidyā] by the principle of the *ahīna* sacrifice (where a subordinate part follows the principal). Regarding the phrase "of that very thing heard in the Chāndogya": the intention is that it is precisely the mention of a contrary fruit that constitutes the differentiator, and not the non-mention of a fruit.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "That which is without fruit is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) [to another]. Its lack of fruit has been stated previously. Furthermore, there is no redundancy regarding the mention of the fruit in this case, because after first stating it as a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), it is subsequently designated as a subsidiary, and the fruit is then concluded [as belonging to the primary act]. || 24 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the Knowledge of the Person (Puruṣavidyā)—sūtra 3.3.25:
"Because of the difference in purpose, such as piercing, and so forth."

The followers of the Atharva Veda recite "śukraṃ pravidhya... at the beginning of their Upaniṣads; this reading is due to its being designated as "divākīrtya" and its inclusion among the "āraṇyaka-anuvākas. || 25 ||

Because of the difference in purpose, such as piercing (*vedha*) and so forth; the connection [of the discussion] arises from the doubt that, just like the *puruṣavidyā* situated in proximity, such mantras as "May Mitra be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no mitra*) might be auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Regarding the phrase "the *pravargya* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the *mahāvrata* and other rites.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the author includes] the speaking of truth (*ṛtavādana*) and other such practices. To the question, "Even though it is clear that these are not auxiliary members (*anaṅga*) [of the ritual], how can piercing (*vedha*) and the rest be considered part of the Sūtra? he says: "This has been stated. "By the power of the mantra" means by the power of the reality understood through the mantra. Then, as to why they are recited in the Upaniṣads, he says: "The Bright" (*śukram*). || 25 ||
Thus ends the section concerning piercing and so forth (sūtra 10).

Now, regarding the sūtra: "But at the time of departure, [the soul takes] the implements, because of the supplementary nature of the word 'taking up' (upāyana), as in the case of the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the praise, and the singing; this has been stated. (3.3.26)

The Chandogas record: "As a horse shakes off its hairs... [and so forth]. The fact that both [versions] are recorded by the Kauṣītakins is not contradictory, as it is a repetition without distinction due to the difference in the practitioners.

But in the case of "losing" (hāni), because it is supplementary to the word "attaining" (upāyana), it is like the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the hymns of praise, and the chanting; this has been stated. It has also been said that even for those things which are proximate, they do not constitute its constituent parts. Thus, the connection [of the present topic] is that the consideration of "losing" and so forth proceeds because of such proximity. "Attaining" (*upāyana*) means going over to another; for the scripture says, "they go over" (*utayanti*).

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), [the author] says "of the word *upāyana*" in order to exclude the status of being subordinate for anything else. The meaning is that the word *upāyana* is the subordinate element. To the question, "Why should it not be the other way around? he replies, "of the sentence concerning *upāyana*. He demonstrates this by saying, "by the knower" (*viduṣā*). For abandonment is what is primarily required by the knower; since *upāyana* (appropriation) is useful for that [abandonment], it is subordinate to it—this is the meaning.

To exclude the possibility that the statements regarding "loss" (*hāni*) and "means" (*upāyana*) function as mere examples in a relationship of primary and subordinate, he says: "In another passage. *Kuśāḥ* refers to specific types of vessels. Regarding the word "likewise" (*tathā*): since the word *deva* has fewer syllables, it could potentially come first; thus, the intended meaning is that the sequence depends on other sentences. *Samayāviṣite* means "when [the sun] has half-risen"; *samayodite* means "when [the sun] has half-risen. *Upākaroti* means "he praises. He states the undesirable consequence if the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) is not accepted: "In this way. The meaning is that it would not be logical, because it would involve the contingency of sublation (*pākṣikabādha*).

The phrase "it has been said" refers to a portion of the Sūtra. He completes it with the words "in the preceding [Sūtra]. Regarding "because they form a single syntactical unit": they constitute a single syntactical unit because they are connected through the relationship of mutual supplement and thing to be supplemented. Regarding "of the isolated [text]": because of its absence—that is, because it lacks authoritative basis. Regarding "of the Kauṣītakins": since the meaning of one is established even when only the other is mentioned, both are stated in all cases; thus, the mention of both is a repetition without distinction, and the meaning is that there is no contradiction due to the difference among the students. || 26 ||
Thus ends the section on the other [state]. 11.
*Sāmparāye tartavyābhāvāt tathā hyanye* (3.3.27): Because there is nothing to be crossed over in the state after death; for thus it is with others.
The relinquishing and taking up of good and evil deeds... "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [in the Absolute]. (7)

Because there is nothing further to be crossed in the hereafter, so it is with others; the meeting has taken place. The Tāṇḍins—namely, the Chandogas—state this in their final conclusion: "to be crossed. The root *tṛ* (to cross) signifies "attainment. || 27 ||
According to one's desire, because there is no contradiction in either case. (3.3.28)
Thus, by virtue of the nature of the meaning, [the phrase] "good and evil deeds" is to be understood as following from the first heard word-part; this is the sense. || 28 ||

Because both [interpretations] are not in conflict with one's preference. Regarding the "words"—that is, the constituent parts of sentences which stand in the place of words in relation to the great sentence (mahāvākya)—he states where and how they are connected: "In the Kauṣītaki [Upaniṣad]," as in "He performs the Agnihotra sacrifice" and "He cooks the gruel. || 28 ||
Here the opponent objects: "The purposefulness of the movement [of the soul] is established in both ways; otherwise, there would be a contradiction. (3.3.29)
...of a portion of good and evil deeds...; therefore, it is not possible that at the time of departure there is a total destruction of the karma of the wise man. || 29 ||

The purposefulness of the movement [of the soul] is established in both ways; otherwise, there would be a contradiction. Even though [the soul] is atomic, because its true resolve has not yet manifested and it is separated from the body, it lacks the capacity for movement. || 29 ||
To this, the following reply is given: "It is established [that the Self exists], because its characteristic object is perceived, as in the case of the world. (3.3.30)

The destruction of all karma occurs precisely at the moment of passing away when one has been reborn... just as those who make that very tank or other structure firm continue to drink water there; it is like that. || 30 ||

"Having been born [there], because of the perception of objects characterized by that [state], as in the world; the perception of objects of a similar class occurs in the form of a body. However, the phrase 'characterized by that' is stated with the intention that this body is not produced solely by karma, and not [merely] because of the perception of that [state]. He explains the greatness of knowledge (vidyā) with the words 'For knowledge...'. The sense is that it is logical for merit and demerit, like [the body], to cause the persistence of the body which is the means for attaining their own fruits. As for the example 'Just as...':
it is an illustration of how something produced from another cause persists for the sake of another effect even in the absence of its [original] cause. || 30 ||

Now, it might be argued: for those who possess knowledge, who have directly realized the supreme reality, there is a continued existence as long as their office lasts; this is the case for those holding an office (ādhikārikāḥ). (Sūtra 3.3.31)

We do not maintain that for all the wise, at the time of the fall of the body... therefore, for them there is no attainment of the path beginning with the Rays (arcir-ādi-gati) immediately after the fall of the body. || 31 ||

He introduces the immediately following sūtra with the words, "Now, it might be argued... The meaning is: "The abiding of those who hold office lasts as long as their office. "Office" means a position. The resolution is that for those who attain the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) immediately after the fall of the body, there is the destruction of merit and demerit at that very same time. || 31 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the next world—12.
There is no restriction for all [the gods]; there is no contradiction, because of both scripture and inference. (3.3.32)
In those meditations such as that of Upakosala, this destination, which is common to all vidyās, is already established and is merely restated in the case of the Upakosala-vidyā and others. || 32 ||

There is no restriction for all; there is no contradiction, on account of both scripture and inference. The path has been introduced. Now, the connection [of this section] is the consideration of whether that [attainment] is restricted or unrestricted. Having raised the seed of the final conclusion as a doubt, he says: "And these who... [and] "they meditate..."—the meaning is "of this sentence. "On account of the absence of proof"—the sense is that there is no evidence for the words *satya* and *tapas* denoting Brahman.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), [the author] shows that all those who know Brahman are indicated in the cited passage by the words "those who know thus" (*itthaṃ viduḥ*). Regarding the word "austerity" (*tapaḥ*): the intention is such passages as "he who performs the highest, great austerity. Regarding the phrase "elsewhere": one should not say that although those two [terms, *tapas* and *vidyā*] refer to Brahman in other contexts, they might not do so here; for it has been stated that [the path] "leads to Brahman," and because the fruit corresponds to the nature of the meditation (*upāsana*). Regarding the phrase "Smṛti also": the meaning is that it is said, "of the knowers of Brahman" (*brahmavidaḥ*). || 32 ||

Thus ends the section on non-restriction (Adhikaraṇa 13): "But there is inclusion of those meditations on the syllable [Om], because of the commonality and the presence of that [state], as in the case of the Upasads; so it has been said. (3.3.33)

It is heard in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "This indeed is that syllable... [and so forth]. [The sūtra states: "In case of a conflict between a secondary and a primary [meaning], the connection with the Veda is determined by the primary, because it is for its sake. (33)

"But there is an inclusion of those [attributes] based on syllables because of their commonality and the existence of that [state]; as in the case of the *aupasada* [sacrifice], so it has been stated. The connection [of this section] is as follows: it was previously stated that the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) is common to all meditations (*vidyā*). Similarly, it is now determined that attributes such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) and so forth are also common; thus the logical connection is established. The phrase "consisting of the nature of being the opposite of the phenomenal world" (*prapañcatyanīkatārūpa*) means that Brahman is the opposite of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Being the opposite of the phenomenal world means having a nature that is contrary to the nature of the phenomenal world—this is what is meant by "not gross" and so forth. Indeed, the words "not gross" and the rest are found within the subject passage (*viṣayavākya*).

"Non-material" (*asthūla*) means other than material. The sense is that by this, the contradiction characterized by having different substrata is established as a consequence. Attributes such as being beyond hunger and so forth, which constitute the specific form of faultlessness, are determined according to their respective meditations (*vidyās*). However, the intention is that the state of being the opposite of everything to be abandoned in general is a limb of all meditations; thus, the term "opposite of the phenomenal world" (*prapañca-pratyanīka*) is used. Truthfulness is also included here, as seen in such scriptural passages as "without blemish" (*niravadya*); yet there is a distinction in that attributes like non-materiality are of the nature of negation.

Therefore, there is no separate consideration [of the object], because of the absence of a means of valid cognition—that is, the absence of a reason. To the objection that the capacity of the thing itself constitutes the reason, he says: "In its own nature" (svarūpe).

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "The universal (*sāmānya*) and its existence (*tadbhāva*) together constitute the means of proof (*hetu*), because they exist in the cognition [of the subject], that is, because they exist as its objects. Since the negation of other attributes is preceded by the cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*), those [negations] which are of the nature of prohibitions do not possess the status of qualities (*guṇa*) invariably concomitant with the cognition of that [substratum]. To this he says: "This has been stated. "By way of its unique form" means "by way of its unique essential nature (*svarūpa*). The use of the instrumental case is figurative; the meaning is "the apprehension of the unique essential nature. Otherwise, the subsequent passage would not be coherent.

"Form" (ākāra) means its own nature (svarūpa). To the objection that even the inner self (pratyagātman) lacks uniqueness because it is free from anything to be discarded, he says: "But of the inner self... Here, "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇya) refers to the opposite—that is, a specific form—and what is intended is merely the possession of attributes that exclude the possibility of being of the same class; it does not mean simply the non-existence [of those attributes] among things of the same or different classes. Even when "changelessness" (avikāratva) is stated, the suspicion of insentience (jaḍatva) does not depart. Even when "non-insentience" (ajaḍatva) is mentioned, the suspicion of grossness, minuteness, and so forth does not depart.

If it is argued that there is no suspicion of grossness (*sthūlatva*) and so forth because of the exclusion of pervasiveness (*vyāpaka*), insentience (*jaḍatva*), and the like, then why should the exclusion of the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*), which is pervaded [by those qualities], not also be suspected? If it is argued that this is because a reality known solely through scripture (*śāstraikagamya*) is not an object of logical pervasion (*vyāpti*), then the same applies to the suspicion of grossness and the like. Consequently, since it is possible for some specific entity that is gross to be non-insentient and so forth, the suspicion regarding the commonality (*sājātya*) of that grossness with its respective entities does not depart.

Therefore, since the suspicion of belonging to this or that genus is pacified precisely by being the opposite of all things to be discarded, such as grossness and so forth, the qualities of "not gross" and so on constitute the unique characteristics (asādhāraṇa-rūpa) because they exclude the suspicion of such generic similarity.

The word "qualified" (*viśeṣita*) refers to that which follows [the general rule]. He states the portion dependent upon the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) with the words "of the qualities" (*guṇānām*). "Jāmadagnya" means performed by Jamadagni. "Puroḍāśī" means having the *puroḍāśa* cake as its substance. "By way of being whispered" (*upāṃśutvena*): because of the scriptural statement "whispered with the *yajus*," and because it is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *upasads* belonging to the Yajurveda, there is whispering. Otherwise, according to the rule "loudly with the *sāman*," there would be loud chanting. || 33 ||
But surely, in this way, [the same applies] to all the vidyās concerning Brahman... because of the teaching of this much [in each]. (3.3.34)

"Āmananam" means reflecting with direct orientation... [they] are established in each respective science (vidyā) as objects of contemplation, even though they follow after the primary subject matter. || 34 ||

He states a doubt regarding the immediately preceding sūtra: "But thus... (nanvevam). [The sūtra says: "Because of this much being taught" (iyadāmananāt). He explains the literal meaning: "Being taught" (āmananam) means... He explains the intended sense: "By which... (yena) || 34 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the syllable *akṣara*—14.

If it be argued that, as in the case of the aggregate of living beings, the distinction [of the individual souls] from the Self would otherwise be untenable, we reply: no, for it is like the case of instruction. (3.3.35)

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the question of Uṣasta is recorded as follows: ... because of the identity of form—established by demonstrating that Brahman is the cause of the life-breath of all living beings and is beyond hunger and other such needs—the two meditations are one.

If it be argued that, as in the case of the "village of beings" (*bhūtagrāma*), there is no possibility of difference [between the two] because they are not other than one's own self, we reply: "No, as in the case of instruction. If the state of being the opposite of all that is to be abandoned (*heyapratyanīkatva*) is unique to the Supreme Self, then Brahman would be beyond hunger and so forth; yet if the individual soul (*jīva*) were endowed with the functions of breathing and so on, such a doubt arises—this constitutes the connection [of the topic]. By the term "Uṣasta’s question," the context (*prakaraṇa*) is indicated. To the objection that there is no difference in form because the questions are uniform, he says: "In the answer..."

To the question of how [the Self] is "within all," he says: "And because it possesses the aggregate of elements" (*bhūtagrāmavataśca*). Anticipating an objection regarding the lack of logical consistency, he says: "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). The passage beginning with "This very [Self]" (*tadidam*) and so forth is the explanation of the sūtra beginning with "between" (*antarā*).

"Regarding this, the answer begins with 'atrottaram' and so forth. By the term 'unconditioned' (nirupādhika), the individual soul (jīva) is excluded. The phrase 'the seer of seeing' (dṛṣṭerdraṣṭāram) is like the expression 'he cooks the cooking of the rice' (odanapākaṃ pacati). The meaning is that the subsequent questions and answers [also address this]. Thus, the distinction between the meditations (vidyābheda) based on the difference of the substrata (dharmibheda) has been refuted. || 35 ||
Now, it might be argued: even though both the question and the answer... [the exchange of attributes] is intended for the sake of glorification, as in other cases. (3.3.36)

There is no difference in the knowledge here, because through the question and the answer... it is established that the object of meditation is presented as distinguished by one quality after another, just like that [in the case of the preceding meditation]. 36.

He states the doubt regarding what immediately follows with the words, "Now, it might be argued" (*atha syāt*). A difference in form was stated due to a difference in attributes; however, the reason for the possibility of a difference in knowledge (*vidyā*) is a difference in the questioners. If there were identity of the questioner, then identity [of the knowledge] would be possible, because of the independence from other knowledges. [The sūtra] says, "They distinguish [the two] by means of exchange, as in the other cases. He explains the "exchange" (*vyatihāra*) with the words, "Of Uṣasta... He states the result of that with the words, "In this way... While stating that very point, he explains the word "they distinguish" (*viśiṣanti*) with the words, "They [distinguish] him as all..."

The objection regarding a difference in form based on the identity of qualities has been answered. The point is that the difference in questioners—as seen in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā and other instances—is an inconsistent [objection]. As for the word "nanu" (but surely): the meaning is that for those whose minds are already distinguished, either the quality of being the sustainer of all living beings or the quality of transcending hunger and so forth is sufficient. To this, the reply is given: "tad ucyate" (that is said); the resolution is that it is for the purpose of generating an excellence of distinguished understanding. || 36 ||
Even there, despite the difference between question and answer, it is that very same [Brahman], for [the attributes] such as truth and so forth are identical. (3.3.37)
For that very [Brahman], denoted by the word "Being" (sat), is the supreme cause; and terms such as "Truth" (satya) and so forth are introduced and concluded in all the various enumerations.

He introduces the subsequent sūtra—"tatrāpi" (even there)—in order to establish the identity of the knowledge [of the two passages]. For it is that very same [knowledge] which consists of "Truth" and so forth. The meaning is that the quality of being the supreme cause is a property of the object of meditation, because qualities such as truthfulness and selfhood, which are conducive to that, are repeated in each successive section (paryāya).
Some, however, [interpret] the two sūtras in the manner already described, by means of arguments such as "the exchange [of attributes] is superior" and "mutual dependence. 37.

Having restated another opinion, he refutes it with the words "But some...". He states that this [opinion] must also be addressed in the Sūtra with the words "But that... (tat tu). Regarding the two Sūtras—"On account of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere" and "The Self"—which concern the identity of the non-sentient and the individual soul, he says "And not here... in response to the claim that there is a mutual superimposition of the nature of the individual soul and the Supreme. He says "That is not true," the sense being that a false superimposition, like the meditation on the *tārkṣya* [as a horse], does not lead to liberation. With the words "And by the subsequent [Sūtra]... and so forth, he asks "What follows from that? and answers with "And not... (na ca).

"Between two"—that is, between two sentences. "And it abandons"—the meaning is that it leaves the body. "Of the two"—of the two meditations mentioned in the subsequent sentences. "The fruit of the qualities"—meaning the fruit of the subordinate members (aṅga-phala). "Due to the absence of proof"—due to the absence of a logical reason. "Of the two"—of the destruction of sin and the abandonment of the body. "Because there is no difference in their connection"—meaning because the primary fruits are identical. By the word "etcetera," the arguments supporting his own view have been stated. || 37 ||
Thus concludes the section on the inner nature (Antaratvādhikaraṇa): "Desire and so forth [belong] elsewhere and there as well, because of the abodes and so forth" (3.3.38).

It is heard in the Chāndogya: "Now, this which is here... [and so on]. From this, it is understood that [the term] denotes space (ākāśa). Therefore, there is identity of the meditations (vidyaikyam). || 38 ||

In other instances, such as those concerning desire and so forth, the identity of the knowledge (*vidya*) was stated because there is no difference in the substratum (*dharmin*) regarding the qualities of being the animator and transcending hunger and so forth. Here, however, there arises the doubt that there is a difference in the substratum because of the eightfold set of qualities (*guṇāṣṭaka*) such as mastery (*vaśitva*) and so on; this constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*). In this context, the exclusion of the one who has transcended space (*vyomātīta*) follows as a result. There is a difference in attributes (*dharmabheda*) consisting of the eightfold set of qualities and mastery and so forth; a difference in substrata (*dharmibheda*) is stated in terms of "space" and "the one reclining therein."

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), [the author], while setting aside the doubt that mere attributes (*dharma-mātra*) might be the object of meditation, explains the phrase "in another [text]" (*itaratra*) by citing the *Vājasaneyaka*: "In the ether," and so forth. The inherent tendency of the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) to refer to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) is set aside in the *Chāndogya* by the hearing of the attributes of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). However, in the *Vājasaneyaka*, there is no such sublation; because the attributes of the Supreme Self are heard in relation to that which rests in the ether, the meaning is that this very [ether] is the Supreme Self.
Now, it might be argued: as it is stated in the Vājasaneyaka...
[the omission does not occur] because of the emphasis. 3.3.39.

Since the qualities of Brahman are not established by any other means of knowledge, when Brahman is being propounded, attributes such as having true desires and so forth are enjoined with respect to it. || 39 ||

He raises a doubt regarding the immediately preceding sūtra with the words "atha" (now). The Dahara-vidyā of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad has the qualified Brahman as its object; this [present] vidyā, however, has the unqualified Brahman as its object. Therefore, the meaning is that they are not identical.

"Non-omission due to reverence": this dispels the suspicion that the statement "of those not [already] obtained" is a mere restatement for the sake of prohibition. Furthermore, its status as a *pūrvapakṣa* (novelty) has been stated as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya-liṅga*). The justification is that what has already been enjoined cannot be prohibited. The fruit is stated by the passage beginning with "Therefore, those here who... and so forth. In that very context, there is repetition for the sake of accomplishment. And as for the words "not," etc., the mention of qualities is not rooted in a desire to deceive.

This is because [the denial of qualities] would follow even from the statement regarding the absence of qualities (*nairguṇya*). Nor is it for the purpose of meditating on a result belonging to this world, since it occurs within the section concerning liberation and because of the scriptural hearing of "Truth" (*satya*); such is the sense. He states the meaning of "neither manifoldness exists here" and so forth with the words "not here. According to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*), difference is enjoined as a mode of Brahman; therefore, the prohibition concerns difference that does not have Brahman as its essence. "In one way," however, expresses uniformity by virtue of having Brahman as its essence. "He is not this" refers to the dissimilarity with the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), in accordance with the context. "Not of this": of this phenomenal world. (39)
But even so, [the objection remains]: "Those here who ... [regard] the self ... [attain the worlds of the fathers]; therefore, because of that statement when [the path] is present. (3.3.40)

Upasthiti—attendance, that is, being present at the service of one who has attained Brahman. For the seeker of liberation, qualities such as the desire for truth (satyakāmatva) and others are to be combined [from various texts]. || 40 ||

Introducing the immediately following sūtra, he raises an objection with the words "nanu" (but surely). [The sūtra states: "Because that is taught when [the means] are present; for this very reason. The intention is that the status of being a reason is implied by what was just stated. To the question, "How can there be dependence on anything else for one who has the experience of Brahman? he replies with the words "tad etat" (this very thing). || 40 ||
Thus ends the section concerning desire and so forth (Kāmādy-adhikaraṇa) – 16.
"There is no rule regarding the determination of that [meditation], because it is seen [in scripture]; for [such meditation] is separate, and its fruit is the absence of obstacles. (3.3.41)

"One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha... ... ... "Like the case of the *godohana* vessel and others, the meditations on the Udgītha and so forth are not to be combined with the ritual acts in a mandatory manner. (Sūtra 4.1.41)

Regarding the rule of non-restriction for that determination: because it is seen separately, there is no obstruction; the fruit [is the attainment of the goal]. It has been stated that qualities such as "having true desires" (satyakāmatva) are to be combined [with other meditations]. Thus, there arises the doubt whether the cognitions of the *udgītha* and so forth must necessarily be combined. This is the connection [of the present discussion]. Although the state of being a subsidiary part of the ritual (*kratvaṅga*) applies to what is mentioned in one branch of the Veda by way of the subsidiaries of the rite studied in another branch—as in the case of sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇa*) and so on—the fact of being made of *parṇa*-wood is cited as an illustrative example.

To the objection—"If it yields no fruit, how can there be its performance; if it does yield fruit, how can it be a subsidiary (aṅga)?"—he says: "By way of being a subsidiary to the ritual action" (*karmāṅgatvena*). To the point that "it is [merely] a hundredfold," he says: "That which indeed... The meaning is that the mention of the fruit is an *arthavāda* (a commendatory statement). Furthermore, it is intended that the fruit is not as proximate as in the case of the *godohana* vessel, because it resides in a different sentence.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the principle of the *Rātrisatra* is stated so that the fruit mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) may be accepted; for the "firm foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*) is indeed accepted as being derived from the explanatory passage. (41)
Thus concludes the section on the non-restriction of that determination (tannirdhāraṇāniyamādhikaraṇa). 17.
"It is stated to be like the offering" (pradānavadeva taduktam). 3.3.42.
In the Dahara-vidyā, it is said: "Those here who worship the Self... and so forth; thus it has been stated: "The deities are indeed manifold because of their distinctness. (42)

That has been stated as being like the giving away [of the sacrificial fee]. What was previously discussed was incidental; therefore, the connection is that this is another inquiry concerning the subject of the *dahara-vidyā* (the "small" meditation), which was considered previously. "Contemplation of the possessor of qualities alone" means contemplation of the essential nature qualified by bliss and so forth. "Contemplation of the qualities" means contemplation of the eightfold qualities. "Only once" means by way of a single, simultaneous treatment (*tantra*).
