In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "The form qualified by attributes" means the nature related to the attributes, the aggregate of both the attribute and the possessor of the attribute (*guṇin*). And that is distinct from the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of Brahman]. Regarding the word "freed" (*apahata*): since words such as "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā*) extend to the substratum (*dharmī*), the meaning is that the meditation upon them is also enjoined in the passage "whose desires are true" (*satyān kāmān*).
Thus ends the section on the offering (pradānādhikaraṇa). 18.
On account of the abundance of indicatory marks; for that is more powerful, and that too [is more powerful]. (3.3.43)
The Taittirīyas study [this] immediately after the Dahara-vidyā... and because it is being determined [as such], it is decided that the second case-ending is used in the sense of the first. || 43 ||

"Because of the abundance of indicatory marks; for that is more powerful; and that also [is so] because it was previously introduced"—thus the connection is made known. By the term "higher knowledge" (*paravidyā*), the notion of mere meditative visualization is excluded. And by the identity of the word "Self" in the passages "the Self in the cave" and "the Self, Nārāyaṇa," the unity of meaning is established.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "The mark" (*cihna*)—this serves to exclude [the possibility of] an indicative mark (*liṅga*) following immediately after the scriptural statement (*śruti*). "Like the calyx of a lotus"—the intention is that this is a statement specifying a particular instance of what was stated in general terms, such as "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*) or "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*). As for "Nor can it be" (*na ca*)—to the objection that one might interpret the nominative case-ending in accordance with the accusative case-endings found in passages such as "By which the sky and heaven are covered," he replies: "Within and without. This means that it would contradict the nature of the object established by a sentence that lacks any injunctive word such as "one should know" (*vidyāt*).

If this were a supplement to what precedes, there would be the necessity of supplying an ellipsis (*vidhy-adhyāhāra*), an awkwardness regarding the nominative case endings, and a contradiction in meaning; however, in the present case, the awkwardness lies in the accusative case endings. The phrase "Nārāyaṇa paraṃ" does not involve the elision of the ablative case (*pañcamī-lopa*). This is because the indication of a case-meaning (*vibhakty-artha-lakṣaṇā*) is untenable. Furthermore, even if it were a compound, the principle of the *niṣādasthapati* (the "chief of the Niṣādas") would apply; moreover, it must be consistent with the *Mahopaniṣad*, and there would be contradictions with other preceding and subsequent scriptural passages, as well as the rule for the substitution of case-endings (*supāṃ suluk*). Such is the intention. As for the word "ātman," in passages such as "The Self, indeed, this [was]" and "The Self, indeed, my dear," it is intended to bring about the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of Nārāyaṇa. || 43 ||
Thus ends the section on the Abundance of Indicative Marks (Liṅgabhūyastvādhikaraṇa). 19.
"There may be an alternative to the previous [view] because of the context; it would be an action, like the mental [sacrifice]. (3.3.44)

In the *Vājasaneyaka-Agnirahasya*, the "mind-made" (*manas-cit*) and other such [fires]—though consisting of knowledge—are of the nature of action because they serve as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) to a sacrifice consisting of action; so it is here as well. || 44 ||

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, due to the context (*prakaraṇa*), these must be ritual actions, like the "mental" [sacrifices]. Since there is no sublation of the context by syntactical connection (*vākya*) and so forth—as in the case of the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*—the "mind-altars" (*manaścita*) and others enter into the sacrifice consisting of action; such is the connection based on this doubt. In accordance with the formulation of the Sūtra, they are designated as being "of the nature of action" and "of the nature of knowledge. The explanation of that is: "by way of entering into the sacrifice consisting of action" and "by way of entering into the sacrifice consisting of knowledge."

There is no disagreement regarding the fact that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the mind-altar (*manaściti*) and the rest consists of knowledge (*vidyā*). However, there is disagreement concerning their being of the nature of knowledge by way of being subordinate members (*aṅga*) [of a sacrifice]. Therefore, in the Sūtra, the word "action" (*kriyā*) is used figuratively; its meaning is "that which is connected to it" by virtue of being a subordinate member of a rite consisting of action.

Because it is the locus of the *homa* (oblation), it possesses the nature of fire (*agni*). The word "built" (*citya*) is used to dispel the doubt that the term applies to fire in general, regardless of its specific function. "Accomplished" means those which have been brought to mind (*anusandhita*). "Proximity" means being present in the intellect. To the objection that there might be independence from the fire-altar built of bricks, he says: "being optionally chosen. "In the *Avivākya*" means devoid of various discourses; or alternatively, "in the *Vivākya*" means where discourse has ceased. Even though the cup (*graha*) does not exist in its own form [at that time], it is considered mental because it is useful as something produced by the mind. || 44 ||
And because of the extension [of the rule]. (3.3.45)
And for this reason, because they enter into a sacrifice consisting of ritual action—specifically one constructed with bricks—they are indeed of the nature of action. || 45 ||
And because of the extended application (*atideśa*). *Vīrya* is the capacity for performing an action. He demonstrates the benefit [of this]: "And therefore," etc. (45).
This being the case, we reply: "But it is knowledge alone [that leads to immortality], because of the specific determination and because of scriptural vision. (3.3.46)
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. ... ... Here, the sacrifice (*kratu*) is also perceived as consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*). || 46 ||

In the final conclusion: "But it is knowledge alone, because of the determination and because of the observation. He explains the portion beginning with "because of the observation" as follows: "And it is observed. Regarding these—the mind-altar and so forth—"whatever ritual act there is in the sacrifice" refers to the principal action; "that which pertains to the sacrifice" refers to the subsidiary action. || 46 ||
But surely—since no word expressing an injunction is heard here, and because the direct Vedic statement (śruti) and other means of proof are more powerful, there can be no sublation. [Sūtra 3.3.47]

Since the direct statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and syntactical connection (vākya) do not find the possibility of entry into a ritual act [in the ordinary sense], they become an indicative mark for entry into a ritual consisting of knowledge (vidyāmaya-kratu). || 47 ||

He states a doubt regarding the immediate [preceding] point with "nanu" (but surely). To the objection that an injunction (*vidhi*) would have to be assumed, he replies with "phalasaṃbandha" (connection with the fruit). Furthermore, there is no sublation [of the meaning] because of the superior force of direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof. Regarding "vidyayā" (by knowledge), it is the cause by way of being the purpose. He states the meaning established by the sentence with "evaṃvit" (one who knows thus). He establishes the indicative mark (*liṅga*) with "sarva" (all). || 47 ||
And as for that which was stated [by the opponent]: "Because no injunction (*vidhi*) is heard...
[it is not a separate meditation] because of the connection (*anubandha*) and so forth, like the distinctness of other cognitions"—that has been answered. (Sūtra 3.3.48)

It is understood that even for those consisting of mind, such as the "mind-altar" (manaścita) and others, there is a fruit by means of their own sacrifice, following the sequence of those built with bricks which consist of ritual action. || 48 ||

To resolve the portion of the previously raised doubt that remains unaddressed regarding the immediate entry [into the fruit], he says: "And as for this... [He continues: "On account of the connection and so forth, it is seen to be like the distinctness of other cognitions; and it has been stated. Regarding the phrase "and it is seen": even though there is a connection with a fruit, the assumption of an injunction would lead to the abandonment of what is heard in the text. That [assumption] is precluded because the cognition consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*) is understood through the direct scriptural statement of its connection and so forth. And he states that the fruit is indeed heard: "And the fruit... (Sūtra 48).

Furthermore, as for the claim that [the prāṇas] have an identical function by way of extended application (atideśa), [it is not so]; for they are perceived even through their commonality, just as in the case of death; for there is no falling into the world [of the senses]. 3-3-49.

It is not necessarily understood from the extended application (atideśa) that even the intermediate operation [of the meditation] results in the fruit by means of the sacrifice consisting of knowledge; rather, this is understood from the extended application itself. || 49 ||

Nor is there [a contradiction] because of perception through generality, for there is no falling into the world as in the case of death; this refers to the intermediate operation—the connection with the ritual (*kratu*) consisting of action. "In the form of space" (*deśarūpa*): "space" (*deśa*) means the substratum (*āśraya*). That which has the limbs as its substratum is the principal (*aṅgī*). || 49 ||
And by another [scriptural passage], this [soul] possesses that same nature; however, because of its multiplicity, it is designated as a "concomitant" (anubandha). (3.3.50)
And by another Brāhmaṇa, because of the greater number of its constituent parts of fire, this connection was made here in its proximity. || 50 ||

Furthermore, the nature of the sound [of the word] is such because of its abundance; thus, there is a connection. It is not only by direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, but also by context (*prakaraṇa*), that the status of being an auxiliary to the sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratvaṅgatā*) is expressed. "Filling" means filling the earth. [The root] *pṛ* is used in the senses of protecting and filling. The change of gender in the word *etat* is for metrical reasons. The meaning is: "this Agni, who is the Veda. (50)
Thus ends the section concerning the prior misconception: 20.
[The opponent argues that] there is only one [self], because [consciousness] exists when the body exists. (3.3.51)

In all higher knowledges (*paravidyā*), there is meditation upon that which is to be meditated upon; for it is not otherwise, because [the scripture] states, "In whatever way they meditate upon Him," since He is the object of meditation. || 51 ||

"Because [the qualities] exist in the body of a single Self. The previous section was incidental. In that preceding part, it was stated that the Lord alone is the object of worship for all sciences (*vidyā*); likewise, it was explained in the *Dīpa* that the individual self (*pratyagātman*) is also such an object. Now, intending to explain how that [individual self], which depends on the *Dīpa*, is included within the category of objects of worship, he says "And he will state... because of its utility therein. To the question "What follows from that?", he replies: "By that much..."
This being the case, we reply: there is a distinction [between the two], because [the cognition] occurs when that [object] exists; it is not, however, like perception. (3.3.52)
But this is not the case—that [the form of] being a knower and so forth... [is required]; rather, only that much is required therein, so nothing is lacking. 52.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "The negative concomitance [is established] because [the result] exists when that [contemplation] exists, but not like perception. To exclude the possibility of considering merely the property of negative concomitance, he says: "His liberation" (*asya mokṣaḥ*). He states the resulting meaning with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*). The sense is that the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the qualified object. For this very reason—namely, because the form of what is to be attained must be recollected—it is said that there is contemplation of what is to be attained. He points out the disparity between the example cited by the opponent: "in the case of ritual acts" (*karmasu*). The meaning is that the disparity lies in the fact that one set of acts is enjoined (*vaidha*) while the other is not (*avaiṃdhatva*). || 52 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the existence [of meditations] in the body (sūtra 20). Now follows the section concerning those [meditations] connected with the limbs:
"But those connected with the limbs do not belong to specific branches, for they are found in every Veda" (3.3.53).
"One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha... there is no specific distinction of proximity for any one [of these], and thus there is no restriction. (Sūtra 53)

However, those [meditations] connected with the limbs (*aṅga*) are not [restricted] to specific branches (*śākhā*), for they belong to every Veda. Wherever Brahman is to be meditated upon, there the status of the pure Self as the object of meditation has been stated. Thus, the connection [of this section] arises from the doubt as to whether or not that meditation exists wherever there is an entry into the *udgītha*. The objection is raised on the grounds that the *udgītha* is one and the same across all branches (*sarva-śākhā*). The resolution is that they are distinct because of their differentiating characteristics (*bhedaka-dharma*). The phrase "in that very [one]" implies the observation that in cases such as "Bring the cow," the meaning culminates in a specific particular.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "Proximity" (*sannidhi*) means residing in the intellect (*dhīsthatva*), for proximity is indeed the state of being present in the mind. And that [proximity] is demonstrated by the power of the word. In cases such as "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), it is the lack of compatibility (*ayogyatva*) that serves as the regulator; the point is that it is not mere physical non-proximity. He states proximity even in terms of meaning with the words "all branches" (*sarvaśākhā*). The meaning is that from the proximity of the principal (*aṅgin*) follows the proximity of the subsidiary (*aṅga*). || 53 ||
Or rather, there is no contradiction, as in the case of mantras and the like. (3.3.54)

The word "or" (vā) has the sense of "and. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is shown that there is no contradiction in its application across all Vedic branches; likewise, here too, there is no contradiction. || 54 ||

Or rather, there is no contradiction, as in the case of mantras and so forth. The example for the recurrence of the udgītha across all recensional branches (śākhās) is mantras and the like; consequently, followers of all branches possess the qualification for this meditation. 54.
Thus concludes the section on the connection with the limbs (aṅgāvabaddha-adhikaraṇa) – 22. "The preeminence of the Bhūman [meditation] is like that of a sacrifice, for so it shows. (3.3.55)
Starting from "Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava" and so forth... because the praise of the knowledge of the earth would otherwise be untenable, therefore meditation on the whole alone is logical. || 55 ||

"The preeminence of the whole [Brahman] is like that of a ritual act; for thus the scripture shows. The meditation on the *udgītha*—which is a constituent part of the *sāman* previously under discussion—is heard in scripture as being to be meditated upon both collectively and individually. Thus, there is a connection [to the present topic] because of the doubt: "In the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, is the whole, the parts, both, or neither to be meditated upon? Regarding the statement "he eats food"—meaning he consumes food—the meditation on Vaiśvānara was introduced; to the question of how there can be meditation on the head alone, he says: "And [the text] declares his nature as Vaiśvānara."

"Of that which was spoken regarding Vaiśvānara"—that is, of that which was spoken as having Vaiśvānara as its object. "A split in the sentence"—meaning a split in the great sentence (*mahāvākya*). The sense is this: as in the case of the passage beginning with "Where one sees nothing else," the multiplicity of incidental matters does not contradict the unity of the primary subject to be established. Since the meditation on the individual parts is incidental, there is no contradiction.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). The meaning is that since the meditation on the whole (*samudāyopāsana*) and its fruit are what are intended to be taught, the mention of a single part thereof is a restatement. Furthermore, this is for the purpose of making known that the specific fruits [of meditating on parts] are included within the fruit of the meditation on the whole; otherwise, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) and because of the mention of sin (*pratyavāya*). Therefore, "this" and so forth. The lack of hearing of any evil [consequence] was stated as a point of difference. He states another point of difference regarding utility by way of its being the counter-correlative to the excess: "name and so forth."

It is heard that there is a superior fruit; therefore, what follows from the unity of the great sentences? To this he says: "From that very [fact]. "Otherwise" means: if it were not intended to be expressed. || 55 ||
Thus concludes the section on the superiority of the Infinite (Bhūman). 23.
[The meditations] are distinct because of the difference in words and so forth. 3.3.56.

In this context, all the knowledges of Brahman (brahmavidyās) have as their nature the attainment of Brahman; thus, the Vedānta passages are intent upon knowledge that is not something to be performed (avidheya-jñāna), for the purpose of removing false views. Therefore, it is established that there is a distinction between these knowledges (vidyābheda). || 56 ||

"Due to the difference in various sounds and so forth. Previously, an inquiry into specific meditations (*vidyā*) was undertaken; now, an inquiry concerning the subject matter of all meditations follows—this is the connection (*saṅgati*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the "supreme secret" is intended. And in the subsequent section, he again removes the charge of tautology with the words "right here" (*atreva*). The meaning is that once it is established as a general rule that repetition without distinction and a change of context constitute differentiators of meditation, the inquiry into the difference or non-difference of specific meditations becomes possible. The identity of form and fruit is the seed for the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is the principal action together with its constituent parts (*sāṅga-pradhāna-karma*). The "connections" (*anubandhas*) are the constituent elements (*avayavas*). Words and so forth are the causes for their differentiation. Due to the difference in these connections, there is a difference in what is to be enjoined. To exclude the notion that there is a difference in form (*rūpa-bheda*) based on a difference in the meaning of the verbal roots (*dhātvartha*), he says: "repetition of the suffix" (*pratyayāvṛtti*). The sense is that "the distinction among cognitions is indeed due to their objects. By the word "Brahman," the difference in context (*prakaraṇabheda*) is stated. He states the result of what is said here [in this section] with the words "in this... (verse 56).
Thus ends the section on the distinction between words and so forth (Sūtra 24). [Sūtra 57:
There is an option [regarding the paths], because the fruit is not distinguished. 3.3.57.

Since the various meditations such as the Sadvidyā and the Daharavidyā have the attainment of Brahman as their fruit, there is indeed an option (vikalpa) among all of them, because their fruits are indistinguishable. || 57 ||

There is an option (vikalpa) because the result is not distinct. For the consideration of whether there is an option or a combination occurs only when a difference [between the means] has been established; such is the logical connection.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): because of the scriptural statement regarding equality, [the soul] would attain equality with Brahman, whose bliss is unlimited. The phrase "of its own" is for the purpose of showing independence from anything else. The term *anavadhikātiśayānanda* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; the meaning is "that which generates bliss. Regarding the combination where some [meditations] are for the purpose of removing the undesirable and others are for the purpose of attaining Brahman, he says: "And all [are for both purposes]. (57)

But those rites whose fruits are distinct from the attainment of Brahman—namely, the optional (kāmya) rites—may be combined according to one's desire, or they may not, because the previously stated reason [for their non-combination] is absent. (3.3.48)
The meaning is that it is because there is an absence of immeasurable fruit. || 58 ||

Connecting the subsequent sūtra with the preceding one, he states its meaning: "distinct from the attainment of Brahman. The sense is that the word *yathākāma* means that desire is the regulating factor regarding both the combination (*samuccaya*) and the option (*vikalpa*) of optional rites.

But the optional rites may or may not be combined according to one's desire, because of the absence of the aforementioned reason; he explains the word "reason" as "because they are not subsidiary. || 58 ||
Thus ends the section on conceptual construction (vikalpādhikaraṇa).
Sūtra 3.3.59: In the case of the auxiliary parts (aṅga), there is the state of being according to their respective bases (yathāśrayabhāva).

The meditations based on the constituent parts of the sacrifice, such as the *udgītha*, are indeed necessarily to be adopted, because they become auxiliary elements of the sacrifice through those very parts. 59.

Just as among the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) there exists a state of dependence on their respective bases, and as the combination or optionality of desired elements has been stated according to one's wish, so too there is the connection [of the present discussion] regarding whether the Udgītha and other meditations (*vidyā*) are to be adopted according to one's wish. [The opponent asks: "But... [To avoid the charge of redundancy, he states what was previously mentioned: "In that case, indeed... [He replies: "Not so... Because the fruit does not belong to its own sentence, there is a delay; thus, there is a difference from the *godohana* passage. It has been stated that there is no contradiction with its being an auxiliary part (*aṅga*). He states a favorable reason: "The Udgītha..."

The sense is that its status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) is established by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) of the accusative case, just as in the expression "vrīhīn" (rice grains). He shows that the fruit resides in another sentence with the words "yadeva" (whatever...). To the question "What follows from that?", he says "svavākyena" (by its own sentence). The meaning is that since the fruit does not reside in its own sentence, once the subsidiary status of the *parṇatā* (being made of *parṇa*-wood) is established through its connection with the *juhū* (ladle)—which has an inseparable connection with the sacrifice—the mention of fruits such as hearing no evil reputation found in another sentence is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says "ataḥ" (therefore).
The injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) is an injunction that has reached the state of being an instigator of action, and not one in the state of being a mere communicator. 59.
And because of the conduct of the learned. (3.3.60)
Instruction means teaching, that is to say, a prescription; for it is understood that the status of being an auxiliary to the *udgītha* alone is what is to be prescribed. || 60 ||

And because of the learned. The reasoning has been stated; now the indicative marks (liṅgas) are being set forth. He states the difference from the *godohana* vessel: "In the case of the *godohana*... (Sūtra 60).
Because of their being combined. (3-3-61)

Furthermore, by stating that even from the seat of the Hotṛ priest a poorly performed *udgītha* may be rectified through knowledge, [the text] demonstrates that such knowledge must necessarily be employed as a remedy for its failure. || 61 ||
Because of the combination. "Combination" (samāhāra) means "concentration" (samādhāna). || 61 ||
And because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of qualities. (3.3.62)

The qualities of the meditation and the substratum of the meditation—such as the *udgītha* and so forth—are to be taken up invariably, just like the *udgītha* itself, in all meditations on the *udgītha* and other such objects. 62.

And because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of qualities (*guṇasādhāraṇya*). The mention of the substratum by the word "quality" (*guṇa*) is intended to express its being an object of meditation (*upāsanārtha*). "Collection" (*samāhāra*) means recurrence (*anuvṛtti*). He explains this with the words "by that" (*tena*).
This being the position reached, it is said: "Or rather not, because their coexistence is not heard [in scripture]. (3.3.63)

And this is not the case, that for the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth... [there would be no fruit]; in that regard, the mention of a fruit would be merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*). || 63 ||

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "Or rather not, because their co-existence is not heard. To the objection that mere co-existence does not constitute being an auxiliary (*aṅga*), he says: "For in the case of being an auxiliary... The meaning is that a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is intended. What is meant is that [the meditation] is a means to a separate fruit, which is incompatible with being an auxiliary. He explains this with: "Even though... It is stated that the status of being a means is what is to be established. In the sentence concerning the *godohana* vessel, the status of being a means must be inferred; thus there is a single delay. Here, however, that need not be inferred, because ritual action (*karman*) alone cannot be the means to achieve knowledge (*vidyā*).

Since the status of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) belongs to that which is qualified by the state of being more intensely vigorous (*vīryavattaratva*), and because this [vigorousness] is what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there is the cognition that the mere act of leading forward (*praṇayana*) alone is to be accomplished by the milking of the cows (*godohana*). It is not, however, [the cognition] of that [act] as qualified by its being a means to cattle (*paśu*), because it lacks the capacity to express such a means. As for the result (*phala*), since it resides in another sentence, there is one delay; thus, what is intended is the similarity in having this single delay.

Regarding the point that the injunction [is established] precisely because it is a means to the fruit, he says: "Therefore" (*tena*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "From the fruit of the sacrifice" (*kratuphalāt*). Then, as to how there is subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) by virtue of the direct statement of the accusative case, he says: "Hence, of the meditation" (*ata upāsanasya*). By the suffix *mātra*, the status of being the principal (*śeṣitva*) is excluded.

The meaning is as follows: just as one might ask, "To what does the *godohana* belong? It is a means for obtaining cattle," so too, when there is an expectation—"What is the object of this meditation? It is a means for attaining a fruit"—and it is found to be connected with the *udgītha* which is in close proximity, the *udgītha* does not stand in a subordinate relationship (*śeṣitva*) toward the meditation, just as the mere act of carrying water stands in relation to the *godohana*. To the objection that if they were separate sentences, it would have to be performed by a different qualified person (*adhikārī*), he says: "And the *udgītha*... The meaning is: just as for one already qualified for the sacrifice, there is a separate qualification based on the desire for cattle in regard to the *godohana*, so it is here.

He states that being more vigorous (*vīryavattara*) is a separate result in the words "In [the case of] vigor" (*vīrye*). He states the difference between [the case of] leafiness (*parṇatā*) and [the case of] vigor in the words "But as for leafiness and so on" (*parṇatādīnāṃ tu*). The meaning is that the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) [of leafiness] is undermined by two delays: because the fruit of leafiness resides in another sentence, and because its status as a means (*sādhanabhāva*) must be inferred. The delay regarding the fruit is not mentioned [for vigor] because it is obvious, since the fruit [of vigor] is stated in the same sentence. It is established by implication that when it is said, "One offers with the *juhū*," there is an expectancy for a specific substance; however, there is no such expectancy for the meditation (*upāsana*) of the *udgītha*. || 63 ||
And because it is seen [in scripture]. (3.3.64)

And scripture shows that there is no fixed rule regarding the adoption of specific modes of meditation; for it is understood from signs such as the combination [of attributes] that these are merely incidental. Therefore, it is established that there is indeed no fixed rule.
Thus ends the section [26] on the existence according to the nature of the substratum.
Thus concludes the third quarter of the third chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.

And because of direct scriptural statement (*darśana*). The argument based on reasoning (*yukti*) has been refuted; now the indicative marks (*liṅga*) are being set aside. "Protection" refers to the non-obstruction of the fruit of the sacrifice and so forth. As for the claim that it is merely "occasional" (*prāyikatva*), the resolution is that such protection would occur only when there is a specific intention (*saṅkalpa*). The same applies to the commonality of the qualities (*guṇasādhāraṇya*). Alternatively, the word "by that" (*tena*) refers exclusively to the *praṇava*, and not to that which is associated with meditation (*upāsana*). Furthermore, the remaining [marks] relate to the connection with the *udgītha*, and not to its being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*). Thus ends the section concerning the state according to the substratum (*yathāśrayabhāvādhikaraṇa*)—26.

Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the *Śrutapradīpikā*, composed by Śrī Sudarśanasūri—the ornament of the illustrious Harita lineage, son of Vāgvijayin, who bore the secondary name Vedavyāsa by the divine command of Śrī Raṅgarāja, and who attained the heart of the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śrī Bhagavadrāmānuja through service at the feet of the venerable Varadācārya.
The Fourth Quarter of the Third Chapter.
"Therefore, the human goal [is attained] from this [scripture], according to Bādarāyaṇa. (3.4.1)

The result [of this discussion] is whether there is a combination or non-combination of qualities... thus: "The knower, liberated from name and form, goes to the divine Person, higher than the high," and so forth. ||1||

"Human purpose [arises] from this, on account of the scriptural statement," so says Bādarāyaṇa. The connection between the sections (pāda-saṅgati) is that the inquiry into the auxiliaries follows immediately after the inquiry into the principal (the possessor of auxiliaries). For it is only when knowledge is established as the principal that its auxiliary can be investigated. Therefore, its status as the principal is first determined. (1)
On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) objects: "Because it is a subordinate element, it is a statement of human purpose, as in other cases; so [says] Jaimini" (3.4.2).

This is not so; that the attainment of the human goal [results] from knowledge... therefore, because knowledge is a subordinate element of the ritual (*kratuśeṣatva*), the human goal does not result from it. || 2 ||

He introduces the second [sūtra] with the words "In this case" (*atra*). "Because it is subordinate, it is a statement of human purpose, as in other cases," says Jaimini. Regarding the phrase "in ritual acts" (*karmasu*): since [the text] says "having studied," knowledge is subordinate to ritual; thus, self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) is also subordinate to that. The meaning is that, just as rice and other grains—which serve as the means for acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)—are subordinate to the sacrifice (*kratu*), so too the Self to be known is subordinate to ritual; therefore, the passage is intent on describing its essential nature. The sense is that, just as there is no unity between the insentient and the sentient, there can likewise be no unity between the insentient and the conscious [Self], as expressed in "All this has that as its essence" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*) and "All this, indeed... (*sarvaṃ khalu*).

The meaning is: "only in the Vedānta statements"—that is, only in those stated by you as having a distinct purpose. "By means of indicative marks" (liṅgaiḥ) means by means of indicators. He raises an objection: "But surely... [the idea that] the knowledge of the *parṇa*-leaf is not a subsidiary part of the sacrifice, like the *juhū* ladle, because it lacks an invariable connection with the sacrifice. He refutes this: "Not so. || 2 ||
What, then, are those marks [of a knower], which, when strengthened by the aforementioned qualities... [are known] from the observation of conduct? (3.4.3)

Since, for those who know Brahman, [meditation] is primarily subordinate to ritual acts—being merely an auxiliary to the ritual—it follows that the human goal is not attained through knowledge alone. || 3 ||

To introduce the immediately following sūtra, he asks: "Which? Because of the observation of established practice; for when there is a conflict between a subordinate and a primary element, the primary must be followed. Therefore, the sense is that action (karman) is predominant. || 3 ||
This is an indicative mark (liṅga); [the opponent asks] "Let the attainment (prāpti) be stated," to which he replies: "Because of its being taught" (tacchruteḥ). 3.4.4.

For scripture itself declares that knowledge is a subordinate element of ritual action; indeed, this scriptural statement—"one performs [the rite] by means of knowledge"—has as its scope knowledge in general. || 4 ||

The *liṅga* (indicative power) is that which assists. *Prāpti* (attainment) is establishment by means of a means of knowledge (*māna*). Because of that [attainment]. Through the direct statement of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-śruti*), there is the understanding of subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*). || 4 ||
Because of the simultaneous undertaking [of the duties]. (3.4.5)
Knowledge and action accompany him... this occurs only when, by logical principle, knowledge is indeed subordinate to action. || 5 ||

Because they are undertaken together. To the objection that even in the case of the opposite (the absence of such undertaking), coexistence is possible, he says: "By what has been stated. That is, by the reasoning [already] set forth—that the Self is a subordinate element of ritual action, and so forth. || 5 ||
Because there is an injunction for one who possesses that [quality]. (3.4.6)
Because there is an injunction for ritual action for one who possesses knowledge, knowledge is employed within those very actions; thus, it cannot be conceived as having a separate fruit. || 6 ||

Because [the study] is enjoined for one who possesses that [text]. The sense is: "having studied," just as in the case of "having bathed, he offers the oblation. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "the comprehension of the meaning. To the question "How is it that the [study] culminates in the cognition of the meaning?", he says: "the meaning. The meaning is: for the purpose of avoiding defects such as the scripture having an unintended meaning. || 6 ||
Because of necessity. 3-4-7.
And since no human goal [is attained] from knowledge alone, it is understood that the fruit belongs to action alone; knowledge, however, is a subsidiary part of action. || 7 ||
Because it is a rule; since the entire lifespan is subsidiary to the sacrifice, the meaning is that everything occurring in the interval is subsidiary to it. || 7 ||
This being the case, we reply: "But because of the teaching of something additional, Bādarāyaṇa [holds] thus, for such is seen [in scripture]. (3.4.8)
By the word "but" (tu), the [previous] position is set aside... it is well said that the fruit being heard is for the sake of the person because of its connection with knowledge. || 8 ||

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "But because of the additional instruction, Bādarāyaṇa [holds] thus, for that is seen. Since the indicative marks (*liṅga*) are present, how can the fruit arise from knowledge? To this he says: "The indicative marks. Because the sentences concerning meditative worship (*upāsanā*) depend upon the qualities mentioned in the sentences defining the essential nature [of the object], it is said "in the sentences teaching knowledge" (*vedanopadeśavākyeṣu*). Just as with the *juhū* ladle, since there is no recognition of the agent [as being the same in both contexts], the meditation cannot be a subordinate part of the ritual action by way of that agent; therefore, the mention of the fruit is not a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). This is the meaning. || 8 ||
The inferential marks are also refuted: "But the perception is equal" (Sūtra 3.4.9).

As it has been said: "Because we observe the performance of ritual action even by those who know Brahman... if knowledge were a subordinate part of ritual action, the renunciation of action would not be possible in any way. (9)

But the observation is equal. The meaning of the word is that the observation is equal even in the case of non-performance. "Inconclusive" (anaikāntika) is a statement of the resulting implication. "Inconclusive" means indefinite; the sense is that it is not restricted to the observation of performance alone. The contradiction between performance and non-performance exists only in your own view, because the fruits of the knowledge of Brahman are merely explanatory passages (arthavāda), and thus the distinction between them being for the sake of liberation or for the sake of the three aims of life (trivarga) is untenable. Intending this, he says: "Of knowledge... (vidyāyāḥ). || 9 ||
As it has been stated: "By the scripture itself, [it is shown that] knowledge is not universal" (3.4.10).
This Vedic revelation does not pertain to all branches of knowledge; for, having designated it by means of the word "yat," its superior potency is indeed stated. || 10 ||

[The word *vidyayā*] is not universally applicable. Regarding the principle that "direct statement (*śruti*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*"), he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*). There is no grammatical connection (*anvaya*) such that "whatever one does, that [one does] by means of knowledge," because that would be strained. When the connection is "whatever one does by means of knowledge, that is more potent," then, since this statement—which restates an action performed through knowledge—requires a source for its application, the context, which provides that source, restricts the scope of the word *vidyā*.

Therefore, since the word *vidyayā*—being dependent on something else due to its nature as a restatement—lacks the capacity for self-determination, the meaning is that there is no "direct statement" in the form of the power inherent in a single word.
And as for that which was stated: "Knowledge and action [lead to different results]...
the division is like that of a hundred. (3.4.11)
"Knowledge and action follow after him..."; just as in that case the division is understood as "a hundred for the sake of jewels," so it is here as well. || 11 ||

The division is like that of a hundred [coins]. Since the scriptural statement regarding "commencement" (samanvārambhaṇa) has as its object both knowledge and action for the sake of liberation, this is the meaning: at the conclusion of the prārabdha karma, knowledge follows in order to grant liberation; and even in other births, action follows in order to produce knowledge. || 11 ||
[The qualification belongs] to one who possesses merely the study [of the Veda]. (3.4.12)

As for what was stated—that because ritual action is prescribed for one who possesses knowledge, and that knowledge is the means for accomplishing the human goal—there is not even a trace of a connection between that [knowledge] and ritual action. || 21 ||

[The opponent argues: "For one who possesses merely the study [of the Veda]," thus showing the natural force of the word *ādhānavat* (like the laying of the sacred fires). He removes the inconsistency regarding the meaning—such as the lack of commencement due to the absence of an impeller—by stating "of that which has been grasped. Everything that needs to be said on this point was already stated in the first sūtra. Accepting that [the injunction] culminates in the understanding of the meaning, he says "even though": the meaning is that since knowledge (*vidyā*) is distinct from what is denoted by the word "study," it is so. "Just as" means: just as the knowledge of the essential nature [of a rite] is a subordinate factor (*śeṣa*) with respect to its performance, so too the knowledge produced by the scripture is a subordinate factor with respect to [the attainment of] knowledge.
Not so, because there is no distinction. (3.4.13)
As for what was said regarding "performing actions here alone... [it refers to the householder], because for the knower, the meditative practice continues until the departure from the body. || 13 ||

"Not so, because there is no distinction. He says "But for the knower" [in sūtra 14] to show that the following of the subordinate elements is justified by the following of the principal element. || 13 ||
Having thus resolved the objection by means of the intrinsic nature of the meaning, [the Sūtra states]:
"Or it is an approval for the sake of praise" (3.4.14).
The word "vā" has the sense of restriction [meaning "only"]. ... "Action does not cling to the man. Therefore, knowledge is not a subsidiary part of action. || 14 ||

The intrinsic nature of the object (*arthasvābhāvyam*) consists in its being distinct from the knowledge of the object, as well as its being an auxiliary to ritual action (*karmāṅgatvam*). Or rather, there is permission for the sake of praise. Regarding the word *īśāvāsyam*: in the word *īṭ*, the instrumental case is used; the sense is "that which is pervaded by the Lord" (*īśena āvāsyam*). One who does not delight is a *nara*. The meaning is: "In you, who are free from attachment, no action clings"—there is nothing other than this, for this is the reality (*tattvam*). || 14 ||
And some [hold that it occurs] by one's own will. (3.4.15)
Moreover, some followers of other Vedic schools [state that] the renunciation of the householder's life is not possible; therefore, knowledge is not an auxiliary part of ritual action. 15.

"And some [hold that renunciation occurs] by one's own will. "By one's own will" (kāmakāra) means the performance of the duties of whichever stage of life (āśrama) one desires; the term "householderhood," etc., is supplied as the context. The meaning is that there can be no abandonment of the principal (the whole) by relying on its subordinate parts (the limbs). || 15 ||
And [the mention of] destruction. || 3-4-6 ||
If that knowledge, which consists of both merit and demerit, were a constituent part of ritual action (*karma*), it would not be logically consistent. || 16 ||
And [there would be] sublation; for the meaning is that there can be no sublation of the whole by a part. || 16 ||
But the term "ūrdhvaretas" indeed occurs in the Śabala hymn. (3.4.17)

The knowledge of Brahman [is prescribed] for those in the stages of life where the semen is drawn up; as for the scriptural injunction regarding "as long as one lives," that refers to those who lack dispassion.

And because [the term] "sound" occurs in the upward-directed [texts], he says "Śruti" regarding the fact that they are recognized in the Smṛtis. "Dharmaskandhas" means the supports of dharma. || 17 ||
Jaimini [holds that there is] a misconception, because it is not an injunction; for [the scripture] indeed refutes it. (3.4.18)
Namely, that there are three groups of dharma... [the teacher] Jaimini considers that there are no stages of life (āśrama). 18.
Jaimini [rejects] the [notion of] "clinging" (parāmarśa), because it is not a scriptural injunction; for he clearly censures it. 18.
Bādarāyaṇa [maintains that the meditation] is to be performed [in both ways], because of the scriptural statement of equality. (3.4.19)

Just as the stage of the householder (gṛhasthāśrama) must be practiced, so too must the other stages of life be practiced; therefore, it must be admitted that even there, the attainment of the path of the gods (devayāna) is possible through the injunctions for it. || 19 ||

Bādarāyaṇa holds that [the fourth stage] is to be practiced because of the scriptural statement of equality; one should not say there is no equality, for there is no mention at all of other stages of life—this is the objection raised with the words "na ca" (nor is it the case). To exclude other interpretations, he says "ato yajñaḥ" (therefore, sacrifice); by the term "etymological," the impossibility of its referring to the fourth stage of life is intended, according to the principle of the *prokṣaṇī* (sprinkling water). He states the impossibility on the grounds of the inconsistency of the meaning as well, with the words "tac ca sarveṣām" (and that [is] for all). Regarding that, he explains the meaning of the phrase "those who partake of the worlds of merit" as "those deficient in steadfastness in Brahman."

In the case of the view that it is a restrictive injunction (*parāmarśa*) and the view that it is a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), [the conclusion is] "or rather, it is an injunction, like the wearing [of the sacred thread]. (3.4.20)

The word "vā" (or) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). ... ... Therefore, since the knowledge of Brahman is prescribed even for those who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*), it is established that the human goal [is attained] through knowledge. || 20 ||

"Or rather, it is an injunction, like the observance [of vows]. The scriptural statement regarding debt is: "One is born with three debts," and so forth. The scriptural statement of exception is: "He is a slayer of heroes," and so forth. "Regarding the duties of their respective stages of life" means they are intent upon the adherence to those specific duties for those belonging to each stage; the meaning is that they do not contradict the status of knowledge as being a limb of the other stages of life. He concludes the meaning of the section with the words "Therefore."
Thus ends the section on the purpose of man (Puruṣārthādhikaraṇa).

3.4.21: "If it be argued that [the mention of fruits] is merely for the sake of praise because of the taking up [of the rite], we say no, because of its being something not previously established (apūrvatva)."

This is now considered: it is indeed logical that this very [Self], which is the most savory among savors, etc., is the injunction for the meditation upon the *udgītha* and so forth as being the most savory, etc. (21).

If it be argued that [these passages] are mere praise because they involve an injunction (*upādāna*), we say no, because they convey something not previously known (*apūrvatvāt*). This connection is made by way of a contextual transition (*prasaṅga*): lest there arise the doubt that other supreme statements, such as those concerning "being the essence of all essences" (*rasatamatva*), are merely for the sake of praise, following the precedent of the scriptural passage regarding "one who is firmly established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*). It is the eighth [chapter] in relation to the seven preceding tastes mentioned earlier. He explains the reason [for this]: "As a subsidiary part of the sacrifice" (*kratvaṅga*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Just as... Even though the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood is preceded by its being enjoined as a subsidiary of the sacrifice, it does not have the purpose of mere praise, because it is capable of being enjoined.
The point is that qualities such as "being the heavenly world" (*svarlokatva*) are incapable [of being enjoined].

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): regarding the claim that even the "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth of the *juhū* ladle and other such items are unestablished, he says: "And not... It is not the case that qualities such as being the "most flavorful" (*rasatamatva*) cannot be adopted just like "earth-ness," because although they cannot be adopted in the form of an origination (*utpatti*), they can be adopted in the form of a cognition (*jñapti*). The sense is that although "earth-ness" and the like could be adopted in the form of a cognition, they do not serve the purpose of an injunction for a meditative vision (*dṛṣṭividhi*) due to the force of the perception of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*). As for the phrase "by whatever [means]": since qualities such as being the "most flavorful" are unestablished, there is no praise by way of restating them.

Because it is inappropriate, there is no praise by means of enjoining what has not been previously established; nor is there praise through the connection with a non-primary quality, because in the absence of a proximate reference to a sacrifice, there is no perception of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*). Therefore, the intention is that this is an injunction of a meditative visualization (*dṛṣṭividhi*). || 21 ||
And because of the word "bhāva" (existence). 3.4.22.

And because of words denoting action such as "one should meditate" (upāsīta), these scriptural passages have the purpose of enjoining meditation. Therefore, these scriptural texts are intended for the injunction of meditation. || 22 ||
The reasoning of the prima facie position has been refuted. Now, the reason for our own position is stated: "And because of the word *bhāva*. *Bhāva* means action (*kriyā*). || 22 ||
Thus ends the section concerning mere praise (Sūtra 2).
"If it be argued that they are for the purpose of the *pāriplava* [narratives], we say no, because of their being specified. (3.4.23)

"Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa... and so forth; these narrative traditions (*ākhyānaśruti*) are not intended for the performance of the *pāriplava* recitations, but rather for the purpose of the injunctions regarding knowledge (*vidyāvidhi*). || 23 ||

If it be argued that [the stories] have the purpose of the *pāriplava* (the sacrificial recitation), we say no, because they are specified. This is an incidental discussion. It was previously argued by the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) that qualities such as being the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*) are for the purpose of praise (*stuti*). Thus, the connection [of this section] is whether the narratives of Prātardana and others are for the purpose of praise or not. "Pāriplava" means the narratives; the meaning is that they are for the purpose of reciting those [stories]. "For the purpose of instruction" means for the purpose of instruction by way of praise. "For the purpose of the injunctions regarding knowledge" means they are subordinate to those very injunctions by virtue of being praises. Otherwise, since the narratives would be infinite, they would be impossible to perform—this is the sense. || 23 ||
And likewise, because of the connection within a single sentence. (3.4.24)

The passages beginning with "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen" do not have the purpose of enjoining ritual action, nor do they have the purpose of mere narrative recitation (pāriplava). || 24 ||
And likewise, because of their connection within a single sentence; "connection" (upabandha) means syntactic relation (anvaya). || 24 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the meaning of the *pāriplava* [narratives].
Therefore, there is no requirement for the kindling of fires and so forth. (3.4.25)

By way of a specific intermediate connection arising from the context of praise... in those [stages], knowledge is independent of ritual action; that is to say, it depends solely on the duties prescribed for one's own stage of life (āśrama). || 25 ||

For this very reason, there is no dependence on fire, fuel, and so forth. Since the two preceding [topics] were incidental, he states the connection with the first section by means of the words "praise" (*stuti*) and so on. This is clear. || 25 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the kindling of fire and so forth. 4.
And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. (3.4.26)
If knowledge were indeed independent of sacrifice and the like... [then it would not be said: "By worshipping Him with one's own duty, a human being attains perfection" (Gītā 18.46). || 26 ||

"And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse; the connection is clear. The sense is that the scriptural injunction regarding sacrifice and so forth also declares that [knowledge] has desire as its means.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the phrase "only when [the desire exists]" implies that there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) regarding the means of fulfilling that desire. [The opponent objects: "There is no need for the sacrifice, since it arises from the scriptural statement itself. To this, he replies: "And knowledge... [and so on]. Regarding the phrase "until death" (*āprayāṇāt*): the sense is that because the principal persists, its constituent parts persist as well. Regarding the claim that sacrifices and the like, which consist of active engagement, lead to mental agitation, he says: "And of such a form... The resolution is that [the sacrifice acts] through the medium of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). || 26 ||
Thus concludes the section on the dependence on all [works].

(Sūtra 3.4.27): "Nevertheless, he should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and so forth; for although that is so, because of the injunction for them, they too must necessarily be practiced as being subordinate members of that [knowledge]."
Even tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth [are required] for the householder... therefore, tranquility, self-restraint, and the like must also be practiced by the householder. || 27 ||

Nevertheless, one should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and so forth, because they are enjoined as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of that [knowledge], and thus must necessarily be practiced. The connection [to the previous topic] in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is clear. The phrase "in those devoid of purpose" was stated for the sake of excluding things such as eating at will. And for one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*), even that which is optional (*kāmya*) is devoid of purpose. "Unenjoined" means other than what is enjoined; this includes both that which is neither enjoined nor prohibited, as well as that which is prohibited. || 27 ||
Thus ends the section concerning tranquility, self-control, and so forth (Sūtra 6).
Now, "And there is permission for all food in case of danger to life, because that is seen [in scripture]. (3.4.28)

In the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) of both the Vājasaneyins and the Chandogas, it is determined that the state of being the eater of all food for the knower of the breath occurs only in the event of the danger of losing one's life. || 28 ||

The permission to eat all food in the event of life-threatening danger is established because that is seen [in scripture]. Since the practice of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth has already been stated, the present discussion concerns the restriction regarding eating, which is a specific form of tranquility; this constitutes the logical connection (*saṅgati*). The intention is to show that even for one who knows the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there is permission to eat all food—how much more so for one who knows Brahman—and so forth. However, this is not explicitly stated in the Sūtra itself.
In the final conclusion: *maṭacī* is a shower of stones; *ibhya* is an elephant-driver.
And because there is no contradiction. (3.4.29)

When food is impure, there is no purity of being... for one who knows the vital breath (prāṇa) but possesses little power, permission to consume all kinds of food is restricted solely to times of distress. 29.
And because there is no contradiction; this is clear. || 29 ||
It is also recorded in Smṛti. (3.4.30)
Moreover, the practice of eating all kinds of food is restricted solely to times of distress; he is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. || 30 ||

Moreover, it is recorded in Smṛti: not only is the state of eating all kinds of food to be understood as pertaining to times of distress for the knower of the Prāṇa, but it is also explicitly stated for all [others]—this is the meaning. || 30 ||
And there is a scriptural statement to this effect regarding the absence of acting according to one's own will. (3.4.31)
The meaning is that, considering that [the prohibition applies] to those who know Brahman as well as others, the Brāhmaṇa does not drink liquor. || 31 ||
And for this reason, the word "śabda" refers to not acting according to one's own will; the sense is that the word "brāhmaṇa," because it is unrestricted, denotes even the knower of Brahman. || 31 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the permission to eat all food (sarvānnānumati).
Now, [the sūtra states]: "And because it is enjoined, the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) must also be performed" (3.4.32).

The meaning is that the knowledge of Brahman has the sacrificial rites and so forth as its constituent parts, because it is prescribed as if it were obligatory by virtue of being a cause for living. || 32 ||

"And because it is prescribed, the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) must also be performed. He states the intermediate connection with the primary subject matter: "sacrifice and so forth. Regarding the phrase "perpetual and non-perpetual": the meaning is that performance throughout one's entire life and performance conducive to the desire for liberation are contradictory.

In the reading "āśramī," the word *kevala* refers to one who does not seek liberation (*amumukṣu*). Regarding the phrase "to be performed," the word *karmāṇi* (actions) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. || 32 ||
Likewise, it is so because it is an auxiliary to knowledge, as in "This very [ātman]... and because it acts as a cooperative factor. (3.4.33)

The meaning is that, by way of the arising of knowledge and as an auxiliary to knowledge, there is no contradiction in its serving both purposes due to the distinctness of their respective applications. || 33 ||

And by way of cooperation. The phrase "the arising of knowledge" serves to exclude the idea of a cumulative combination (samuccaya). Regarding the objection that there is a contradiction in the conjunction of the eternal and the non-eternal, he says: "The Agnihotra," etc. *Viniyoga* is an injunction that makes known the status of being an auxiliary (*śeṣatva*). || 33 ||
In the same way, he states that there is no difference in the ritual action itself: "In every respect, they are those very same [mantras], because of the dual characteristic. (3.4.34)

In every respect—whether for the purpose of knowledge or for the purpose of the stages of life (āśrama)—because of their application [to the same acts] and because there is no evidence for a difference in the essential nature of the rituals themselves. || 34 ||

In every respect, they are indeed those same [fires], because of the twofold characteristic. To the objection that even when the word is identical, a difference is observed—as in the case of the Agnihotra within the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana—he says: "Regarding the nature of the ritual action. The result of the determination "they are indeed those same" is the independence from repetition and from other auxiliary elements. || 34 ||
And it demonstrates non-overpowering. (3.4.35)

And by such statements as "one dispels evil through dharma," [these acts] are progressively refined day by day for the sake of the arising of knowledge; therefore, these very sacrifices and other rites belong to both [stages]. || 35 ||

And it demonstrates non-overpowering. The word "etcetera" (ādi) refers to statements concerning sacrifice and so forth. The meaning is that the statement indicating both the status of being an auxiliary (aṅgatva) and the slight effect produced by that [auxiliary] points to sacrifice and the like either by using the word "sacrifice" (yajñādi) or by using a word synonymous with it. || 35 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the injunction [of the study of the Veda].
Now, [the next sūtra]: "But also in the interval, because that is seen. (3.4.36)
For the four stages of life (āśramas), the grace of knowledge regarding the science of Brahman can be bestowed through such means as the propitiation of deities. || 36 ||

"But even in the interval, because that is seen. He states the connection [with the previous argument] by saying "of the four. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), one who has not yet taken a wife is included. The meaning is that there is support through the duties pertaining to the social classes (varṇa). "Of the non-exclusive"—that is, of those that are not fixed. || 36 ||
It is also recorded in Smṛti. (3.4.37)

Moreover, the meaning is that even for those who do not belong to any stage of life (āśrama), one becomes perfected through knowledge supported by practices such as the recitation of prayers (japa). || 37 ||

It is also recorded in the Smṛti: "A Brāhmaṇa is one who has studied that [Veda]," meaning "one who knows that. To the question, "How does grace come about through recitation (japa) and so forth? he says: "Recitation and so forth" (verse 37).
And there is a special favor. (3-4-38)
This point is established not only by logic and traditional law (smṛti), but also by the scriptural injunction: "One should seek the Self through knowledge. || 38 ||
And there is a special favor; this is clear. 38.
But the other [the path of knowledge] is superior to this, also because of an indicative mark (liṅga). 3.4.39.

The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis. Therefore—due to not belonging to any stage of life (anāśramitva)... [and] for one whose wife has died, if there is no dispassion (avairāgya), the acquisition of a wife becomes an unavoidable contingency (āpad). 39.

To the objection that even those who are capable should neglect the stages of life (āśramas), he says: "But therefore the other is superior, and because of the indicative mark. This means that for one who is capable, the other [the householder's stage] is superior, since their duties are not equal. He teaches [how to handle] adversity with the word "having desisted" (*nivṛtta*). There is no contradiction, as there is detachment inherent in those established in Brahman, an indifference toward enjoyments to be experienced at other times, and a desire for the duties of the householder's stage. (39)
Thus ends the section concerning the "Separated One" (Vidhurādhikaraṇa) — 9.
But for one who has become that [state], there is no non-becoming of that state, even according to Jaimini, because of the restrictive rule and because of the absence of that form. 3.4.40.

By showing that there is no disagreement even with Jaimini regarding the stages of life (āśramas) of the lifelong student, the forest-dweller, and the wandering mendicant, he confirms his own intended position. || 40 ||

"But for one who has become that [an āśrama], there is no non-becoming of that state, even according to Jaimini, because of the restrictive rule and because of the absence of the characteristics of those [other stages]. The connection [of this sūtra] arises from the doubt as to whether those who have fallen from their stage—such as the *vidhura* (the widower) and others—are eligible for knowledge (*vidyā*) due to their similarity in being without an āśrama, just like others. The term *vaikhānasa* refers to the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). The scriptural passage beginning with "the student" (*brahmacārī*) refers to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*). || 40 ||
Now, it might be argued that for those who have taken lifelong vows (naiṣṭhika) and so forth, [there is no such sin].
But this is not so; for even though they hold an office [of religious duty], there is a possibility of their falling from grace, as that [office] is incompatible with such a lapse. (Sūtra 3.4.41)

Even though the penance described in the section on qualification (*adhikāralakṣaṇa*) [is mentioned], it is for others; therefore, the penance described in the section on qualification pertains to a *brahmacārin* other than [the one under discussion]. (41) He states the doubt regarding what follows: "Now, it might be argued" (*atha syāt*). The sixth book is the section on qualification (*adhikāralakṣaṇa*). The animal sacrifice for the *avakīrṇin* involves a donkey. One who has fallen from the status of a *brahmacārin* while still a student (*upakurvāṇa*) is an *avakīrṇin*. Nor can that penance prescribed for the qualified [householder] apply here, because of the inference of his fall [from the vow]. To the question, "In that case, what is the scope of that penance?", he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). (41)
Some say that even when preceded by *upa*, it expresses the sense of "becoming," just like the word *aśana*; this has been stated [in the Vārttika]. 3.4.42.

Even for those such as the *naiṣṭhika* perpetual celibates who have fallen from their vow of chastity, there exists the fitness for the knowledge of Brahman, because the possibility of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) remains. || 42 ||

Some say that [the term] "even with a prefix" [is used here], as in the case of the word *bhāva* (existence) being like *aśana* (eating). It has been stated that the expiation for a *upapātaka* (minor offense), such as the breach of celibacy by a student (*upakurvāṇa*), is extended by analogy to those who have taken lifelong vows (*naiṣṭhika*) and others; thus, the meaning is that there is fitness for knowledge (*vidyā*). Because expiations for sexual intercourse and so forth would not apply to householders and others, the word [refers to an act] that does not contradict one's own stage of life (*āśrama*). || 42 ||
But outside [the body], it is in both ways, according to Smṛti and traditional practice. (3.4.43)
The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude other opinions. ... ... Therefore, these [gods] have no qualification for the knowledge of Brahman. || 43 ||

"But outside [the Vedic fold], it is in both ways, because of Smṛti and custom. (2.4.43) The meaning is as follows: although there is a contradiction between the Smṛti stating that [a lapse] constitutes a fall (*patana*) and the scriptural injunctions regarding the penance (*prāyaścitta*) for it, one must establish the following distinction: the Smṛti concerning the fall refers to cases where, due to the commission of a sinful act, there is an absence of penance capable of destroying the power that results in the loss of eligibility for Vedic rites; whereas the injunction for penance refers to cases where the power to produce a taste for actions similar to the transgression has been destroyed. He states the result of such avoidance: "They do not instruct [them]. (2.4.43)
Thus ends the section on "That which has come into being" (tadbhūtādhikaraṇa). 10.
Ātreya [maintains] that the fruit belongs to the master, because of the scriptural declaration of the fruit. 3.4.44.

The meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth have as their basis the constituent parts of the ritual action; however, the contemplation upon [the *udgītha*] as being the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*) can be performed by the sacrificer alone. 44.

"Ātreya [holds that] the fruit belongs to the master, because the scripture declares the fruit [for him]. Following the inquiry into the distinction between the performers of meditation, this investigation into the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth is undertaken; thus, there is a connection by way of topical relevance (*prasaṅga*). This is clear.
This being the position reached, it is replied: "The priest is to be hired; so says Auḍulomi, for he is hired for that purpose. (3.4.45)

The term *ātvijyam* refers to the work of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Furthermore, according to the principle that "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer," it is indeed the agent who desires the fruit who performs the action. || 45 ||

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "Ātreya [says] that the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is for the sake of the sacrifice; for he is hired for that purpose. The meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) has been explained as the means to the fruit (*phala-sādhana*). The sense of the dative case in "for the purpose" (*prayojanāya*) has been stated. He states the meaning of "he is hired" (*parikrīyate*) with the words "in the injunctions regarding ritual acts" (*karma-vidhiṣu*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "They are included within that. Regarding the point that the status of being performed by the priests (*ṛtvij-kartṛkatva*) follows only when there is subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*), he says: "Even though," and so forth. The phrase "one authorized for the sacrifice" (*kratv-adhikṛta*) refers to the principle of the foremost course (*agryaprāya-naya*).

Furthermore, because of its internal connection, the knowledge that serves as the means for making an action performed by a priest more powerful would itself have that priest as its agent; this also accords with the natural sense of the statement, "He performs [the action] aided by that knowledge. He states the distinction regarding the meditations on the *dahara* (the small ether) and so forth, if they were not of that nature: "In the case of the *dahara* and others... (45).
Thus ends the section on the Master (the Lord).

11. *Sahakāryantaravidhiḥ*: "There is an injunction for another auxiliary [to meditation] in the case of one who possesses that [meditation], as in the case of the beginning of an injunction; this is the third [point]. (3.4.46)
Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa [should attain] scholarship... [and so forth]; scholarship and the rest, with mauna as the third, are enjoined as further auxiliary means for knowledge. || 46 ||

The injunction of another auxiliary, as a third [alternative], belongs to one who possesses that [prior qualification], like the beginning of the injunction. Previously, sacrifices and so forth, as well as tranquility and so forth, were established as auxiliaries. The connection [of this section] is that, in the same manner, another auxiliary is now being established. For the word *mauna* (silence/contemplation) has the sense of "reflecting" (*manana*). Therefore, it was said: "because it has the purpose of knowledge. Regarding the phrase "it is enjoined," the meanings of the individual words have been stated. He states the meaning of the sentence: "This has been said. To the objection that it is a mere restatement because its purpose is knowledge, he replies: "And contemplation..."

It should be explained as "by one side" (*pakṣeṇa*). The meaning is that since a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) would be purposeless, even a partial meaning must be accepted if it is conducive to being an injunction (*vidhi*).

What is the meaning of the terms "scholarship" (*pāṇḍitya*), "childhood" (*bālya*), "silence" (*mauna*), and "Brāhmaṇa"? Regarding the apparent contradiction—that in the passages "therefore he is a Brāhmaṇa" and "then he is a Brāhmaṇa," scholarship and so forth belong to the Brāhmaṇa, yet Brāhmaṇahood consists of scholarship and so forth—the author says: "Thus, in this way. The first word "Brāhmaṇa" refers to the mere learned person; the second, however, refers to one who has reached the pinnacle of knowledge. "Perfection" (*paripūrti*) refers to auspicious qualities. The state of possessing both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatva*) is expressed by the two words.

"Feeling what has not been attained" refers to the ultimate knowledge of faultlessness and auspicious qualities; that is dependent solely upon instruction. That is wisdom (*pāṇḍitya*). Non-silence consists of wisdom, childhood, sacrifice, and so forth. (46)
Now, it might be argued: "If [the duties] apply to all stages of life... [but] because of their completeness, the conclusion is made with reference to the householder. (3.4.47)
The word "tu" (but) sets aside an objection. The intention is that the conclusion with the householder is for the purpose of demonstrating the duties of all the stages of life (āśramas). || 47 ||

He introduces [the next point] immediately: "Now, it might be argued... [The sūtra states: "But because of the totality, there is a conclusion with the householder. The statement in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad regarding the life of a knower of Brahman being established in the state of a householder is for the sake of illustration; the meaning is that it does not contradict the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. || 47 ||
Likewise, in this statement as well...
[there is no contradiction], because there is instruction even for those who speak with silence. 3.4.48.

For one who is completely free from all desires, the practice of begging for alms, silence as the third [practice], and the like, beginning with scholarship, are prescribed as auxiliaries to knowledge. || 48 ||

Summarizing this point for the sake of connection, he introduces the following sūtra with the word "tathā" (likewise). This is because, just as in the case of the sage, there is instruction regarding others as well. Such a word refers to being preceded by the renunciation of desires and so forth. He concludes the meaning of the section with the word "ataḥ" (therefore). || 48 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the injunction of another auxiliary means (sahakāryantaravidhi). 12.
"Not manifesting [his power], on account of the connection" (3.4.49).
Therefore, [it is said] "the Brahmin should [attain] wisdom... and so forth, in such passages as "from purity of food comes purity of being" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23). || 49 ||
"Because it does not manifest [itself] through logical connection. The consistency is clear. They are sublated—meaning they have as their object those who do not know Brahman.
In the final conclusion (rāddhānta): the meaning is that the divisions of the scope of restrictive injunctions (niyama-śāstra) are contrary to the restrictive rule. || 49 ||
Thus ends the section on non-manifestation (13): "That which belongs to this life [occurs] when there is no obstruction of what has been commenced, because that is observed. (3.4.50)

Knowledge is of two kinds: that which has prosperity as its fruit... because it is heard [in scripture] that there is no obstruction to the fruit of ritual action when it is conjoined with the knowledge of the *udgītha*. 50.

"Because that [result] is seen when there is no obstacle to what is currently undertaken, the consideration of the subsidiaries has been completed; now the time for considering the perfection residing in the principal (the *aṅgin*) is being examined—this is the connection (*saṅgati*). An inquiry is conducted here and in the subsequent sūtra regarding the accomplishment of those meditations (*vidyā*) which are subsidiary to ritual actions but are devoid of the *udgītha* and other such elements. For this inquiry is only possible if the meditation is to be accomplished through merit (*sukṛta*); thus he says: 'As has been stated. (50)
Thus ends the section concerning the present life (Aihikādhikaraṇa). 14.
Thus there is no such restriction regarding the fruit of liberation, because that state is definitively determined; because that state is definitively determined. (3.4.51)
The repetition [of the word "meditation"] even regarding meditation that has liberation as its fruit indicates the completion of the chapter. || 51 ||
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
And the chapter is completed.

Thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the fruit of liberation, because that state is determined; because that state is determined, this is another section [of the work]. The connection is clear. "Of that" refers to what was stated in the preceding sūtra. "To all," and so forth. Its "superiority" is caused by its bringing about an excellence of the Lord’s pleasure. The resolution is that the offense against a knower of Brahman, which produces an excellence of displeasure, acts as an obstacle. || 51 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth section, concerning the fruit of liberation.

Thus concludes the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the *Śrutapradīpikā*, composed by Śrī Sudarśanasūri—the ornament of the illustrious Harit lineage, son of Vāgvijaya, who assumed the name Vedavyāsa by the divine command of Śrī Raṅgarāja, and who attained the heart of the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śrī Bhagavad Rāmānuja through service at the feet of the venerable Padmanābhācārya.
And the chapter is concluded.
The first quarter of the fourth chapter.
There is repetition [of the path], because of the repeated instruction. 4.1.1.
It is determined that in the third chapter, knowledge (vidyā), along with its means, is designated by such terms as "knowing" (vedana) and so forth. || 1 ||

"Repetition [is required] because of the repeated instruction. He states the connection with the chapter: "In the third [chapter]. Knowledge was considered along with its own appropriate means; now follows the consideration of the fruit—this is the connection. First, that part regarding knowledge which was not previously determined is now determined, for the purpose of making known the relationship between the end and the means, and for the purpose of making known its nature as a fruit, since it consists of bliss. Regarding the point that repetition is sometimes performed even when not explicitly heard in the text, he says: "And not..."
