In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the application [of the meditation] in each individual Upaniṣad and their synonymy have been shown by the words "paryāyatvaṃ ca" and so forth. He shows the application across many Upaniṣads with the word "tathā" (likewise). Here, the principle of the goat and the animal (*chāgapaśunaya*) is intended. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And meditation" (*dhyānaṃ ca*). || 1 ||
And because of the indicative mark (liṅga). 4-1-2.

The indicative mark is the traditional scripture (smṛti). And the meaning of this scripture is as follows: ... therefore, knowledge that has been repeated many times alone is the purpose of the teaching. || 2 ||
And it is clear from the indicative mark (liṅga). || 2 ||
Thus ends the section on repetition (āvṛttyadhikaraṇa). Now:
"But [the Self] as the Self, they approach and cause others to grasp. (4.1.3)
Now this is considered: what is the object of worship? ... Therefore, it is established that Brahman is to be worshipped as the very Self of the worshipper. || 3 ||

However, people accept [the Self] as "the Self" and cause others to grasp it as such. Regarding the Brahman that has been described as the object of meditation (*upāsana*), there arises a doubt: is it to be meditated upon as being devoid of a relationship characterized by non-separation (*ayutasiddhi*), or rather as having the meditator as its body? This constitutes the connection [of the present topic]. Just as the section beginning with *puruṣārtho 'taḥ* (Sūtra 3.4.1) arises through an implication of the meaning of scripture (*śruti*), so too does this [present discussion] arise through an implication of the meaning of the scriptures on non-difference (*abheda*). The word "other" (*anya*) denotes a relationship devoid of the nature of the body-and-self relation.

Because it is employed in a context devoid of any specific relationship, such as "this one is not ours, but rather another," [the distinction is established]. Since, if the object of meditation were the self of the meditator, the relationship between the meditator and the meditated would be that of body and soul, leading to the understanding that the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are like a subject and a king; and since the cognition of difference is the means to liberation, the intended meaning is that the non-duality taught in the scriptures is set aside by the force of those statements concerning the means [to liberation], whereby difference is shown to be real.
"It would be unreal" means that it would result in the state of being subject to saṃsāra.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), he explains the word "Self" (*ātman*) as "the worshipper. [The roots] *upa-gam* and others have the sense of "understanding" (*buddhi*); thus, the meaning is "they worship" (*upāsate*). Since non-difference is seen precisely in the injunctions for worship, the meaning is that the object of worship is to be understood as having the worshipper as its body. Then, with the intention of raising the objection that this contradicts the injunctions for worship based on difference, he asks: "How do they accept [this]? He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "having Being as their root" (*sanmūlāḥ*) and ending with "that which is in the Self" (*ya ātmani*), by saying "of everything.
The syntactical connection is: "They establish what is logical."

He states the non-contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning unity and plurality with the words "And thus. He clarifies that with the words "I am. He establishes this with the words "Of the additional. The word "this" (eṣaḥ) refers to the individual soul (jīva), because it is masculine; and because the Supreme is denoted by the word "Deity" (devatā). The mere qualification is incomplete; the meaning is that only the qualified [entity] is complete. || 3 ||
Here begins the section on the meditation on [the Self] as the Self (ātmatvopāsanādhikaraṇa): "Not in a symbol (pratīka), for he is not that" (4.1.4).

"One should meditate upon the mind as Brahman" ... [this is] not to be contemplated in that manner, because the mind, being a mere symbol (*pratīka*), lacks the status of being the self of the meditator. || 4 ||

"Not in a symbol, for he [is not there]. The discussion concerns whether the meditation taught as being upon the Self should likewise be performed with respect to symbols (*pratīka*), or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because of the designation by the word "Brahman," that alone is to be meditated upon; whereas the mind and so forth are merely qualifications of the vision.

In the final conclusion: regarding the statement "for Brahman is the object of meditation," he says, "in the case of meditations on symbols. Regarding the question "how [can it be] the word 'Brahman'?", he says, "but Brahman... (Sūtra 4).
But is it not the case that here too Brahman alone is to be meditated upon? [The answer is:
"The perception of Brahman [is to be applied to the other] because of its excellence. (4.1.5)
The view of Brahman alone is appropriate regarding the mind and other [internal organs]... whereas the view of a king toward a servant leads to prosperity. (5)

To introduce the immediate [topic], he says: "Now, however" (*nanu*). "The vision of Brahman [is to be applied] because of excellence. It is not merely the insentient mind and so forth that is to be meditated upon; rather, it is the presiding deity (*abhimānidevatā*). Thus, there is no contradiction. || 5 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the Pratīkas (3).
Now, "The meditations on the Āditya and so forth [are] on Brahman, because of the appropriateness. (4.1.6)

"That very one who shines [in the sun] is the Udgītha... ... [and thus] even ritual actions possess the quality of being means to a result; therefore, the perception of that [Sun] is to be applied to the subordinate parts such as the Udgītha. 6.

"And the notions of Āditya and so forth [are to be applied] to the subsidiary parts, because it is logical. Here too, the connection [of the discussion] is the consideration of specific meditative views (*dṛṣṭi*). The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the *udgītha* is both Brahman and something to be practiced; this is for the sake of the purpose [of the meditation]. "From those that are fruitless" means from those which are not means to a fruit.

In the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), it is because of the statement that the mind and so forth possess the quality of being the object of the vision of Brahman, and not because of the sequence of the text. Here, however, by the word "meditated upon" (*upāsya*), the word *udgītha*—which is immediately adjacent—is intended as the primary object of meditation required first. The words *āditya* and so forth, though separated [by other terms], fulfill the subsequent requirement for qualifying attributes.
Thus concludes the section concerning the meditations on the Āditya and others. Now follows:
"He should sit, for that is possible. (4.1.7)

For the sake of attaining liberation, according to the Vedānta scriptures... [one] should perform [the practice] while seated with support for the purpose of withdrawing from worldly expansion. || 7 ||

[The sūtra states: "Because it is possible for one who is seated. Since the two preceding [topics] were incidental, he states the connection with what precedes that by saying, "Liberation" (mokṣa). The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that the mention of sitting is intended to convey mental comfort. The refutation of that is based on its necessary occurrence. || 7 ||
And because of meditation. 4-1-8.
Regarding the instruction "it should be meditated upon" (nididhyāsitavya), meditation is defined as one-pointed reflection uninterrupted by any other heterogeneous cognitions. || 8 ||
And because of meditation; the word "meditation" (dhyāna) has the abstract state as its primary meaning.
And with reference to immovability. 4-1-9.
And with respect to immobility, [the comparison] between the earth, the intermediate space, and so forth, would be possible for the meditator only while remaining seated. || 9 ||
And with reference to immobility: "Water" refers to water from ponds and the like; its similarity [to the mind] lies in its steadiness while performing a single-pointed task. || 9 ||
And they remember it. || 4.1.10 ||
And they remember that meditation belongs only to one who is seated: "Having sat down upon a seat, one should apply oneself to yoga for the purification of the self. (10)
And they remember it clearly. || 10 ||
Wherever there is one-pointedness [of mind], there [the result follows] without distinction. (4.1.11)
"...in a place and time exceeding [the requirements for] one-pointedness... [and] agreeable to the mind," because of the completion of the sentence [with these words]. || 11 ||
Where there is one-pointedness, there [the practice occurs] without distinction; that is to say, "time"—meaning there is no restriction regarding lunar days and so forth. || 11 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the seated one (āsīna-adhikaraṇa). 5.
"Until departure; for that too is seen there. (4.1.12)
This aforementioned means for attaining liberation leads one to reach the world of Brahmā for the duration of one's life. || 12 ||
For even there, until the final departure, attachment and so forth are clearly observed. (12)
Thus concludes the section on "until departure" (6).
Now, [sūtra] 4.1.13: Upon attaining that [Self], there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the designation thereof.
Thus, having purified the nature of knowledge (vidyā), [one should understand that] it is to be accomplished through the cessation of misconduct regarding knowledge. || 13 ||

Upon the attainment of that [knowledge], there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the designation thereof. Regarding the phrase "upon the attainment of knowledge" (*vidyāprāptau*), the reason for not using the expression "at the commencement of meditation" (*upāsanaprārambhe*) is based on the intention that the completion of the knowledge of that which is not of that nature [i.e., the Self] is also intended by the Sūtra. The fact that the non-clinging and destruction pertain to subsequent and prior sins depends upon their capacity to be so designated. For indeed, the non-clinging of what is already adhered is not logical; therefore, in its case, there is only destruction. As for the subsequent [sin], there is non-clinging. To the objection that destruction is observed even in the absence of adherence, he says: "And not... (*na ca*).

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), he demonstrates the absence of contradiction due to the difference in subject matter with the words "as for example" (*yathā*). He explains non-attachment and destruction with the words "of sin" (*aghasya*). He states the logical consistency of what has been said with the words "thus, in this way" (*tadevam*). Since [the fruit] is to be accomplished in the form of heaven and so forth, the ritual action that causes it does not have the power to remove sin; however, in this case, since the removal of obstacles alone is what is to be accomplished, knowledge is equivalent to an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). For one who has begun the practice of meditation, there is the resolve: "Upon the completion of that, I shall forgive everything."
Therefore, there is no contradiction with the section concerning the future life; at that time, the intention is "it is endured. || 13 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the attainment of that [knowledge]. Now:
"In the same way, there is non-attachment for the other as well; but upon death. (4.1.14)

The non-clinging and destruction of future and past sins [respectively] occur through knowledge... the meaning is that meritorious deeds whose fruits are seen to conform to that knowledge perish. || 14 ||

For the other [type of karma] as well, there is likewise no connection [to future results], but [this occurs] at the time of death; the mention of "attachment" and so forth is clear. He states a further doubt with the words "of what has been done. He introduces another section of the Sūtra with "But surely... The phrase "they perish" means that if they are obstructed from their fruit, they perish. || 14 ||
Thus ends the section concerning others (Itarādhikaraṇa). 8.
But only those [karmas] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], for that is the limit. 4.1.15.

There is no evidence for the existence of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) that serve as the cause for the maintenance of the body prior to or subsequent to the arising of the knowledge of Brahman. || 15 ||

"But the former [works] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], because that is their limit. He states the connection [with the previous section] with the words "brahma" (Brahman). "Thence" means from the arising of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
In the final conclusion, he states that the persistence of the body is due to the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the words "And not... (sūtra 15).
Thus ends the section concerning those whose karma has not yet begun to bear fruit (Anārabdhakāryādhikaraṇa) – 9.
But the Agnihotra and other such rites are for that very purpose [of exhausting remaining karma], because that is seen in scripture (agnihotrādi tu tatkāryāyaiva taddarśanāt). 4.1.16.

In the same way, there would be no connection for the other [the seeker] either; thus, for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is defiled, the very arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) would not occur. || 16 ||

"But the Agnihotra and so forth are for the sake of that [state], because it is seen [in scripture]. He states the connection with the words "of the other. Since in the previous [section] non-performance was refuted on the grounds of the observation of such [acts] among those whose vital energy is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*) and because of the contradiction between the obligatory and the non-obligatory, as well as here because of the non-adherence of the fruits of good deeds, there is no tautology.
In the conclusion [of the discussion], he says "vidyāyāśca" [and of knowledge] regarding the point that it should therefore be performed only once. || 16 ||
"If [the soul departs] with its good deeds such as the Agnihotra...
for from this [text], some maintain that there is another [path] for both. (4.1.17)
Therefore, the scriptural statements regarding the non-clinging and destruction of good deeds such as the Agnihotra and so forth refer specifically to that [knowledge]. || 17 ||

He states a doubt regarding the immediately preceding [verse]: "If [the works] such as the Agnihotra... The scope of the phrase beginning with "those who hate" must be sought; for since subsequent sins have not been experienced and have not yet begun to bear fruit, it is logical that they constitute the object [of the destruction], and thus the term "friends" is employed.

Therefore, for some, the object [of the knowledge] consists of both types of merit: that performed previously as a cause for rain, food, and so forth, and that performed subsequently whose fruit has been obstructed. This is the meaning. || 17 ||
Even for an action that has been performed, there may be an obstruction to its fruit...
"For [it is said] 'by knowledge alone'. (4.1.18)
"Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone [is effective]... [the evil deeds go to the enemies and] the good deeds to friends; thus says the Śāṭyāyanaka. (18)

He states the connection with the immediately preceding sūtra: "Even though it has been performed... This refers to what was stated previously: "For the fruit is indeed unobstructed when separate [from other causes]."
For it is clearly stated: "By knowledge alone."
Thus ends the section concerning the Agnihotra and other rites—10.
But having exhausted the others by means of experience, he then attains [the Self]. (4.1.19)

Regarding those two, merit and demerit, for which non-attachment and destruction have been stated... [the former] friends take away, and the latter enemies [take away]; thus, it is faultless. || 19 ||
Thus ends the section on the destruction of other [impurities]—11.
Thus concludes the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.

"But having exhausted the others through experience, he then attains [the Self]. This connection is clear. In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he removes the seed of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "Of that [person], for as long as... Here, the body and its limit are not explicitly stated in the scripture. In the phrase "having shaken off" (*dhūtvā*), the body is mentioned, but not its limit. The singular number is intended to signify the genus (*jāti*), just as in the expression "shaking off evil"; this is stated because no restriction regarding a limit is heard in the text.
He summarizes the matter stated in the preceding sections for the sake of easy comprehension: "Thus, in this way" (tadevam) || 19 ||
Thus ends the eleventh section, concerning the destruction of other [karmas].

Thus concludes the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Śrutapradīpikā*, composed by Śrī Sudarśanasūri—the ornament of the illustrious Harit lineage, son of Vāgvijayin, who bears the secondary name Vedavyāsa by the divine command of Śrī Raṅgarāja, and who has grasped the heart of the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śrī Bhagavadrāmānuja through service at the feet of the venerable Varadācārya.
The second quarter of the fourth chapter.
Speech [is merged] in the mind, because it is so seen and because of scriptural statement. (4.2.1)
Now, in order to consider the manner of the departure of the wise one... it must be resolved that the mind is joined with speech, but it does not dissolve into it. || 1 ||

"Speech [merges] into the mind, because it is so seen and because of scriptural statement. The connection between the sections (*pāda-saṅgati*) is as follows: the fruit of knowledge has been stated in relation to the stability of the body; now, the departure (*utkrānti*), which consists of the commencement of the journey, is being considered. The intended meaning is that speech is characterized by a state consisting in its being the cause for the activity of speech in some manner.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), it is said: "For it is seen. The sense is that speech is absorbed into the mind, just as fire whose own function has ceased is absorbed into wood whose own function has ceased. Regarding what was stated [by the opponent]: because both terms—*vāk-sampatti* (attainment of speech) and *sampatti* (attainment)—are secondary, there is a lack of natural consistency (*asvārasya*) with the term *parama-sampatti* (supreme attainment). Yet, even in that case, there is no absolute lack of natural consistency; for the two terms "seeing" (*darśana*) and "word" (*śabda*) serve as cumulative reasons. || 1 ||
For this very reason, all [the qualities] follow. 4-2-2.
"From which [state] there is merely the conjunction of speech and mind... [attaining] non-return through the senses merging into the mind. (2)
Therefore, all [the others] follow. "Anu" means afterwards. || 2 ||
Thus ends the section concerning speech.
Now follows the section concerning the mind: "That [is] the mind; the vital breath [is] higher. (4.2.3)
That [mind], conjoined with all the sense organs—the mind... and there would be an indication (lakṣaṇā) of the waters by the word "prāṇa"—thus [it is said]. || 3 ||
That mind [is merged] in the vital breath, according to the subsequent [scriptural passage]. This means by way of a succession—namely, through its own cause, which is earth. || 3 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the mind (manas). Now follows:
"But [the soul] [is merged] in the presiding deity, because of its approaching that [deity], and so forth" (4.2.4).
Just as the statement "speech merges into the mind" and "the Yamunā flows into the ocean" is not contradictory, so it is in this case as well. || 4 ||

"He [the individual soul] [merges] into the presiding deity (adhyakṣa), because of the scriptural statements regarding 'approaching it' and so forth. The connection is clear. The word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to the passages concerning departure (utkrānti) and re-establishment (pratiṣṭhā). He provides an illustration for the case where, even when moving from one object to another after having conjoined with it, the designation is made by means of the word denoting either one of the two—stating: "Just as... (yathā) || 4 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the presiding deities (Adhyakṣādhikaraṇa). 3.
"Because of its existence in the elements" (bhūteṣu tacchruteḥ) [Sūtra 4.2.5].
"The vital breath [merges] into heat" refers to the soul accompanied by the subtle body; for scripture declares that as the soul migrates, it consists of all beings. || 5 ||
Because that [consciousness] exists in the elements; the connection is clear. || 5 ||
But is it not the case that [the qualities] are perceived in each one individually among fire and the rest?
No, for [the scripture] shows them in each one. 4.2.6.
The light is not designated as belonging to each one individually; therefore, the merging occurs only within the elements.

He introduces the next section with the words "Now, [an objection]... (*nanu*). [The Sūtra states: "For [the scriptures] show that [the three deities] do not [individually produce the world], for they enter into each one of them and make each one threefold" (*naikasmin darśayato hi*). Since it is taught that for the purpose of creation one must enter into those principles [of fire, water, and earth] and make each one threefold—based on the instruction that each one is to be made threefold—it is understood that each triad of elements, having been made threefold, possesses causal efficiency. The sense is that since the commencement of a body is impossible through non-triplicated elements, the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) must be combined to produce their respective effects. || 6 ||
Thus ends the section on the elements (bhūtādhikaraṇa). Now, [the sūtra]:
"And [the meditation] is the same up to the beginning of the departure from the body; and immortality is attained without having burned away [the remainder of karma]. (4.2.7)
The intention is that this departure belongs to both the knower and the ignorant; it refers to the subject matter of that experience of Brahman. || 7 ||

"And [the path] is common up to the commencement of the journey toward the immortal, even without having burned away [the body]. Although the two subjects to be established—the states of the knower and the non-knower—are common, this particular section does not concern what occurs after that [commencement], because its subject matter is not contested by the knowers. Therefore, the connection [of the section] is established by demonstrating the commonality of those points that are contested.
In the final conclusion—regarding the statement that "equality [of the path] exists when there is departure"—he says: "For even for the knower... Then he establishes that equality: "And that... (7).
Even then [the soul remains associated with subtle elements], because until its final absorption (apiti), there is the designation of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). 4.2.8.
And that must necessarily be immortality... "Having made myself what was unmade, may I attain the world of Brahman," so it is said. || 8 ||

"Even then [liberation occurs] until absorption, because of the designation of transmigratory existence. By the scriptural statement that [the soul] remains attached until the final body, the impossibility of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) has been stated. || 8 ||
And it is subtle by measure, because it is perceived as such. (4.2.9)
For this reason as well, even for the wise man, bondage persists as the subtle body continues to exist; therefore, his bondage has not been burnt away. || 9 ||
And it is subtle by measure, because it is perceived in that way; here, its non-connection [with the gross body] is stated by virtue of its abiding in the subtle body.
Therefore, one should not approach [the teacher] with a burden. 4-2-10.
Therefore, when all are completely liberated... this statement does not declare immortality through the crushing of bondage. || 10 ||

"Not by suppression" (nopamardena). Here, the impossibility [of the soul's departure] through such means is intended, based on many scriptural passages concerning the nature of meditation as constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*), its form as vision (*darśana*), its form as joy (*prīti*), its persistence until death, the shaking off of very difficult karma, the exit through a specific channel, the specific path, and the state of the subtle body. After the primary argument, the conclusion was made by the preceding Sūtra; likewise, the corroborative argument (*abhyuccaya-yukti*) is now stated. || 10 ||
And from this very same reasoning, heat [is established]. (4.2.11)
Regarding this subtle body, it has been well stated that its departure is uniform from whatever point the journey begins. || 11 ||

And from this very reasoning follows its heat. The meaning is that because the ash—which was mentioned in the phrase "it causes burning," etc.—is universal, the perception of heat here [in the subtle body] is due to the fact that some part of the subtle body possesses the capacity for departure (utkramaṇa). He concludes the present topic with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). || 11 ||

If it be argued that there is no departure for the wise [soul] because of a prohibition, we say: No, because [the departure is] from the embodied soul; for in some [scriptural passages], it is clearly stated. 4.2.12.

Thus, it is faultless that the statement "even for the wise there is departure... establishes that [the subtle elements] go along embracing the individual soul (jīva), just as they do the subtle elements themselves. || 12 ||

If it is argued that [the soul does not depart] because of a prohibition, we say no; for in some [scriptural texts], the departure from the body is clearly stated. "The subtle elements" (taijomātrāḥ) refers to the minute portions of the gross elements. "The heart" means it departs from the heart. The three words beginning with "akāmayamānaḥ" (free from desire) refer to the absence of the three types of craving.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), [the author states] "of that," and so forth. The meaning is: let the embodied self (*śārīra*) be the one indicated by the word "that" ending in the genitive case; however, the body itself is the point of departure (*apādāna*) for the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) which belong to it. He offers a rebuttal by accepting that the genitive case expresses a relationship characterized by the instrument and its possessor: "No. The meaning is: since it is better to assume the status of the point of departure for the subject under discussion (*prastuta*) itself, rather than assuming the status of the point of departure for an unrelated substratum (*dharmī*).

He establishes that the genitive case itself implies the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*) through the arguments of redundancy and semantic power, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). He addresses the point that a thing is only fit for negation when its occurrence would otherwise be undesirable, saying "And therefore" (*tataśca*). "The grasper" (*grahaḥ*) means the rope; the meaning is that one conquers death by means of the rope. To the question, "In that case, how is there no departure of the vital breaths? he replies, "But for the ignorant person" (*aviduṣastu*). || 12 ||
And it is recorded in tradition. ||4-2-13||
And it is recorded that even for the wise man, by means of the suṣumnā nerve... having transcended the world of Brahmā, he goes by that path to the supreme goal. 13.
And it is recorded in tradition; this is clear. 13.
Thus ends the section on the commencement of rebirth (āsṛtyupakrama).
Now follows: "Those [elements] pass over to the other [state], for so he says. (4.2.14)

Just as [the individual soul], together with the collection of organs, endowed with vital breath, and presiding over the instruments, finds rest from the exertion of experiencing pleasure and pain through union with the Supreme Self, so it is here as well. 14.

Regarding those [points], the other [author] says: "For this very [sūtra]... The meaning is that the disagreement concerning this much portion has been resolved; thus the connection [of the sūtras] is stated. The rest is clear. || 14 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the excellence of others (parasaṃpattyadhikaraṇa). 6.
Non-distinction [of the individual soul from Brahman] because of the scriptural statement: 4.2.15.
This is the merging into the Supreme Self... because, moreover, there is no mention there of the creation of the unmanifest (avyakta) and so forth. || 15 ||

There is no division, because of the scriptural statement. The connection [of the words] is clear. If the word *tejas* were taken as referring merely to the individual soul (*jīva*), there would be a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*), and a discrepancy with the meaning of the word *sampatti* (merging). Therefore, as in deep sleep, there is no dissolution of the substantive element (*viśeṣya*). Nor is there dissolution of the qualified whole (*viśiṣṭa*), because due to the loosening of the subtle body, it is impossible for the subtle elements—which constitute its qualifying attributes—to dissolve into their collective totality (*tatsamaṣṭi*); and for that very reason, it is impossible for them to dissolve into darkness.

Furthermore, because there is no mention of the creation of the unmanifest (*avyakta*) and so forth for the purpose of initiating a subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), and because [liberation] would be impossible if such a body were not initiated, "merging" (*saṃpatti*) means merely a state of contact. By the phrase "and because there is no mention of the creation of the unmanifest and so forth," the absence of a cause for its re-emergence has been stated.
Thus ends the section on non-distinction (Avibhāgādhikaraṇa). 7.

His abode [the heart] first blazes up; the door [of the skull] being illuminated by that, he—favored by Him who dwells in the heart—proceeds through the hundred-and-first artery, by virtue of the power of knowledge and through connection with the recollection of the path which is a remainder of that [knowledge]. 4.2.16.

Thus, regarding the commencement of the journey up to the point of departure for both the wise and the ignorant... since the wise man knows that channel, the departure of the wise man by means of it is logically established. || 16 ||

The flame of the top of that [heart] blazes up; its door being illumined by that, [the soul], favored by the one dwelling in the heart, proceeds through the hundred-and-first artery by the power of knowledge and by the application of the recollection of the path which is the remainder of that [knowledge].
He states the connection [between the verses] with the word "evam" (thus). This is clear. || 16 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the abode;
[the soul] follows the path of the rays. 4.2.17.
By means of [the path] exceeding a hundred [nerves] from the heart of the wise... for the wise, there is indeed the attainment of Brahman solely by following the rays. || 17 ||
It follows the rays; the connection and so forth are clear. (17)
Thus concludes the section on following the rays (Raśmyanusārādhikaraṇa).
9. "Not at night; if it be so argued, we say no, because the connection lasts as long as the body exists; and scripture also shows this. (4.2.18)
This is now considered: the statement beginning with "for the wise man... by day and during the bright fortnight" refers to the subject of the ignorant person. || 18 ||

If it is argued that [the soul does not depart] at night, we say no; for the connection [of the soul with the body] persists as long as the body exists, and scripture shows this. This point has been settled. In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): how can there be a persistence as long as the body exists for *prārabdha* karma, which is to be experienced through multiple bodies? Even so, another [residual] karma remains possible. How then is the statement of censure avoided? And how is its non-futility explained? To this he says: "This has been stated" (verse 18).
Thus ends the section on the night (niśādhikaraṇa). 10.
And [the sacrifice] may also take place during the southern course of the sun. 4.2.19.

Even for a learned man who dies at night, his attainment of Brahman is certain; however, such a practice [of dying during the northern solstice] is intended to demonstrate the excellence of the northern solstice for the purpose of encouraging the performance of religious duties. || 19 ||

[This applies] even during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*). The connection and so forth are clear. [Objection: If one dies at night or during the southern solstice, the body would not possess "finality" (*caramatva*); and if that were the case, there would be an absence of binding karma. [Response: This is not so—because even for one who dies during the southern solstice, the attainment of Brahman is heard in the supplementary portion of the text, namely: "he attains the greatness of Brahman. This is the intended meaning.

Nor does the phrase "and then he who is on the right" refer to another qualified person, because such a person has not been introduced as a topic; furthermore, there is the perception of identity in the statement "he conquers the two glories. Nor can there be the syntactical connection "the knower [conquers] the two glories," because the word "knower" (vidvat) refers to the very same qualified person under discussion, namely "of one who knows thus" (*tasyaivaṃ viduṣaḥ*); moreover, the verb *ji* (to conquer) is inherently transitive, and there are Vedic usages such as "he conquers the world" (*lokam abhijayati*). || 19 ||
But surely these two [paths] are recorded in Smṛti with reference to the wise who are about to die, and they pertain to yogins; for these two are indeed taught in Smṛti. (4.2.20)
In this context, [the practice] is prescribed for those established in knowledge, not for those facing death; nor is a specific time of death prescribed for those facing death. || 20 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the southern course (Dakṣiṇāyanādhikaraṇa) — 11.
Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the Śrī Śārīrakamīmāṃsā Bhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.

He introduces the subsequent sūtra with the words "But [is it not the case]? These two are remembered for the sake of yogins, and they are of the nature of recollection (*smārta*). He states the meaning of the term *smārta*: "recollection" (*smṛti*), which means "by way of being recollected. This is clarified by the word "to remember" (*smartum*). By intending to show the strength of the natural sense of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) through its opening member, he demonstrates that the subject matter is the path at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end. || 20 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the southern solstice (Dakṣiṇāyanādhikaraṇa) — 11.

Thus concludes the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Śrutapradīpikā*, composed by Śrī Sudarśanasūri—the ornament of the illustrious Harita lineage, son of Vāgvijayin, who bears the secondary name Vedavyāsa by the divine command of Śrī Raṅgarāja, and who has grasped the heart of the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śrī Bhagavad Rāmānuja through service at the feet of the venerable Varadācārya.
The third quarter of the fourth chapter.
[The soul departs] by way of the path beginning with light, because that is well-known from scripture. 4.3.1.
For the wise man who has departed [from the body] by means of a specific channel... elsewhere too, Agni, Āditya, and others are recognized everywhere. || 1 ||

"By the path beginning with light, because that [attainment] is well-known. He states the connection with the preceding section [of the *Pāda*] by saying "of the knower" (*viduṣaḥ*). The phrase "as... and so forth is employed to indicate the relationship with one who knows Brahman. "Śavyam" means "fit for a corpse" (*śava-arham*). The meaning is that there is multiplicity of form due to the difference in sequence and the difference in those who follow the sequence.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), there is little difference; the sense is that the mention of the world of the gods (*devaloka*) stands in place of the year. The scriptural passage, "Those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship faith and truth," is the authority for the identity of the path. Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) serves as a supporting factor.

This scripture does not concern the meditation on a specific path that has not been previously taught; for there would be a circularity of dependence: the distinction between paths would result from the restriction [of the scripture], and the restriction would result from the distinction between paths. On the contrary, their identity is established by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Furthermore, the unity of the paths is established by the natural force of the scriptural statement regarding the duality of the paths of the gods and the ancestors: "Now, of these two paths... The reason this is not mentioned in this particular commentary is that it has already been stated in another commentary.

Although the fruit—consisting of Brahman and the attainment thereof—is recognized as identical across all extraneous sciences (*paravidyā*), it is not accepted that they are one and the same because of the impossibility of synthesizing them due to the infinity of their attributes; however, regarding the path, since it is suitable for contemplation without exceeding twelve categories, it is logical to accept their identity through recognition.
Thus ends the section concerning the Path beginning with Light (Arcirādyadhikaraṇa).
Now: "Vāyu [is reached] after the year, on account of both non-distinction and distinction. (Sūtra 4.3.2)
"The wise go by the path beginning with light... he who blows here is the house of the gods. (2)

"Vāyu [comes] after the year, by way of both non-distinction and distinction. The connection is clear. He clears up the context in order to state the doubt, beginning with the words "Therein," etc. Having determined the sequence of the year and the world of the gods (devaloka) immediately after the month, there arises a doubt regarding the world of the gods and Vāyu. Regarding the phrase "and because of the absence of distinction": although the sequence stated in the fifth [sūtra] is the same for the year and the world of the gods, a distinction was previously mentioned in the case of the year following the month—namely, that a longer period is placed immediately after a shorter period; however, such is not the case here. This is the meaning.
In the final conclusion (rāddhānta): the word "world of the gods" (devaloka) is a general term. To exclude the sense of [any] world in general, he says: "and this is Vāyu. || 2 ||
Thus ends the section concerning Vāyu (2).
Now, Varuṇa [is to be understood] after lightning, because of the connection (sūtra 4.3.3).
According to the Koṣītakins, this path of the gods (devayāna) ... [is such that] Varuṇa should be placed above Indra and the others. || 3 ||

Varuṇa follows Taṭita due to their relationship. He states that there is no contradiction with the Kauṣītaki text regarding the previously mentioned sequences for the purpose of making known the portions to be defined which have already been defined, whereas in those parts where there is a contradiction, that [Kauṣītaki] text is weak—beginning with the words "Of the Kauṣītakins," and so forth. The phrase "to avoid the futility of the instruction" implies the thought that, since both sequences would be sublated, it is more reasonable to sublate one sequence rather than both. The mention of "Indra and Prajāpati as well" implies the thought that, between two sequences being broken, it is better to break only one sequence.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): Lightning is below the waters, because it is clearly visible from there. The meaning is that the relationship between those two is like the relationship between their presiding deities. [Objection: Let there be a connection with lightning within the belly of the clouds; how then can Varuṇa be placed above lightning by overriding the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*)? Or how is there room for Indra and Prajāpati there? To this he says: "This has been stated. Because the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the order of the text, Varuṇa is above lightning.
According to the reading of the Kauṣītaki school, because adventitious elements are placed at the end, the meaning is that Indra and Prajāpati follow after them. || 3 ||
Thus ends the section concerning Varuṇa. 3.
Those [deities] are conductors, because of the indicative mark thereof. 4.3.4.

This is now considered: Are the "flames" (arcis) and so forth... [the names of] specific presiding deities whose essence consists of the flames and so on? As in the passage, "The earth said to him... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3). || 4 ||

Regarding the statement that "the *ātivāhikas* [are so called] because of their characteristic marks, and they are not denotative even of the worlds of experience," he says here: "These very [ones]. The opponent's intention is that the "worlds" are those designated as "day" (*ahar*) and so forth. To the question, "Why is it not the reverse? he says: "For this very reason. The sense is that even the word "expands" (*vijihīte*) is a characteristic mark of a world.
In the final conclusion—regarding how the words "light" (arcis) and so forth denote deities—he says: "And they say."
If this is so, then that non-human person leads him...
by means of the lightning itself from there [to the world of Brahman]. (4.3.5)
Then, above the lightning, by means of the Vaidyuta [deities]... for them too, there certainly exists a connection by way of being *ātivāhika* (conveying deities). || 5 ||
He introduces [the next point] immediately after: "If it is so... [The descent occurs] by means of the lightning alone, because of the speed [of that path]. This is clear. || 5 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the *ātivāhika* (the guide-soul)—Section 4.
Bādari [holds that the soul] has a task [to perform], because its going [to the sun] is logically consistent. (4.3.6)
The knower goes by way of light and so forth; therefore, the group of conductors beginning with light leads him alone. || 6 ||

Bādari [holds that the soul goes] to the effected [Brahman], because the movement [of the soul] is thus logically established. He states the connection [with the previous section]: "By the path of light alone. Regarding the two paths—worship (*upāsti*) and ritual action (*karman*)—the four-faced Brahmā is the goal. Because he is omnipresent, because his qualities such as omniscience are complete, and because there is no partiality in his relationship [to all souls], there is no need for movement; this is the intended meaning of terms such as "perfect" (*paripūrṇa*). He removes the objection regarding the futility of worship: "Because it is eternally attained. (6)
And because of being specified. (4.3.7)
A non-human person, having approached, leads [the soul] to the worlds of Brahman; one who has traveled by way of the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) attains proximity to Hiraṇyagarbha. || 7 ||
And because of being specified: regarding the phrase "this world of Brahman," he says "and by the plural number" in order to exclude the accepted *karmadhāraya* compound. || 7 ||
But if this is so, [one might object that] the non-human *tatpuruṣa* leads them... [but] the designation [of him as Brahman] is due to proximity. (4.3.8)

The meaning is that by the reasons already stated—such as the impossibility of [Hiraṇyagarbha’s] going and specific qualifying attributes—it is determined that the one who "ordains Brahmā" is Hiraṇyagarbha. || 8 ||
But that designation [of the Self] is due to proximity; by the word "and so forth" in the phrase "by qualifications and so forth," the logical possibility of movement is included. || 8 ||

Now, it might be argued that upon reaching Hiraṇyagarbha by way of the path beginning with light (arcirādi), [the soul returns] because of the scriptural statement: "At the dissolution of the effected world, together with its presiding deity, he goes to the highest. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9).
This is understood from the scriptural statement: "Upon the passing away of the effected world—the world of Brahman—all are completely liberated through the supreme immortality. (Sūtra 9)

Because it is stated that upon the completion of their task, they go beyond [the world] together with its presiding deity, one might ask: what is the authority for this meaning? To this he says: "Those [who reach] Brahman. From the supreme immortality (*parāmṛtāt*)—that is, having attained the supreme immortality. The ablative case is used here due to the elision of the suffix *lyap*. || 9 ||
And because of Smṛti. (4.3.10)
And from this Smṛti passage, the following meaning is understood: the group beginning with light leads only one who is engaged in the work [of meditation]; this is the opinion of Bādari. 10.
And because of the Smṛti; [it refers to] that of the other—the lifespan of Brahmā. || 10 ||
On this point, Jaimini objects by adopting a different position: "Jaimini [holds that the word refers to] the Supreme [Brahman], because of its primary meaning. (4.3.11)

The path beginning with light leads those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman... and non-material worlds do not absolutely not exist, because of the authority of the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇa. || 11 ||

"By adopting another alternative"—meaning by something other than the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), but not by the entire established conclusion (*siddhānta*). "Jaimini [says] the highest [state], because it is primary. "Without remainder" means the completion of knowledge—the attainment of the state where knowledge performs its function—or its total expansion. The sense is that just as there is a dependence on a specific time even though [the soul] is eternal, so too is a dependence on a specific place appropriate even though it is omnipresent. Regarding the objection that "there is no movement because departure [of the soul] is untenable," he says: "Of the knower."

"Conceived by one's own will" means conceived by eternal will. "Not absolutely" means not that they do not exist—that is, it is not the case that they do not exist; rather, they certainly exist, they indeed exist eternally—this is the intended meaning. By the words "in that Imperishable, in the highest heaven," etc., the firmness of this proof is intended to be expressed. || 11 ||
And because of the scriptural statement. 4-3-12.
Scripture shows that [the soul] proceeds by way of the channel in the crown of the head... having attained the supreme light, it manifests in its own true form. || 12 ||
And because of the scriptural vision [of this path]. [The word] "having arisen" establishes that the journey is by way of the path of the gods (devayāna). || 12 ||
As it has been said: "I enter the abode of Prajāpati... and there is no expectation regarding any result. (4.3.13)
There is no intention regarding the request... it is the opinion of Jaimini that the group of superhuman guides beginning with Light leads only one who meditates upon the Supreme Brahman. 13.
And there is no intention directed toward the effect; this is clear. 13.

Now the venerable Bādarāyaṇa states the established conclusion according to his own view: "Bādarāyaṇa [holds that the Lord] leads those who do not rely on symbols; for there would be faults in both cases, and because of the nature of their resolve. (4.3.14)

For those who do not have the symbols as their object—that is, for those other than those whose meditation is based on symbols—there is no journey by way of the path beginning with light nor attainment of Brahman, because of the principle that "as is one's resolve, so is one's destination" (tatkratu-nyāya) regarding meditation on the mixed [symbolic] Brahman. || 14 ||

"Bādarāyaṇa [holds that the Lord] leads [the meditator] because of the absence of meditation on symbols (apratīkālambanāt), and because there would be faults in both cases, and because of the nature of his resolve (tatkratuḥ). To the question, "What is the distinction from the view of Jaimini?", he says: "This has been stated. And in the passage beginning with "na ca," the term *pratīkālambana* refers, according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*), to those who meditate on [the Self] through specific views (*dṛṣṭyupāsaka*), since those who meditate on the effected [Brahman] (*kāryamupāsīnān*) are mentioned separately. He states this as follows: for one who meditates on the effected [Brahman], only the effected is to be attained, not the Supreme Brahman; this is because of the principle of "according to one's resolve" (*tatkratu*). Therefore, the meaning is that the path of light (*arcirādi*) which leads to the Supreme does not belong to him.

The proposition that "he leads those who do not have a support consisting of symbols" would be contradicted; for the passage beginning with "those who [know] thus" has as its object supports consisting of symbols. To this he replies: "Those who [know] the five fires. Furthermore, the portion of the Sūtra stating "and according to his resolve" (tat-kratuś-ca) serves to establish that both of the two groups previously mentioned have supports that are not symbols. Since the fruit corresponds to the mode of meditation, even one who knows the five fires—who is devoted to the meditation on the attainment of Brahman as the fruit—is likewise devoted to the meditation on Brahman.

Therefore, because they are conducive to the attainment of Brahman, the separate mention [of the two paths] would otherwise be purposeless; thus, their distinction is exactly as stated. To the question, "Who then are those who take hold of symbols (pratīka)? he says: "Name and so forth" (nāmādi). || 14 ||
The author states that scripture itself demonstrates this distinction: "And it shows a distinction" (4.3.15).

As far as the reach of name extends, there he has freedom of movement... it is established that for those who meditate on Brahman as the Self, free from primordial nature (prakṛti), the group of conducting deities (ativāhika-gaṇa) leads them [to their destination]. || 15 ||
Thus ends the section on the effect (kāryādhikaraṇa) — 5.
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavadrāmānuja.
And he shows the distinction: "the range of names" means the domain of the names of gods and so forth. He concludes: "therefore."

The Smṛti statement "together with Brahmā" does not refer to the person who has traveled by way of the path beginning with light (arcirādi); rather, it refers to yogins residing in the world of Caturmukha (Brahmā). And regarding the phrase "they [attain] Brahman," following the principle of the Niṣādasthapati rule, the meaning is that those abiding in the world called Brahman are liberated at the end of their final body solely on account of the gracious Brahmā, who is the Supreme Immortal. This is because both the *karmadhāraya* compound and the ablative case used in the sense of cause are natural in this context. || 15 ||
Thus ends the section on the "Effect" (Kāryādhikaraṇa) — 5.

This concludes the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Śrutapradīpikā*, composed by Śrī Sudarśanasūri—the ornament of the Harita lineage, son of Vāgvijayin, who bears the secondary name Vedavyāsa by the divine command of Śrī Raṅgarāja, and who has grasped the heart of the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śrī Rāmānuja through service at the feet of the illustrious Varadācārya.
The fourth quarter of the fourth chapter.
The manifestation [of the soul] upon reaching [the highest light] occurs by its own nature, because of the scriptural statement. 4.4.1.

For those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman and upon the Self as dissociated from primordial matter (prakṛti), the qualification "in its own form" would be redundant; for even without such a qualification, its being its own form is already established. || 1 ||

"Manifestation by means of its own [nature], because of the word [in the scripture]. He states the connection with the preceding section: "the supreme," etc. "By form" means by appearance. Regarding the phrase "nor [is there] suffering": the cessation of suffering is desired, while the cessation of happiness is undesired; thus, because both would be present, the consequence would follow that liberation is a mixture of what is beneficial for man (*puruṣārtha*) and what is not. This is the sense. "It would be meaningless": the meaning is that the word "manifestation" (*abhiniṣpatti*) would be purposeless.

Regarding the question "How by its own [nature]?"—it is answered: "By its own. The word "own" (sva) refers to what is unique (asādhāraṇa), and not to that which is not to be accomplished (asādhyatva), because of the mention of "manifestation" (abhiniṣpatti). "He manifests in form"—that is, he is accomplished as characterized by form; the meaning is that the form is what is to be accomplished.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "It would be meaningless. For one thing is not produced by means of the form of another; since this uniqueness is established by the very fact of the matter, the meaning is that the word itself would be rendered purposeless. || 1 ||
As for what was said—that because one's own nature is eternally attained... [the Self is] liberated, because it is so declared [in scripture]. 4.4.2.
"Completely liberated from the connection with karma and the body etc. produced by it... this meaning is established through reasoning," and so forth. || 2 ||

He introduces the immediately following sūtra with the words, "But since it has been said... [The term] "liberated" refers to the thesis. He explains the thesis-statement "liberated" with the word "karma. To the question "What follows from that?", he says, "Therefore... The meaning is that there is no futility of the word "manifestation" (abhiniṣpatti), because it denotes the cessation of the previously non-existent concealment. For that [cessation]... [is indeed the case].

That is the cessation of concealment (*tirodhāna*). The meaning is that the essential nature (*svarūpa*), which was promised as being free from concealment, has been declared. To explain this, he asks, "Whence [is this]? and so forth, beginning with "The Self (*ātmā*)... Since the word "this" (*etam*) refers to the subject under discussion as characterized by the eight qualities, and since those eight qualities were concealed at the time of waking and so on, the repeated use of the word "this" in each successive stage intends to refer to the innate form that is not concealed by karma. The purpose of describing the states of waking and so on is to examine the disposition of the listener.

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). He states the denotative power of the word: "even upon the manifestation of its own form" (*svarūpāvirbhāve 'pi*). This should be understood as beginning with the phrase "this one thing is produced by the sage" (*idamekaṃ muninirvṛttam*), and so forth.
And as it has been stated: "The Self [is meant], because of the context" (Sūtra 4.4.3), regarding the nature of the Self in deep sleep... [and so forth].

He introduces [the next section] immediately with the words "And as for what was said. The subject is the Self (*ātman*), because of the context. To address the doubt that this might concern something other than the Self, he says: "And this... The requirement for a cause regarding bliss (*ānanda*) is not due to its nature as bliss; rather, it is because bliss is concealed during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) that there is a need for it. In liberation (*mukti*), there is merely the manifestation of that which is self-established; thus, it has no dependence on external adjuncts (*upādhi*). Therefore, the meaning is that the scripture concerning liberation does not culminate in something that is not the supreme human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). || 3 ||
Thus concludes the section on the manifestation [of the soul] upon reaching [Brahman].
4.4.4: [The souls are] non-differentiated, because that is how it is seen [in scripture].

"Has this one, having approached the supreme light, become entirely liberated from all bonds...? But [it is not so], because of the mention of difference and because of the teaching of superiority," and so forth. (Sūtra 4)

Because it is perceived as non-different; the connection is clear. The terms *sāmya* (equality) and *sādharmya* (similarity) are included because they appear in the text, not because there is any difference in their meaning. Since [the soul] is heard of as being simultaneous with [Brahman], and through the expression of equality and similarity, just as in the cases of Śrī and Rodanī, or like two red objects, one understands its own state of independence; and since the nature existing in the state of liberation is real, it is impossible for statements concerning means (*upāya*) and so forth to have a meaning that contradicts that [liberation]; therefore, the experience of Brahman as one's own self is not tenable—this is the introduction [of the objection] by way of challenging the meaning of the scriptures on non-difference.

In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): let there be "perceptibility" (*d�ṛṣṭatva*); [the opponent asks] "What follows from that? To this he says: "His own self" (*svātmānaḥ*). Regarding the word "together" (*saha*): the meaning is that the experience [of the soul] up to Brahman is justified by the scriptural mention of "together," because that [mention] intends the accompaniment of objects of enjoyment. Since non-difference is seen precisely in the scriptural passages concerning liberation, and since that [non-difference] does not contradict the scriptural texts on difference maintained by the constituent parts [of the system], the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is an experience of Brahman whose body is one's own self.
He points out the inconsistency between what precedes and what follows according to the view of another commentator: "as a mode of Brahman" (*brahmaprakāratayā*). || 4 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the perception [of the soul] as non-distinct [from Brahman].
Jaimini [holds that the soul attains its true nature] through the state of Brahman, on account of the introductory statements and so forth. (4.4.5)
The view of Jaimini is that it is not possible for the inner self (pratyagātman) to have consciousness alone as its essential nature after it has attained the supreme light. || 5 ||

Jaimini [asserts] that [the Self] is of the nature of Brahman on account of the introductory statements and so forth; he states the connection of this with the first section by saying "of the inner self" (*pratyagātmanaḥ*). To the question "In what sense is it Brahman?", he says: "For [qualities] such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*)... Jaimini's view is that since it is impossible for that which is knowledge to be the substratum of knowledge and other qualities, its essential nature must be insentient (*jaḍa*). || 5 ||
"By consciousness alone [the soul exists], because it has that as its essence; thus says Auḍulomi. (4.4.6)
"Pure consciousness alone is its true nature; thus, its manifestation in the form of that [consciousness] alone within the intellect (citi) is the opinion of Auḍulomi. (Sūtra 6)

"Auḍulomi [holds that] it consists of consciousness alone, because its nature is that; the mention of the instrumental case is figurative. Regarding the phrase 'the pleasure of modification,' the word 'etc. includes indifference (*upekṣā*). 'Having true desires' means the absence of occasional pleasure; 'having true resolves' means the absence of indifference. For one who is indifferent is not one whose resolves are true—such is the position of the opponent. (6)

Now the venerable Bādarāyaṇa states the final conclusion according to his own view: "Even so, because of the introductory statement and because of the prior existence, there is no contradiction; thus [says] Bādarāyaṇa. (4.4.7)

Even so—that is, even when the nature of being mere consciousness has been established... [there is] the nature of consciousness everywhere; the meaning is that it is of the nature of self-luminosity. || 7 ||

"Even so, because of the introductory statement and because [the qualities] exist previously, Bādarāyaṇa maintains there is no contradiction. Regarding the doubt that the eight qualities might have been presented as a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) despite the existence of the statement concerning them, he states the intended meaning: "It is equal. The particle *eva* is a remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), not an independent word; for a restriction requires something specific to be restricted. Therefore, it is not right to break up many sentences belonging to disciples. Thus, by avoiding the breaking of the particle *eva*, the non-contradiction between the meanings of the two statements is to be understood.

Contradiction with reality (*vastuvirodha*)—the impossibility of cognition being the locus of cognition and so forth—has already been refuted previously. "Incapable" (*aśakya*) means incapable of being sublated (*bādhitum*).

Even so, he establishes the extreme clarity [of the meaning] through the illustrative sentence which is a part of that very passage, beginning with "sa yathā" (Just as...). He states the lack of contradiction even in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with "na caivam" (And it is not thus). To the question of how there is no contradiction even in the illustrative sentence, he says "yathā" (Just as). To the questions of what is the meaning of the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) found in the illustrative sentence and what is the portion upon which it depends there, he says "idam atra vākya" (This is the meaning of the sentence here). He explains the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-svarūpatva*) by saying "svaprakāśa" (self-luminous). || 7 ||
Thus ends the section concerning Brahman—3. [Sūtra 4.4.8: "Because of the scriptural statement that it is by mere volition alone [that he creates]."
The liberated one, having attained the supreme Brahman, is established as being "nothing but a mass of consciousness," as it were. || 8 ||

"From mere volition alone, because that [power] exists. He states the connection [of the sūtra] with the words "the liberated one" (*mukta*). The word *prayatna* refers to an activity distinct from volition (*saṅkalpa*). The opponent's position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the particle *eva* excludes non-connection (*ayoga-vyavacchedaka*).
In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the intention is that, since there is no restrictive factor, it also excludes connection with something else (*anyayoga-vyavacchedaka*).
And for this very reason, it has no other presiding lord. (4.4.9)
Since he is liberated and possesses the power of true resolve, for that very reason... for that very reason it is said: "He becomes his own ruler. || 9 ||

For this very reason, he is "one who has no other lord. Here, another quality caused by his *satya-saṅkalpa* (truthful resolve) is stated. "One who has no other lord" means that he is not dependent upon anything distinct from the Supreme Self; otherwise, the word "ananya" (non-other) would be redundant. He states the meaning with the words "for this very reason."
Thus ends the section concerning volition (saṅkalpādhikaraṇa). 4.4.10:
Bādari declares non-existence, for thus [the scripture] says.
"Do the body and senses not exist for one who is liberated?"—thus indeed does the Śruti declare the bodilessness of the liberated one. || 10 ||
Bādari declares non-existence, for so it is stated; the connection [of this view] with the inquiry is clear. (10)
Jaimini [holds that the soul] exists [after death], because of the mention of various options. (4.4.11)
Jaimini [holds that] for one who is liberated there is still the state of body and senses... for it is that very body which is the cause of pleasure and pain. 11.

Jaimini [maintains that there is] existence [of the soul], because of the mention of alternatives. Even though the soul is bodiless, since pleasure and pain are rooted in karma, the meaning is that what is prohibited is a body commenced by karma. || 11 ||
But the Blessed Bādarāyaṇa states his own settled conclusion: "Therefore, according to Bādarāyaṇa, it is of both kinds, like the door-panels. (4.4.12)

By the word "from intention alone" (saṅkalpād eva) in this [sūtra], and by the words "he approaches" and "he sacrifices," through the distinction of intention, there arises both the *satra* and the *ahīna*. || 12 ||

Therefore, Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) is of both kinds, because of the injunctions for "performing" and "offering," and because of the plurality and singularity of the sacrificers; the meaning is that it is both a *satra* and an *ahīna*, just like the twelve-day sacrifice. || 12 ||
When there is possession of a body and other instruments... [this is] because it is possible even in the absence of a body, as in the case of the intermediate state (sandhya). 4.4.13.

In the absence of instruments such as a body created by Himself, the Lord, engaged in divine play (*līlā*), experiences the essence of that play through the worlds of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) and others created for His sport. || 13 ||

He connects it with the immediately following Sūtra with the words: "When... [The soul exists] even in the absence of a body, because its existence is possible as in the state of deep sleep (saṃdhyā). [It exists] by means of those created by the Supreme Person—i.e., those created without an intermediate agent. || 13 ||
The state [of the subtle body] is like that of waking. || 4-4-14 ||
It is entirely logical that they themselves create their own bodies and so forth, as well as their own worlds such as the world of the ancestors, solely through their own volition. || 14 ||

As in the case of a waking person; [the Lord] addresses the objection that for the liberated soul there would be a deficiency in objects of enjoyment due to the creation of fathers and so forth by Brahmā, that this [creation] would be directed toward another [end], and that the desire of the fathers and others is caused by karma—by refuting these, He states that the creation of fathers and others, whether mediated or immediate, is included within His own sport: "The Supreme Person also... (14).
But has it not been stated that the Self is of medium size?
[To this we reply: "Its entry is like that of a lamp; for thus Scripture shows" (4.4.15).

Just as for a single lamp in a single location... [the movement of] one that is not liberated is governed by karma; however, for one who is liberated, it is by his own will—this is the distinction. || 15 ||

He raises a doubt regarding the immediately preceding sūtra with the words "nanu" (but surely). [The sūtra states: "Like a lamp, there is an entry; for thus it shows. To the objection that, in that case, one might preside over other objects by means of knowledge as well, he replies with the words "ityādi" (and so on). "Conformity with the conceit of self" means the possession of the specific power of being an instigator. "The body" is that which is to be impelled. "Conformity with the apprehension of 'this'" means being endowed solely with the power of illumination. By this property, the scripture has as its object a pervasion across many instances.

"What is the difference between him and those such as Saubhari who are already liberated? If he is capable of presiding over multiple bodies, let him do so even in his previous state. To this, he says: "Of one not yet liberated" (amuktasya). || 15 ||
Now, an objection: "Is it not the case that for one who has attained the supreme Brahman, there is a cessation of internal and external cognition? ...
[This] is indeed declared to depend on either deep sleep (svāpyaya) or union [with the Self] (saṃpatti). (4.4.16)
This statement does not refer to one who has attained liberation; rather, the statement refers to either deep sleep or union [with the Supreme]. 16.

He states the doubt regarding what follows with the words "nanu" (but surely). For [the state] is declared to depend on either deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) or union (*saṃpatti*), since "union with Being" (*satā saumya*) is well-known as union with Brahman; and the statement regarding union with Brahman at the time of departure has been shown in the passage, "The light [merges] into the highest. That this refers to the subject of death is made known by the passage beginning with "Speech [merges] into the mind" (*vāṅ manasi*). The grammatical connection is that these two exist because of such a statement.

He explains the interval between the two scriptural passages with the words "in deep sleep. Both [passages], "By the Being, my dear, [the breath] goes to heat" and "[it merges] into the Supreme," are to be considered here. || 16 ||
Thus ends the section on non-existence (Abhāvādhikaraṇa). 5.
"Excluding the activity of the world, because of the context and because of being not proximate. (4.4.17)

What sovereignty, such as the creation of the world and so forth—which is unique to the Supreme Person—could belong to the liberated one? For the liberated one possesses no proximity [to the Lord] by virtue of which the activity of the world would also belong to him. || 17 ||

"Excluding the activity of the world" because of the context and because [the individual soul] is not proximate [to that activity]. "The creation of the world and so forth constitute the state of being the Lord of all. For the manner of lordship consists precisely in creation and the rest; therefore it has been stated thus. There is a logical connection because this constitutes an investigation into the nature of having true volitions (*satyasaṅkalpatā*).

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): the word "unfeigned" (*nirvyāja*) refers to that which exists exactly as it is. The mind is "kanyā" because of its luminosity; for the root *kan* signifies shining. By means of the two reasons stated in the Sūtra, there is the exclusion of both under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the causality that constitutes the definition of Brahman. || 17 ||

If it be argued that [the soul does not depart] because of the direct teaching [to the contrary], we say no; for that teaching refers to one who occupies a specific station within the [celestial] spheres as an authorized agent.
"He becomes self-ruling; he experiences [all] in all worlds"—this is what is expressed by this sentence; it does not refer to the activity of creating the world. || 18 ||

Lest it be argued that while the activity of the world is mentioned for the liberated soul in another context, it does not exist in its own specific context, he says: "Not so, because of the direct teaching; [it exists] because of the mention of one who resides in the spheres of authority. To the question, "How can there be a need for anything other than the experience of Brahman for one who is no longer subject to karma?", he says: "Unobstructed by karma. He concludes the meaning of the Sūtra with: "Thus, therefore... (18).
If the liberated one were like those in saṃsāra... [and] "He does not participate in modifications; for thus he declares his state"—4.4.19.

Regarding the phrase "does not engage in modification"—meaning birth and so forth—it is stated [in the scriptures] that he has "freedom of action" and so on; however, the activity of governing the world does not belong to the liberated one. || 19 ||

He introduces the immediately following sūtra with the words "yadi" (if). The suspicion that [the Lord] might be subject to impermanent enjoyments is refuted by the phrase "and it does not abide in transformation; for thus it declares its state—'it abides in transformation'. The term "transformations" (vikārāḥ) is clear. [The opponent might say: "Let him experience them; what of it? To this he replies: "His manifestation" (tadvibhūti). The phrase "for thus" (tathā hi) is to be explained as follows: by means of this explanation, the proof for [the Lord's] being the experiencer of Brahman is shown. He shows the proof for the inclusion of the manifestation within that [experience] with the words "in Him" (tasmin). He states the final conclusion with the word "therefore" (ataḥ). || 19 ||
And thus, perception and inference have been demonstrated. 4-4-20.
For this liberated inner self, there is the power of realizing true intentions and equality with the Supreme Person, with the exception of the activity of creating and governing the world. 20.

Even those scriptural passages concerning the Supreme that refer to His being the Controller and so forth might be intended for the purpose of [His] enjoyment; if that were not the case, then even those passages concerning the individual soul (jīva) would have to be intended as referring to Him as the Controller. To this, he says: "And thus both perception and inference show it," beginning with "Out of fear of Him... The sense is that, unlike the case of passages concerning the individual soul, no other interpretation is possible here. "He is the Lord of all," etc.; the sense is that because there is no restriction [to the state of bondage], the fact that the liberated one is also subject to His control is established. He shows specifically that the liberated one is subject to His control with the word "likewise."
Brahman is the individual soul; immortality is liberation; the eternal dharma is knowledge; and bliss is joy.

Anticipating the objection regarding the contradiction between [the soul's] dependence on another and its eternity, he refutes it with the words beginning "Even though," and so forth. "Of that" refers to the state of being free from sin and the like; "being of such a nature" means being innate. He establishes that the inner self (pratyagātman) is dependent upon that by saying "of the Supreme Person. It is not only the nature of the liberated one and so forth; he states with the word "thus" that other eternal entities as well have their very existence and excellence dependent upon Him.

For one who is liberated and directly perceives his own self as the supreme remainder (paraśeṣa) without limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), the state of being a controller is contrary because it is inconsistent with the absence of self-identification (ātmābhimāna). Thus, the absence of the status of a controller does not bring about a deficiency in bliss; rather, it brings about its fullness. The arrangement of objects of enjoyment in accordance with self-identification is observed among humans, cattle, and so forth. || 20 ||
And because there is a mark indicating equality in respect to enjoyment alone. (4.4.21)

Since the liberated one’s experience consists solely in the enjoyment of the realization of the true nature of Brahman, it must be described in accordance with the Śruti that the liberated one’s sovereignty excludes the activity of creating and maintaining the world. Thus, the liberated one’s lordship is indeed devoid of the cosmic operation. 21.

"And because the similarity consists merely in enjoyment. In the previous sūtra, it was stated that the scriptural texts concerning equality and the fulfillment of true resolves must be restricted according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (where the general term 'cow' excludes the specific 'bull'), due to the contradiction with the unassailable statements "He makes them happy" and "He rules all this," as well as the contradiction with logical arguments such as the impossibility of [the soul] being the material cause. Here, however, it is said that the equality understood in a general sense must—according to the maxim of "the goat and the sheep" (where the specific excludes the general)—be limited to the similarity characterized by enjoyment, as seen in other passages, and because this accords with scriptural texts concerning being governed [by the Lord]. He concludes the meaning of the section with the words "Therefore... (21).
If the sovereignty of the liberated depends upon the Supreme Person...
non-return [is established] on the basis of scripture; non-return, on the basis of scripture. (4.4.22)

Just as Vāsudeva—who is solely composed of auspiciousness that is the antithesis of every thing to be abandoned—is difficult for even the gods to attain, so too is that Great Soul (mahātman) rare. The repetition of the aphorism indicates the completion of the treatise. Thus, everything is consistent. 22.
Thus ends the section [6] concerning the exclusion from the activities of the world;
thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
And the chapter is completed.
And the treatise is completed.

He introduces the doubt regarding the immediately preceding Sūtra with the words "yadi" (if). [The Sūtra states: "Non-return, on account of the scriptural statement; non-return, on account of the scriptural statement. The mention of qualities such as being the opposite of the Veda is intended as an illustration of how the Lord establishes that the liberated one is not to be abandoned, and thus serves as a proof that no desire to abandon the experience of Brahman arises in him. The phrase "abode of suffering," and so forth, is employed to exclude [the possibility of returning to] the world of the fathers and other such realms attained through mere wish. Therefore, what is prohibited here is return caused by karma; it is not, however, the movement [of the soul] understood from the Upaniṣadic passage beginning with "these worlds."

Regarding the one whose pride has been shattered, [the author] states the favoring [of that person] with the words beginning "And not... Cessation [of transmigratory existence) may occur through another person, or by one's own will, or through karma, or by the Lord. Among these, the first alternative is rejected because the Lord lacks anyone equal or superior to Him. The second and third positions are refuted by the passage beginning "Nor is it cut off...": for it is impossible for a conscious being to desire to abandon infinite bliss, and because karma, once its own latent impressions have been destroyed so as never to sprout again, cannot persist.

He refutes the fourth [position] with the words, "And not for one who possesses a supreme form. The meaning is that there can be no suspicion of a cessation [of the Lord's grace] by the will of the Blessed One, because it would follow that the resolve "I shall not cause [him] to return"—which is based on the extreme dearness of the Knower—would be rendered untrue.

Thus, everything is consistent (*samañjasam*). By the word "all" (*sarva*), there is intended the entire collection of statements that establish difference and non-difference, those enjoining or prohibiting attributes and so forth, as well as the means of valid cognition such as perception, and the words of the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas that have been cited, along with the mass of reasoning that supports them. The word "thus" (*iti*) refers back to the entirety of the meaning stated in the passage beginning with "the whole world" (*akhilabhuvana*). The consistency of all these [statements] is to be seen in this manner; and the avoidance of contradictory means of knowledge and reasoning is to be understood according to the direction already stated.

In this discourse, which is moderately profound, everything is intended to be implicit; for those who plunge into it, both the establishment of one's own position and the refutation of opposing positions become easy—this is the underlying intention. Thus, it is said that "everything is consistent. || 22 ||

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Śrutapradīpikā*, composed by Śrī Sudarśanasūri—the ornament of the illustrious Harita lineage and son of Vāgvijayin; who, having received the divine command of the illustrious Raṅgarāja, assumed the secondary name Vedavyāsa; and who, through service at the feet of the venerable Varadarājārya, mastered the heart of the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the illustrious Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
The chapter is concluded; and the treatise is completed.
Hariḥ oṃ.
